additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model Additions

New Stocks Added

Four new stocks were introduced as described:

  • Outrances (initial: 150): gains a constant 20/hour, loses 40% and 10% of its current level per hour — two separate balancing loops driving it toward equilibrium.
  • Illigents (initial: 30): gains 40% of current outrances per hour (cross-stock coupling), loses a constant 5/hour.
  • Yelbs (initial: 65): gains 10% of current outrances per hour, loses 12% of current trazes per hour — a cross-stock drain creating a dependency between trazes and yelbs.
  • Trazes (initial: 85): gains a constant 15/hour, loses 18% of its current level per hour — a classic balancing loop.

Key Feedback Structures

  • Outrances has two simultaneous balancing (negative) feedback loops via its two fractional outflows, both driven by its own level.
  • Trazes has a single balancing loop via its 18% fractional outflow.
  • Outrances → Illigents: A reinforcing cross-link where outrances drive illigents inflow, creating a dependency chain.
  • Outrances → Yelbs and Trazes → Yelbs: Yelbs is influenced by two separate stocks — outrances feeds it while trazes drains it, creating an interesting cross-stock interaction.

Constants Separated

All numerical constants (rates and fixed flows) were given their own named variable nodes per modeling best practices, ensuring no embedded constants in equations with other variables.

testParams.prompt:
Please add the following to my model...
In my business, we start the period with one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory is enhanced by 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each year the stock loses a constant three whatajigs.  Meanwhile, we begin with two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory gains from 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock is reduced through 3% of whatever existing_store_lambdas are currently available.  Meanwhile, we have on hand two hundred whoziewhats. Every year, this inventory is enhanced by 5% of the current balacks count. Simultaneously, each year the stock gets diminished by 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we have on hand twelve funkados. Every year, this inventory receives new additions of 5% of the current whoziewhats count. Simultaneously, each year the stock is reduced through 3% of whatever maxabizers are currently available.  Meanwhile, we begin with eighty-eight maxabizers. Every year, this inventory gets replenished by 5% of the current funkados count. Simultaneously, each year the stock gets diminished by 3% of whatever existing_store_mus are currently available.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model Extension: Chained Inventory System with Feedback Loops

The existing model (with existing_store_lambda and existing_store_mu) was preserved intact, with only the supply_mu flow corrected to be driven by 3% of maxabizers (as specified) rather than a constant.

New Stocks Added

Five new stocks were introduced: whatajigs, balacks, whoziewhats, funkados, and maxabizers. Each follows a standard stock-and-flow structure with a proportional inflow and a separate outflow.

Causal Chain

The system forms a reinforcing chain threading through all inventories:

  • whatajigs grows from itself (5%) and feeds balacks
  • balacks grows from whatajigs (5%) and is depleted by existing_store_lambda (3%)
  • whoziewhats grows from balacks (5%) and depletes itself (3%)
  • funkados grows from whoziewhats (5%) and is depleted by maxabizers (3%)
  • maxabizers grows from funkados (5%) and is depleted by existing_store_mu (3%)

Feedback Loop Closure

Two key feedback loops are closed:

  1. Maxabizers → supply_mu → existing_store_mu → maxabizers_outflow → maxabizers: A balancing loop where maxabizers build up mu, which then drains maxabizers.
  2. existing_store_lambda → balacks_outflow → balacks: Lambda stock acts as a drain on balacks, linking the original model into the new chain.

All rate constants were extracted as named auxiliary variables to comply with modeling best practices.
supportingInfo.title: Chained Inventory System with Closing Feedback Loops

supportingInfo.explanation: This model captures the exponential growth dynamics of frimbulator inventory. The structure represents a reinforcing feedback loop (R1): Frimbulators → Daily Growth → Frimbulators. This is a classic "Success to the Successful" or exponential growth archetype where the stock reinforces its own growth. The current inventory level determines the absolute amount of daily growth (2% of current inventory), which then adds back to the inventory, creating compound growth. I separated the growth rate (0.02) into its own variable rather than embedding it directly in the flow equation, following best practices for constant handling. This structure will produce exponential growth behavior where the inventory grows increasingly faster over time as the base (current inventory) increases.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model Structure

This model captures a Balancing Process with Exponential Growth archetype. The frimulator inventory is a stock that experiences two simultaneous processes: percentage-based growth and constant reduction.

Key Causal Relationships

Reinforcing Loop (R1): Frimbulators → Incoming_Frimbulators → Frimbulators. This creates exponential growth because the incoming flow is proportional to the current stock size. As inventory grows, the 5% growth produces increasingly larger absolute additions.

Balancing Process: The Constant_Reduction creates a steady drain of 5 frimbulators per week through Outgoing_Frimbulators, which opposes the growth.

Model Behavior

Initially, the 5% growth on 100 frimbulators produces 5 units per week, exactly balancing the 5-unit constant reduction. As inventory grows beyond 100, the percentage-based incoming flow exceeds the constant outgoing flow, causing net accumulation. The reinforcing loop dominates over time, leading to exponential growth despite the constant reduction.
supportingInfo.title: Frimulator Inventory Growth with Constant Reduction

This model captures a two-stock system with mutual interdependence between whatajigs and balacks inventories.

Whatajigs Stock Dynamics:

  • Whatajigs grows through self-reinforcement: the stock drives its own 5% annual growth (reinforcing loop)
  • Whatajigs is depleted by balacks at a 300% rate, creating a negative feedback connection from balacks to whatajigs

Balacks Stock Dynamics:

  • Balacks grows based on whatajigs at a 5% rate, creating a positive feedback connection from whatajigs to balacks
  • Balacks experiences self-limiting decay at 3% annually (balancing loop)

Cross-Stock Feedback Structure:

  • A reinforcing loop exists: whatajigs increases balacks growth, which increases balacks, which increases whatajigs reduction, which decreases whatajigs
  • This creates oscillatory potential as the two stocks influence each other in opposing ways

Constants Separated

All numerical constants (growth rates and multipliers) are extracted as separate variables to follow best practices and enable easy parameter adjustment.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Complete Causal Discovery Model

This model captures all cause-and-effect relationships described in the background information across three independent inventory systems.

Marticatenes System

I created a stock-and-flow structure with marticatenes as the central stock starting at 50 units. The stock has two flows: a constant inflow of 10 units per month and an outflow equal to 20% of current inventory. This creates a balancing feedback loop where higher marticatenes levels increase the outflow, which then reduces the stock.

Refluppers System

I modeled refluppers as a stock starting at 75 units with two flows. The critical causal link is that refluppers inflow depends on marticatenes count (20% of current marticatenes), creating a cross-system causal relationship. The outflow is constant at 8 units per month. This means marticatenes directly influences refluppers accumulation.

Exemintes System

I structured exemintes as an independent stock starting at 120 units. It has a constant inflow of 8 units per month and an outflow of 10% of current inventory, creating another balancing feedback loop similar to marticatenes.

Key Causal Relationships

Each system exhibits internal balancing feedback where the stock level influences its own outflow. The unique cross-system causality is marticatenes driving refluppers inflow. All constants are separated into distinct variables to make causal relationships explicit and modifiable.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Complete Causal Structure Extraction

This model captures all cause-and-effect relationships from the provided information through three interconnected inventory systems:

Three-Stock Chain Structure: The system forms a causal chain: dominitoxings → povals → auspongs. Each stock influences the next through fractional inflows.

Dominitoxings System:

  • Receives constant daily additions (12 units)
  • Experiences fractional outflow (30% daily)
  • Drives inflow to povals through positive causal link

Povals System:

  • Receives fractional inflow from dominitoxings (30% of dominitoxings)
  • Experiences fractional outflow (20% of itself)
  • Drives inflow to auspongs through positive causal link

Auspongs System:

  • Receives fractional inflow from povals (20% of povals)
  • Experiences constant outflow (12 units daily)

Key Causal Relationships: All fractional rates create positive polarity relationships (stock increases → flow increases). All flows create their expected stock relationships: inflows add positively, outflows subtract negatively. Constants influence their respective flows with positive polarity.

This structure represents a cascading inventory system where upstream stocks causally influence downstream accumulations.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In the system, we begin with one hundred ten pablanksills. Every quarter, this inventory gets replenished by 6% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock loses a constant eighteen pablanksills.  Meanwhile, we start the period with seventy posistorathers. Every quarter, this inventory is enhanced by exactly twenty-five new posistorathers. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock has outgoing 35% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows ninety-five crypterals. Every quarter, this inventory is enhanced by exactly eighteen new crypterals. Every quarter, this inventory benefits from 35% of the current posistorathers count. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock suffers depletion of 22% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model Structure

I created a complete stock-and-flow model capturing all causal relationships described in the background information. The model contains three independent subsystems, each representing a distinct inventory with its own dynamics.

Pablanksills Subsystem

The pablanksills stock begins at 110 units and has two flows: a reinforcing growth loop (6% quarterly growth) and a constant depletion (18 units per quarter). The growth creates a positive feedback where larger inventory generates more growth. Following the mandatory constant handling rule, I separated the 6% rate into growth_rate_pablanksills and the 18-unit depletion into constant_depletion_pablanksills as distinct variables.

Posistorathers Subsystem

The posistorathers stock starts at 70 units with constant additions (25 units per quarter) and fractional outflow (35% per quarter). This creates a balancing structure where the stock seeks equilibrium between constant inflow and proportional outflow. I extracted constant_addition_posistorathers and outflow_rate_posistorathers as separate variables per the constant handling requirement.

Crypterals Subsystem

The crypterals stock (initial value 95) has the most complex structure with three flows: constant additions (18 per quarter), contributions from posistorathers (35% of posistorathers stock), and fractional depletion (22% of crypterals). This creates a cross-subsystem linkage where posistorathers directly influences crypterals accumulation. All constants were separated into distinct variables: constant_addition_crypterals, contribution_rate_posistorathers, and depletion_rate_crypterals.

Causal Relationships

Every cause-and-effect relationship is explicitly captured with correct polarity. Stocks positively influence their proportional flows (reinforcing). Flows positively influence their destination stocks (inflows) or negatively influence them (outflows). Rate constants positively influence their respective flows. The model contains 18 causal relationships total, forming two reinforcing loops (pablanksills growth, crypterals self-reinforcement) and multiple balancing loops (all outflows).

supportingInfo.explanation:
Complete Causal Structure Extraction

I created a comprehensive stock and flow model capturing all causal relationships from the provided information. The model contains four interconnected inventory systems:

Primary Stock-Flow Structures:

  • Ocs inventory: Starts at 25, gains from proptimatires (15% weekly), loses constant 3 units weekly
  • Proptimatires inventory: Starts at 40, gains constant 5 units weekly, loses 25% of itself weekly
  • Priaries inventory: Starts at 80, gains from proptimatires (10% weekly), loses based on houtals (5% weekly)
  • Houtals inventory: Starts at 60, gains constant 7 units weekly, loses 8% of itself weekly

Key Cross-Stock Causal Relationships:

  1. Proptimatires drives ocs inflow (positive feedback)
  2. Proptimatires drives priaries inflow (positive feedback)
  3. Houtals drives priaries outflow (creates depletion pressure)

Structural Decisions: All numerical constants were separated into distinct variables following best practices. Each flow has explicit rate variables, enabling clear causal tracing. The model captures both self-regulating loops (stocks affecting their own outflows) and cross-system dependencies (proptimatires affecting multiple other stocks, houtals affecting priaries).

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Throughout the process, we have on hand one hundred fifty outrances. Every hour, this inventory gains from exactly twenty new outrances. Simultaneously, each hour the stock gets diminished by 40% of its current amount. Simultaneously, each hour the stock loses 10% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we start the period with thirty illigents. Every hour, this inventory gains from 40% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock suffers depletion of a constant five illigents.  Meanwhile, we have on hand sixty-five yelbs. Every hour, this inventory benefits from 10% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock is reduced through 12% of whatever trazes are currently available.  Meanwhile, our records indicate eighty-five trazes. Every hour, this inventory gets replenished by exactly fifteen new trazes. Simultaneously, each hour the stock loses 18% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model Structure

This model captures four interconnected inventory systems with their respective accumulation and depletion processes.

Stock-Flow Structures

Outrances System: A stock with constant inflow (20 per hour) and two fractional outflows (40% and 10% per hour). This creates a balancing feedback loop where higher outrances lead to greater depletion.

Illigents System: A stock that gains from outrances (40% conversion rate) and depletes at a constant rate (5 per hour). This creates a reinforcing connection from outrances to illigents.

Yelbs System: A stock that gains from outrances (10% conversion rate) and is reduced based on trazes (12% conversion rate). This creates two cross-system dependencies.

Trazes System: A stock with constant inflow (15 per hour) and fractional outflow (18% per hour). This creates a balancing feedback loop.

Key Causal Relationships

The model exhibits a cascade structure where outrances serves as a source for both illigents and yelbs. Additionally, trazes influences yelbs through its reduction effect, creating an inter-system dependency. Each stock has its own balancing loop through fractional depletion, while the constant inflows provide steady replenishment.

Constant Separation

All numerical constants have been extracted into separate named variables following best practices, ensuring model transparency and ease of modification.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: At the facility, our records indicate one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory gets replenished by 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each year the stock decreases by a constant three whatajigs.  Meanwhile, our records indicate two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory grows through incoming 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock gets diminished by 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we have on hand two hundred whoziewhats. Every year, this inventory increases due to 5% of the current balacks count. Simultaneously, each year the stock experiences losses of 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, there are initially twelve funkados. Every year, this inventory gains from 5% of the current whoziewhats count. Simultaneously, each year the stock suffers depletion of 3% of whatever maxabizers are currently available.  Meanwhile, we start the period with eighty-eight maxabizers. Every year, this inventory increases due to 5% of the current funkados count. Simultaneously, each year the stock experiences losses of 3% of whatever whoziewhats are currently available.

supportingInfo.explanation:
This model captures a cascade system with five interconnected inventory stocks. Each stock has growth and depletion flows with specific causal relationships:

Whatajigs forms the foundation, growing from its own stock (5% self-reinforcing growth) while depleting at a constant rate. This creates a reinforcing feedback loop where whatajigs drives its own growth.

Balacks receives inflow from whatajigs (5% of whatajigs) and depletes proportionally to itself (3%). This creates a cross-stock cascade where whatajigs influences balacks growth.

Whoziewhats receives inflow from balacks (5% of balacks) and depletes proportionally to itself (3%). This extends the cascade chain further.

Funkados and Maxabizers form a mutual interdependency: funkados grows from whoziewhats but depletes based on maxabizers, while maxabizers grows from funkados but depletes based on whoziewhats. This creates two balancing feedback loops that couple these final two stocks together.

The model reveals a complex causal structure: a linear cascade (whatajigs → balacks → whoziewhats) feeding into a circular interdependency (funkados ⇄ maxabizers via whoziewhats). All constants are extracted as separate variables to make relationships explicit and enable sensitivity analysis.
supportingInfo.title: Cascading Inventory System with Circular Interdependency

supportingInfo.explanation:
Added Frimbulator Inventory System

I added a new stock called frimbulators with an initial value of 20 units, representing the organization's inventory. This stock accumulates through a single inflow called frimbulator_incoming.

The incoming flow is calculated as 2% of the current existing_stock_a count, creating a causal link between the existing stock and the frimbulator inventory growth. I created a separate constant variable frimbulator_growth_rate (0.02) to represent this 2% rate, following the best practice of never embedding numerical constants directly in equations.

This creates a reinforcing feedback loop: as existing_stock_a grows through its own growth_flow, it drives higher frimbulator_incoming, which accumulates in the frimbulators stock. The structure captures the dependency where frimbulator inventory growth is tied to the existing_stock_a level rather than being independent.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model Updates: Closing Feedback Loops

Initial Inventory Correction: Changed existing_inventory initial value from 75 to 100 frimbulators as specified.

New Reinforcing Loop (R1): Added enhancement_flow (5% of existing_inventory weekly) as a new inflow to existing_inventory. This creates a reinforcing feedback loop: existing_inventory → enhancement_flow → existing_inventory. As inventory grows, enhancement grows proportionally, accelerating inventory growth. Created enhancement_rate constant (0.05) following best practices.

New Balancing Loop (B1): Added buffer_depletion_flow (3% of existing_buffer weekly) as a new outflow from existing_inventory. This creates a balancing feedback loop connecting the two stocks: existing_buffer → buffer_depletion_flow → existing_inventory. Higher buffer levels increase inventory depletion. Created buffer_depletion_rate constant (0.03).

Constant Extraction: Following XMILE best practices, extracted all numerical rates into separate named variables (consumption_rate, enhancement_rate, buffer_depletion_rate) rather than embedding them directly in flow equations.

Feedback Structure: The model now contains one reinforcing loop (inventory self-enhancement) and two balancing loops (consumption and buffer-driven depletion), creating dynamic tension between growth and depletion forces.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model Extension: Warehouse Inventory System

I've extended the original two-pool model by adding three new warehouse inventory stocks (marticatenes, refluppers, and exemintes) that create feedback loops connecting back to the original pools.

New Feedback Loops Created:

  1. existing_pool_alpha → marticatenes → refluppers → existing_pool_beta loop: This creates an indirect connection where existing_pool_alpha feeds marticatenes (15% monthly), which then feeds refluppers (20% monthly), which finally depletes based on existing_pool_beta (10% monthly). This closes a feedback path between the two original pools.

  2. existing_pool_beta → refluppers outflow: The existing_pool_beta now has a second outflow (refluppers_outflow) in addition to its original feed_beta inflow, creating a balancing effect on the refluppers inventory.

Structural Changes:

  • Separated all constant values into named variables (feed_alpha_rate, drain_alpha_fraction, etc.) following best practices
  • Added marticatenes stock with fractional inflow from existing_pool_alpha and fractional outflow from itself
  • Added refluppers stock with fractional inflow from marticatenes and fractional outflow driven by existing_pool_beta
  • Added exemintes stock with constant inflow and fractional outflow from itself (independent subsystem)

System Behavior:

The model now exhibits cascading dynamics where changes in existing_pool_alpha propagate through marticatenes to refluppers, which then affects existing_pool_beta through depletion. This creates interdependencies across all warehouse inventories and the original pools.
supportingInfo.title: Warehouse Inventory Feedback Loop Integration

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model Extension: Three New Inventory Systems

I added three new stock-and-flow structures to represent the inventory systems described:

Pablanksills System (Reinforcing Loop R1): Created a stock starting at 110 units with proportional growth (6% per quarter) and constant depletion (18 units per quarter). This creates a reinforcing feedback loop where higher inventory leads to higher growth, which further increases inventory.

Posistorathers System (Balancing Loop B1): Created a stock starting at 70 units with constant additions (25 units per quarter) and proportional depletion (35% per quarter). The proportional outflow creates a balancing loop that limits growth as the stock increases.

Crypterals System (Mixed Dynamics): Created a stock starting at 95 units with two inflows and one outflow. The constant replenishment (18 units) and proportional enhancement from posistorathers (35% of posistorathers level) add to the stock, while proportional depletion (22% of crypterals) removes from it. This creates a cross-stock linkage where posistorathers directly influences crypterals growth.

Key Structural Pattern: All three systems follow the classic stock-flow archetype with separate variables for all constants, ensuring model transparency and ease of parameter adjustment. The posistorathers-to-crypterals connection represents an inter-system dependency.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model Expansion: Adding Four New Stock-Flow Chains

I expanded the original two-stock model by adding four new interconnected stock-flow structures that create multiple feedback loops.

New Stocks Added:

  • ocs (initial: 25 units): Receives inflow from proptimatires (15% weekly) and has outflow driven by existing_chamber_eta (4% weekly)
  • proptimatires (initial: 40 units): Receives inflow from existing_chamber_theta (9% weekly) and has outflow proportional to itself (25% weekly)
  • priaries (initial: 80 units): Receives inflow from proptimatires (10% weekly) and has outflow driven by houtals (5% weekly)
  • houtals (initial: 60 units): Receives constant inflow (7 units weekly) and has outflow proportional to itself (8% weekly)

Feedback Loops Created:

  1. existing_chamber_theta → proptimatires → ocs → existing_chamber_eta: This creates a reinforcing connection where theta influences eta through intermediate stocks

  2. proptimatires → priaries → houtals: A cascade where proptimatires drives priaries growth, which is then constrained by houtals

  3. proptimatires self-regulation: The 25% outflow creates a balancing loop limiting proptimatires accumulation

  4. houtals self-regulation: The 8% outflow creates a balancing loop limiting houtals accumulation

All constants were extracted as separate variables following best practices, and all causal relationships were documented with appropriate positive polarities since all relationships involve variables moving in the same direction.
supportingInfo.title: Four Interconnected Stock Flow Chains with Feedback

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model Extension: Five Interconnected Inventory Chains

I added five new inventory stocks (whatajigs, balacks, whoziewhats, funkados, and maxabizers) that form a complex chain of interdependencies with the existing model.

New Feedback Loops Created:

  1. Whatajigs → Balacks → Whoziewhats → Funkados → Maxabizers Chain: Each inventory feeds forward to enhance the next inventory at 5% annually, creating a cascading positive reinforcement structure.

  2. Existing Store Lambda → Balacks Feedback: The original existing_store_lambda now influences balacks reduction (3% drain), connecting the original model to the new chain.

  3. Existing Store Mu → Maxabizers Feedback: The original existing_store_mu drains maxabizers at 3%, creating another connection point that closes the loop back to the original model.

  4. Maxabizers → Funkados Negative Loop: Maxabizers reduces funkados, while funkados enhances maxabizers, creating a balancing feedback loop between these two stocks.

Structural Pattern: This represents a "Limits to Growth" archetype where growth-promoting processes (5% enhancements) are constrained by draining processes (3% reductions), with cross-connections to the original lambda and mu stores creating system-wide interdependencies. Each stock has both self-reinforcing growth and external draining mechanisms, preventing unlimited accumulation.

Causal loop

The phrase "grows relative to its current size" defines a reinforcing loop: inventory raises the growth flow, and the growth flow raises inventory. This is the classic exponential-growth archetype, and it is the only feedback loop present because no draining or limiting process is described.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: At the facility, we have on hand one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory receives new additions of 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each year the stock suffers depletion of 300% of whatever balacks are currently available.  Meanwhile, we have on hand two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory increases due to 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock suffers depletion of 3% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

The description contains two accumulations, each with one inflow and one outflow, so the model uses two stocks and four flows.

  • Whatajigs (starts at 100): gains from whatajig additions (5% of its own level) and loses through whatajig depletion (300% of the balacks available).
  • Balacks (starts at 200): gains from balack additions (5% of the whatajig level) and loses through balack depletion (3% of its own level).

Causal loops captured

  1. Reinforcing loop on whatajigs — more whatajigs → more additions → more whatajigs (exponential self-growth).
  2. Balancing loop on balacks — more balacks → more depletion → fewer balacks (exponential self-decay).
  3. Balancing cross-loop — more whatajigs → more balack additions → more balacks → more whatajig depletion → fewer whatajigs. This is the classic predator–prey style coupling, which is why the two inventories can oscillate; the model uses a small time step and Euler integration accordingly.

Modeling choices

  • All four percentage rates (5%, 300%, 5%, 3%) and both starting quantities were pulled out into separately named constants rather than being embedded in the flow equations, keeping every equation a simple product of a level and a rate.
  • Each stock's equation is only its initial value; the accumulation is expressed through the inflow/outflow attachments rather than an integral expression.
  • All four flows are one-directional (additions and depletions are physical processes that cannot run backwards), so they are constrained to stay non-negative.
  • No aggregate totals were introduced, and no conditional logic is used anywhere.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: During operations, there are initially fifty marticatenes. Every month, this inventory is enhanced by exactly ten new marticatenes. Simultaneously, each month the stock is reduced through 20% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, our records indicate seventy-five refluppers. Every month, this inventory gains from 20% of the current marticatenes count. Simultaneously, each month the stock suffers depletion of a constant eight refluppers.  Meanwhile, we have on hand one hundred twenty exemintes. Every month, this inventory grows through incoming exactly eight new exemintes. Simultaneously, each month the stock is reduced through 10% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Three accumulations were identified, each with one inflow and one outflow:

  • Marticatenes — starts at fifty, gains a fixed ten per month, and loses twenty percent of its current level each month. Because the loss is proportional to the level, this forms a balancing (goal-seeking) loop that drives the stock toward an equilibrium of fifty units.
  • Refluppers — starts at seventy-five, gains twenty percent of the current marticatene count each month, and loses a fixed eight per month. This stock has no internal feedback; it is driven entirely by the marticatene level and a constant drain, so it drifts rather than settling on its own.
  • Exemintes — starts at one hundred twenty, gains a fixed eight per month, and loses ten percent of its current level each month. Another balancing loop, seeking eighty units.

Causal couplings captured

The only cross-stock cause and effect is Marticatenes → reflupper gain → Refluppers, making the marticatene inventory the upstream driver of reflupper accumulation.

Modeling choices

  • Every numeric value stated in the description (initial levels, constant rates, and fractional loss rates) was abstracted into its own named constant so that no arbitrary number appears inside an equation, and so each stated fact appears explicitly as a cause.
  • Stock equations contain only initial values; the integration is expressed through the inflow and outflow attachments.
  • All flows are one-directional (never negative), since additions, gains, reductions, and depletions are physically one-way processes.
  • No flow serves as both an inflow and an outflow to the same stock.
  • The time step is a quarter month so the proportional drains are integrated smoothly.
supportingInfo.title: Three Coupled Inventory Stocks With Feedback

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In my business, we have on hand thirty-five povals. Every day, this inventory receives new additions of 30% of the current dominitoxings count. Simultaneously, each day the stock gets diminished by 20% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we have on hand ninety auspongs. Every day, this inventory receives new additions of 20% of the current povals count. Simultaneously, each day the stock loses a constant twelve auspongs.  Meanwhile, we have on hand forty-five dominitoxings. Every day, this inventory grows through incoming exactly twelve new dominitoxings. Simultaneously, each day the stock is reduced through 30% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Three accumulations are represented as stocks, each with its own inflow and outflow, since inventories change only through their flows:

  • povals (starts at 35): gains 30% of the current dominitoxings each day, loses 20% of itself each day.
  • auspongs (starts at 90): gains 20% of the current povals each day, loses a fixed twelve per day.
  • dominitoxings (starts at 45): gains a fixed twelve per day, loses 30% of itself each day.

Causal chain

The information contains a one-way cascade: dominitoxings drive poval additions, and povals drive auspong additions. Each stock also drives its own percentage-based outflow, creating three separate balancing (self-correcting) loops that pull each inventory toward an equilibrium. The two constant flows (twelve per day) have no feedback from any stock, so they act as external drivers only.

Constants abstracted

Every numeric value from the description was pulled out into its own named variable — initial levels (initial povals, initial auspongs, initial dominitoxings), fractional rates (poval addition rate, poval loss rate, auspong addition rate, dominitoxing loss rate), and fixed quantities (auspong loss constant, dominitoxing addition constant) — so no arbitrary numbers appear inside equations.

Flow direction checks

No flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow of the same stock, and all flows are marked one-directional because additions and reductions of physical inventory cannot run backwards.

Note that the auspong stock can trend downward because its fixed loss of twelve per day may exceed the additions coming from povals; the model reports this faithfully rather than masking it.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In the system, our records indicate one hundred ten pablanksills. Every quarter, this inventory benefits from 6% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock suffers depletion of a constant eighteen pablanksills.  Meanwhile, our records indicate seventy posistorathers. Every quarter, this inventory gets replenished by exactly twenty-five new posistorathers. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock has outgoing 35% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, there are initially ninety-five crypterals. Every quarter, this inventory is enhanced by exactly eighteen new crypterals. Every quarter, this inventory grows through incoming 35% of the current posistorathers count. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock decreases by 22% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Three accumulations were identified, each changing only through its own flows:

Pablanksills (starts at 110) — a reinforcing loop: growth is a fraction (6%) of the current stock, so the stock feeds its own inflow. Depletion is a fixed eighteen units per quarter, independent of the stock, so it cannot balance the compounding growth — this stock grows without bound.

Posistorathers (starts at 70) — a classic balancing (goal-seeking) structure: a constant inflow of twenty-five units per quarter against an outflow that is 35% of the current stock. The stock settles toward its equilibrium of roughly 71 units, where inflow equals outflow.

Crypterals (starts at 95) — also goal-seeking, but coupled to posistorathers. It receives a constant eighteen units per quarter plus a transfer equal to 35% of the posistorathers stock, and loses 22% of its own level each quarter. The transfer inflow is defined directly as the posistorathers outflow, making the material coupling between the two stocks explicit rather than duplicating the arithmetic.

Modeling choices

  • Every percentage and constant amount (6%, 18, 25, 35%, 18, 22%) was abstracted into its own named constant rather than embedded in an equation, so each numeric assumption is visible and separately adjustable.
  • All flows are one-directional (births/additions and removals), so each is constrained to be non-negative.
  • Stock equations contain only initial values; accumulation is expressed purely through inflow and outflow attachments.
  • No flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow of the same stock; the posistorathers departure is represented once as its outflow and once as the corresponding crypterals inflow.
  • Time is measured in quarters with a quarter-step-based solution interval to keep the fractional rates faithful to the stated per-quarter behavior.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Four accumulations were identified, each changing only through its own inflow and outflow:

  • Ocs (start 25): grows by 15% of the proptimatires stock, drains at a constant 3 per week.
  • Proptimatires (start 40): grows by a constant 5 per week, drains at 25% of itself — a classic balancing loop that drives it toward an equilibrium of 20.
  • Priaries (start 80): grows by 10% of proptimatires, drains at 5% of houtals — driven entirely by other stocks, so it has no self-regulation of its own.
  • Houtals (start 60): grows by a constant 7 per week, drains at 8% of itself — another balancing loop, settling near 87.5.

Causal couplings

Two cross-stock links were made explicit: proptimatires drives both the ocs inflow and the priaries inflow, and houtals drives the priaries outflow. These are the only inter-stock causes in the description; the remaining causes are the two self-referencing (percentage-of-self) drains.

  • Every percentage and constant quantity was abstracted into its own named variable (growth fractions, depletion fractions, arrival quantities, decline quantity) rather than being hard-coded inside a flow equation.
  • Stock equations contain only initial values; accumulation is expressed through the inflow/outflow attachments.
  • All flows were marked one-directional, since each represents a physical arrival or removal that cannot legitimately run backwards.
  • No flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow of the same stock.
  • Weekly time units with a quarter-week time step keep the percentage-based drains numerically stable.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In my business, our records indicate one hundred fifty outrances. Every hour, this inventory grows through incoming exactly twenty new outrances. Simultaneously, each hour the stock has outgoing 40% of its current amount. Simultaneously, each hour the stock has outgoing 10% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows thirty illigents. Every hour, this inventory is enhanced by 40% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock decreases by a constant five illigents.  Meanwhile, our records indicate sixty-five yelbs. Every hour, this inventory increases due to 10% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock suffers depletion of 12% of whatever trazes are currently available.  Meanwhile, we begin with eighty-five trazes. Every hour, this inventory grows through incoming exactly fifteen new trazes. Simultaneously, each hour the stock has outgoing 18% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Four accumulations were identified, each with explicit initial values and their own flows:

  • Outrances (starts at 150): one constant inflow of 20 per hour and two separate proportional outflows (40% and 10% of the current stock). These were kept as two distinct flows rather than combined into a single 50% drain, because the description names them as two separate depletion processes.
  • Illigents (starts at 30): an inflow driven by 40% of the current outrance stock, and a constant outflow of 5 per hour.
  • Yelbs (starts at 65): an inflow driven by 10% of the current outrance stock, and an outflow driven by 12% of the traze stock — a cross-stock coupling, not a self-drain.
  • Trazes (starts at 85): a constant inflow of 15 per hour and a proportional outflow of 18% of the stock.

Modeling choices

  • No hard-coded constants in equations. Every rate, fraction, and constant (20, 0.4, 0.1, 0.4, 5, 0.1, 0.12, 15, 0.18) was abstracted into its own clearly named auxiliary variable so each equation reads in plain language.
  • Stock initial values are set as plain numbers; accumulation is handled purely through the flow structure.
  • All flows marked one-directional, since arrivals and depletions here are physical processes that cannot run backwards.
  • No flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow of any stock.

Causal structure

The outrance stock drains itself through two proportional loops (balancing loops that drive it toward an equilibrium of about 33 units), and the traze stock has its own balancing drain loop (settling near 83 units). Outrances act as the upstream driver of both illigents and yelbs, while trazes act as the depleting driver of yelbs — so yelbs sit at the junction of two independent upstream stocks. Illigents grow on a constant-drain structure, meaning their long-run behavior depends on whether the outrance-driven inflow exceeds the fixed loss of 5 per hour.
supportingInfo.title: Four Coupled Inventories With Cross Stock Drivers

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Throughout the process, we start the period with one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory increases due to 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each year the stock suffers depletion of a constant three whatajigs.  Meanwhile, our records indicate two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory increases due to 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock has outgoing 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we begin with two hundred whoziewhats. Every year, this inventory gains from 5% of the current balacks count. Simultaneously, each year the stock has outgoing 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we have on hand twelve funkados. Every year, this inventory receives new additions of 5% of the current whoziewhats count. Simultaneously, each year the stock decreases by 3% of whatever maxabizers are currently available.  Meanwhile, our records indicate eighty-eight maxabizers. Every year, this inventory gains from 5% of the current funkados count. Simultaneously, each year the stock suffers depletion of 3% of whatever whoziewhats are currently available.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure extracted

Five accumulations were identified, each with exactly one inflow and one outflow:

  • whatajigs (starts at 100): grows by a fraction of itself — a self-reinforcing loop — and loses a fixed quantity each year. Because the loss is constant while the gain is proportional, this stock eventually escapes the drain and grows exponentially.
  • balacks (starts at 200): fed by a fraction of whatajigs, drained by a fraction of itself (a balancing loop on its own level).
  • whoziewhats (starts at 200): fed by a fraction of balacks, drained by a fraction of itself.
  • funkados (starts at 12): fed by a fraction of whoziewhats, drained in proportion to the maxabizers level.
  • maxabizers (starts at 88): fed by a fraction of funkados, drained in proportion to the whoziewhats level.

Cross couplings

The chain whatajigs → balacks → whoziewhats → funkados → maxabizers is a cascade of material transfers. Two extra cross-links were captured explicitly: funkados are drained by maxabizers and maxabizers are drained by funkados' upstream driver, whoziewhats. The funkados–maxabizers pair therefore forms a coupled loop where each stock's outflow is set outside itself.

Constants abstracted

Rather than embedding numbers in equations, three named parameters were created: a common growth fraction (5% per year) driving every addition, a common decline fraction (3% per year) driving every proportional removal, and a constant whatajigs depletion (3 units per year) for the one fixed-size loss. This makes every rate visible as an explicit cause in the causal map.

Type choices

All five inventories are stocks since they change only through their flows; all ten rates are flows marked one-directional, since each describes a strictly additive or strictly subtractive yearly process.

testParams.prompt: Please give me a quantitative model that captures the key causal processes described in the background information.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.
            
            Epidemiologists understand that infectious disease spread follows well-established patterns that typically evolve over daily intervals. 
            The susceptible population becomes exposed when they come into contact with infectious individuals. 
            After an incubation period, exposed individuals become infectious and can transmit the disease. 
            Infectious individuals then recover and develop immunity, or in some cases may die from the disease.
            The basic reproduction number (R0) determines how many new infections each infectious person generates.
            Public health interventions like vaccination can move people directly from susceptible to recovered,
            while social distancing measures reduce the contact rate between infectious and susceptible individuals.
            Contact tracing and quarantine can remove exposed individuals from circulation before they become infectious.
            Disease progression involves distinct compartments of people moving through the infection cycle.
            
            Use these variable names: 
            susceptible, exposed, infectious, recovered, infecting, incubating, recovering, contacts, vaccination

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

The model is a classic SEIR chain of stocks with two intervention pathways, built exactly around the requested vocabulary.

Stocks (accumulations): susceptible, exposed, infectious, recovered, plus deceased to close the accounting for disease deaths.

Flows (rates of progression):

  • infecting moves people from susceptible to exposed and equals contacts * infectivity.
  • incubating moves exposed to infectious after the incubation period.
  • quarantining removes traced exposed people before they can transmit (splitting the exposed outflow so total drainage still equals exposed / incubation_period).
  • recovering and dying split the infectious outflow by the case fatality ratio.
  • vaccination moves people directly from susceptible to recovered, as public health interventions do.

All of these are one-directional (uniflows) because people cannot un-infect or un-die.

contacts captures random mixing: each infectious person makes contact_rate contacts per day, and the susceptible share of the population determines how many of those are risky.

Key feedback loops

  1. Contagion (reinforcing): infectious → contacts → infecting → exposed → incubating → infectious. This drives exponential takeoff.
  2. Susceptible depletion (balancing): as susceptible falls, the susceptible fraction in contacts falls, shutting down the epidemic — the limit that turns the growth curve over.
  3. Behavioral response (balancing): rising perceived_prevalence raises relative_prevalence, which lowers the social_distancing_effect multiplier on the contact rate, cutting transmission. Because perception is smoothed by a reporting delay, this loop reacts late and can generate successive waves — a classic delayed-correction archetype.
  4. Intervention leakage: vaccination and contact tracing drain the susceptible and exposed stocks respectively, weakening the contagion loop before it acts.

Formulation choices

  • total_population is an auxiliary sum, not a stock, since it is a pure algebraic aggregation of the compartments.
  • perceived_prevalence uses SMOOTH (a true moving average of perception), not a pure delay function.
  • The social distancing table function is normalized on relative prevalence and passes through (1, 1), so normal conditions yield normal contacts and higher prevalence yields progressively fewer contacts.
  • No numeric constants are buried in equations; every parameter (contact rate, infectivity, incubation period, illness duration, fatality ratio, quarantine effectiveness, vaccination fraction, seeds) is an explicit named variable that can be tested.
  • basic_reproduction_number and effective_reproduction_number are reported as diagnostics: the epidemic grows while Rt exceeds 1 and peaks exactly when it crosses 1.
  • Divisions by population and time constants use the protected division operator to avoid division-by-zero.
supportingInfo.title: SEIR model with distancing, tracing, vaccination

variables.name: susceptible
variables.documentation: People who have not yet been infected and have no immunity. They leave only by becoming exposed through contact with infectious people or by being vaccinated.

variables.name: exposed
variables.documentation: People who have been infected but are still in the incubation period and not yet able to transmit the disease. They either progress to infectious or are removed by contact tracing and quarantine.

variables.name: infectious
variables.documentation: People currently able to transmit the disease. This stock drives new infections and is drained by recovery and disease death.

variables.name: recovered
variables.documentation: People who are immune and no longer participate in transmission, whether through natural recovery, vaccination, or removal by quarantine.

variables.name: deceased
variables.documentation: Cumulative deaths caused by the disease, accumulated from the dying flow.

variables.name: infecting
variables.documentation: Rate at which susceptible people become exposed. It is the number of risky contacts between susceptible and infectious people multiplied by the probability that a contact transmits the infection.

variables.name: contacts
variables.documentation: Contacts per day between infectious and susceptible people. Each infectious person makes contact_rate contacts per day, and the fraction of those contacts that fall on susceptible people equals the susceptible share of the population (random mixing).

variables.name: contact_rate
variables.documentation: Actual contacts per person per day, equal to the normal rate scaled down by social distancing behaviour.

variables.name: normal_contact_rate
variables.documentation: Contacts per person per day in the absence of any social distancing.

variables.name: social_distancing_effect
variables.documentation: Multiplier on the normal contact rate reflecting voluntary and mandated social distancing. At or below reference prevalence (relative prevalence of 1) behaviour is normal (multiplier 1); as perceived prevalence rises above the reference, contacts are progressively cut back.

variables.name: perceived_prevalence
variables.documentation: The share of the population currently infectious as perceived by the public, smoothed to represent reporting and awareness delays. A smoothing (moving average) function is used rather than a pure delay because perceptions average recent information.

variables.name: reporting_delay
variables.documentation: Time for case information to be reported and absorbed into public perception.

variables.name: relative_prevalence
variables.documentation: Perceived prevalence expressed relative to the level of prevalence at which people begin to change behaviour. This normalization makes the social distancing function dimensionless and equal to 1 under reference conditions.

variables.name: reference_prevalence
variables.documentation: Prevalence of infectious cases considered normal or tolerable; above this level distancing responses begin.

variables.name: infectivity
variables.documentation: Probability that a single contact between an infectious and a susceptible person transmits the disease.

variables.name: incubating
variables.documentation: Rate at which exposed people finish incubation and become infectious. Only the fraction not intercepted by contact tracing and quarantine reaches the infectious stock.

variables.name: quarantining
variables.documentation: Rate at which exposed people are found by contact tracing and isolated before they can transmit, moving them directly out of the transmission chain.

variables.name: quarantine_effectiveness
variables.documentation: Fraction of exposed people identified and isolated by contact tracing before becoming infectious.

variables.name: incubation_period
variables.documentation: Average time between infection and becoming infectious.

variables.name: recovering
variables.documentation: Rate at which infectious people stop transmitting and gain immunity. Only survivors flow to recovered.

variables.name: dying
variables.documentation: Rate at which infectious people die from the disease, the fatal share of the infectious outflow.

variables.name: case_fatality_ratio
variables.documentation: Fraction of infectious cases that end in death rather than recovery.

variables.name: duration_of_illness
variables.documentation: Average time a person remains infectious before recovering or dying.

variables.name: vaccination
variables.documentation: Rate at which susceptible people are immunized, moving them directly to the recovered (immune) stock without passing through infection.

variables.name: vaccination_fraction
variables.documentation: Fraction of the remaining susceptible population vaccinated each day; represents public health campaign intensity.

variables.name: total_population
variables.documentation: Living population participating in mixing. This is a simple algebraic sum of the compartments, so it is an auxiliary rather than a stock.

variables.name: initial_population
variables.documentation: Size of the population at the start of the epidemic.

variables.name: initial_infectious
variables.documentation: Number of infectious people seeding the epidemic.

variables.name: basic_reproduction_number
variables.documentation: R0: the number of new infections one infectious person would generate in a fully susceptible population, equal to contacts per day times transmission probability times infectious duration.

variables.name: effective_reproduction_number
variables.documentation: Rt: actual infections generated per infectious person given the shrinking susceptible pool and current contact rate. The epidemic grows while this exceeds 1.

testParams.name: Healthcare capacity model with resource constraints
testParams.prompt: Please give me a quantitative model that captures the key causal processes described in the background information.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.
            
            Healthcare systems have limited capacity that affects patient outcomes during health crises that unfold over weekly cycles.
            Patients requiring care enter the system through admissions, but bed capacity limits how many can be treated.
            When demand exceeds capacity, patients face delays or are turned away, potentially worsening their condition.
            Healthcare workers are the key resource - they can treat patients but also become sick themselves,
            reducing available capacity. Staff burnout increases when workload is high, leading to turnover.
            Hospitals can surge capacity by opening additional beds and hiring temporary staff, but this takes time.
            Recovery times vary - some patients recover quickly while others require long-term care.
            The system involves managing patient flows, workforce dynamics, and available bed resources.
            
            Use these variable names:
            patients, available beds, healthcare workers, workload, burnout, staff turnover.

supportingInfo.explanation:
What the model represents

The model is built around four accumulations and the delays between them:

  • patients (census) fills from admissions and drains through discharges
  • available beds (open physical capacity) grows with bed surge and shrinks with bed closure
  • healthcare workers (on-duty staff) gains from hiring and returning sick workers, and loses to staff turnover and worker illness
  • burnout builds with workload pressure and dissipates only slowly with rest

Key causal mechanisms captured

Capacity rationing. Admissions are the smaller of demand and admission capacity. Capacity comes from usable beds, which is the minimum of physical beds and the beds the effective workforce can actually staff — so beds without staff are not capacity. This is the classic "limits to growth" constraint.

Turned-away patients come back sicker (reinforcing loop). Unmet demand accumulates in deferred patients and re-enters as returning patients after a delay, so under-capacity today raises demand tomorrow.

Burnout / turnover death spiral (reinforcing loop). High workload accelerates burnout accumulation; burnout both raises staff turnover and cuts worker productivity via effective workers. Fewer effective workers means fewer staffed beds and even higher workload — capacity erodes exactly when it is needed.

Infection of caregivers (reinforcing loop). worker illness scales with the patient census, pulling caregivers out of service during a surge, with a delay before they recover.

Care quality feedback. Overload lengthens the effective length of stay, which keeps beds occupied longer and further reduces admission capacity.

Balancing loops with delays. bed surge and hiring both close the gap between what is needed and what exists, but each is slowed by a delay (three weeks for beds, four for staff), which is why the system overshoots into crisis before relief arrives.

Formulation choices

  • Aggregate quantities like workload, care demand, usable beds, desired beds, desired workers and effective workers are auxiliaries, not stocks, because they are algebraic calculations rather than accumulations.
  • All nonlinear responses (burnout build-up, quit amplification, productivity loss, length-of-stay stretch) are graphical functions normalized to pass through the point (1, 1), so "normal" input gives "normal" output and both directions of deviation are expressible.
  • All rate constants, delays and benchmarks are named variables rather than numbers buried in equations; the epidemic driver is a single time-based wave of new arrivals.
  • Every physically one-directional flow (admissions, discharges, turn aways, hiring, turnover, illness, recoveries, bed opening and closing) is constrained to be non-negative.
  • Parameters are calibrated so the system rests near equilibrium before the wave arrives, so the behavior seen is caused by the crisis and the feedback loops, not by arbitrary initial imbalance.

variables.name: patients
variables.documentation: The census of patients currently being treated in the hospital. It is an accumulation that rises with admissions and falls with discharges, so it can only change through those flows.

variables.name: admissions
variables.documentation: Patients actually taken into care each week. It is the lesser of the demand for care and the capacity of the hospital to accept patients, which is how a limited-capacity system rations service.

variables.name: discharges
variables.documentation: Rate at which treated patients leave care. Modeled as the census divided by the effective average length of stay, the standard first-order draining of a stock.

variables.name: care demand
variables.documentation: Total weekly requests for care: newly sick people plus previously turned-away people who come back needing care.

variables.name: new arrivals
variables.documentation: Exogenous wave of newly ill people seeking care over the weeks of the health crisis. Represents the epidemic driver that stresses the system.

variables.name: deferred patients
variables.documentation: Patients who could not be admitted and are waiting in the community, often worsening. Accumulating them lets the model capture the delayed re-presentation of unmet need.

variables.name: turn aways
variables.documentation: Unmet demand each week: the part of care demand that capacity cannot absorb. Since admissions is the minimum of demand and capacity, this is never negative.

variables.name: returning patients
variables.documentation: Rate at which deferred patients come back and re-enter the demand stream, creating a reinforcing pressure on an already overloaded system.

variables.name: deferral delay
variables.documentation: Average time a turned-away patient waits before seeking care again.

variables.name: admission capacity
variables.documentation: How many patients per week the hospital can accept, set by the free usable beds and the time needed to process an admission. This is the physical capacity limit of the system.

variables.name: admission processing time
variables.documentation: Time required to prepare a free bed and admit a patient.

variables.name: usable beds
variables.documentation: Beds that can actually be used: the smaller of physical beds and the beds the present, effective workforce can staff. This makes workers, not walls, the binding constraint under stress.

variables.name: beds per worker
variables.documentation: Maximum number of beds one healthcare worker can cover.

variables.name: available beds
variables.documentation: Physical bed capacity currently open and available for use. It grows when surge beds are opened and shrinks when surge beds are closed again, with delays in both directions.

variables.name: bed surge
variables.documentation: Rate of opening additional beds when the census indicates more capacity is needed. The surge time captures the delay in bringing capacity online.

variables.name: bed closure
variables.documentation: Rate of closing surge beds once the crisis passes, returning capacity gradually toward its baseline level.

variables.name: desired beds
variables.documentation: Bed capacity managers want, equal to the current census divided by the target occupancy so that some headroom is maintained.

variables.name: target occupancy
variables.documentation: Fraction of beds managers aim to have filled, leaving a buffer for new admissions.

variables.name: bed surge time
variables.documentation: Time needed to open and equip additional beds.

variables.name: bed closure time
variables.documentation: Time over which surge beds are wound down after demand falls.

variables.name: baseline bed capacity
variables.documentation: Normal, permanently staffed bed capacity of the hospital; the floor below which beds are not closed.

variables.name: healthcare workers
variables.documentation: Healthy staff currently available to treat patients. It gains from hiring and from sick colleagues returning, and loses from turnover and from workers falling ill.

variables.name: hiring
variables.documentation: Recruitment of permanent and temporary staff to close the gap between needed and available workers, delayed by the time it takes to hire and onboard.

variables.name: hiring time
variables.documentation: Average delay in recruiting and deploying additional staff.

variables.name: desired workers
variables.documentation: Staff needed to care for the current census at the normal caseload per worker.

variables.name: normal patients per worker
variables.documentation: Caseload per worker that constitutes a normal, sustainable workload.

variables.name: staff turnover
variables.documentation: Staff quitting each week. Normal attrition is amplified when burnout is above its reference level, which is the core reinforcing loop that erodes capacity.

variables.name: normal turnover fraction
variables.documentation: Fraction of staff who leave each week under normal, non-burnout conditions.

variables.name: effect of burnout on turnover
variables.documentation: Multiplier on quit rates from burnout relative to normal. Normal burnout (ratio of one) leaves turnover unchanged; severe burnout multiplies quitting several fold.

variables.name: burnout ratio
variables.documentation: Current burnout compared with its normal level, used as the normalized input to the burnout effect functions.

variables.name: reference burnout
variables.documentation: Burnout level observed under normal workload, used as the benchmark for comparison.

variables.name: burnout
variables.documentation: Accumulated exhaustion and stress in the workforce. It builds up while workload is high and dissipates only slowly with rest, so it is a stock rather than an instantaneous condition.

variables.name: burnout accumulation
variables.documentation: Rate at which fatigue builds, rising steeply once caseloads per worker exceed normal.

variables.name: baseline burnout rate
variables.documentation: Rate of burnout build-up at normal workload, calibrated so that burnout sits at its reference level in normal times.

variables.name: effect of workload on burnout
variables.documentation: Nonlinear multiplier showing how far above normal fatigue accrues as workload rises. Normal workload of one gives the normal rate of one.

variables.name: burnout recovery
variables.documentation: Gradual recuperation of the workforce when pressure eases, draining the burnout stock.

variables.name: burnout recovery time
variables.documentation: Time constant for recovery from accumulated burnout.

variables.name: workload
variables.documentation: Caseload per effective worker relative to the normal caseload. A value of one is normal; above one staff are stretched.

variables.name: effective workers
variables.documentation: Effective staffing after accounting for reduced productivity of burned-out workers. This is the labor actually available to staff beds and treat patients.

variables.name: effect of burnout on productivity
variables.documentation: Multiplier on worker output from burnout. Normal burnout gives normal productivity; high burnout reduces it, tightening the capacity constraint further.

variables.name: worker illness
variables.documentation: Staff falling sick each week. Risk scales with the patient census because more patients mean more exposure, so a surge directly removes caregivers.

variables.name: baseline infection fraction
variables.documentation: Weekly fraction of staff who become ill when the patient census is at its reference level.

variables.name: reference patients
variables.documentation: Normal patient census used as the benchmark for staff exposure risk.

variables.name: sick workers
variables.documentation: Staff off duty because they are ill. Holding them in a separate stock captures the delay before they return to duty.

variables.name: worker recovery
variables.documentation: Rate at which sick staff recover and rejoin the working workforce.

variables.name: illness duration
variables.documentation: Average time a worker is off duty when sick.

variables.name: effective length of stay
variables.documentation: Average time patients spend in care, lengthened when overstretched staff cannot deliver timely treatment. Longer stays keep beds occupied and tighten capacity.

variables.name: base length of stay
variables.documentation: Average treatment time under normal staffing, blending quick recoveries with longer-term cases.

variables.name: effect of workload on length of stay
variables.documentation: Multiplier on length of stay from care quality degradation as workload rises. Normal workload gives the normal stay.

testParams.name: Traffic congestion model with induced demand
testParams.prompt: Please give me a quantitative model that captures the key causal processes described in the background information.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.
            
            Transportation engineers recognize that building more roads often fails to reduce congestion due to induced demand effects that emerge over annual planning cycles.
            When new road capacity is added, it initially reduces travel time and congestion. However, this improvement
            attracts new drivers who switch from other routes, times, or modes of transport. Some people who previously
            didn't make trips now find driving more attractive. Over time, this increased traffic volume can return
            congestion to previous levels or even make it worse. The phenomenon demonstrates that transportation is not
            just about moving vehicles, but about the complex behavioral responses to changes in the system.
            Traffic also creates negative externalities like air pollution and noise, which affect quality of life.
            The system involves road infrastructure, traveler behavior, and traffic volume dynamics.
            
            Use these variable names: 
            road capacity, travelers, travel time, congestion.

supportingInfo.explanation:
What the model captures

The model is built around two accumulations and two balancing loops that fight each other — the classic "Fixes that Fail" structure behind induced demand.

Stocks

  • road capacity — changes only through capacity expansion, a one-directional construction flow with a multi-year lead time.
  • travelers — the stock of daily trips on the network, changing through a single bidirectional net flow (change in travelers). Traffic is a stock, not an instant calculation, because route, departure-time, mode and even location habits adjust gradually.

Loop 1 — the intended fix (balancing, slow): congestion → indicated road capacity → capacity expansion → road capacity → reduces congestion. Planners size projects to serve current traffic at a target volume-to-capacity ratio, and delivery takes years.

Loop 2 — induced demand (balancing, faster): lower congestion → shorter travel time → higher driving attractiveness → more desired travelers → more travelers → raises congestion back up. This is the behavioral response the background emphasizes: the latent pool (potential traveler pool) contains trips currently taken on other routes, at other times, by other modes, or not taken at all.

Because loop 2 acts faster than loop 3-year construction cycle, capacity relief is eroded before it is even fully delivered, and the system settles back near its original congestion level with more vehicles on the road.

Externalities: traffic volume drives air pollution and noise, which degrades quality of life. This is the ratchet in the system — congestion may return to where it started, but pollution and lost livability do not, because they scale with the higher traffic volume rather than with the congestion ratio.

Formulation choices

  • Both non-linear relationships are expressed as normalized graphical functions passing through (1, 1): the congestion delay multiplier rises steeply as volume approaches capacity, and driving attractiveness falls as travel time exceeds the normal reference.
  • All numeric constants are held in their own named variables (construction time, adjustment time, target congestion, latent pool, emission intensity) so no arbitrary numbers sit inside equations.
  • Capacity expansion is a uniflow (roads are not un-built); change in travelers is bidirectional since traffic can fall when conditions worsen.
  • Divisions use the protected operator to avoid division by zero.
  • Quality of life and pollution are computed algebraically as outcome indicators, not as stocks, since they are simple functions of current traffic.

variables.name: road capacity
variables.documentation: The stock of usable road infrastructure, measured as the number of vehicle trips per day the network can carry at normal service levels. It only changes through construction projects.

variables.name: capacity expansion
variables.documentation: Rate at which new road capacity is delivered. Planners compare the capacity implied by current traffic at their target congestion level with existing capacity and close the gap over the typical construction lead time. Capacity is never removed, so this flow is one-directional.

variables.name: indicated road capacity
variables.documentation: The amount of capacity that would be needed to serve current traffic volume at the congestion level planners consider acceptable.

variables.name: target congestion
variables.documentation: The volume-to-capacity ratio that transportation agencies aim for. Below one means they want a capacity cushion.

variables.name: capacity construction time
variables.documentation: Average years from recognizing a capacity shortfall to opening new lanes, covering planning, funding and building.

variables.name: initial road capacity
variables.documentation: Starting road capacity of the network.

variables.name: travelers
variables.documentation: The stock of people currently driving on this road network each day. It accumulates behavioral shifts: people switching routes, times, or modes, and latent trips being made or abandoned. It is a stock because habits and location choices adjust gradually, not instantly.

variables.name: change in travelers
variables.documentation: Net rate at which drivers join or leave the network as actual usage adjusts toward the level implied by current driving attractiveness. It is bidirectional because traffic can both grow and shrink.

variables.name: traveler adjustment time
variables.documentation: Average time for travelers to change route, departure time, or mode choices in response to changed travel conditions.

variables.name: initial travelers
variables.documentation: Starting daily traffic volume on the network.

variables.name: desired travelers
variables.documentation: The traffic volume that would occur if everyone had fully adjusted to current travel conditions: the latent pool of possible trips scaled by how attractive driving currently is.

variables.name: potential traveler pool
variables.documentation: The latent demand: trips that would be driven on this network if travel time were at the normal reference level. It includes trips currently made by other routes, at other times, by other modes, or not made at all.

variables.name: driving attractiveness
variables.documentation: Multiplier on latent demand reflecting how appealing driving is given current travel times. At the normal travel time (ratio of one) attractiveness is one; faster travel makes driving more attractive and induces new trips, slower travel suppresses them.

variables.name: travel time ratio
variables.documentation: Current travel time compared with the historically normal travel time, used as a dimensionless signal for traveler decisions.

variables.name: travel time
variables.documentation: Average door-to-door trip duration on the network. It equals the reference trip time inflated by the delay that congestion imposes.

variables.name: normal travel time
variables.documentation: Reference average trip duration when the network operates at its normal congestion level.

variables.name: congestion delay multiplier
variables.documentation: How much congestion stretches trip duration. Passes through one at normal congestion and rises steeply and non-linearly as volume approaches and exceeds capacity, reflecting standard traffic flow behavior.

variables.name: congestion ratio
variables.documentation: Current congestion relative to the reference congestion level, providing a normalized input to the delay function.

variables.name: congestion
variables.documentation: The volume-to-capacity ratio of the network, the standard engineering measure of how crowded roads are.

variables.name: normal congestion
variables.documentation: Reference volume-to-capacity ratio against which current congestion is judged.

variables.name: air pollution and noise
variables.documentation: Negative externalities generated by traffic, scaling with the number of vehicles on the road.

variables.name: externality per traveler
variables.documentation: Emissions and noise generated per daily trip.

variables.name: pollution ratio
variables.documentation: Current externality burden relative to the historically tolerated level.

variables.name: reference pollution
variables.documentation: The pollution and noise level associated with the initial traffic volume, used as a benchmark.

variables.name: quality of life effect
variables.documentation: Multiplier showing how the externality burden degrades livability. Equals one at the reference pollution level and declines as pollution and noise rise.

variables.name: quality of life
variables.documentation: Index of livability along the corridor, degraded by traffic externalities. It is an outcome indicator rather than a driver of behavior in this model.

variables.name: baseline quality of life
variables.documentation: Livability index at the reference pollution level.
