additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Additions

  • frimbulator_inventory (stock): starts at twenty frimbulators, driven only by its enhancement inflow, since a physical inventory is an accumulation.
  • frimbulator_enhancement (flow): two percent of the current existing_stock_a each day. Marked one-directional because an "enhancement" can only add.
  • frimbulator_enhancement_fraction and initial_frimbulators: named parameters so no arbitrary numbers sit inside equations.

Feedback structure

The self-referencing growth of stock A is an explicit reinforcing loop (stock A → growth flow → stock A), and it now also drives an exponentially rising frimbulator supply. Stock B retains its balancing (goal-seeking) loop: the fuller it gets, the faster it drains, so it settles where inflow equals drain. No feedback from frimbulators back into stock A was added, because the description gives no evidence that frimbulators influence anything upstream — inventing one would misrepresent the system.

Formulation errors corrected in the prior model

  1. growth_flow had the hard-coded 0.1 embedded; abstracted into growth_fraction.
  2. drain_flow had the hard-coded 0.05 embedded; abstracted into drain_fraction.
  3. input_flow was a bare 5; abstracted into base_input_rate.
  4. Missing flow-to-stock relationships (growth_flow → existing_stock_a, input_flow/drain_flow → existing_stock_b) were absent from the causal list, so the reinforcing and balancing loops were not visible; they are now explicit.
  5. Missing uniflow settings and units/documentation on all original variables were supplied.

testParams.name: Add a single stock with two flows
testParams.prompt:
Please add the following to my model...
In our organization, we start the period with one hundred frimbulators. Every week, this inventory gets replenished by 5% of the current existing_inventory count. Simultaneously, each week the stock decreases by 3% of whatever existing_buffer are currently available.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Errors corrected in the prior model

  • existing_inventory — its initial value was 75 and hard coded. It now starts from initial inventory (100), matching the stated one hundred frimbulators, and the arbitrary number is abstracted into a named variable.
  • supply_flow — was a bare constant of 8, which had no stated basis. It is now five percent of the current existing inventory count, using the named inventory replenishment fraction. This is the structure described in the new information.
  • consumption_flow — was driven by inventory (existing_inventory * 0.02), with an embedded numeric rate. The description says the decrease is three percent of whatever buffer is currently available, so it is now driven by existing buffer through the named buffer depletion fraction. The old inventory-to-consumption link was removed and replaced.
  • replenish_flow — was a disconnected constant of 3, leaving the buffer as an unbounded open-ended stock with no feedback. It is now a standard stock adjustment: the gap between target buffer and the actual buffer, closed over a buffer adjustment time.
  • existing_buffer — initial value moved into the named initial buffer variable.

Feedback loops now closed

  1. Reinforcing loop (growth engine): inventory → supply flow → inventory. Because resupply is a percentage of the stock itself, inventory compounds — classic exponential growth.
  2. Balancing loop (buffer correction): buffer → replenish flow → buffer. Any shortfall against the target is closed over time, and any excess slows the rebuild.
  3. Balancing loop (cross-stock drain): inventory → target buffer → replenish flow → buffer → consumption flow → inventory. Larger inventories justify a larger reserve, a larger reserve drives a larger three percent weekly drawdown, which pulls inventory back down. This is the link that ties the two originally separate stocks into a single closed system rather than two unconnected accumulations.

With five percent compounding growth against a drawdown of only three percent of a reserve worth a quarter of inventory, the reinforcing loop dominates and inventory grows over the period.

All numeric rates are held in explicitly named variables, and no conditional logic is used; the division in the rebuild rate uses the protected operator.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Added warehouse structure

  • whatajigs stock starting at one hundred, filled by whatajigs_inflow (five percent of base_stock_x) and drained by whatajigs_outflow (three hundred percent of the current balacks level).
  • balacks stock starting at two hundred, filled by balacks_inflow (five percent of the current whatajigs level) and drained by balacks_outflow (three percent of base_stock_y).

Feedback loops closed

  • Warehouse balancing loop: more whatajigs produce more balacks, and more balacks drive a much larger withdrawal of whatajigs, which pulls the whatajigs level back down. Because the withdrawal multiplier (three hundred percent) is far stronger than the conversion (five percent), this loop dominates and drives strong self correction, so the two inventories cannot both run away.
  • base_stock_y balancing loop: the description says balacks decrease by an amount set by base_stock_y, but with no counterpart the material would appear from nowhere and base_stock_y would grow without limit. I added base_stock_y_outflow, an equal transfer leaving base_stock_y, which conserves material and closes a balancing loop against the existing reinforcing self growth of base_stock_y.
  • base_stock_x now also drives the warehouse, linking the previously separate base system to the inventory system.

Formulation cleanups

  • Hard coded numbers in the original flows were abstracted into explicitly named constants: constant_input_rate_x, output_fraction_x, input_fraction_y, plus new ones for each warehouse percentage and each initial inventory level. No existing variable names were changed.
  • total_warehouse_inventory was added as an auxiliary (a simple sum), not a stock, since it is an algebraic aggregation rather than an accumulation with its own flows.
  • All flows are one directional (uniflow) because deliveries, withdrawals, conversions and drains cannot physically run backwards here.

Please add the following to my model...
In our organization, we start the period with fifty marticatenes. Every month, this inventory receives new additions of 15% of the current existing_pool_alpha count. Simultaneously, each month the stock loses 20% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we have on hand seventy-five refluppers. Every month, this inventory benefits from 20% of the current marticatenes count. Simultaneously, each month the stock is reduced through 10% of whatever existing_pool_beta are currently available.  Meanwhile, we start the period with one hundred twenty exemintes. Every month, this inventory is enhanced by exactly eight new exemintes. additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.

supportingInfo.explanation:
What was added

Three new inventories (stocks)

  • marticatenes — starts at 50; gains fifteen percent of the alpha pool each month and loses twenty percent of itself.
  • refluppers — starts at 75; gains twenty percent of the marticatenes count each month and is reduced by ten percent of the beta pool.
  • exemintes — starts at 120; gains a constant eight units per month and loses ten percent of itself.

Six flows were created (one inflow and one outflow per inventory) so each stock changes only through its own flows, and no flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow.

Named parameters instead of buried numbers. Every percentage and the constant addition amount were pulled out into their own clearly named constants (addition fractions, loss fractions, and the exemintes addition rate) so no arbitrary numbers are hidden inside equations.

Feedback loops closed

  • marticatenes: the stock drives its own percentage loss, and that loss reduces the stock — a classic balancing loop that pushes the inventory toward the level where inflow and outflow match.
  • exemintes: the same balancing loop structure — a fixed inflow against a stock-proportional outflow, converging on a steady state.
  • The stock-to-flow-to-stock links for the original alpha pool (balancing) and beta pool (reinforcing growth) were made explicit so both existing loops are fully closed in the causal map.

Cross-chain causal links

A one-way chain now runs alpha pool → marticatenes → refluppers, while the beta pool acts as the drain on refluppers. These are genuine causal links stated in the description, but they are open chains, not loops — no return path was invented, since there is no evidence in the description that refluppers or marticatenes feed anything back to the alpha or beta pools.

Housekeeping

No existing variable names or equations were altered. Model settings were made explicit: monthly time units, a three-year horizon, and a quarter-month time step for accurate integration of the fractional drains.

Please add the following to my model...
In my business, our records indicate thirty-five povals. Every day, this inventory benefits from 30% of the current dominitoxings count. Simultaneously, each day the stock experiences losses of 20% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we begin with ninety auspongs. Every day, this inventory gets replenished by 20% of the current povals count. Simultaneously, each day the stock loses a constant twelve auspongs.  Meanwhile, there are initially forty-five dominitoxings. Every day, this inventory increases due to 8% of the current existing_reservoir_delta count. Simultaneously, each day the stock has outgoing 30% of its current amount.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.

supportingInfo.explanation:
What was added

Three new inventories (stocks)

  • povals starts at 35, gains 30% of dominitoxings per day, loses 20% of itself per day.
  • auspongs starts at 90, gains 20% of povals per day, loses a fixed 12 per day.
  • dominitoxings starts at 45, gains 8% of the delta reservoir per day, releases 30% of itself per day.

Conserved transfer flows to close loops

  • Because the description says povals gain exactly 30% of dominitoxings while dominitoxings lose exactly 30% of themselves, these are the same physical movement, so a single flow (dominitoxings to povals) serves as an outflow of one stock and the inflow of the next. The same logic links povals and auspongs through one shared 20% flow.
  • The 8% draw on the delta reservoir is likewise treated as a real transfer, so it is now also an outflow of the existing delta reservoir. This closes a balancing loop on delta (more delta, bigger draw, less delta) that counteracts the existing reinforcing self-growth loop, and it connects the previously isolated new chain to the original model.

Self correcting (balancing) loops now exist within each new inventory where the outflow is a percentage of the stock itself: dominitoxings and povals each drain faster when fuller. Auspongs has no such loop because its loss is a fixed quantity, so it can be driven to zero if inflow falls below twelve per day; the uniflow setting keeps flows from running backwards.

Constants abstracted All percentages and fixed rates were pulled out of the equations into clearly named parameters (gamma supply rate, gamma output fraction, delta input fraction, delta drain rate, dominitoxings gain fraction, dominitoxings transfer fraction, povals transfer fraction, auspongs loss rate) so no arbitrary numbers sit inside formulas.

No existing variable names were changed.

Please add the following to my model...
At the warehouse, we have on hand one hundred ten pablanksills. Every quarter, this inventory benefits from 6% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock is reduced through a constant eighteen pablanksills.  Meanwhile, we begin with seventy posistorathers. Every quarter, this inventory grows through incoming exactly twenty-five new posistorathers. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock has outgoing 35% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we start the period with ninety-five crypterals. Every quarter, this inventory receives new additions of exactly eighteen new crypterals. Every quarter, this inventory increases due to 35% of the current posistorathers count. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock gets diminished by 22% of its current amount.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Additions to the model

  • Pablanksills: added a stock starting at 110 with a proportional growth inflow (6% of current inventory) and a constant outflow of 18 per quarter. The growth flow depends on the stock itself, closing a reinforcing loop (more inventory → more growth → more inventory), while the fixed withdrawal acts as a constant drain that determines whether the stock takes off or collapses.

  • Posistorathers: added a stock starting at 70 with a constant inflow of 25 per quarter and a proportional outflow of 35% of the current amount. The proportional outflow closes a balancing loop (more stock → more leaving → less stock), which drives the stock toward a goal level set by the arrival rate divided by the outflow fraction.

  • Crypterals: added a stock starting at 95 with a constant inflow of 18 per quarter and a proportional outflow of 22%, again a balancing loop.

  • Chain link between the two new stocks: the described outflow of posistorathers (35% of the count) and the described crypteral inflow (35% of the posistorather count) are the same quantity, so they are represented by a single conserved transfer flow that drains posistorathers and fills crypterals. This makes the two stocks an explicit upstream/downstream cascade rather than two disconnected accumulations.

Formulation cleanups

  • All hard-coded rates and fractions were pulled out of flow equations into clearly named constants (growth fractions, arrival rates, reduction rates, depletion fraction) and initial values were given named constants as well. This applies both to the new material and to the previously supplied epsilon and zeta structure, whose 0.08, 12 and 9 values were embedded directly in equations.

  • All rate flows were marked one-directional, since inventory can only physically be added or removed, never flow backwards.

  • No existing variable names were changed, and no simple sums were represented as stocks.

Please add the following to my model...
Throughout the process, the baseline inventory shows one hundred fifty outrances. Every hour, this inventory gets replenished by exactly twenty new outrances. Simultaneously, each hour the stock loses 40% of its current amount. Simultaneously, each hour the stock loses 10% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, our records indicate thirty illigents. Every hour, this inventory gains from 40% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock decreases by a constant five illigents.  Meanwhile, we start the period with sixty-five yelbs. Every hour, this inventory is enhanced by 10% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock has outgoing 12% of whatever trazes are currently available.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows eighty-five trazes. Every hour, this inventory gains from exactly fifteen new trazes. Simultaneously, each hour the stock suffers depletion of 18% of its current amount.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.

supportingInfo.explanation:
What was added

Outrances is a new accumulation starting at its baseline inventory. It receives a fixed hourly replenishment and is drained by two separate proportional losses (a 40 percent channel and a 10 percent channel). Because both losses are computed from the stock itself, each forms its own balancing (goal-seeking) loop: the bigger the stock grows, the harder the drains pull it back, so the stock settles at an equilibrium where inflow equals total outflow.

Illigents accumulates a share of the current outrance level each hour and loses a fixed quantity each hour. This makes illigents a downstream consequence of outrances rather than an independent stock.

Yelbs is enhanced by a share of the current outrance level and drained by a share of the currently available trazes. This creates a cross-stock coupling in which the traze inventory governs how quickly yelbs leave.

Trazes accumulates a fixed hourly replenishment and loses a proportional share of itself, another balancing loop that drives it toward a steady state; that steady state in turn sets the long-run drain on yelbs.

Formulation choices

  • Every numeric value from the description (baselines, fixed hourly amounts, and every percentage) was abstracted into its own clearly named constant, so no arbitrary numbers appear inside flow equations.
  • All proportional and fixed-quantity flows were marked one-directional, since none of them can physically run backwards.
  • No flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow of the same stock.
  • The two distinct percentage losses on outrances were kept as two separate outflows rather than merged, preserving the causal detail in the source description.
  • Existing variables (vessel iota, vessel kappa, and their flows) were left untouched; their implicit relationships were made explicit in the causal list so the accumulation feedback from iota back through charging is visible as a reinforcing loop.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Added five new inventories — whatajigs, balacks, whoziewhats, funkados, and maxabizers — each as a stock with its own explicit inflow and outflow, initialized at 100, 200, 200, 12, and 88 units respectively.

Feedback structure captured:

  • Whatajigs grow on themselves (5% of their own level) while losing a fixed three units per year — a reinforcing growth loop restrained by a constant drain.
  • Whoziewhats drain at 3% of their own level — a classic balancing (self-correcting) loop.
  • Funkados and maxabizers form a closed two-stock balancing loop: funkados feed maxabizers at 5%, while maxabizers pull funkados down at 3%. Both directions were needed to close this loop.

Links back to the original model: the balacks outflow is driven by the existing lambda store, and the maxabizers outflow is driven by the existing mu store, so the pre-existing inventories now propagate their behavior into the new chain (whatajigs → balacks → whoziewhats → funkados → maxabizers).

Formulation cleanups:

  • The hard-coded 0.04, 15, and 10 buried inside replenish_lambda, deplete_lambda, and supply_mu were pulled out into named constants (lambda_replenishment_rate, lambda_depletion_amount, mu_supply_amount). No variable names were changed.
  • The repeated 5% and 3% rates are represented once each as standard_growth_fraction and standard_depletion_fraction, and the fixed whatajigs loss as whatajigs_outflow_amount, so no arbitrary numbers appear inside flow equations.
  • All flows are marked one-directional, since gains and losses of physical items cannot run backwards.
  • No flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow of the same stock, and every stock's level is changed only through its flows.

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include at least 10 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
What the model says

The Revolution is represented as an escalation archetype (mutual, tit-for-tat reinforcement) sitting on top of a fix that fails and a success-to-the-successful shift in identity. Six accumulations carry the story forward in time: British War Debt, Colonial Resentment, Coercive Legislation, British Troop Presence, American Colonial Identity, and Colonial Militia Mobilization. Everything else is a rate or an algebraic consequence.

The trigger: a debt looking for a taxpayer

The French and Indian War leaves the war-debt stock at its peak. Debt drives Fiscal Pressure to Tax, which drives the Colonial Tax Burden (Sugar, Stamp, Townshend, Tea Acts).

R1 — Taxation and resistance spiral

Tax burden multiplied by Lack of Representation becomes Perceived Injustice, which accumulates as Colonial Resentment. Resentment is a stock, not a flow: repealing the Stamp Act removed the tax but not the memory, which is why each new measure landed on a higher base.

B1 — The fix that fails

Taxes were supposed to pay down the debt. But resentment destroys Colonial Tax Compliance through boycotts, smuggling and intimidation (a nonlinear effect curve normalized to 1 at tolerable resentment). Revenue therefore rises far less than the burden, the debt is not retired, and Parliament tries harder. The intended balancing loop is defeated by the very resistance it provokes.

R2 — Defiance and coercion (the core escalation)

Resentment plus identity produces Acts of Defiance (Stamp Act riots, non-importation, the Boston Tea Party). After a transatlantic perception delay — modeled with a SMOOTH, not a delay, since London judged a running impression of colonial behaviour — this becomes New Coercive Acts (Declaratory Act, the Intolerable Acts). Punitive law raises perceived injustice, which raises resentment, which raises defiance. Merchant lobbying provides the only conciliatory outflow (repeal) and it is weak and slow.

R3 — Troops, blood and propaganda

Perceived disorder also sends regiments. Troops among a hostile population produce Violent Incidents — the Boston Massacre. Amplified by colonial newspapers and committees of correspondence, these become Propaganda Intensity, feeding straight back into grievance.

R4 — Troops make the debt worse

Garrisons cost money, so Military Spending refills the war-debt stock, renewing the demand for colonial revenue. Coercion literally pays for the next round of taxation.

R5 — The identity loop

Punishment aimed at Boston and publicised violence create Shared Grievance, which builds American Colonial Identity. Identity is treated as essentially irreversible: once thirteen colonies learned to act together, that capability persisted. Identity then multiplies both defiance and militia recruitment, so British repression manufactured the very nation it was trying to suppress.

The outcome

Resentment plus identity accumulate Colonial Militia Mobilization. Hostilities break out as the product of two stocks — armed colonists and British regulars — which is precisely what happened when Gage's column marched to seize militia stores at Lexington and Concord in 1775. War was not caused by any single act; it was the delayed output of twelve years of mutually reinforcing accumulation, in which every British attempt to restore authority strengthened the resistance and every colonial protest hardened British resolve.
supportingInfo.title: Escalation Spiral Driving Colonies Toward Armed Revolt

variables.name: British War Debt
variables.documentation: Normalized index of the British Crown's debt left by the French and Indian War (1754-63) plus the ongoing cost of garrisoning North America. It starts at its post-war peak (index = 1) and is the fiscal engine that drives the search for colonial revenue.

variables.name: Military Spending
variables.documentation: Cost of keeping regular troops in America. Every soldier sent to enforce order adds to the debt that must be repaid, which is what closes the vicious circle between coercion and taxation.

variables.name: Debt Repayment
variables.documentation: Debt actually retired using revenue collected from the colonies. It is the intended balancing action of the whole British fiscal program.

variables.name: Reference Debt
variables.documentation: The level of debt London considered manageable; used to normalize fiscal pressure.

variables.name: Fiscal Pressure to Tax
variables.documentation: How urgently Parliament feels it must raise money. The larger the war debt relative to what is tolerable, the harder ministers push new revenue measures such as the Sugar, Stamp and Townshend Acts.

variables.name: Baseline Tax Rate
variables.documentation: The tax load Parliament would impose on the colonies at normal fiscal pressure.

variables.name: Colonial Tax Burden
variables.documentation: The stamp duties, customs duties and tea duties actually laid on the colonies. It rises directly with British fiscal pressure.

variables.name: Lack of Representation
variables.documentation: Multiplier capturing the fact that colonists had no members in Parliament, so every shilling of tax was experienced as illegitimate ('no taxation without representation'). If representation had been granted this multiplier would fall and the same taxes would generate far less grievance.

variables.name: Reference Resentment
variables.documentation: The level of colonial grievance that could be absorbed without disrupting normal trade and tax collection; used to normalize the compliance effect.

variables.name: Effect of Resentment on Compliance
variables.documentation: Nonlinear effect of grievance on willingness to pay. At normal resentment (input 1) compliance is normal (output 1); as resentment climbs, non-importation agreements, smuggling and the destruction of tea collapse collections.

variables.name: Normal Compliance
variables.documentation: Fraction of levied taxes that would be collected in a calm colony.

variables.name: Colonial Tax Compliance
variables.documentation: Share of the levied taxes actually paid, degraded by boycotts, intimidation of stamp distributors and smuggling.

variables.name: Colonial Tax Revenue
variables.documentation: Money actually reaching the Treasury from America. Because resistance destroys compliance, revenue rises far less than the burden imposed, so the debt is never paid down and the pressure to tax persists.

variables.name: Colonial Resentment
variables.documentation: The accumulated store of colonial anger and distrust toward Britain. It is a stock because grievances are remembered: the Stamp Act was repealed but the memory of it was not, so each new measure landed on top of the old.

variables.name: Perceived Injustice
variables.documentation: Total current provocation felt by colonists: unrepresented taxation, punitive laws such as the Intolerable Acts, and the circulation of atrocity stories like Revere's engraving of the Boston Massacre.

variables.name: Resentment Sensitivity
variables.documentation: How strongly a given provocation converts into lasting anger.

variables.name: Resentment Growth
variables.documentation: Rate at which new grievance is added to the colonial stock of anger.

variables.name: Resentment Memory Time
variables.documentation: Average time over which grievances fade if no new provocation occurs. It is long, which is why conciliation had to be fast to work.

variables.name: Resentment Decay
variables.documentation: Natural cooling of anger over time in the absence of fresh insults.

variables.name: Defiance Propensity
variables.documentation: Conversion of anger plus solidarity into overt public action.
variables.units: defiance index per year per resentment index

variables.name: Acts of Defiance
variables.documentation: Riots against stamp distributors, non-importation agreements, the Gaspee affair and the Boston Tea Party. Defiance requires both anger and enough shared identity to organize it collectively.

variables.name: British Response Time
variables.documentation: Time for news to cross the Atlantic and for Parliament to legislate. This delay is a key reason policy always answered the last crisis rather than the current one.

variables.name: British Perception of Disorder
variables.documentation: London's smoothed, delayed picture of American lawlessness. Modelled as a smooth (a moving average), not a pure delay, because ministers judged a running impression of colonial behaviour.

variables.name: British Resolve
variables.documentation: Parliament's determination to assert sovereignty, expressed in the Declaratory Act and later the Coercive Acts. It is what turns perceived disorder into punishment rather than negotiation.

variables.name: Coercive Legislation
variables.documentation: The standing body of punitive law in force: Quartering Acts, the Declaratory Act, and above all the Intolerable Acts that closed Boston's port and altered the Massachusetts charter. It accumulates because acts stay on the books until repealed.

variables.name: New Coercive Acts
variables.documentation: Rate of enacting new punitive legislation in response to colonial defiance. This is the British half of the escalation spiral.

variables.name: Merchant Lobby Strength
variables.documentation: Political weight of British merchants hurt by colonial boycotts, the force behind the repeal of the Stamp Act and most Townshend duties. It is the only conciliatory pressure in the system and it is weak relative to British resolve.

variables.name: Repeal of Acts
variables.documentation: Partial rollback of punitive laws under commercial pressure. Because repeals were slow and partial, they removed the tax but not the accumulated distrust.

variables.name: British Troop Presence
variables.documentation: Regulars stationed in American towns, notably the regiments sent to Boston in 1768. Troops both cost money and create daily friction with civilians.

variables.name: Deployment Rate
variables.documentation: How many troops London sends per unit of perceived disorder.

variables.name: Troop Deployment
variables.documentation: Sending of regiments to enforce the acts and protect customs officials.

variables.name: Troop Tour Duration
variables.documentation: Average time before garrisons are withdrawn or reduced.

variables.name: Troop Withdrawal
variables.documentation: Slow removal of garrisons, such as the pullback from Boston town after the Massacre.

variables.name: Cost per Troop
variables.documentation: Annual cost of maintaining a unit of troops in America, charged to the debt.
variables.units: debt index per troop index per year

variables.name: Friction Coefficient
variables.documentation: Likelihood that armed soldiers among an angry population produce a violent clash.

variables.name: Violent Incidents
variables.documentation: Street confrontations culminating in the Boston Massacre of 1770. Violence requires both troops on the ground and a hostile population.

variables.name: Propaganda Intensity
variables.documentation: Pamphlets, engravings and newspaper accounts that turn each incident into a shared political lesson. The committees of correspondence, a product of colonial identity, amplify the effect of every clash.

variables.name: Shared Grievance
variables.documentation: The common experience of punishment and publicised violence that made thirteen separate colonies see themselves as one people. Closing Boston's port made Boston's cause everyone's cause.

variables.name: Identity Sensitivity
variables.documentation: Rate at which shared grievance is converted into durable American self-identification and inter-colonial institutions.

variables.name: Identity Formation
variables.documentation: Growth of a common American political identity through the Stamp Act Congress, committees of correspondence and the Continental Congress.

variables.name: Initial Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: The modest sense of common Americanness existing in 1763, when most colonists still thought of themselves as loyal Britons.

variables.name: American Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: Accumulated sense of being one American people with a right to self-government. It is treated as effectively irreversible: once colonists learned to act together, that capability did not disappear.

variables.name: Mobilization Rate
variables.documentation: Speed at which angry, organized communities form and arm militia companies.

variables.name: Militia Recruitment
variables.documentation: Enlistment and drilling of minutemen and the stockpiling of powder and arms after 1774.

variables.name: Colonial Militia Mobilization
variables.documentation: Armed and organized colonial military capacity. Once this accumulates alongside a British garrison determined to seize colonial stores, an armed clash becomes nearly unavoidable.

variables.name: Confrontation Probability
variables.documentation: Chance per year that armed colonists and regulars meet in a shooting confrontation.

variables.name: Outbreak of Hostilities
variables.documentation: Indicator of open war, realised at Lexington and Concord in April 1775 when a British column marching to seize militia stores met armed minutemen. It is the product of two accumulations that the escalation loops built up over twelve years.

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include at least 10 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
What the model says about why road rage happens

Road rage is not caused by "bad drivers" alone; it emerges from a small number of accumulations that feed back on each other. The model has four accumulations (stocks) and three engines of change (feedback loops).

The accumulations

  • Driver Stress builds from frustration, impatience and fatigue and drains only slowly through rest. Because it is a stock, a bad week of commuting leaves drivers primed for the next week.
  • Traffic Congestion is a queue that accumulates when demand, poor road design, weather and crash blockages exceed clearing capacity.
  • Aggressive Driving Norm accumulates learned behavior: what drivers repeatedly see becomes what they consider acceptable.
  • Enforcement and Awareness accumulates policing and public education, and erodes as attention fades.

Loop R1 – the congestion/stress escalation (reinforcing) Congestion → frustration and impatience → accumulated stress → higher aggression propensity → more road rage incidents → more crashes → more lane blockage → more congestion. This is a classic "fixes that fail"-style vicious circle: the aggression that drivers use to escape delay is exactly what manufactures more delay.

Loop R2 – the contagion of aggression (reinforcing) Each visible incident strengthens the aggressive driving norm, which increases the number of perceived provocations (being cut off, tailgated, honked at) that every other driver experiences, which produces more retaliation. This is an "escalation" archetype: my aggression is your provocation.

Loop B1 – societal response (balancing) Rising incidents mobilize enforcement and awareness, which both deters individual aggression and erodes the aggressive norm. Because enforcement decays with the public's attention span, this loop produces the boom-and-bust pattern seen in real campaigns: incidents rise, a crackdown follows, incidents fall, attention wanders, incidents creep back.

Structural choices

  • Stress, congestion, norms and enforcement are modeled as stocks because they are genuine accumulations with memory; the incident rate is a flow, and the running total of incidents is a simple accumulation of that flow.
  • Perceived provocations and aggression propensity are auxiliaries (algebraic), not stocks, because they are computed instantaneously from current conditions.
  • Two nonlinear response curves are used instead of hidden constants: stress escalates aggression sharply then saturates, and enforcement restrains aggression with diminishing returns. Both pass through (1, 1) so that normal conditions give normal behavior.
  • Personality traits, road design, weather, schedule pressure, fatigue and distraction enter as exogenous drivers, since they set the level around which the loops operate rather than being caused by road rage itself.

Implication for the future If demand growth, distraction or fatigue rise while enforcement attention stays short-lived, the two reinforcing loops dominate and incidents grow superlinearly. The highest-leverage interventions are the ones that break loops rather than punish individuals: reducing congestion buildup (road design, demand management), shortening stress recovery time, and — most powerfully — sustaining enforcement and awareness long enough to erode the learned norm rather than letting it decay with the news cycle.
supportingInfo.title: Feedback loops driving road rage escalation

variables.name: Driver Stress
variables.documentation: Average stress and arousal level carried by drivers, expressed as an index where 1 is the normal level. Stress is a stock because it builds up over repeated frustrating trips and decays only gradually through rest and recovery.

variables.name: Stress Accumulation
variables.documentation: Rate at which driving conditions add to driver stress. It is the average of the three main psychological pressures (blocked progress, time pressure, tiredness) scaled by how sensitive drivers are to pressure.

variables.name: Stress Recovery
variables.documentation: Rate at which accumulated stress dissipates through rest, sleep and calm driving. Modeled as first order decay: the more stress present, the faster it drains.

variables.name: Stress Sensitivity
variables.documentation: How strongly everyday driving pressures translate into felt stress for the average driver.

variables.name: Stress Recovery Time
variables.documentation: Average time for accumulated driver stress to dissipate when pressures are removed.

variables.name: Frustration
variables.documentation: Felt sense of being blocked or thwarted while driving. It rises with congestion and is amplified by poor road design such as narrow lanes and confusing intersections.

variables.name: Impatience
variables.documentation: Low tolerance for delay. Delay only matters when drivers are under schedule pressure, so impatience is congestion multiplied by how tightly scheduled drivers are.

variables.name: Fatigue Prevalence
variables.documentation: Relative prevalence of sleep deprivation and tiredness among drivers, which impairs judgement and lowers the anger threshold.

variables.name: Schedule Pressure
variables.documentation: Degree to which drivers are running late or have tight commitments, indexed to 1 at normal conditions.

variables.name: Road Design Deficiency
variables.documentation: Index of how poorly the road network is designed (merges, narrow lanes, confusing intersections). Higher values both create congestion and directly amplify frustration.

variables.name: Traffic Congestion
variables.documentation: Index of crowding, delay and stop-and-go conditions on the network. It is a stock because queues accumulate: vehicles and blockages enter faster than they clear and the backlog persists.

variables.name: Congestion Buildup
variables.documentation: Rate at which delay is created, driven by underlying travel demand, poor road design, bad weather, and extra blockage caused by crashes.

variables.name: Congestion Clearing
variables.documentation: Rate at which queues dissipate once the disruption passes, modeled as first order decay of the congestion backlog.

variables.name: Baseline Traffic Demand
variables.documentation: Underlying volume of trips people wish to make relative to road capacity.

variables.name: Weather Difficulty
variables.documentation: Index of adverse weather (rain, snow, fog) that slows traffic and raises crash risk.

variables.name: Congestion Clearing Time
variables.documentation: Average time for a queue or delay to clear from the network.

variables.name: Crash Disruption Sensitivity
variables.documentation: How much extra congestion each unit of crash activity creates through lane blockage and rubbernecking.

variables.name: Crash Rate
variables.documentation: Rate of collisions and near misses. It comes from ordinary distracted or weather related driving plus the extra crashes generated by aggressive road rage behavior.

variables.name: Baseline Crash Rate
variables.documentation: Crash rate that would occur from ordinary inattentive driving in normal weather.

variables.name: Crashes per Rage Incident
variables.documentation: Average number of collisions or hard-braking events produced by each road rage incident.

variables.name: Distracted Driving Prevalence
variables.documentation: Index of phone use, texting and eating behind the wheel. Distraction both raises crashes and creates erratic behavior that other drivers read as provocation.

variables.name: Aggressive Driving Norm
variables.documentation: The socially learned expectation that tailgating, cutting off and honking are normal ways to drive. It is a stock because norms accumulate from what drivers repeatedly observe and fade only slowly.

variables.name: Norm Reinforcement
variables.documentation: Rate at which witnessed aggression normalizes aggressive driving. This is the learned-behavior channel: every visible incident teaches onlookers that aggression is acceptable.

variables.name: Norm Erosion
variables.documentation: Rate at which the aggressive norm decays, accelerated by enforcement and public awareness campaigns that re-label aggression as unacceptable.

variables.name: Norm Learning Rate
variables.documentation: How strongly each observed aggressive incident spreads to other drivers' expectations of normal behavior.

variables.name: Norm Erosion Time
variables.documentation: Time constant for an established driving norm to fade under normal levels of enforcement and awareness.

variables.name: Enforcement and Awareness
variables.documentation: Accumulated policing presence, penalties and public education aimed at aggressive driving. It is a stock because capability and public attention build up and then erode as concern fades.

variables.name: Enforcement Investment
variables.documentation: Rate at which society adds enforcement and awareness effort in reaction to visible road rage incidents.

variables.name: Enforcement Decay
variables.documentation: Rate at which enforcement and public attention wear off when the problem is out of the headlines.

variables.name: Public Concern Sensitivity
variables.documentation: How responsive authorities and the public are in mobilizing enforcement per road rage incident.

variables.name: Enforcement Attention Span
variables.documentation: Average time enforcement pressure and public attention persist before decaying.

variables.name: Perceived Provocations
variables.documentation: Number of times per trip a driver feels cut off, tailgated or honked at. More aggressive norms, more crowding (more interactions) and more distraction all raise the supply of provocations.

variables.name: Aggression Propensity
variables.documentation: Probability that a given provocation is answered with aggression. It combines stable personality traits, the current stress state, and the restraining effect of enforcement.

variables.name: Hostile Personality Prevalence
variables.documentation: Share of drivers with impulsive, hostile or highly competitive dispositions who are predisposed to retaliate.

variables.name: Effect of Stress on Aggression

variables.name: Deterrence Effect

variables.name: Road Rage Incident Rate

variables.name: Cumulative Road Rage Incidents

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include no more than 5 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
The core story: two reinforcing loops that outran one balancing loop

Stock: Colonial Resentment. Grievance is treated as an accumulation, not an event. It begins at a modest level in 1763 because Britain, saddled with French and Indian War debt, decided the colonies should pay for their own defence — the Stamp Act, taxation without representation, and troops.

Reinforcing Loop R1 — Escalation (the classic Escalation archetype): Colonial Resentment → Colonial Defiance (riots, boycotts, the Boston Tea Party) → British Coercion (troops in Boston and the Massacre, the Intolerable Acts closing the port) → more Colonial Resentment. Each side read the other's move as proof that firmness was required. This is the engine that turned a tax dispute into gunfire at Lexington.

Reinforcing Loop R2 — Identity formation (Success to the Successful for the patriot cause): Colonial Defiance → Colonial Identity → still more Defiance. Committees of correspondence, the Continental Congress and shared martyrs converted thirteen separate provinces into one "American" people, giving anger an organised channel and making each round of resistance broader than the last.

Balancing Loop B1 — Reconciliation, progressively disabled: High resentment normally creates pressure to settle (the Stamp Act repeal of 1766, repeal of most Townshend duties). That cooling outflow is the only brake in the system. But it is divided by Colonial Identity: the stronger the sense of being a separate people, the more any compromise inside the empire looked like surrender. As R2 built identity, it silently weakened the very loop that could have kept the system stable — a fixes that fail / eroding brake dynamic.

Why hostilities broke out: at first the brake matched the escalation and the system merely oscillated (crisis, repeal, calm). Once identity had accumulated enough, reconciliation could no longer drain grievance as fast as coercion added it, so resentment ran away and defiance became armed resistance. War was the output of loop dominance shifting from the balancing loop to the escalation loop, not of any single tax or massacre.

Formulation notes: all arbitrary magnitudes were avoided; only the safe division operator (//) is used so that identity can never cause a divide by zero. Defiance and Coercion are one directional flows (they cannot be negative), while the stocks accumulate them. Nothing here is a simple sum, so no aggregation was mis typed as a stock.
supportingInfo.title: Escalation Loop Overwhelms Colonial Reconciliation Brake

variables.name: Colonial Resentment
variables.documentation: The accumulated stock of colonial grievance against British rule. It starts at a modest level in 1763, reflecting the post French and Indian War decision to make the colonies pay for imperial defense through measures such as the Stamp Act, taxation without representation, and the stationing of troops. Resentment is a stock because anger accumulates over time from a sequence of episodes (Stamp Act, Boston Massacre, Intolerable Acts) and drains only slowly when London relents.

variables.name: Colonial Defiance
variables.documentation: The rate of open acts of colonial resistance: Stamp Act riots, non importation agreements, the Boston Tea Party, committees of correspondence and the Continental Congress. Defiance is the product of how much resentment has accumulated and how strongly colonists see themselves as one American people, since anger only becomes collective action when there is a shared identity to act through. It also serves as the inflow that builds Colonial Identity, because shared resistance forged shared nationhood.

variables.name: British Coercion
variables.documentation: The rate at which Britain answers defiance with force and punishment: new revenue acts, troops in Boston (leading to the Massacre), the Coercive or Intolerable Acts closing Boston harbour, and finally the march on Concord. Parliament treated each act of defiance as a challenge to sovereignty that had to be met with a firmer hand, so coercion tracks defiance and pours straight back into colonial resentment.

variables.name: Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: The accumulated sense of a common American identity and inter colonial solidarity. Every joint act of resistance (congresses, boycotts, relief sent to blockaded Boston) leaves behind durable networks and a stronger 'we', so identity is a stock fed by defiance. Stronger identity both amplifies future defiance and makes quiet submission or reconciliation on British terms less acceptable.

variables.name: Reconciliation
variables.documentation: The rate at which grievances are settled and anger cools through repeal, petition and compromise, as with the repeal of the Stamp Act and most Townshend duties. High resentment creates pressure to negotiate, but a strong separate American identity makes accommodation within the empire look like surrender, so this balancing outflow is progressively weakened as identity grows. Safe division is used so identity can never cause a divide by zero.

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include no more than 5 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
The story in one loop set

Road rage is best explained not as a list of causes but as an escalating (reinforcing) feedback structure with one weak balancing brake.

Stock: Aggressive Driving Norm — the only true accumulation here. Personality, stress and weather are momentary; what persists and compounds in a society is the learned, culturally accepted level of aggression behind the wheel. Norms build slowly and erode slowly, which is exactly what a stock represents.

R1 – The provocation loop: Incidents → Driver Stress → more Incidents. Each aggressive act is somebody else's perceived provocation, and the erratic driving, near-misses and crashes it causes add delay and congestion, which raises impatience and stress for everyone. Stress then makes the next act more likely.

R2 – The learned-behavior loop: Incidents → Normalization Rate → Aggressive Driving Norm → more Incidents. Watching others tailgate, weave and honk teaches drivers that this is how the road works, which feeds the norm stock and produces still more incidents. This is the classic escalation / success-to-the-successful dynamic applied to a behavioral norm.

B1 – The erosion loop: Aggressive Driving Norm → Norm Decay → less norm. Enforcement, driver education, courtesy campaigns and generational turnover continuously drain the stock. This is the only thing holding the system in check.

Why the future depends on a tipping point

Because incidents are the product of the norm and driver stress, the two amplify each other. Driver Stress is a saturating graphical function of incidents whose value at zero incidents (0.7) captures the irreducible background load from congestion, poor road design, bad weather, fatigue and distraction — the situational and environmental factors you listed.

If background stress is low, the balancing erosion loop out-runs the two reinforcing loops and aggression fades. Once background stress and the norm cross a threshold — which is where the model is initialized — the reinforcing loops dominate and incidents grow steadily and then accelerate. Interventions that only punish individual drivers act on the outflow alone; interventions that reduce congestion, delay and provocation (road design, staggered travel, fatigue and phone-use reduction) weaken the reinforcing loops at their source and are what actually flip the system back below the tipping point.

Formulation notes

  • Road Rage Incidents is an auxiliary, not a stock: it is a rate of occurrence computed algebraically each moment, not something that accumulates.
  • Driver Stress uses a normalized graphical function passing through (1,1) with saturation, so normal conditions give normal stress and stress cannot rise without limit.
  • Both flows are one-directional (a norm cannot be un-learned through the learning channel), so they are constrained to be non-negative.
supportingInfo.title: Learned Aggression And Provocation Escalation Loops

variables.name: Aggressive Driving Norm
variables.documentation: The accumulated pool of learned, socially normalized aggressive driving behavior in the driving population (tailgating, cutting off, honking, retaliating). It is a stock because norms are learned over time through repeated exposure and only erode slowly; they cannot jump instantly. Initialized slightly above the neutral index value of 1 to represent a driving culture already tipped a little toward aggression.

variables.name: Normalization Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which witnessing aggressive driving teaches and legitimizes it for other drivers. The more incidents drivers observe on the road, the faster aggression is copied and normalized. Formulated as the observed incident level spread over an adoption period (the division by two represents the averaging of exposure over the learning period).

variables.name: Norm Decay
variables.documentation: The gradual erosion of aggressive driving norms through driver turnover, enforcement, education, courtesy campaigns and simple forgetting. Proportional to the current norm spread over the same forgetting period, giving the balancing loop that would return the culture to calm in the absence of new provocation.

variables.name: Road Rage Incidents
variables.documentation: The current rate of aggressive-driving/road-rage events on the road. It is an algebraic result, not an accumulation: at any moment it is the product of how acceptable aggression currently is (the norm) and how stressed, hurried and provoked drivers currently feel. Both must be present for an incident to occur, so they multiply.

variables.name: Driver Stress
variables.documentation: The overall arousal level of drivers: stress, impatience, fatigue, distraction and the frustration of congestion, bad weather and poor road design. The value at zero incidents (0.7) represents this irreducible background load from traffic and life. Incidents feed back into stress because each aggressive act is a perceived provocation for someone else and because aggressive driving, near-misses and crashes themselves create the delays and congestion that frustrate everyone. The curve passes through (1,1) so a normal incident level yields normal stress, and it saturates because there is a ceiling on how agitated drivers can get.

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include at least 8 feedback loops.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.

In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.

supportingInfo.explanation:
What this model says

The Revolution is not explained by any single grievance but by a set of interlocking feedback loops that turned a fiscal problem into a war. An exogenous shock (war spending, 1754-63) enters a system whose loops then amplify almost every attempt to control it — a classic fixes that fail / escalation structure.

The core stocks

British War Debt, Colonial Tax Level, Colonial Grievance, American Identity, Coercive Legislation, Intercolonial Coordination, British Troop Presence, British Perceived Rebelliousness, Martyr Narrative and Militia Mobilization. These are accumulations with memory: grievances, statutes, institutions and armed men persist, which is why the crisis was cumulative rather than episodic. Sums and multipliers (tax revenue, defiance, hostilities) are auxiliaries, not stocks.

The feedback loops

B1 — Debt repayment (balancing, the intended fix). Debt → fiscal pressure → new taxes on the colonies → revenue → debt falls. This is the only loop London consciously designed.

R1 — Taxation delegitimizes taxation (reinforcing). Taxes imposed without representation → grievance → collapse of Parliament's perceived legitimacy → smuggling and evasion → less revenue → higher debt → still more taxes. The fix undermines itself.

R2 — Coercion spiral (reinforcing). Defiance (Stamp Act riots, the Tea Party) → London perceives rebellion → punitive statutes (Quartering, Declaratory, Intolerable Acts) → fresh grievance → more defiance. Firmness manufactured the disloyalty it was meant to punish.

R3 — Troops, blood and propaganda (reinforcing). Perceived rebellion → troops garrisoned among civilians → friction → the Boston Massacre → a martyr narrative kept alive by prints and annual orations → grievance → defiance → more troops.

R4 — Identity forging (reinforcing). Shared grievance, shared committees and shared martyrs → American identity → willingness to resist → more defiance → more repression → more shared grievance. Identity has no outflow here: it ratchets.

R5 — Punish one, unite all (reinforcing). Closing Boston's port taught twelve other colonies they were next → committees of correspondence and the Continental Congress → far more effective collective resistance → more alarm in London → more coercion.

R6 — Coercion is expensive (reinforcing). Resistance → troops and customs enforcement → enforcement spending → debt rises again → more taxes → more grievance. Empire paid for its own unravelling.

R7 — Arms race (reinforcing). Troops and annulled charters → perceived British threat → militia drilling and powder stockpiles → London sees armed rebellion → more troops and attempts to seize arms → Lexington and Concord → still more mobilization. This loop closes the model: hostilities feed both grievance and recruitment.

B2 — Merchant conciliation (balancing). Grievance plus coordination → boycotts → British merchants lose orders → lobbying → repeal (Stamp Act 1766, most Townshend duties 1770). This loop genuinely cooled things twice, which is why 1770-72 was quiet. It is weak because Parliament treated repeal of coercion, unlike repeal of duties, as surrendering sovereignty (a deliberately slow reversal rate).

B3 — Deterrence (balancing, and it fails). Troops intimidate crowds, suppressing open defiance. But the deterrent multiplier saturates while the outrage troops generate does not, so beyond a point R3 overwhelms B3 — the signature of escalation.

Why hostilities broke out

Before 1763 the loops are dormant. War debt switches on B1, which switches on R1, R2 and R6; each British corrective move strengthens the reinforcing loops more than the balancing ones. Perception delays (roughly two years of dispatches) mean London always responded to a colonial mood that had already moved on, so its measures arrived calibrated to yesterday's problem and provoked tomorrow's. The Intolerable Acts finally activate R5 at full strength, R5 and R4 together activate R7, and once both an army and a militia exist in the same countryside, armed hostilities become an accounting certainty rather than a decision.

variables.name: British War Debt
variables.documentation: Accumulated British public debt, driven up sharply by the French and Indian War (1754-63) and by the later cost of garrisoning and policing America. It is the fiscal engine behind colonial taxation.

variables.name: War Spending
variables.documentation: Time-based profile of war expenditure for the French and Indian War, which ends in 1763. This is the exogenous shock that starts the whole story.

variables.name: Enforcement Spending
variables.documentation: The cost of keeping soldiers and customs enforcement in America. Coercion is not free, so it adds back onto the debt that coercion was meant to relieve.

variables.name: Debt Repayment
variables.documentation: Revenue actually collected in America and applied against the debt. Represents the intended purpose of the Stamp, Sugar and Townshend duties.

variables.name: Cost per Troop Unit
variables.documentation: Annual fiscal cost of maintaining one unit of military presence in the colonies.
variables.units: debt units per troop unit per year

variables.name: Reference Debt Level
variables.documentation: The debt level considered normal or tolerable by Parliament, used to scale fiscal pressure.

variables.name: Fiscal Pressure
variables.documentation: How urgently Parliament feels it must raise revenue, expressed relative to a tolerable debt level.

variables.name: Tax Enactment
variables.documentation: Passage of new revenue measures on the colonies (Sugar Act, Stamp Act, Townshend Duties, Tea Act) in response to fiscal pressure.

variables.name: Tax Enactment Sensitivity
variables.documentation: How readily Parliament converts fiscal pressure into new colonial taxes.

variables.name: Colonial Tax Level
variables.documentation: The standing burden of British taxes and duties on the colonies. It is a stock because laws accumulate until repealed.

variables.name: Tax Repeal
variables.documentation: Repeal or partial repeal of taxes (Stamp Act 1766, most Townshend duties 1770) driven by British merchants hurt by colonial boycotts.

variables.name: Repeal Responsiveness
variables.documentation: How quickly Parliament yields to commercial lobbying and repeals taxes.

variables.name: Boycott Effectiveness
variables.documentation: How much economic damage an organized colonial boycott inflicts on British trade.

variables.name: Boycott Intensity
variables.documentation: Non importation and non consumption agreements. Grievance supplies the motive and intercolonial organization supplies the enforcement.

variables.name: Merchant Lobby Pressure
variables.documentation: Pressure from British merchants and manufacturers on Parliament to repeal colonial taxes. Normal boycott pressure (input 1) yields normal lobbying (output 1), with saturation at extremes.

variables.name: Colonial Tax Base
variables.documentation: Size of the taxable colonial economy, held constant here to isolate political dynamics.

variables.name: Colonial Tax Revenue
variables.documentation: Money actually collected. It depends not just on the law but on whether colonists obey it, which is why smuggling and evasion mattered so much.

variables.name: Tax Compliance
variables.documentation: Willingness to pay duties rather than smuggle, tar collectors, or intimidate stamp distributors. Normal legitimacy (input 1) gives normal compliance (output 1).

variables.name: Representation Deficit
variables.documentation: The absence of colonial representatives in Parliament, the constitutional fact that turned ordinary taxes into a grievance of principle: no taxation without representation.

variables.name: Grievance Pressure on Legitimacy
variables.documentation: The combined constitutional and emotional case against Parliament's authority, which erodes its claim to obedience.

variables.name: Perceived Legitimacy of Parliament
variables.documentation: How far colonists accept Parliament's right to legislate for them. Normal grievance pressure (input 1) leaves legitimacy at its normal value (output 1); high grievance destroys it.

variables.name: Colonial Grievance
variables.documentation: The reservoir of colonial resentment against British rule. It is a stock because grievances were remembered and compounded rather than felt and forgotten.

variables.name: Taxation Grievance
variables.documentation: Resentment generated by taxes imposed by a body in which colonists had no voice. Taxes alone would anger less; taxes without representation anger far more.

variables.name: Taxation Grievance Weight
variables.documentation: Grievance generated per unit of unrepresented taxation per year.
variables.units: grievance units per tax index per year

variables.name: Coercion Grievance
variables.documentation: Resentment produced by punitive laws such as the Quartering Acts and the Intolerable Acts, including closing Boston's port and revoking the Massachusetts charter.

variables.name: Coercion Grievance Weight
variables.documentation: Grievance generated per unit of coercive legislation per year.
variables.units: grievance units per law index per year

variables.name: Outrage from Violence
variables.documentation: Grievance generated by bloodshed and by the way it was retold: the Boston Massacre engravings, and later Lexington and Concord.

variables.name: Outrage Weight
variables.documentation: Grievance generated per unit of circulating atrocity narrative and armed clash per year.
variables.units: grievance units per narrative unit per year

variables.name: Grievance Accumulation
variables.documentation: Total rate at which new resentment is added, from taxes, punitive laws and violence.

variables.name: Grievance Dissipation
variables.documentation: Slow cooling of resentment when nothing new happens, as in the quiet years 1770 to 1772.

variables.name: Grievance Memory Time
variables.documentation: Average time over which a grievance fades if not renewed. Long memory is what made the crisis cumulative.

variables.name: American Identity
variables.documentation: The accumulated sense of being one American people with rights distinct from British subjects abroad. It ratchets upward and does not easily reverse.

variables.name: Identity Formation
variables.documentation: Shared suffering, shared institutions and shared stories forge a common identity. Committees of correspondence and a common press made local quarrels continental.

variables.name: Identity Formation Rate
variables.documentation: Speed at which shared grievance and organization crystallize into national identity.
variables.units: identity units per year per grievance unit

variables.name: Willingness to Resist
variables.documentation: How far colonists are prepared to go in open defiance. Normal identity (input 1) gives normal willingness (output 1); a strong identity multiplies it.

variables.name: Coordination Effect
variables.documentation: Force multiplier on resistance from congresses, committees and correspondence networks. Normal coordination (input 1) gives normal effect (output 1).

variables.name: Repression Deterrence Effect
variables.documentation: The short run intimidating effect of redcoats and warships, which suppresses open defiance. Normal troop presence (input 1) gives normal defiance (output 1). Note the deterrent effect saturates while the outrage it creates does not.

variables.name: Acts of Defiance
variables.documentation: Overt resistance: Stamp Act riots, tarring customs officers, the Boston Tea Party, seizure of powder stores. Requires motive, willingness and organization, and is dampened by fear of troops.

variables.name: Confrontation Friction
variables.documentation: Probability that armed men and defiant crowds occupying the same streets produce actual bloodshed.

variables.name: Violent Incidents
variables.documentation: Clashes between soldiers and civilians, of which the Boston Massacre of 1770 is the archetype. Requires both troops and crowds to be present.

variables.name: Martyr Narrative
variables.documentation: The stock of circulating atrocity stories, pamphlets and prints (Revere's engraving, annual Massacre orations) that keeps past violence politically alive.

variables.name: Propaganda Production
variables.documentation: Conversion of an incident into durable political ammunition by printers, orators and committees.

variables.name: Propaganda Amplification
variables.documentation: How effectively the colonial press magnified each incident into a symbol of tyranny.

variables.name: Narrative Fading
variables.documentation: Gradual loss of emotional force of old stories as attention shifts.

variables.name: Narrative Half Life
variables.documentation: Average persistence of a propaganda narrative in public memory.

variables.name: Militia Threat Weight
variables.documentation: How heavily British officials weighted colonial arming and militia drilling when judging rebelliousness.

variables.name: Observed Colonial Resistance
variables.documentation: What London and its governors actually see: riots, tea destroyed, militias drilling, powder stockpiled, shots fired.

variables.name: British Perceived Rebelliousness
variables.documentation: London's judgment of how disloyal the colonies are. It is a stock because perception adjusts slowly across a three thousand mile information delay.

variables.name: Threat Perception Change
variables.documentation: Belated updating of British beliefs about America. Bidirectional, since perceptions could relax as well as harden.
variables.units: defiance units per year per year

variables.name: Perception Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: Delay in ships, dispatches and parliamentary sessions before London reacts to American events.

variables.name: Coercive Legislation
variables.documentation: Standing punitive statutes: Quartering Acts, Declaratory Act, and above all the Coercive or Intolerable Acts of 1774 that closed Boston's port.

variables.name: Coercive Act Passage
variables.documentation: Parliament's reflex to answer defiance with punishment in order to assert sovereignty.

variables.name: Coercion Propensity
variables.documentation: How strongly the British ministry believed that firmness rather than concession was the answer to colonial disorder.
variables.units: law index per year per defiance unit

variables.name: Coercive Act Repeal
variables.documentation: Rare softening of punitive statutes. Deliberately slow, because Parliament treated repeal of coercion as a surrender of sovereignty.

variables.name: Legislative Reversal Rate
variables.documentation: Fraction of standing coercive legislation reversed per year.

variables.name: Intercolonial Coordination
variables.documentation: Shared institutions of resistance: Stamp Act Congress, committees of correspondence, Sons of Liberty, the Continental Congresses.

variables.name: Coordination Building
variables.documentation: Punishing one colony taught the others they were next, which is exactly why the Intolerable Acts produced the First Continental Congress.

variables.name: Coordination Formation Rate
variables.documentation: Speed at which shared threat converts into joint political machinery.
variables.units: coordination units per year per grievance unit

variables.name: Coordination Decay
variables.documentation: Lapsing of committees and agreements during quiet periods.

variables.name: Coordination Duration
variables.documentation: Average life of a resistance organization absent renewed provocation.

variables.name: British Troop Presence
variables.documentation: Regulars and customs enforcement stationed in America, notably the Boston garrison from 1768 and Gage's army after 1774.

variables.name: Troop Deployment
variables.documentation: Sending soldiers to restore order where authority is seen to be collapsing.

variables.name: Deployment Propensity
variables.documentation: Troops deployed per unit of perceived rebelliousness per year.
variables.units: troop units per year per defiance unit

variables.name: Troop Withdrawal
variables.documentation: Redeployment or drawdown of garrisons when calm appears to return.

variables.name: Troop Deployment Duration
variables.documentation: Average time a garrison remains in place.

variables.name: Perceived British Threat
variables.documentation: Colonial reading of British intentions: standing armies, charters annulled, ports closed, and finally powder seized and shots fired.

variables.name: Militia Mobilization
variables.documentation: Armed and drilled colonial forces, minutemen, and stockpiled munitions. This is the stock that turns political conflict into a shooting war.

variables.name: Militia Recruitment
variables.documentation: Arming and training in self defence, organized by provincial congresses once British force appeared aimed at them.

variables.name: Recruitment Responsiveness
variables.documentation: How readily perceived threat converts into men under arms.
variables.units: militia units per year per threat unit

variables.name: Militia Demobilization
variables.documentation: Militiamen returning to farms and shops when alarm passes.

variables.name: Militia Commitment Time
variables.documentation: Average time a mobilized militiaman stays mobilized.

variables.name: Armed Hostilities
variables.documentation: Open fighting between organized armed forces, the outcome of interest: Lexington, Concord and Bunker Hill. It requires both a mobilized militia and a British army in the field.
