variables.name: Traffic Congestion
variables.documentation: A normalized index of how congested the road network is (1 = normal congestion). It accumulates as traffic volume, poor road design, bad weather and crash blockages build queues, and it drains as queues clear.

variables.name: Congestion Buildup
variables.documentation: Rate at which congestion builds toward the level implied by traffic volume, road design, weather and crash blockages.

variables.name: Congestion Clearing
variables.documentation: Rate at which existing queues dissipate; the natural balancing drain of the congestion stock.

variables.name: Target Congestion
variables.documentation: The congestion level the road system is currently heading toward, given demand, design quality, weather and blockages from crashes.

variables.name: Effective Traffic Volume
variables.documentation: Traffic actually on the road after some drivers cancel, delay or reroute trips because of congestion.

variables.name: Trip Deterrence Effect
variables.documentation: Nonlinear effect by which worsening congestion suppresses discretionary travel. Passes through (1,1) so normal congestion gives normal traffic.

variables.name: Road Design Effect on Congestion
variables.documentation: Narrow lanes and confusing intersections multiply congestion; good design reduces it. Normal design quality (1) gives a multiplier of 1.

variables.name: Crash Blockage Effect
variables.documentation: Crashes and near-miss incidents block lanes and add congestion. Normal crash levels (1) give a multiplier of 1.

variables.name: Crashes and Blockages
variables.documentation: Collisions and lane blockages produced by aggressive manoeuvres and by phone use, texting and eating at the wheel.

variables.name: Driver Stress Level
variables.documentation: Average psychological stress and anxiety carried by the driving population (1 = normal). Stress accumulates from congestion, weather and exposure to incidents and decays with rest and recovery.

variables.name: Stress Accumulation
variables.documentation: Rate at which driving conditions load stress onto drivers.

variables.name: Stress Recovery
variables.documentation: Natural relaxation and recovery that drains accumulated stress; the balancing drain of the stress stock.

variables.name: Target Stress
variables.documentation: The stress level current conditions would eventually produce, given congestion, weather, exposure to road rage incidents, and the calming effect of awareness and education.

variables.name: Congestion Effect on Stress
variables.documentation: Stop-and-go traffic and delays raise stress more than proportionally. Normal congestion (1) gives a multiplier of 1.

variables.name: Incident Effect on Stress
variables.documentation: Witnessing or experiencing road rage makes the road feel hostile and raises baseline anxiety. Normal incident severity (1) gives a multiplier of 1.

variables.name: Emotional Regulation Effect
variables.documentation: Public awareness campaigns and driver education teach coping skills that lower the stress produced by the same conditions. Normal awareness (1) gives a multiplier of 1.

variables.name: Perceived Incident Severity
variables.documentation: How bad the road rage problem looks relative to what society tolerates; drives both public stress and the political response.

variables.name: Aggressive Driving Norm
variables.documentation: The socially learned expectation that aggressive driving is normal. It accumulates as drivers observe aggression around them and decays slowly, faster when enforcement and awareness are strong.

variables.name: Norm Reinforcement
variables.documentation: Rate at which observed aggressive driving is absorbed and normalized by other drivers.

variables.name: Norm Decay
variables.documentation: Rate at which the aggressive norm fades through turnover, courtesy campaigns and visible sanctioning.

variables.name: Enforcement Effect on Norm Decay
variables.documentation: Visible enforcement and campaigns de-normalize aggression, speeding the erosion of the aggressive driving norm. Normal enforcement (1) gives a multiplier of 1.

variables.name: Road Rage Incidents
variables.documentation: The pool of active or recent road rage incidents in society. It rises with new confrontations and falls as they are resolved and fade from attention.

variables.name: Incident Occurrence
variables.documentation: New road rage confrontations, produced by aggressive driving and amplified when provoked drivers retaliate.

variables.name: Incident Resolution
variables.documentation: Incidents cooling down, being resolved or dropping out of public salience.

variables.name: Retaliation Escalation
variables.documentation: Being cut off, tailgated or honked at triggers tit-for-tat responses that turn ordinary aggression into full incidents. Normal provocation (1) gives a multiplier of 1.

variables.name: Enforcement and Awareness
variables.documentation: Accumulated policing presence, penalties and public education about aggressive driving. It builds when the incident problem looks severe and erodes as attention and budgets fade.

variables.name: Enforcement Investment
variables.documentation: Society's response rate: the worse the incident problem appears, the more enforcement and awareness capacity is added.

variables.name: Enforcement Erosion
variables.documentation: Decay of enforcement intensity and campaign memory once attention moves elsewhere.

variables.name: Aggressive Driving Behavior
variables.equation: Baseline_Aggressive_Driving * Stress_Effect_on_Aggression * Frustration_Effect_on_Aggression * Aggressive_Driving_Norm * Fatigue_Effect_on_Aggression * Enforcement_Effect_on_Aggression * Impulsive_Personality_Prevalence
variables.documentation: The prevailing rate of aggressive manoeuvres on the road (tailgating, weaving, hostile gestures). It is the product of stress, frustration, learned norms, fatigue, personality mix and deterrence.

variables.name: Stress Effect on Aggression
variables.documentation: Stressed and anxious drivers are more irritable and quicker to react aggressively. Normal stress (1) gives a multiplier of 1.

variables.name: Frustration Effect on Aggression
variables.documentation: Feeling blocked or thwarted converts directly into aggressive action. Normal frustration (1) gives a multiplier of 1.

variables.name: Fatigue Effect on Aggression
variables.documentation: Tired drivers have impaired judgement and weaker impulse control. Normal fatigue (1) gives a multiplier of 1.

variables.name: Enforcement Effect on Aggression
variables.documentation: Deterrence: visible policing and penalties suppress aggressive manoeuvres. Normal enforcement (1) gives a multiplier of 1.

variables.name: Driver Fatigue
variables.documentation: Tiredness in the driving population, driven mainly by stress-related sleep loss. Normal stress (1) gives normal fatigue (1).

variables.name: Frustration
variables.documentation: The sense of being blocked and thwarted on the road, produced by congestion, by perceived provocations from others, and by impatience.

variables.name: Congestion Effect on Frustration
variables.documentation: Heavy traffic and delays are the classic frustration trigger. Normal congestion (1) gives a multiplier of 1.

variables.name: Provocation Effect on Frustration
variables.documentation: Being cut off or tailgated is experienced as a personal affront and sharply increases frustration. Normal provocation (1) gives a multiplier of 1.

variables.name: Perceived Provocations
variables.documentation: How often the average driver feels wronged by others. One driver's aggression is another driver's provocation, so this rises steeply with aggressive driving. Normal aggression (1) gives normal provocation (1).

variables.name: Impatience Level
variables.documentation: Low tolerance for delay, driven by tight schedules and running late, and amplified when drivers are already stressed.

variables.name: Congestion Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: How quickly congestion adjusts to changes in demand and blockages.

variables.name: Stress Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: How long it takes driver stress to build up or unwind.

variables.name: Norm Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: How slowly social norms about acceptable driving change; this long delay is what makes the learned-behavior loop so persistent.

variables.name: Incident Duration
variables.documentation: Average time an incident stays active or salient.

variables.name: Enforcement Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: Delay in mounting and sustaining an enforcement and awareness response.

variables.name: Baseline Traffic Volume
variables.documentation: Underlying travel demand relative to road capacity (1 = normal).

variables.name: Road Design Quality
variables.documentation: Quality of lanes, merges and intersections (1 = normal). A policy lever.

variables.name: Weather Severity
variables.documentation: Adverse weather index (1 = normal). Bad weather slows traffic and makes driving more demanding and stressful.

variables.name: Distracted Driving Prevalence
variables.documentation: How common phone use, texting and eating at the wheel are (1 = normal); raises crash and blockage risk.

variables.name: Baseline Stress
variables.documentation: Stress drivers carry from life outside the car under normal conditions.

variables.name: Baseline Aggressive Driving
variables.documentation: Reference level of aggressive driving under normal conditions.

variables.name: Impulsive Personality Prevalence
variables.documentation: Share of the driving population with impulsive, hostile or competitive traits (1 = normal mix).

variables.name: Schedule Pressure
variables.documentation: How tightly drivers are scheduled and how often they are running late (1 = normal).

variables.name: Normal Incident Rate
variables.documentation: Incidents per week produced when aggression and retaliation are at normal levels.

variables.name: Tolerable Incident Level
variables.documentation: The incident level society treats as normal; deviations from it drive both public anxiety and the enforcement response.

variables.name: Enforcement Response Strength
variables.documentation: How strongly society converts a perceived road rage problem into enforcement and awareness capacity. A key policy lever.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
How the model reads the Revolution

The model treats the Revolution as an escalation system rather than a chain of events. Four accumulations carry the story: British War Debt (from the French and Indian War), Colonial Grievance, Coercive Measures in force (troops, customs crackdowns, the Intolerable Acts), and Militia Mobilization, plus the slowly built Colonial Identity.

Loop B1 — Fiscal balancing (the intended policy)

Debt raises Tax Burden, taxes produce Revenue Collected, and revenue pays down the debt. This is the only balancing loop in the system and the only one Parliament consciously designed. Left alone it would work.

Loop R1 — Provocation and repression (the escalation spiral)

Taxes without representation build Colonial Grievance, grievance drives Colonial Resistance (Stamp Act riots, nonimportation, the Boston Tea Party), resistance provokes Coercive Escalation into more Coercive Measures, and those measures — quartered troops that fire on crowds, a closed port — generate still more grievance. This is a classic escalation archetype: each side's defensive move is the other side's provocation.

Loop R2 — Identity forged by repression

Grievance and coercion feed Identity Formation, which accumulates into Colonial Identity; identity multiplies resistance, which brings more coercion. Punishing Boston taught twelve other colonies that they were one people, converting local riots into a continental movement. This is why concessions came too late: identity does not decay when a tax is repealed.

Loop R3 — Revenue erosion (why fiscal policy backfired)

Resistance destroys Tax Compliance through boycotts, smuggling and intimidation of collectors (captured by a nonlinear compliance curve normalized so customary resistance yields normal compliance). Falling revenue, plus the rising cost of enforcement, keeps the debt high, which demands more taxation — feeding grievance again. The fix-that-fails: every attempt to make the colonies pay made them pay less and resist more.

From resentment to gunfire

Resistance combined with visible military coercion drives Mobilization Rate and the stock of armed Militia. Hostilities Intensity requires both armed colonists and enforcing troops in the same place — which is exactly what happened when regulars marched to seize powder at Concord. Hostilities were not chosen; they were the intersection of two stocks that the escalation loops had been filling for a decade.

Formulation notes

  • Grievance, coercion, identity and armed readiness are stocks because they persist and decay slowly; resistance and hostilities intensity are auxiliaries computed from them.
  • The compliance effect uses a graphical function passing through (1,1) so it expresses deviation from customary behavior.
  • All rate constants (repayment pressure, relief and repeal times, sensitivities) are named variables rather than buried numbers, and decay flows are marked one-directional so grievance, coercion and militias cannot flow backwards.

variables.name: British War Debt
variables.documentation: The accumulated imperial debt, largely from the French and Indian War (1754-63), that Parliament sought to service by taxing the colonies. It is a stock because it accumulates spending and is drawn down by revenue.

variables.name: War and Enforcement Spending
variables.documentation: Ongoing military and administrative outlays, which rise as more troops, customs enforcement and punitive acts (troops in Boston, port closure) must be maintained.

variables.name: Baseline Military Spending
variables.documentation: Normal cost of defending and administering the North American colonies absent extra coercion.

variables.name: Cost per Coercive Measure
variables.documentation: Additional annual cost of garrisoning troops and enforcing each punitive act.

variables.name: Revenue Collected
variables.documentation: Money actually reaching the Treasury: the tax demanded times the share the colonists are willing to pay rather than boycott or smuggle.

variables.name: Tax Burden
variables.documentation: The level of taxation Parliament demands from the colonies (Stamp Act, Townshend duties, tea duty). It is set in proportion to the debt to be serviced.

variables.name: Debt Repayment Pressure
variables.documentation: Fraction of outstanding debt Parliament tries to raise from the colonies each year.

variables.name: Tax Compliance
variables.documentation: Share of demanded tax actually paid, eroded by boycotts, smuggling, intimidation of stamp agents and destruction of taxed goods.

variables.name: Normal Compliance
variables.documentation: Compliance that would be obtained at customary levels of colonial resistance.

variables.name: Compliance Multiplier
variables.documentation: Nonlinear effect of organized resistance on tax collection. At customary resistance (ratio of one) the multiplier is one; as resistance grows, collection collapses toward zero.

variables.name: Resistance Ratio
variables.documentation: Colonial resistance expressed relative to its customary level, so effects can be stated as deviations from normal.

variables.name: Reference Resistance
variables.documentation: Customary level of colonial protest activity used as a benchmark.

variables.name: Colonial Resistance
variables.documentation: Organized defiance: nonimportation agreements, Sons of Liberty actions, the Boston Tea Party, committees of correspondence and the Continental Congress. It requires both grievance and a shared identity capable of coordinating action, hence the product.

variables.name: Resistance Propensity
variables.documentation: Willingness to translate grievance and solidarity into overt defiance.
variables.units: resistance units per grievance unit per identity unit

variables.name: Colonial Grievance
variables.documentation: Accumulated colonial anger at taxation without representation, standing armies, the Boston Massacre and the Intolerable Acts. A stock because outrage builds up over years and only slowly fades.

variables.name: Grievance Accumulation
variables.documentation: New outrage generated each year by taxes levied without colonial consent and by punitive measures such as troops firing on a Boston crowd or closing the port.

variables.name: Perceived Injustice from No Representation
variables.documentation: How much outrage each pound of tax creates because colonists had no members in Parliament.

variables.name: Coercion Grievance Effect
variables.documentation: Outrage produced by each coercive measure in force, including quartered troops, the Massacre and the Intolerable Acts.
variables.units: grievance units per measure per year

variables.name: Grievance Relief
variables.documentation: Gradual cooling of anger when grievances are not renewed, as after the repeal of the Stamp Act.

variables.name: Grievance Relief Time
variables.documentation: Average time for accumulated resentment to fade if nothing new inflames it.

variables.name: Coercive Measures
variables.documentation: The stock of British punitive and enforcement actions in force: troops in Boston, customs crackdowns, the Intolerable Acts and the closure of the port. A stock because measures remain in force until repealed.

variables.name: Coercive Escalation
variables.documentation: Parliament's answer to defiance: more troops and harsher laws to reassert sovereignty after events like the Tea Party.

variables.name: British Determination to Assert Authority
variables.documentation: Strength of the ministry's belief that defiance must be punished rather than accommodated.

variables.name: Concession and Repeal
variables.documentation: Withdrawal of coercive measures, as with repeal of the Stamp Act and most Townshend duties.

variables.name: Policy Reversal Time
variables.documentation: Average time before a coercive measure is softened or repealed.

variables.name: Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: The accumulating sense of being one American people rather than separate British provinces, built through shared grievance and intercolonial cooperation. A stock because identity, once formed, persists.

variables.name: Identity Formation

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include no more than 4 feedback loops and at least 5 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
What the model says drives road rage

Road rage is treated not as a one-off event but as the output of four accumulations that feed each other: congestion, driver stress, the learned norm of aggressive driving, and the visible pool of road rage incidents, plus a societal enforcement and awareness stock.

Structure

  • Stocks (things that accumulate): Traffic Congestion, Driver Stress, Aggressive Driving Norm, Road Rage Incidents, Enforcement and Awareness. Each changes only through its own inflow and outflow, and each flow is either an inflow or an outflow — never both.
  • Auxiliaries: perceived provocations, perceived problem severity, and four nonlinear effect multipliers, all normalized so that a normal input of one returns an output of one. This makes every curve read as a deviation from today's conditions.
  • Exogenous pressures: road design quality, weather severity, fatigue and distraction, and the baseline propensity of impulsive or hostile personalities. These do not sit in loops; they are the external dials that set how hard the loops run.

The four feedback loops

  1. R1 — Congestion trap (reinforcing). Congestion raises stress, stress produces incidents, incidents block lanes and cause rubbernecking, which deepens congestion. This is a classic escalating vicious cycle.
  2. R2 — Provocation and retaliation (reinforcing). Each incident is experienced by other drivers as being cut off, tailgated or honked at. That perceived provocation loads more stress, which produces more incidents — an escalation archetype where each side's aggression justifies the other's.
  3. R3 — Learned behaviour (reinforcing). Witnessed aggression slowly builds the social norm that aggressive driving is acceptable, and a stronger norm produces more aggression. Because norms accumulate and erode slowly, this loop is the source of long-run drift: it is what makes road rage worse a decade later even if traffic stabilizes.
  4. B1 — Enforcement response (balancing). Rising incidents raise perceived severity, which mobilizes policing and awareness campaigns, which deter acting out. Crucially this loop is delayed — enforcement takes time to build and fades in about a year — so it is a "fixes that fail / shifting the burden" style correction that arrives late and slips away, allowing the three reinforcing loops to regain the upper hand.

What this implies for the future

With travel demand set slightly above clearing capacity, congestion drifts up, stress follows, incidents rise, and the norm loop locks in the higher level. Enforcement pushes back but only after the problem is already visible, producing overshoot-and-oscillation around a rising trend rather than a return to today's level. Leverage therefore lies less in reacting to incidents (B1) and more in weakening the reinforcing loops upstream: improving road design and clearing capacity, reducing fatigue and distraction, and interrupting the normalization of aggressive driving before it accumulates.

Formulation checks applied

  • Perceived provocations and perceived problem severity are auxiliaries, not stocks, because they are instantaneous ratios rather than accumulations.
  • No conditional logic is used anywhere; all nonlinearity is carried by normalized lookup curves passing through the point (1, 1).
  • Physically one-directional flows (incidents, stress buildup and recovery, norm reinforcement and decay, enforcement investment and erosion) are constrained to stay non-negative.
  • All arbitrary magnitudes are named constants (clearing time, recovery time, erosion time, adoption rate, policy response strength) rather than numbers buried in equations.

variables.name: Traffic Congestion
variables.documentation: An index of how congested the road network is, where 1 is the normal historical level. Congestion accumulates when traffic loading and incident-related blockages exceed the rate at which the network clears vehicles.

variables.name: Congestion Buildup
variables.documentation: Rate at which congestion accumulates from ordinary travel demand, amplified when road rage incidents block lanes and cause rubbernecking.

variables.name: Congestion Clearing
variables.documentation: Rate at which the network dissipates congestion. Good road design speeds clearing; adverse weather slows it.

variables.name: Traffic Demand Pressure
variables.documentation: Baseline loading of vehicles onto the network per month, expressed relative to clearing capacity. A value slightly above one represents growing travel demand.

variables.name: Normal Clearing Time
variables.documentation: Average time for a normal amount of congestion to dissipate under normal design and weather.

variables.name: Road Design Quality
variables.documentation: Quality of road geometry, lane width and intersection clarity relative to normal. Poor design (below one) keeps congestion in place longer.

variables.name: Weather Severity
variables.documentation: Severity of driving conditions such as rain, snow or fog relative to normal. Worse weather slows the clearing of congestion.

variables.name: Incident Blockage Effect
variables.documentation: Multiplier showing how aggressive driving episodes, collisions and confrontations add to traffic loading by blocking lanes. Normal incidents give a multiplier of one.

variables.name: Driver Stress
variables.documentation: Average level of accumulated stress, anxiety and impatience carried by drivers in the population, indexed so that one is the normal level. Stress accumulates faster than it dissipates when congestion and provocations are high.

variables.name: Stress Accumulation
variables.documentation: Rate at which drivers take on stress from delays, being cut off or tailgated, and from fatigue and distraction while driving.

variables.name: Stress Recovery
variables.documentation: Rate at which drivers unwind and recover from accumulated stress between trips.

variables.name: Stress Buildup Rate
variables.documentation: Normal monthly rate of stress loading on drivers under normal congestion, provocation and alertness.

variables.name: Stress Recovery Time
variables.documentation: Average time it takes a driver to shed accumulated driving stress.

variables.name: Fatigue and Distraction
variables.documentation: Index of sleep loss and phone or in-car distraction relative to normal. Tired, distracted drivers absorb stress faster and judge situations more poorly.

variables.name: Congestion Stress Effect
variables.documentation: Multiplier capturing how stop-and-go traffic and delay raise driver stress. At normal congestion the multiplier is one; heavy congestion more than doubles stress loading.

variables.name: Provocation Stress Effect
variables.documentation: Multiplier capturing how being cut off, tailgated or honked at raises anger and stress. Normal provocation yields a multiplier of one.

variables.name: Perceived Provocations
variables.documentation: How often the typical driver feels personally wronged on the road. It rises both with the number of active aggressive episodes and with how aggressively drivers generally behave.

variables.name: Aggressive Driving Norm
variables.documentation: The socially learned acceptability of aggressive driving, indexed to one at the normal level. It is a stock because norms are learned slowly by watching others and forgotten slowly.

variables.name: Norm Reinforcement
variables.documentation: Rate at which witnessing aggressive driving normalizes and spreads that behaviour to other drivers.

variables.name: Norm Decay
variables.documentation: Rate at which the acceptability of aggressive driving fades as drivers turn over and memories of aggressive examples fade.

variables.name: Norm Adoption Rate
variables.documentation: How strongly exposure to a normal level of aggressive episodes reinforces the aggressive driving norm each month.

variables.name: Norm Erosion Time
variables.documentation: Average time over which a learned driving norm fades if it is no longer reinforced.

variables.name: Road Rage Incidents
variables.documentation: The number of active or recent road rage episodes visible in society. Incidents accumulate as they occur and drain away as they are resolved and forgotten.

variables.name: Incident Rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which new road rage episodes occur. Stressed drivers who have learned that aggression is normal act out more often, while visible enforcement holds them back.

variables.name: Incident Resolution
variables.documentation: Rate at which episodes end, are cleared from the road and fade from public attention.

variables.name: Baseline Incident Rate
variables.documentation: Number of road rage episodes per month that would occur under normal stress, normal norms and normal enforcement, reflecting the underlying share of impulsive and hostile personalities.

variables.name: Incident Duration
variables.documentation: Average time an incident stays active and salient on the road and in public awareness.

variables.name: Reference Incidents

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include at least 6 feedback loops and no more than 15 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
How the Revolution came about: a system of escalation

The model treats the Revolution not as a chain of events but as four accumulations — British War Debt, Colonial Resentment, British Coercive Measures, and Colonial Unity — locked together by reinforcing loops that overwhelmed the balancing loops that had kept the empire stable before 1763.

The balancing loops that were supposed to work

  • B1 Debt service: Debt → Tax Burden → Tax Revenue Collection → debt falls. This is the loop London was actually trying to close after the French and Indian War.
  • B2 Repeal: Coercive Measures → Repeal Pressure → Coercion Relaxation → coercion falls. The Stamp Act repeal (1766) and the withdrawal of troops from Boston (1770) are this loop working.
  • B3 Grievance cooling: Resentment → Resentment Decay → resentment falls, but only when Britain concedes. The quiet years 1770–73 are this loop working.

The reinforcing loops that broke the system

  • R1 Uncollectable revenue: Debt → Tax Burden → Resentment → Resistance → less revenue collected → debt stays high → more taxes. Boycotts and smuggling meant taxation produced grievance without producing money, so the pressure to tax never let up.
  • R2 Coercion spiral: Resistance → Coercion Escalation → Coercive Measures → Resentment → Resistance. The Tea Party produced the Intolerable Acts, which produced the Continental Congress.
  • R3 Bloodshed and propaganda: Coercion × Resistance → Armed Clashes → Resentment → Resistance → more clashes. The Boston Massacre converted a policing presence into martyrdom and propaganda.
  • R4 Imperial identity-making: Coercive Measures → Unity Building → Colonial Unity → Resistance → more coercion. Punishing Boston collectively created the very American people Britain denied existed.
  • R5 Rally round the flag: Armed Clashes → Unity → Resistance → more clashes.
  • R6 Cost of empire: Coercion → Garrison Spending → Debt → Tax Burden → Resentment → Resistance → more coercion. Repression was expensive, and its expense justified the taxes that made repression necessary.

The tipping point

The crucial nonlinearity is Repeal Pressure, drawn as a curve that rises with moderate resistance and then collapses. Merchant boycotts made repeal cheap and attractive in 1766 and 1770; outright defiance of Parliament's sovereignty in 1773–74 made concession look like surrender. The moment that curve turned down, both balancing loops (B2 and B3) were switched off while all six reinforcing loops kept running. That is an escalation archetype fused with a fixes that fail archetype — coercion applied to suppress resistance was the very thing manufacturing it — and once conciliation was withdrawn, hostilities at Lexington were the arithmetic result rather than an accident.

Structural notes

  • Resistance is the product of resentment and unity, not their sum: anger without organisation is a riot, organisation without anger is a debating society. Only both together produce a revolution.
  • Armed Clashes is likewise a product of coercion and resistance — violence needs both soldiers and crowds in the same street.
  • Unity is formulated as a bounded contagion so that identity spreads through existing networks but cannot exceed complete union.
  • Total sums and indices are auxiliaries; only genuine accumulations (debt, grievance, statutes-and-troops, identity) are stocks.
supportingInfo.title: Escalation Loops Driving Colonial Revolt

variables.name: British War Debt
variables.documentation: The accumulated imperial debt left by the French and Indian War (1754-63) plus the ongoing cost of garrisoning and policing North America. Indexed to 1 at the end of the war. This stock is the original driver of the whole crisis: Britain needed the colonies to help pay it down.

variables.name: War and Garrison Spending
variables.documentation: New borrowing required to keep troops, customs officers and warships in America. The more coercive the imperial posture, the more expensive the empire becomes - a cost that flows straight back into the debt.

variables.name: Tax Revenue Collection
variables.documentation: Money actually collected from the colonies and applied to the debt. It equals the taxes levied, discounted by resistance: boycotts, smuggling, tarring of stamp distributors and the destruction of tea meant that levying a tax and collecting it were very different things.

variables.name: Tax Burden
variables.documentation: The severity of taxes and revenue measures imposed on the colonies (Sugar Act, Stamp Act, Townshend duties, Tea Act). It rises with the debt Parliament is trying to service, but saturates because there is a practical political ceiling on how much can be demanded at once. Normalised so that the post-war debt level (1) produces the normal tax burden (1).

variables.name: Colonial Resentment
variables.documentation: The accumulated store of colonial grievance - 'no taxation without representation', anger at standing armies, memories of the Boston Massacre. Grievance is a stock, not an event: it builds up over a decade and only drains slowly when London conciliates.

variables.name: Resentment Growth
variables.documentation: The rate at which new grievance is created, by taxes levied without colonial representation, by troops and punitive laws such as the Intolerable Acts, and above all by bloodshed that can be turned into propaganda.

variables.name: Resentment Decay
variables.documentation: The cooling of grievance when Britain backs down. The repeal of the Stamp Act in 1766 and of most Townshend duties in 1770 genuinely calmed the colonies for several years; grievance only fades when concessions are actually made.

variables.name: British Coercive Measures
variables.documentation: The accumulated apparatus of imperial force and punishment: troops quartered in Boston, vice-admiralty courts, the Declaratory Act, and finally the Intolerable Acts closing Boston harbour. It is a stock because each measure stays on the books until it is repealed.

variables.name: Coercion Escalation
variables.documentation: New troops and punitive statutes sent in response to colonial defiance. The Tea Party produced the Intolerable Acts; every act of resistance made Parliament feel its authority had to be vindicated.

variables.name: Coercion Relaxation
variables.documentation: Repeal and withdrawal of coercive measures when London judges conciliation to be cheaper than confrontation, as with the Stamp Act repeal and the removal of troops from Boston after the Massacre.

variables.name: Colonial Unity
variables.documentation: The degree to which thirteen separate provinces see themselves as one American people with common institutions - committees of correspondence, the Stamp Act Congress, the Continental Congress, the militia. Bounded between 0 and 1 (complete union). Once built it does not easily dissolve.

variables.name: Unity Building
variables.documentation: The rate at which a common American identity spreads. It is contagious (proportional to how much unity already exists) and it saturates as it approaches complete union. Shared punishment - especially the closing of Boston's port and the blood spilled at the Massacre and at Lexington - is what recruits the uncommitted.

variables.name: Colonial Resistance
variables.documentation: Organised defiance: non-importation boycotts, smuggling, the Sons of Liberty, the Tea Party, congresses and militia drilling. Anger alone accomplishes little and organisation without anger has no cause - resistance requires both grievance and unity together, which is why it is their product.

variables.name: Armed Clashes
variables.documentation: Violent contact between soldiers and colonists - the Boston Massacre of 1770, and ultimately Lexington and Concord. Violence requires both an armed imperial presence and a defiant population in the same street, so it is the product of coercion and resistance. This is the variable that measures the outbreak of hostilities.

variables.name: Repeal Pressure
variables.documentation: Britain's willingness to conciliate. Moderate colonial resistance - merchant boycotts hurting London trade - produced repeal of the Stamp Act and the Townshend duties. But once resistance became outright defiance of sovereignty, ministers concluded that concession would be fatal to the empire and conciliation collapsed. Normalised so normal resistance (1) gives normal repeal pressure (1).

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include at least 6 feedback loops and no more than 15 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
What the model says

Road rage is treated not as an event but as the output of three slowly-moving accumulations — Driver Stress, the socially learned Aggressive Driving Norm, and Traffic Congestion — each of which is fed by the incidents it helps create. Everything is indexed so that 1 = today's normal, and the whole system sits in equilibrium at 1 until Driving Conditions Quality (road design plus weather, the one exogenous driver) begins to degrade.

The reinforcing loops that generate escalation

  1. Stress spiral (R1): Incidents → provocations → stress accumulation → driver stress → more incidents. Angry drivers provoke each other, and the provocation is stored as stress that carries into the next trip.
  2. Congestion-rage spiral (R2): Incidents → congestion buildup → congestion → stress accumulation → stress → incidents. Aggression causes crashes and blockages; the resulting jams are themselves the biggest stressor.
  3. Learned-behaviour spiral (R3): Incidents → norm reinforcement → aggressive driving norm → incidents. This is the contagion loop the background material calls learned behaviour — every witnessed outburst normalises the next one.
  4. Provocation-contagion spiral (R4): Norm → perceived provocations → incidents → norm. A more aggressive culture means everyone genuinely is being cut off more often, which justifies retaliating.
  5. Fatigue spiral (R5): Congestion → driver fatigue → incidents → congestion. Long crawling commutes steal sleep; tired drivers lose impulse control.
  6. Distraction spiral (R6): Congestion → distracted driving → perceived provocations → incidents → congestion. Stop-and-go traffic invites phone use, and inattentive manoeuvres read to other drivers as deliberate discourtesy.

The balancing loops that keep it bounded

  1. Enforcement response (B1): Norm → enforcement intensity → both suppresses incidents and accelerates norm decay. Society reacts to a visibly worsening driving culture — but it reacts to the norm, which is slow to become visible, so the correction always lags the escalation.
  2. Stress recovery (B2), congestion clearing (B3) and norm decay (B4) are the ordinary draining loops that stop each stock running away.

What the future looks like

Because the six reinforcing loops share the same three stocks, a modest, permanent worsening of road and weather conditions does not produce a modest, proportional rise in road rage. The congestion it creates is amplified through fatigue, distraction and stress, and then locked in by the learned norm, so incidents settle at a materially higher plateau than the external shock alone would suggest. The system behaves like "fixes that fail" on the enforcement side: crackdowns work, but because they respond to a slow-moving cultural stock rather than to conditions, they arrive after the norm has already shifted. The high-leverage interventions are the ones that break the loops early — protecting road capacity and trip-time reliability (weakening R2, R5, R6) and suppressing the observability of aggression (weakening R3, R4) — rather than punishing incidents after the culture has already re-set.

Formulation notes

  • Road rage incidents, perceived provocations, fatigue, distraction and enforcement are auxiliaries, not stocks: they are algebraic combinations of conditions at a point in time, not accumulations.
  • Enforcement is driven by the norm stock rather than by incidents; had it been driven by incidents directly it would have created a simultaneous algebraic loop with no state variable to break it.
  • All flows are marked one-directional, since stress cannot un-accumulate through its inflow and queues cannot clear negatively.
  • Fatigue, distraction and enforcement use graphical relationships normalised through the point (1,1), so normal input gives normal output and the curves express saturating deviation in both directions.
supportingInfo.title: Feedback engine driving societal road rage escalation

variables.name: Traffic Congestion
variables.documentation: Dimensionless index of how congested the road network is relative to normal conditions (1 = normal). Congestion is a genuine accumulation: it builds up faster than it clears and persists, so it is modelled as a stock rather than an instantaneous calculation.

variables.name: Congestion Buildup
variables.documentation: Rate at which congestion accumulates. Road rage incidents create blockages, crashes, defensive slow-downs and rubber-necking that add traffic delay, and poor road design or bad weather (low driving conditions quality) multiplies the delay created by any given level of disruption.

variables.name: Congestion Clearing
variables.documentation: Rate at which traffic queues dissipate. The more congestion there is, the more of it clears per unit time, which is the classic balancing drain that gives congestion a finite equilibrium level.

variables.name: Driver Stress
variables.documentation: Average level of stress, anxiety and impatience carried by drivers, indexed to 1 at normal conditions. Stress is a stock because it builds over repeated trips and dissipates only gradually through rest and recovery.

variables.name: Stress Accumulation
variables.documentation: Rate at which driving experience adds to driver stress. Sitting in stop-and-go traffic and being cut off, tailgated or honked at are the two main stress inputs, combined here as a simple average of the two pressures.

variables.name: Stress Recovery
variables.documentation: Rate at which accumulated stress dissipates once drivers are off the road. Recovery is proportional to the stress carried, which is the balancing drain that keeps stress bounded.

variables.name: Aggressive Driving Norm
variables.documentation: The socially learned acceptability of aggressive driving, indexed to 1 at normal conditions. Because road rage is largely learned by observation, the norm accumulates from witnessed incidents and erodes only slowly, making it a stock.

variables.name: Norm Reinforcement
variables.documentation: Rate at which witnessing aggressive driving normalises it. Every incident is observed by other drivers and teaches them that tailgating, weaving and horn-blasting are acceptable responses.

variables.name: Norm Decay
variables.documentation: Rate at which the aggressive driving norm erodes through forgetting, driver turnover, education and, above all, visible enforcement and public awareness campaigns that de-legitimise the behaviour.

variables.name: Road Rage Incidents
variables.documentation: Rate of aggressive-driving episodes in society, indexed to 1 at normal conditions. It is an algebraic combination of the four proximate drivers named in the background material (stress, learned norms, fatigue, and perceived provocation), averaged so no single driver dominates, and damped by enforcement and public awareness.

variables.name: Perceived Provocations
variables.documentation: How often a driver feels cut off, tailgated, blocked or disrespected. Provocations come both from other drivers deliberately behaving aggressively (the norm) and from erratic, inattentive manoeuvres by distracted drivers.

variables.name: Driver Fatigue
variables.documentation: Tiredness and impaired judgement among drivers. Longer, slower commutes eat into sleep and demand sustained low-grade concentration, so fatigue rises with congestion. Normalised so that normal congestion (1) produces normal fatigue (1), with diminishing additional effect at extreme congestion.

variables.name: Distracted Driving
variables.documentation: Phone use, texting and eating behind the wheel. Stop-and-go crawling invites drivers to fill dead time with their phones, so distraction rises with congestion. Normalised so that normal congestion yields normal distraction.

variables.name: Enforcement Intensity
variables.documentation: Policing, penalties and public awareness campaigns directed at aggressive driving. Society responds to a visibly worsening culture of aggression on the roads by increasing enforcement, though with saturating returns. It is driven by the observable norm rather than by instantaneous incidents so that the societal response has a real lag.

variables.name: Driving Conditions Quality
variables.documentation: Exogenous index of road design adequacy and weather favourability (1 = normal). This is the external driver of the model: narrowing effective lane capacity, confusing intersections and more frequent adverse weather progressively degrade conditions over the simulated period.

supportingInfo.explanation:
What the model says

The Revolution is represented not as a chain of events but as a set of interacting feedback loops built on five accumulations: British War Debt, Anti British Sentiment, Colonial Identity, British Coercion, and Armed Hostilities.

The trigger (an exogenous shock). War Spending during the French and Indian War (1754-63) loads Britain with debt. Spreading that debt over a repayment horizon creates a Revenue Need, which is the engine behind Taxation (Sugar, Stamp, Townshend, Tea Acts).

Loop R1 - Taxation without representation. Taxation, amplified by Perceived Lack of Representation, feeds Grievance from Taxation into Anti British Sentiment, which produces Colonial Resistance (riots, boycotts, the Tea Party). Resistance destroys Tax Compliance, so collections fall, the debt is not retired, Revenue Need stays high and taxes are pressed harder. This is a classic fixes that fail / vicious reinforcing loop: the revenue measure undermines the very revenue it seeks.

Loop R2 - Defiance and imperial resolve. Resistance also raises Parliamentary Resolve, so defiance produces heavier rather than lighter taxation - the Tea Party answered by the Intolerable Acts.

Loop R3 - Escalation (the arms-race archetype). Resistance raises Desired Coercion, which accumulates as British Coercion (customs commissioners, troops in Boston, the closed port). Coercion is itself a grievance, which raises sentiment, which raises resistance. The one-year Coercion Adjustment Time is the transatlantic delay that made every British measure arrive after tempers had already risen - the classic cause of overshoot in escalation systems.

Loop R4 - Bloodshed and propaganda. Coercion multiplied by resistance yields Violent Incidents (the Boston Massacre). Propaganda Amplification turns five deaths into a colony-wide symbol, adding sharply to sentiment.

Loop R5 - Identity as the accelerator. Shared Grievance Recognition (sentiment seen through Intercolonial Coordination) builds Colonial Identity, which strengthens the Committees of Correspondence and Congress, which in turn makes anger far more effective as organized resistance and militia mobilization. Identity is a slow stock drained by loyalist attachment, which is why the system took two decades to tip.

The break to war. Militia Mobilization combined with British Coercion, once past an Escalation Threshold, produces the Outbreak of Fighting that accumulates as Armed Hostilities (Lexington and Concord). Fighting then feeds back into both sentiment and identity, closing the loops and making reconciliation impossible.

The only balancing loop is weak: collected revenue pays down debt and lowers the revenue need. Because resistance strangles compliance, this stabilizing loop is defeated by the reinforcing ones - which is precisely why hostilities broke out.

Formulation notes

  • Aggregations and indices (Taxation, Colonial Resistance, Violent Incidents, Militia Mobilization) are auxiliaries, not stocks, since they are algebraic combinations rather than accumulations.
  • All numerical parameters are named variables (reference levels, adjustment times, thresholds) rather than constants buried in equations.
  • Uniflow is set true on one-directional processes (War Spending, Debt Repayment, Sentiment Escalation and Decay, Identity Formation and Erosion, Outbreak of Fighting) and false on Coercion Adjustment, which could legitimately reverse when acts were repealed.

variables.name: Initial War Debt
variables.documentation: Debt already carried by Britain when the French and Indian War begins, expressed as an index of millions of pounds. Sets the starting point of the fiscal pressure that later drives colonial taxation.

variables.name: War Spending
variables.documentation: Borrowing to fight the French and Indian War (1754-1763). A time-based graphical function turns spending on during the war and off afterward, leaving a debt overhang that Parliament wanted the colonies to help repay.

variables.name: British War Debt
variables.documentation: Accumulated imperial debt. It is a true stock because it only changes through borrowing (war spending) and repayment from tax revenue. This debt is the root cause that pushed Parliament toward colonial taxation.

variables.name: Debt Repayment Target Time
variables.documentation: The period over which the Treasury aimed to retire the war debt. A shorter target time means a heavier annual revenue demand on the colonies.

variables.name: Revenue Need
variables.documentation: Annual revenue Parliament believes it must raise from the colonies, derived by spreading the outstanding debt over the intended repayment period.

variables.name: Reference Resistance
variables.documentation: Normal, pre-crisis level of colonial resistance used to normalize resistance into a relative index so that graphical effects pass through the point (1,1).

variables.name: Relative Resistance
variables.documentation: Colonial resistance measured against its normal historical level. Used as the input to both British political resolve and tax compliance.

variables.name: Parliamentary Resolve
variables.documentation: Britain's determination to assert the principle of parliamentary supremacy. Defiance such as the Tea Party stiffened rather than softened Parliament, so more resistance raises the tax and revenue demands imposed. Normalized to 1 at normal resistance.

variables.name: Taxation
variables.documentation: The tax burden Parliament imposes on the colonies (Sugar Act, Stamp Act, Townshend duties, Tea Act). It grows with the revenue need created by war debt and with Parliament's determination to assert its authority.

variables.name: Tax Compliance
variables.documentation: Fraction of the imposed tax actually collected. Boycotts, non-importation agreements, smuggling and intimidation of stamp distributors cut collections sharply as resistance rises. Normalized to 1 at normal resistance.

variables.name: Debt Repayment
variables.documentation: Revenue actually collected from the colonies and applied to the debt. It is the product of the tax imposed and the share that colonists actually pay.

variables.name: Reference Taxation
variables.documentation: The level of taxation colonists regarded as customary and tolerable, used to convert the tax burden into a grievance index.

variables.name: Perceived Lack of Representation
variables.documentation: Amplifier capturing 'no taxation without representation'. Because colonists had no members in Parliament, each pound of tax produced more outrage than the same tax levied by their own assemblies.

variables.name: Grievance from Taxation
variables.documentation: Outrage generated by taxes imposed without consent, relative to customary tax levels.

variables.name: Reference Coercion
variables.documentation: Normal peacetime level of imperial enforcement, used to scale coercion into a grievance index.

variables.name: Grievance from Coercion
variables.documentation: Anger produced by troops quartered in Boston, customs enforcement, the closing of the port and the other Intolerable Acts.

variables.name: Confrontation Intensity
variables.documentation: How readily contact between armed enforcement and defiant crowds turns violent. It converts the mixture of coercion and resistance into bloody incidents.

variables.name: Violent Incidents
variables.documentation: Bloodshed such as the Boston Massacre of 1770. Incidents require both a coercive presence (soldiers, customs officers) and a resisting population, so they are the product of the two.

variables.name: Propaganda Effectiveness
variables.documentation: How powerfully patriot printers, engravings and Committees of Correspondence magnified each incident into a shared symbol of tyranny.

variables.name: Propaganda Amplification
variables.documentation: The emotional impact of violent incidents once broadcast as propaganda throughout the colonies.

variables.name: Reference Hostilities
variables.documentation: Scaling constant that converts accumulated fighting into a dimensionless index of shared wartime experience.

variables.name: Hostility Feedback
variables.documentation: Once blood is shed at Lexington and Concord, the fighting itself becomes a cause of further hatred and of a common American identity. This variable carries that feedback back into sentiment and identity.

variables.name: Sentiment Formation Time
variables.documentation: Time required for grievances to be absorbed into settled public opinion across the colonies.

variables.name: Sentiment Escalation
variables.documentation: Rate at which grievances over taxes, coercion, massacres and fighting are converted into hostility toward Britain. Uniflow because grievances can only add anger; forgetting is handled by the separate decay flow.

variables.name: Sentiment Decay Time
variables.documentation: Average time over which anger fades when no new provocations occur, as happened during the quiet years after the Townshend repeal.

variables.name: Sentiment Decay
variables.documentation: Cooling of resentment through habit, repeal of taxes and continuing loyalty to the Crown.

variables.name: Initial Anti British Sentiment
variables.documentation: Low background level of colonial resentment in 1754, when most colonists considered themselves loyal British subjects.

variables.name: Anti British Sentiment
variables.documentation: Accumulated colonial hostility toward Britain. It is a stock because outrage builds up over years of provocations and drains only slowly, which is why the memory of the Stamp Act and the Boston Massacre still shaped reactions in 1774.

variables.name: Committee Network Strength
variables.documentation: Effectiveness of Committees of Correspondence, newspapers and the Continental Congress in linking a shared identity into practical joint action.

variables.name: Intercolonial Coordination
variables.documentation: The degree to which thirteen separate colonies act as one. It rises with a common American identity and with the strength of the communication networks that identity supports.

variables.name: Shared Grievance Recognition
variables.documentation: Recognition that grievances suffered in Boston are grievances of all the colonies. Anger only forges identity when it is communicated and seen as shared, so it is multiplied by coordination.

variables.name: Identity Formation Time
variables.documentation: Time needed for shared grievance to harden into a self-conscious American identity.

variables.name: Identity Formation
variables.documentation: Rate at which colonists come to see themselves as Americans rather than provincial Britons.

variables.name: Loyalist Attachment Time
variables.documentation: Time constant for the pull of loyalty to Crown, trade and English tradition, which continually erodes a separate American identity.

variables.name: Identity Erosion
variables.documentation: Loss of distinct American identity through loyalism, commercial ties and provincial rivalries.

variables.name: Initial Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: Weak sense of common American identity in 1754, when the Albany Plan of Union failed.

variables.name: Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: Accumulated sense of being a single American people. A stock because identity is built slowly out of shared experience and, once formed, persists and enables coordinated resistance.

variables.name: Coordination Effect on Resistance
variables.documentation: Multiplier showing how much more effective anger becomes when colonies act together through congresses, boycotts and committees. Normalized so that normal coordination gives a multiplier of 1.

variables.name: Colonial Resistance
variables.documentation: Active defiance: stamp riots, non-importation, the Boston Tea Party, tarring of customs officers. It requires both anger and the organization to act on it.

variables.name: Coercion Response Strength
variables.documentation: How forcefully Britain answers defiance. Values above one mean each act of resistance is met with a harsher measure, as the Tea Party was met with the Intolerable Acts.

variables.name: Desired Coercion
variables.documentation: The level of enforcement Parliament thinks is necessary to restore obedience, given the amount of defiance it observes.

variables.name: Coercion Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: Delay in legislating and shipping enforcement across the Atlantic. This delay is why British measures always arrived after tempers had already risen.

variables.name: Coercion Adjustment
variables.documentation: Net change in imperial coercion as Parliament adds troops and acts, or repeals them. Bidirectional because coercion could be relaxed, as with the repeal of the Stamp Act.

variables.name: Initial British Coercion
variables.documentation: Light imperial enforcement before 1763, the era of 'salutary neglect'.

variables.name: British Coercion
variables.documentation: Accumulated apparatus of enforcement: customs commissioners, warships, troops in Boston, the closed port and the Intolerable Acts. A stock because each measure stayed on the books and added to the previous ones.

variables.name: Militia Mobilization
variables.documentation: Minutemen, powder stores and provincial congresses. Armed readiness grows when determined resistance is organized across colonies.

variables.name: Escalation Threshold
variables.documentation: How much combined armed readiness and coercive enforcement is required before confrontation becomes actual fighting. A higher threshold means more provocation is needed before shots are fired.

variables.name: Outbreak of Fighting
variables.documentation: Rate at which armed clashes occur, as when troops marched to seize colonial munitions at Concord. Fighting needs both an armed populace and an enforcing army, so it is the product of the two divided by the escalation threshold.

variables.name: Armed Hostilities
variables.documentation: Accumulated open warfare between colonists and Crown forces, beginning at Lexington and Concord. Starts at zero and accumulates once the escalation loops overwhelm restraint.

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include the variables "Traffic Congestion", "Driver Stress" and "Accidents".

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
How the model explains road rage

Road rage is represented not as a one-off event but as the output of several interlocking feedback loops, so that future incident levels depend on how these loops gain or lose strength.

Accumulations (stocks). Five things genuinely build up over time and are therefore modelled as stocks: Traffic Congestion, Driver Stress, Road Rage Incidents, Accidents (crashes awaiting clearance) and the socially learned Aggressive Driving Norm, plus Enforcement and Awareness and Vehicle Volume. Everything else — impatience, provocations, propensity, risk multipliers — is an algebraic auxiliary, because these are instantaneous calculations rather than accumulations.

R1 — The congestion–rage–crash spiral (the core reinforcing loop). Traffic demand relative to effective road capacity builds congestion → congestion raises driver stress and impatience → stress and impatience raise aggression propensity → more rage incidents start → aggressive manoeuvres raise crash occurrence → crash scenes block lanes and add back into congestion. This is the engine that can make incidents escalate rather than settle.

R2 — Learned behaviour loop. Visible rage episodes reinforce the aggressive driving norm; a stronger norm makes individual aggression more acceptable and also generates more perceived provocations (being cut off, tailgated, honked at), which both stress drivers and directly trigger retaliation. This is a classic reinforcing 'escalation/normalisation' structure and explains why road rage can become culturally entrenched.

R3 — Provocation retaliation loop. Provocations raise stress, stress raises propensity, propensity produces incidents, and incidents (through the norm) create more provocations — tit-for-tat escalation between drivers.

B1 — Societal correction. Rising incidents and crashes raise the perceived road safety problem, which draws enforcement and public awareness. Enforcement both deters aggression directly and accelerates the unlearning of the aggressive norm. Because enforcement erodes when attention fades, this loop produces the familiar 'crack down, forget, relapse' cycle — a fixes-that-fail pattern if the underlying congestion driver is never addressed.

B2 — Trip avoidance. Severe congestion pushes some drivers off the road, relieving demand. This limits how far the congestion spiral can run, but only weakly and with delay.

B3 — Natural relief. Stress recovery, incident de-escalation, queue clearing and crash clearance are all first-order drains that keep the system bounded.

Exogenous drivers are represented as separate inputs so scenarios can be tested: weather severity (which cuts effective capacity and adds stress), road design capacity, share of aggressive personalities, driver fatigue and distracted driving (which act mainly through crash risk and therefore feed the congestion spiral).

Formulation choices. No arbitrary numbers are buried in equations — all rates, times and reference levels are named constants, and every nonlinear relationship is a normalised graphical function passing through (1,1) so that normal input produces normal behaviour and deviations are visible in both directions. All flows are one-directional (uniflow) since none of them can meaningfully run backwards. All divisions use the safe division operator. The model is initialised in equilibrium at index value 1, so any change you make to weather, road capacity, fatigue, distraction, traffic growth or enforcement responsiveness reveals purely the feedback response of the system.
