testParams.name: Logistic Growth Pattern
testParams.prompt: Please create a model that demonstrates logistic growth (S-curve) behavior. The model must include a variable named 'output' that shows this behavior over time.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a model that exhibits logistic growth (S-curve) behavior in the 'output' variable.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Logistic growth combines reinforcing and balancing feedback. Initially, growth is exponential due to reinforcing feedback. As the system approaches its carrying capacity, balancing feedback becomes dominant, slowing growth until the system stabilizes at the maximum sustainable level. Examples include population growth with limited resources, market adoption of new products, and epidemic spread with limited susceptible population. The output should start with exponential growth but gradually slow and level off as it approaches a carrying capacity or maximum limit.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

The model is the classic limits to growth archetype expressed in its simplest form: a single stock with one net flow, driven by two coupled loops.

Reinforcing loop (growth engine): output → net growth → output. Because growth is proportional to the existing level, an initial seed compounds and produces exponential takeoff in the early phase.

Balancing loop (the limit): output → remaining capacity fraction → fractional growth rate → net growth → output. As the stock fills the available carrying capacity, the unused fraction falls toward zero, which throttles the fractional growth rate and finally halts growth.

Formulation choices

  • output is a stock — it is a genuine accumulation, changing only through its flow, which is what generates the S-shape.
  • net growth is the single flow, written as level × fractional growth rate. It is left bidirectional so that if the stock ever starts above the limit it is corrected downward rather than frozen.
  • remaining capacity fraction uses the structural complement 1 - x, and the safe division operator, so no arbitrary constants appear inside equations.
  • All numeric values (carrying capacity, intrinsic growth rate, initial output) are isolated as named constants rather than buried in formulas, so the limit and the steepness of the curve can each be changed independently.

Expected behavior

Starting from a small seed well below the limit, output grows nearly exponentially, passes its steepest point around half of carrying capacity, then decelerates smoothly and levels off at the maximum sustainable level — a textbook logistic S-curve.

testParams.name: Logistic Decay Pattern
testParams.prompt: Please create a model that demonstrates logistic decay (inverse S-curve) behavior. The model must include a variable named 'output' that shows this behavior over time.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a model that exhibits logistic decay (inverse S-curve) behavior in the 'output' variable.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Logistic decay follows an S-shaped (sigmoid) decline and is the mirror image of logistic growth. The output starts high and declines only slowly at first while it is near its initial level. The decline then accelerates, reaching its maximum rate around the midpoint between the starting value and the floor, before slowing again as balancing feedback becomes dominant near the floor, until the system stabilizes at a lower equilibrium. Because the decline is slow at both the top and the bottom and fastest in the middle, the curve has an inflection point (it is NOT exponential decay, which declines fastest at the very start). A natural structure is an outflow proportional to both the distance still remaining above the floor and the distance already fallen from the initial value (for example, rate proportional to (initial - output) * (output - floor)), which is near zero at both ends and largest in between. Examples include the decline phase of a product life cycle and the abandonment of a technology following an inverse S-curve. The output should start high and nearly flat, decline most steeply through the middle, and then level off as it approaches a minimum sustainable level or floor.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure created

  • output (stock) — the accumulation that must display the inverse S-curve. It starts near its historical peak and is drained only by its single outflow, so all behavior comes from feedback rather than an imposed time path.
  • decline (flow, uniflow) — formulated as the classic logistic-decay rate: proportional to the distance already fallen (upper reference level − output) times the distance still remaining above the floor (output − floor level), normalized by the total range so the coefficient is a pure fractional rate per time.

Why this produces logistic decay rather than exponential decay

The product term is near zero at both extremes and maximal in the middle:

  • Near the top, almost nothing has fallen yet, so the decline is tiny → the curve starts high and nearly flat.
  • A reinforcing loop then takes over: every unit lost widens the fallen-from-peak gap, which speeds the loss further, so the decline accelerates and is steepest around the midpoint between peak and floor (the inflection point).
  • Near the bottom, the balancing loop dominates: the remaining gap above the floor collapses, shutting the outflow down so output levels off at a lower equilibrium instead of crashing to zero.

This reinforcing-then-balancing hand-off (a shifted "limits to growth" archetype, mirrored) is exactly what distinguishes an S-shaped decline from exponential decay, which would fall fastest immediately at the start.

Formulation care taken

  • initial offset was introduced as an explicit named parameter because a stock started exactly at the peak makes the product term identically zero — a degenerate equilibrium where nothing would ever happen. The small offset seeds the decline and controls the length of the flat top.
  • No arbitrary constants appear inside equations; the peak, floor, decay speed, and seed erosion are all named variables. The only bare number in the flow is a structural range normalization.
  • decline is marked one-directional, so the loss process can never reverse and push output back up.
  • No conditional logic, no delay-based averaging, and no sums misclassified as stocks.
supportingInfo.title: Logistic decay via reinforcing then balancing loops

testParams.name: Standing Oscillation Pattern
testParams.prompt: Please create a model that demonstrates sustained oscillation behavior. The model must include a variable named 'output' that shows this behavior over time.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a model that exhibits sustained oscillation behavior in the 'output' variable.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Standing oscillations occur in systems with delays and feedback loops that create periodic behavior. The system oscillates around an equilibrium point with relatively constant amplitude. Examples include predator-prey models (Lotka-Volterra), inventory management with ordering delays, economic business cycles, and many engineering control systems. The oscillation is sustained rather than dampening out. The output should oscillate periodically with relatively constant amplitude over time.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure created

The model is a two-stock balancing loop with an embedded delay, the canonical structure that produces standing (undamped) oscillation.

  • output (stock) accumulates output change rate.
  • output change rate is driven entirely by corrective momentum, a second stock.
  • corrective momentum accumulates momentum change rate, which is proportional to the gap between the equilibrium level and output.

Why it oscillates rather than settles

Tracing the loop: output → gap (−) → momentum change rate (+) → corrective momentum (+) → output change rate (+) → output (+). One negative link makes this a balancing loop, so it seeks the goal. But the correction must pass through two accumulations, so it arrives a quarter-cycle late: when output finally reaches the goal, momentum is at its maximum and carries output straight past it. The system therefore continuously overshoots in alternating directions.

Critically, no damping term exists anywhere in the loop — nothing removes corrective momentum except the reversal of the gap itself. This is what distinguishes standing oscillation from damped oscillation: energy is traded back and forth between the two stocks and never dissipated, so the amplitude stays constant indefinitely.

Modeling choices

  • All numeric values (goal, responsiveness, initial shock) are abstracted into named constants rather than buried inside equations.
  • Both flows are marked bidirectional (not uniflows), since output must be able to fall as well as rise — forcing them non-negative would destroy the oscillation.
  • RK4 integration with dt = 0.25 is used because Euler integration adds artificial energy to oscillating systems, causing the amplitude to grow spuriously. RK4 preserves the constant amplitude.
  • restoring strength = 0.25 gives an angular frequency of 0.5 and a period of about 12.6 time units, so the 100-unit run shows roughly eight clean cycles.
supportingInfo.title: Two-stock delayed balancing loop drives sustained oscillation

testParams.name: Simple Pendulum
testParams.prompt: Create a System Dynamics model of a simple pendulum with a small initial displacement. The model must include variables named 'angle' (angular position in radians), 'angular_velocity' (angular velocity in radians/second), and 'angular_acceleration' (angular acceleration in radians/second²). The model should obey Newton's laws of motion.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a pendulum model that accurately represents a simple pendulum with a small initial displacement and follows Newton's laws.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A simple pendulum consists of a mass suspended from a fixed point by a massless string. For small angles, the motion approximates simple harmonic motion. Newton's second law for rotational motion states: τ = I*α, where τ is torque, I is moment of inertia, and α is angular acceleration. For a simple pendulum: α = -(g/L)*sin(θ), where g is gravitational acceleration (9.8 m/s²), L is length, and θ is angle. For small angles, sin(θ) ≈ θ, giving α ≈ -(g/L)*θ. The angular velocity ω = dθ/dt, and angular acceleration α = dω/dt. Energy is conserved: E = (1/2)*I*ω² + mgh, where potential energy depends on height h = L*(1-cos(θ)).

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

The pendulum is built as a classic second-order oscillator: two stocks in a chain linked by a balancing (negative) feedback loop.

  • angle (stock) accumulates change_in_angle, whose equation is simply angular_velocity — this enforces dθ/dt = ω.
  • angular_velocity (stock) accumulates angular_acceleration — this enforces dω/dt = α.
  • angular_acceleration (flow) is -(gravitational_acceleration / length) * SIN(angle), the exact rotational form of Newton's second law (τ = Iα with τ = −mgL·sinθ and I = mL², so the mass cancels). The full sine is kept rather than the small-angle approximation, so the model is correct for any amplitude while still reproducing simple harmonic motion at the small initial displacement of 0.1 rad.

The negative loop angle → angular_acceleration → angular_velocity → change_in_angle → angle, with two stocks inside it, produces the sustained oscillation. Because the restoring force acts through two accumulations, the response is a 90°-lagged sinusoid rather than simple decay.

Modeling choices and error avoidance

  • No hard-coded constants inside equations. Gravity (9.8 m/s²), string length, mass, the initial angle and the initial angular velocity are each their own named parameter. The only bare numbers left are structurally required ones: the exponent 2, the ½ in kinetic energy, the 1 in 1 − cos θ, and 2π in the reference period.
  • Both flows are bidirectional (uniflow = false). A pendulum's angle and velocity legitimately go negative; clamping them at zero would destroy the physics. This is the most common failure mode in oscillator models.
  • total_energy is an auxiliary, not a stock. It is an algebraic sum of kinetic and potential energy, not an accumulation via flows. It doubles as a validity check: if it drifts, the integration is inaccurate.
  • Energy accounting uses moment of inertia I = mL² and height h = L(1 − cos θ), exactly as given.
  • period = 2π√(L/g) is included purely as a benchmark so the simulated oscillation frequency can be verified against theory (≈2.007 s for a 1 m pendulum).

Simulation settings

Euler integration systematically pumps energy into an undamped oscillator, causing the amplitude to grow artificially. RK4 with a small time step (0.01 s) is used instead so total energy stays constant and the pendulum neither grows nor decays over the 10-second run — roughly five full swings.
supportingInfo.title: Newtonian Pendulum With Conserved Mechanical Energy

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a pendulum model that accurately represents a damped pendulum with friction and follows Newton's laws.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A damped pendulum experiences a resistive force proportional to velocity. The equation of motion becomes: α = -(g/L)*sin(θ) - (b/I)*ω, where b is the damping coefficient. Newton's second law still applies: τ_total = τ_gravity + τ_damping = I*α. The system loses energy over time due to friction, causing oscillation amplitude to decrease exponentially. Angular acceleration must still be the derivative of angular velocity, and angular velocity the derivative of angle.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

The model is built as a proper second-order physical system, so the chain angular acceleration → angular velocity → angle is preserved exactly as Newton's laws require.

  • angle is a stock whose only inflow is change_in_angle, which equals angular_velocity. This guarantees angular velocity is the true derivative of the angle rather than an independent guess.
  • angular_velocity is a stock whose only inflow is change_in_angular_velocity, which equals angular_acceleration. This guarantees angular acceleration is the true derivative of angular velocity.
  • Both flows are bidirectional (not one-way), because a swinging pendulum legitimately reverses direction each half cycle. Forcing them to be non-negative would break the physics.

Newton's second law with damping

angular_acceleration is an algebraic auxiliary (not a stock — it is an instantaneous consequence of the current state, not an accumulation). It implements total torque divided by inertia:

  • Gravitational restoring term: gravity divided by length, times the sine of the angle, with a negative sign. Using the sine (rather than the small-angle shortcut) keeps the model valid for large swings.
  • Frictional term: the damping coefficient divided by the moment of inertia, times angular velocity, with a negative sign. Because it always carries the opposite sign to the velocity, it always opposes motion and drains energy.

moment_of_inertia is derived from mass and length squared rather than being asserted, so the damping torque is converted to acceleration consistently.

No hard-coded values inside structural equations

Gravity, length, mass, the friction coefficient, and both initial conditions are each their own named parameter. The acceleration equation therefore contains only named quantities and structural operations.

Behavior check

total_mechanical_energy (rotational kinetic plus gravitational potential) was added as a diagnostic. In the undamped case it stays flat; with friction present it decays monotonically, which is the signature of the balancing feedback that friction introduces on top of the oscillatory loop between angle and velocity. The result is the expected exponentially decaying oscillation envelope.

Solver settings

Runge-Kutta integration with a small time step is used because oscillatory systems accumulate noticeable phase and amplitude error under simple Euler integration — with Euler the amplitude would grow artificially, which would falsely mask or invert the damping.

testParams.name: Pendulum with Moderate Initial Angle
testParams.prompt: Create a System Dynamics model of a simple pendulum with a moderate initial displacement (30 degrees). The model must include variables named 'angle' (angular position in radians), 'angular_velocity' (angular velocity in radians/second), and 'angular_acceleration' (angular acceleration in radians/second²). The model should obey Newton's laws of motion.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a pendulum model that accurately represents a simple pendulum with a moderate initial displacement (30 degrees) and follows Newton's laws.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: For larger angles, the small-angle approximation breaks down and we must use the full equation: α = -(g/L)*sin(θ). This introduces non-linearity, making the period slightly longer than predicted by the small-angle approximation. Newton's laws still govern the motion: the restoring torque is τ = -m*g*L*sin(θ), and τ = I*α. Energy conservation still holds (in the absence of damping): KE + PE = constant, where PE = m*g*L*(1-cos(θ)). The motion is still periodic but not exactly sinusoidal due to the nonlinear restoring force.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

The pendulum is represented as a classic second-order oscillator built from two coupled accumulations:

  • angle (stock) accumulates change in angle, whose equation is simply angular_velocity — the definition of angular position as the integral of angular velocity. It is initialized at 30 degrees converted to radians.
  • angular velocity (stock) accumulates change in angular velocity, whose equation is angular_acceleration. It starts at zero because the bob is released from rest.

Both flows are bidirectional (the pendulum swings back and forth), so neither is constrained to be one-directional.

Newton's laws, not the small-angle approximation

Rather than hard-wiring a linearized spring law, the model derives acceleration the way Newton's second law for rotation does:

  • restoring torque = -mass*gravity*length*SIN(angle) — the exact gravitational torque.
  • moment of inertia = mass*length^2 for a point-mass bob.
  • angular acceleration = torque divided by inertia, which reduces exactly to α = −(g/L)·sin(θ).

Because the sine is retained, the restoring force is genuinely nonlinear, the motion is periodic but not perfectly sinusoidal, and the simulated period is slightly longer than the linear prediction — precisely the behavior expected at 30 degrees.

Energy check

Kinetic energy (I·ω²/2), potential energy (m·g·L·(1−cos θ)), and their sum are computed as auxiliaries. In this undamped system the total should remain flat, which acts as a diagnostic on numerical accuracy. RK4 integration with a small time step is used so this conservation actually holds; Euler with a coarse step would artificially pump energy into the swing.

Reference comparison

Small angle period (2π√(L/g)) and nonlinear period (the same value scaled by the leading amplitude correction) are included as passive reference calculations so the roughly 1.7% period lengthening at 30 degrees can be compared with the simulated swing. They do not feed back into the motion.

Constants

No arbitrary numbers are buried inside equations: gravity, length, mass, the initial displacement in degrees, the degree-to-radian conversion, and the series coefficient are all separate named variables. All aggregations (total energy) are auxiliaries, not stocks, since they are algebraic sums rather than accumulations.

testParams.name: Simple Spring-Mass System
testParams.prompt: Create a System Dynamics model of a simple spring-mass system with a small initial displacement. The model must include variables named 'position' (displacement from equilibrium in meters), 'velocity' (velocity in meters/second), and 'acceleration' (acceleration in meters/second²). The model should obey Hooke's law and Newton's second law.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a spring-mass system model that accurately represents a simple spring-mass system with a small initial displacement and follows physical laws.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A spring-mass system consists of a mass attached to a spring. Hooke's law states that the force exerted by a spring is F = -kx, where k is the spring constant and x is displacement. Newton's second law: F = ma, so ma = -kx, giving a = -(k/m)*x. This produces simple harmonic motion with angular frequency ω = sqrt(k/m). The velocity v = dx/dt, and acceleration a = dv/dt. Energy is conserved: E = (1/2)*m*v² + (1/2)*k*x², where kinetic energy KE = (1/2)*m*v² and potential energy PE = (1/2)*k*x².

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

The oscillator is built as the classic two-stock integration chain:

  • position (stock, starts at a small initial_displacement of 0.1 m) is filled by the flow change in position, which simply equals velocity — the definition dx/dt = v.
  • velocity (stock, starts at rest) is filled by the flow acceleration, which equals -(spring constant / mass) * position — Hooke's law (F = -kx) combined with Newton's second law (F = ma).

Both flows are bidirectional (not uniflows) because the mass physically moves back and forth through equilibrium; forcing them non-negative would destroy the oscillation.

Balancing loop

Position → acceleration → velocity → position forms a single balancing loop with a delay, which is exactly what generates sustained oscillation: the restoring force always points back toward equilibrium, but the accumulated momentum in the velocity stock carries the mass past it, producing simple harmonic motion.

Parameters as named variables

No physical constants are buried inside equations. Spring stiffness, mass, initial displacement and initial velocity are each their own named variable so they can be varied independently. angular_frequency = sqrt(k/m) is included as a diagnostic so the simulated period can be checked against the theoretical 2π/ω.

Energy accounting

kinetic_energy = ½mv², potential_energy = ½kx², and total_energy = their sum. These are auxiliaries, not stocks — they are algebraic calculations from the state variables, not accumulations. Total energy should stay flat, providing a built-in check on numerical accuracy.

Simulation settings

Oscillatory systems integrated with Euler artificially gain energy every step, so the model uses RK4 with a small time step (dt = 0.03125 s, about 200 steps per cycle) over 20 seconds — roughly three full oscillations with energy conserved to a high degree.

testParams.name: Damped Spring-Mass System
testParams.prompt: Create a System Dynamics model of a spring-mass system with damping (friction). The model must include variables named 'position' (displacement from equilibrium in meters), 'velocity' (velocity in meters/second), and 'acceleration' (acceleration in meters/second²). The model should obey Hooke's law and Newton's second law.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a spring-mass system model that accurately represents a spring-mass system with damping (friction) and follows physical laws.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A damped spring-mass system experiences both spring force and damping force. The total force is F = -kx - bv, where k is spring constant, b is damping coefficient, and v is velocity. Newton's second law gives: ma = -kx - bv, or a = -(k/m)*x - (b/m)*v. The system loses energy over time due to damping, causing oscillation amplitude to decrease exponentially. Acceleration must still be the derivative of velocity, and velocity the derivative of position.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Two coupled integrations (the physics core)

  • position is a stock whose only flow, change_in_position, equals velocity. This enforces that velocity is the derivative of position.
  • velocity is a stock whose only flow, change_in_velocity, equals acceleration. This enforces that acceleration is the derivative of velocity.
  • Both flows are bidirectional (not uniflows) because the mass moves and accelerates in both directions during oscillation.

Forces and Newton's second law

  • spring_force = negative stiffness times displacement (Hooke's law) — the restoring, balancing loop that creates oscillation.
  • damping_force = negative damping coefficient times velocity — friction always opposing motion.
  • net_force sums the two, and acceleration = net force / mass, exactly Newton's second law, equivalent to a = -(k/m)x - (b/m)v.

Named parameters instead of buried constants spring_constant, damping_coefficient, mass, initial_position, and initial_velocity are separate variables, so every physical value is explicit and adjustable rather than hard-coded inside a formula.

Energy check total_mechanical_energy is an auxiliary (a simple algebraic sum of elastic potential and kinetic energy), not a stock, because it is calculated from the state variables rather than accumulated. With damping present it decays steadily, and oscillation amplitude decays exponentially — the expected behavior of a dissipative system.

Formulation safeguards applied

  • No flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow of the same stock; each stock has a single net flow.
  • Stocks are used only for true integrations (position, velocity); the derived quantities (acceleration, forces, energy) are auxiliaries.
  • Because this is a lightly damped oscillator, the model uses 4th-order Runge–Kutta with a small time step so numerical error does not artificially add or remove energy (Euler with a coarse step would spuriously damp or amplify the oscillation).

testParams.name: Spring-Mass System with Large Displacement
testParams.prompt: Create a System Dynamics model of a spring-mass system with a large initial displacement. The model must include variables named 'position' (displacement from equilibrium in meters), 'velocity' (velocity in meters/second), and 'acceleration' (acceleration in meters/second²). The model should obey Hooke's law and Newton's second law.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a spring-mass system model that accurately represents a spring-mass system with a large initial displacement and follows physical laws.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: For larger displacements, Hooke's law F = -kx still applies (assuming the spring remains in the linear regime). Newton's second law: F = ma = -kx, so a = -(k/m)*x. The system exhibits simple harmonic motion regardless of amplitude (unlike a pendulum where nonlinearity appears). Energy conservation: total energy E = (1/2)*m*v² + (1/2)*k*x² remains constant. Maximum velocity occurs at equilibrium (x=0), and maximum displacement occurs when v=0.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

The model is the classic two-stock oscillator (a balancing loop with delay, which is what produces oscillation rather than smooth goal-seeking):

  • position — a stock, because displacement accumulates velocity. Initialized at a named initial_displacement (10 m, a large amplitude).
  • velocity — a stock, because velocity accumulates acceleration. Initialized at initial_velocity (released from rest).
  • acceleration — an auxiliary, computed as -(spring_constant/mass) * position. This is Hooke's law (F = -kx) substituted into Newton's second law (F = ma), so no separate force variable is needed and the restoring relationship stays exactly linear at any amplitude.

The two stocks are linked by flows that are pure definitions: change_in_position = velocity and change_in_velocity = acceleration. Both flows are bidirectional (not uniflows), since the mass legitimately moves and accelerates in both directions each cycle.

Why it obeys the physics

  • The negative feedback from position to acceleration back through velocity to position is the restoring loop; because velocity is an intervening accumulation, the loop overshoots and produces undamped simple harmonic motion.
  • No damping or driving term is included, so total energy is conserved.
  • angular_frequency = sqrt(k/m) is included so the simulated period can be checked against theory; note it contains no amplitude term, confirming that a large displacement does not change the period (unlike a pendulum, where the restoring term would be sin of the angle).

Energy checks

kinetic_energy (m·v²/2), potential_energy (k·x²/2), and total_energy are auxiliaries — not stocks — because they are algebraic functions of the state variables, not independent accumulations. Treating total energy as a stock would be a formulation error. Total energy should trace a flat line; kinetic energy peaks at x = 0 and potential energy peaks where v = 0, as required.

Numerical settings

Conservative oscillators are sensitive to integration error: Euler integration artificially pumps energy into the system and the amplitude grows. The model therefore uses RK4 integration with a small time step (0.01 s) relative to the natural period (~3.1 s), which keeps total energy flat and the amplitude constant over the 20-second run.

All parameters (stiffness, mass, initial conditions) are named variables, so no physical constants are buried inside equations.

testParams.name: Isothermal Gas Process
testParams.prompt: Create a System Dynamics model of an isothermal process where gas temperature remains constant while volume changes. The model must include variables named 'pressure' (pressure in Pascals), 'volume' (volume in cubic meters), and 'temperature' (absolute temperature in Kelvin). The model should obey the ideal gas law (PV = nRT).

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a gas system model that accurately represents an isothermal process where gas temperature remains constant while volume changes and follows the ideal gas law.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: For an ideal gas, PV = nRT, where P is pressure, V is volume, n is moles, R is gas constant, and T is temperature. In an isothermal process, temperature T is constant, so PV = constant. If volume increases, pressure must decrease proportionally to maintain PV = nRT. If volume decreases, pressure increases. The relationship is P = nRT/V, showing inverse proportionality. All variables (P, V, T) must remain positive throughout the process.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure chosen

  • volume is the only genuine accumulation being driven: it is a stock changed solely by a single bidirectional flow, volume expansion rate. That flow is written as a fraction of the current volume (a named fractional expansion rate), which guarantees volume decays or grows smoothly and can never hit or pass zero — an essential safeguard because volume sits in the denominator of the gas law.
  • temperature is a stock whose net flow, temperature change rate, is explicitly zero. This makes the isothermal assumption visible structure rather than a hidden assumption, and guarantees the temperature holds its positive initial reservoir value for the entire run.
  • pressure is an auxiliary, not a stock. Pressure is instantaneously determined by the state of the gas, so it is computed algebraically from the rearranged ideal gas law, P = nRT/V, using protected division. Treating pressure as a stock with its own flows would be a classic formulation error: it would let pressure drift away from the value the gas law requires.
  • moles and gas constant are separate named constants so no physical constant is buried inside an equation.

Verification built in

  • pressure volume product multiplies pressure by volume; because temperature and moles are constant, this diagnostic must remain flat at nRT for the whole simulation. If it moves, the model is wrong.
  • work rate, work done by gas, heat transfer rate, and heat absorbed from reservoir close the energy account: heat in is set equal to work out at every instant, which is exactly the physical mechanism that keeps internal energy — and therefore temperature — unchanged. Cumulative heat and cumulative work should track each other identically.

Feedback present

The model contains a balancing loop: as volume rises, pressure falls, which reduces the rate of work done and hence the heat that must be drawn from the reservoir. This is the self-limiting behavior characteristic of isothermal expansion, where work grows only logarithmically with the volume ratio.
supportingInfo.title: Isothermal Gas Model With Energy Verification

testParams.name: Isobaric Gas Process
testParams.prompt: Create a System Dynamics model of an isobaric process where gas pressure remains constant while temperature changes. The model must include variables named 'pressure' (pressure in Pascals), 'volume' (volume in cubic meters), and 'temperature' (absolute temperature in Kelvin). The model should obey the ideal gas law (PV = nRT).

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a gas system model that accurately represents an isobaric process where gas pressure remains constant while temperature changes and follows the ideal gas law.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: For an ideal gas at constant pressure, V/T = nR/P = constant (Charles's Law). If temperature increases, volume must increase proportionally to maintain the ideal gas law PV = nRT. If temperature decreases, volume decreases. The relationship is V = (nR/P)*T. Pressure remains constant while volume and temperature vary together. Temperature must be measured in absolute scale (Kelvin) and cannot be negative.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure chosen

One true state variable. In an isobaric process the only independent accumulation is thermal energy, represented here as the temperature stock (Kelvin, starting at a strictly positive initial value). It changes solely through the heating rate flow, which is heat supplied per second divided by the total constant-pressure heat capacity. That flow is bidirectional (not a uniflow) so that removing heat correctly cools the gas.

Volume is an auxiliary, not a stock. This is the key formulation point. Because pressure is held constant, the ideal gas law fixes volume instantaneously as volume = moles * gas_constant * temperature / pressure, i.e. Charles's Law V/T = nR/P = constant. Making volume a stock with its own independent flows would let it drift away from the ideal gas law and would double-count the state of the system; as an algebraic auxiliary it satisfies PV = nRT exactly at every time step.

Pressure is a fixed parameter, the defining condition of the isobaric process, and it feeds volume negatively (it sits in the denominator of nRT/P).

No hard-coded constants inside equations. The universal gas constant, the amount of gas, the molar constant-pressure heat capacity, the applied pressure, the heat input and the initial temperature are each their own named variable, so every equation reads as a plain-language statement of physics.

Energy bookkeeping. An expansion-work rate (pressure times the rate of volume change, obtained by differentiating V = nRT/P at constant pressure) accumulates into a work done by gas stock. This is a legitimate accumulation and makes the isobaric energy balance visible: part of the heat added raises temperature, part leaves as expansion work, which is exactly why the constant-pressure molar heat capacity is used rather than the constant-volume one.

Reinforcing/balancing behavior. With a steady heat input the temperature ramps linearly and the volume ramps with it in strict proportion, the signature behavior of an isobaric process; no feedback loop distorts the gas law because volume is derived rather than accumulated.

testParams.prompt: Create a System Dynamics model of an isochoric process where gas volume remains constant while temperature changes. The model must include variables named 'pressure' (pressure in Pascals), 'volume' (volume in cubic meters), and 'temperature' (absolute temperature in Kelvin). The model should obey the ideal gas law (PV = nRT).

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a gas system model that accurately represents an isochoric process where gas volume remains constant while temperature changes and follows the ideal gas law.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: For an ideal gas at constant volume, P/T = nR/V = constant (Gay-Lussac's Law). If temperature increases, pressure must increase proportionally to maintain PV = nRT. If temperature decreases, pressure decreases. The relationship is P = (nR/V)*T. Volume remains constant while pressure and temperature vary together. This represents heating or cooling a gas in a rigid container.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure chosen

Temperature is the only accumulation. Heat delivered to a sealed rigid container accumulates as internal energy, so temperature is modeled as a stock driven by a single bidirectional flow, temperature change rate. That rate comes from the first law at constant volume: heat input divided by thermal mass (moles × molar heat capacity at constant volume). No work term appears because the volume cannot change.

Volume is a constant, not a stock. In an isochoric process the vessel is rigid, so volume is an algebraic constant fed by container volume. Making it a stock with flows would wrongly imply it can accumulate change.

Pressure is algebraic, not a stock. With n, R and V fixed, the ideal gas law forces pressure = moles × R × temperature / volume. Pressure has no independent dynamics — it is instantaneously slaved to temperature, which is exactly Gay-Lussac's law (P/T = nR/V = constant). Modeling pressure as a stock would have allowed it to drift away from the state equation.

Constants abstracted

Every physical/empirical number was pulled out into its own named variable — universal gas constant (8.314 J/mol·K), molar heat capacity constant volume (Cv ≈ 5/2 R for a diatomic gas), moles of gas, container volume, initial temperature, and nominal heat input rate — so no arbitrary constant sits inside a structural equation.

Verification variables

  • ideal gas law check computes PV/(nRT) and must stay exactly 1 for the whole run, proving the state equation holds.
  • pressure to temperature ratio must stay flat at nR/V, proving the isochoric (Gay-Lussac) proportionality.
  • internal energy (n·Cv·T) makes explicit that all added heat becomes internal energy since no expansion work is done.

Behavior

With constant heating power, temperature rises linearly and pressure rises linearly in lockstep; setting nominal heat input rate negative cools the gas and pressure falls proportionally. The flow is left bidirectional (not a uniflow) precisely so cooling can be simulated.
supportingInfo.title: Isochoric Gas Model With Ideal Law

variables.name: temperature
variables.documentation: Absolute temperature of the gas in Kelvin. It is a stock because thermal energy added to the gas accumulates in the rigid container, raising temperature over time. Initialized at ambient temperature.

variables.name: initial temperature
variables.documentation: Starting absolute temperature of the gas (room temperature, ~300 K). Named separately so no arbitrary number appears inside a structural equation.

variables.name: temperature change rate
variables.documentation: Rate of temperature change from the first law of thermodynamics at constant volume: dT/dt = Qdot / (n * Cv). Because no work is done (volume fixed), all heat goes into internal energy and hence temperature. It is bidirectional (uniflow = false) because the gas can be cooled as well as heated.

variables.name: heat input rate
variables.documentation: Net rate of heat transfer into the gas through the rigid container walls. Positive values heat the gas, negative values cool it. This is the external driver of the isochoric process.

variables.name: nominal heat input rate
variables.documentation: Constant setting of the heater/cooler power applied to the container. Change its sign to simulate cooling instead of heating.

variables.name: molar heat capacity constant volume
variables.documentation: Molar heat capacity of the gas at constant volume (Cv). For a diatomic ideal gas Cv is about 5/2 R = 20.8 J/(mol K). It converts heat added into temperature rise.

variables.name: moles of gas
variables.documentation: Fixed amount of gas sealed in the rigid container (n in PV = nRT). It is constant because the container is closed.

variables.name: universal gas constant
variables.documentation: The universal (ideal) gas constant R = 8.314 J/(mol K), abstracted into its own named variable rather than embedded in equations.

variables.name: volume
variables.documentation: Volume occupied by the gas in cubic meters. In an isochoric (constant volume) process the gas is held in a rigid container, so volume is an unchanging constant, not an accumulation with flows. It appears in the ideal gas law as the denominator determining pressure.

variables.name: container volume
variables.documentation: Fixed internal volume of the rigid vessel (10 liters). Defined as its own parameter so the isochoric constraint is explicit and adjustable.

variables.name: pressure
variables.documentation: Absolute gas pressure in Pascals, computed algebraically from the ideal gas law P = nRT/V. Pressure is not an independent accumulation: with n, R and V fixed it is instantaneously determined by temperature, which is exactly Gay-Lussac's law (P proportional to T at constant volume). The // operator protects against division by zero.

variables.name: pressure to temperature ratio
variables.documentation: Diagnostic check of Gay-Lussac's law: P/T should remain constant and equal to nR/V throughout the isochoric process. Useful for verifying the model behaves for the right reasons.

variables.name: ideal gas law check
variables.documentation: Dimensionless validity check equal to PV/(nRT). It should remain exactly 1 at all times, confirming the model obeys the ideal gas law.

variables.name: internal energy
variables.documentation: Internal energy of the ideal gas, U = n * Cv * T. Shown to make explicit that in an isochoric process all heat added becomes internal energy because no expansion work is performed.

testParams.name: Population Growth variable documentation
testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete stock-and-flow model of population growth. Make sure that every variable in the model is clearly documented, describing what it represents and its role within the system.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how a population grows and shrinks over time so I can project its size into the future.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A population increases through births and decreases through deaths. The number of births and deaths in a period both scale with the current size of the population. A fractional birth rate and a fractional death rate control how quickly each process happens.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how a population grows and shrinks over time so I can project its size into the future.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model structure

One stock, two flows. Population is the only accumulation in the system: it can change solely through its inflow (births) and its outflow (deaths). Its equation is just an initial value, supplied by the separate parameter initial population so the starting condition is explicit and easy to vary when projecting scenarios.

Flows scale with the stock. Both births and deaths are the product of the current Population and a fractional rate. This captures the stated behaviour that the number of events in a period is proportional to how many people there are. Both are marked as one-directional flows, since neither births nor deaths can be negative.

Two named rate parameters. fractional birth rate and fractional death rate are separate constants rather than numbers buried inside the flow equations, so the two driving assumptions of the projection are visible and adjustable.

Feedback structure

  • Population → births → Population is a reinforcing loop: more people produce more births, which produce still more people. This is the engine of exponential growth.
  • Population → deaths → Population is a balancing loop: more people produce more deaths, which drain the stock.

Which loop dominates depends entirely on the relative size of the two fractional rates. If births exceed deaths the reinforcing loop wins and the population grows exponentially; if deaths exceed births the balancing loop wins and the population decays exponentially toward zero; if they are equal the population holds steady.

Diagnostic

net population growth rate is included as an auxiliary (not a stock, since it is a simple algebraic calculation, not an accumulation). It reports net change as a fraction of current size, making loop dominance immediately visible. Safe division protects against a zero population.

Settings

The model runs 100 years with a quarterly time step, which is fine enough that Euler integration tracks the exponential accurately.
supportingInfo.title: Exponential Population Stock With Birth Death Flows

variables.name: Population
variables.documentation: The stock of people in the region being studied. It is the central accumulation of the model: it can only change through the flows of births (adding people) and deaths (removing people). Its initial value is set by the initial population parameter.

variables.name: initial population
variables.documentation: The size of the population at the start of the simulation. It is separated out as its own named parameter so the starting condition can be changed easily when projecting different scenarios.

variables.name: births
variables.documentation: The number of people added to the population per year. Births scale with the current size of the population because more people means more potential parents; multiplying the population by the fractional birth rate gives the number of new arrivals per year. This flow creates the reinforcing loop that drives exponential growth. It is a uniflow because births can never be negative.

variables.name: deaths
variables.documentation: The number of people removed from the population per year. Deaths scale with the current size of the population because a larger population exposes more people to mortality; multiplying the population by the fractional death rate gives annual deaths. This flow creates the balancing loop that drains the stock. It is a uniflow because deaths can never be negative.

variables.name: fractional birth rate
variables.documentation: The fraction of the existing population that gives rise to a new birth each year. It controls how quickly the reinforcing birth process operates. Held constant here so the model produces a clean projection of exponential behaviour.

variables.name: fractional death rate
variables.documentation: The fraction of the existing population that dies each year. It controls how quickly the balancing death process operates. Held constant here so the model produces a clean projection of exponential behaviour.

variables.name: net population growth rate
variables.documentation: The fractional rate at which the population is expanding or contracting each year, computed as the net change (births minus deaths) divided by the current population. It is a diagnostic indicator that makes it easy to see whether the reinforcing birth loop or the balancing death loop dominates. The safe-division operator prevents an error if the population reaches zero.

testParams.name: Savings Account variable documentation
testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete stock-and-flow model of savings account. Make sure that every variable in the model is clearly documented, describing what it represents and its role within the system.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how the balance of a savings account changes over time as money is added, earns interest, and is withdrawn.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A savings account has a balance that grows when the account holder makes deposits and when interest accrues, and shrinks when the account holder makes withdrawals. Interest earned each period is a fraction (the interest rate) of the current balance.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how the balance of a savings account changes over time as money is added, earns interest, and is withdrawn.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

One stock: Balance is the only accumulation — money can enter or leave the account only through its flows, so nothing else in the model is a stock.

Two inflows, one outflow:

  • Deposits — money the saver adds, driven by the external Deposit Rate.
  • Interest Earned — the bank's credit, computed as Balance × Interest Rate.
  • Withdrawals — money the saver removes, driven by the external Withdrawal Rate.

Each flow is assigned to exactly one side of the stock (never both inflow and outflow), and all three are one-directional (uniflows), since deposits, interest payments, and withdrawals cannot physically run backwards.

Parameters were pulled out as named variables — Initial Balance, Deposit Rate, Withdrawal Rate, and Interest Rate — so no bare numbers appear inside any flow equation and each assumption can be inspected or changed on its own.

Feedback behavior

The Balance → Interest Earned → Balance link forms a reinforcing loop (compounding): the more money in the account, the more interest it earns, which adds still more money. This drives exponential growth whenever deposits plus interest exceed withdrawals. There is no balancing loop in the basic account, so behavior is either exponential growth or, if withdrawals dominate, accelerating depletion toward zero.

Formulation checks applied

  • Net Cash Flow is a simple sum of the flows, so it is modeled as an auxiliary, not a stock — treating a running total like that as an accumulation would double-count the account.
  • No conditional logic or hard-coded constants appear in the equations; interest uses a plain product of the balance and the rate.
  • The time step is small relative to the compounding period so the interest calculation stays accurate.
supportingInfo.title: Savings Balance With Compounding Interest Loop

variables.name: Balance
variables.documentation: The amount of money currently held in the savings account. It is the single accumulation in the system: it rises with deposits and accrued interest and falls with withdrawals. Because it is an accumulation that can only change through its flows, it is modeled as a stock.

variables.name: Initial Balance
variables.documentation: The money already in the account at the start of the simulation. It sets the starting value of the Balance stock and is separated out as its own variable so the opening amount is explicit and easy to change.

variables.name: Deposits
variables.documentation: The rate at which the account holder puts new money into the account. It is an inflow to Balance and is set equal to the planned deposit rate. It is a uniflow because a deposit can only add money; taking money out is represented separately as a withdrawal.

variables.name: Deposit Rate
variables.documentation: The account holder's planned saving contribution per year. It is an external decision by the saver rather than something generated inside the account, so it is a constant input that drives the Deposits flow.

variables.name: Withdrawals
variables.documentation: The rate at which the account holder takes money out of the account. It is an outflow from Balance and is set equal to the planned withdrawal rate. It is a uniflow because a withdrawal can only remove money; putting money in is captured by the Deposits flow.

variables.name: Withdrawal Rate
variables.documentation: The account holder's planned spending out of savings per year. Like the deposit rate, it is an external behavioral choice, so it is modeled as a constant input that drives the Withdrawals flow.

variables.name: Interest Earned
variables.documentation: The money credited to the account by the bank each period. It is an inflow to Balance calculated as the interest rate applied to the current balance, which creates the reinforcing compounding loop: a bigger balance earns more interest, which makes the balance bigger still. It is a uniflow because a positive interest rate can only add money.

variables.name: Interest Rate
variables.documentation: The fraction of the current balance paid by the bank as interest per year. It is set by the bank, so it is treated as a constant parameter, and it converts the balance into an interest inflow.

variables.name: Net Cash Flow
variables.documentation: The overall rate of change of the account, computed algebraically as all inflows minus all outflows. It is an auxiliary (not a stock) because it is a simple sum used for reporting whether the account is growing or shrinking at any moment.

testParams.name: Inventory Management variable documentation
testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete stock-and-flow model of inventory management. Make sure that every variable in the model is clearly documented, describing what it represents and its role within the system.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how a store's inventory of a product fluctuates as it is restocked and sold.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A store holds an inventory of a product. Inventory rises as new units are produced or delivered and falls as units are sold to customers. The store tries to keep inventory near a desired coverage of expected sales, ordering more when inventory is low. Sales depend on customer demand, which can be limited by how much inventory is available.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how a store's inventory of a product fluctuates as it is restocked and sold.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure built

Two stocks, three flows. Inventory accumulates arrivals (Production) and is drained by Sales. A second stock, Work In Process, holds units that have been ordered or started but not yet delivered; it is filled by Production Start Rate and emptied by Production. This supply line is essential — without it restocking would be instantaneous and inventory could not fluctuate.

Inventory control balancing loop. The store forecasts sales with a smoothed average of demand (Expected Sales, using SMOOTH rather than a delay function, since a forecast is an average, not a time shift). Desired Inventory is that forecast times Desired Coverage. The difference (Inventory Gap) is closed over Inventory Adjustment Time and added to the replacement of expected sales to give Desired Production. Because the correction acts through a delivery delay, this balancing-loop-with-delay archetype generates overshoot and oscillation — exactly the fluctuation behavior of interest.

Demand-side constraint on sales. Maximum Shipment Rate is stock divided by Minimum Order Processing Time; compared with demand it gives dimensionless Inventory Adequacy, which feeds a graphical Order Fulfillment Ratio passing through (1,1) so that adequate stock yields full service and short stock throttles sales. Sales is demand times this ratio, capturing that demand can be limited by availability.

Test input. A time-based multiplier (Demand Variation) steps demand up 20% at week 10 so the restocking dynamics are visible.

Formulation safeguards

  • No conditional logic; the availability constraint is handled with a graphical function, and protected division (//) guards the adequacy ratio against zero demand.
  • All numeric parameters are named variables (delays, coverage, base demand); stock initial values are expressed in terms of those parameters so the model starts in equilibrium.
  • Production Start Rate, Production and Sales are marked one-directional, preventing physically impossible negative ordering, delivery or selling. Stock-adjustment flows never appear as both inflow and outflow of the same stock.
  • Aggregate calculations such as Desired Inventory and Expected Sales are auxiliaries, not stocks, since they are algebraic results rather than accumulations.
supportingInfo.title: Inventory Restocking Model With Supply Delay

variables.name: Inventory
variables.documentation: The physical stock of finished units held in the store. It accumulates units arriving from production or delivery and is depleted by units sold to customers. It is initialized in balance with normal demand, holding exactly the desired number of weeks of coverage.

variables.name: Work In Process
variables.documentation: Units that have been ordered or started into production but have not yet arrived at the store. This stock creates the supply-line delay that is the main source of inventory oscillation. It is initialized at the amount needed to sustain normal throughput over the production delay.

variables.name: Production Start Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which new units are ordered from the supplier or released into production. It follows the desired production rate but can never be negative, since orders once placed cannot be un-placed.

variables.name: Production
variables.documentation: The rate at which units complete production or delivery and enter store inventory. Modeled as a first-order delay of the work in process stock, representing the average time between ordering and arrival.

variables.name: Sales
variables.documentation: The rate at which units actually leave the store into customers' hands. Equals customer demand multiplied by the fraction of demand that can be filled from available inventory, so sales are constrained when stock is short. Sales can never be negative.

variables.name: Customer Demand
variables.documentation: The rate at which customers want to buy the product, independent of whether the store can supply it. It is the normal demand level scaled by a time-varying multiplier so the model can be tested with a demand shift.

variables.name: Base Demand
variables.documentation: The normal, reference level of customer demand for the product. Used both to scale demand variation and to set consistent initial conditions for the stocks.

variables.name: Demand Variation
variables.documentation: A dimensionless multiplier on normal demand driven by simulation time. It equals one until week 10 and then steps up by twenty percent, providing the disturbance that reveals how inventory fluctuates as the store restocks.

variables.name: Expected Sales
variables.documentation: The store's forecast of future sales, formed as an exponentially smoothed (moving average) view of recent customer demand. SMOOTH is used because managers average recent experience rather than reacting to every momentary change.

variables.name: Forecast Averaging Time
variables.documentation: The time constant over which recent demand is averaged to form the sales forecast. Longer averaging makes the forecast steadier but slower to recognize a real change in demand.

variables.name: Desired Coverage
variables.documentation: The number of weeks of expected sales the store wants to hold on the shelf as a service buffer. It converts the sales forecast into a target inventory level.

variables.name: Desired Inventory
variables.documentation: The target stock level, equal to the desired weeks of coverage times expected sales. It is the goal of the inventory control balancing loop.

variables.name: Inventory Gap
variables.documentation: The shortfall (or surplus, when negative) of actual inventory relative to the target. It is the error signal that drives ordering above or below the replacement rate.

variables.name: Inventory Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: The time over which the store intends to close any gap between actual and desired inventory. Shorter adjustment times mean more aggressive ordering, which combined with the delivery delay produces stronger oscillation.

variables.name: Desired Production
variables.documentation: The order rate the store would like: enough to replace expected sales plus a correction to close the inventory gap over the adjustment time. This anchor-and-adjust rule is the core inventory control policy.

variables.name: Production Delay
variables.documentation: The average time between placing an order or starting production and the units arriving in store inventory. This delay is what makes the balancing inventory loop overshoot and fluctuate rather than settle immediately.

variables.name: Minimum Order Processing Time
variables.documentation: The shortest time in which the store could physically clear its entire shelf stock. It sets the maximum possible shipment rate given available inventory.

variables.name: Maximum Shipment Rate
variables.documentation: The largest rate at which units could be sold given the stock on hand and the minimum time needed to process an order. It is the physical capacity constraint on sales.

variables.name: Inventory Adequacy
variables.documentation: The ratio of the maximum feasible shipment rate to customer demand. A value of one or more means stock is sufficient to serve all demand; below one signals a stockout condition. Protected division avoids dividing by zero demand.

variables.name: Order Fulfillment Ratio
variables.documentation: The fraction of customer demand the store can actually satisfy, as a function of inventory adequacy. It equals one when stock is adequate (input of one gives output of one) and falls toward zero as inventory becomes insufficient, capturing how availability limits sales.

testParams.name: Infectious Disease Spread variable documentation
testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete stock-and-flow model of infectious disease spread. Make sure that every variable in the model is clearly documented, describing what it represents and its role within the system.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how an infectious disease spreads through a population over the course of an outbreak.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In a classic epidemic model a population is divided into people who are susceptible, people who are currently infected, and people who have recovered. Susceptible people become infected through contact with infected people, at a rate that depends on the contact rate and the infectivity of the disease. Infected people recover after an average duration of illness, moving into the recovered group.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how an infectious disease spreads through a population over the course of an outbreak.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure built

Three stocks (the SIR chain): Susceptible Population, Infected Population, and Recovered Population. People flow one way down the chain, so each flow is attached to exactly one side of each stock — Infection Rate drains susceptibles and fills the infected; Recovery Rate drains the infected and fills the recovered. Both flows are one-directional (people cannot un-catch or un-recover from a disease), so they are constrained to be non-negative.

Two flows:

  • Infection Rate = contacts per infected person per day × probability of transmission per contact × number of infected × the share of contacts that land on a susceptible person (susceptible ÷ total population). No arbitrary constants are buried in the formula; contact rate, infectivity, and population size are all named, adjustable variables.
  • Recovery Rate = infected ÷ average duration of illness, the standard first-order drain in which the average person stays sick for the illness duration.

Auxiliaries: Contact Rate, Infectivity, and Average Duration of Illness are the policy- and pathogen-relevant parameters. Initial Population and Initial Infected seed the stocks, with the seed cases subtracted from susceptibles so no one is counted twice.

Total Population is an auxiliary, not a stock, because it is a simple algebraic sum of the three states rather than something that accumulates through flows of its own. Making it a stock would be a formulation error.

Feedback behavior

The model contains the two loops that generate the classic epidemic curve: a reinforcing contagion loop (more infected → more infectious contacts → more new infections → more infected) that drives the exponential take-off, and a balancing depletion loop (more infections → fewer susceptibles → smaller share of contacts with vulnerable people → fewer new infections) that, together with recovery, turns the curve over and ends the outbreak. This is the limits to growth archetype: the epidemic grows until it exhausts its own resource, the pool of susceptible people.

The run is set for 200 days with a small time step so the fast exponential growth phase is integrated accurately.
supportingInfo.title: Classic SIR Epidemic Stock and Flow Model

variables.name: Susceptible Population
variables.documentation: The number of people who have not yet had the disease and can still catch it. It is a stock because it accumulates (in this simple outbreak model it only drains) through the flow of new infections. It starts as everyone in the population except the initial handful of infected people.

variables.name: Infected Population
variables.documentation: The number of people currently sick and contagious. It is a stock because people accumulate in this state: they enter when they become infected and leave when they recover. This stock drives the contagion process, creating the reinforcing loop that produces epidemic growth.

variables.name: Recovered Population
variables.documentation: The number of people who have had the disease, are no longer contagious, and are assumed immune. It accumulates everyone who leaves the infected stock. It starts empty at the beginning of the outbreak.

variables.name: Infection Rate
variables.documentation: The number of people per day who catch the disease. It is calculated as the contacts each infected person makes per day, times the probability that a contact transmits the disease, times the fraction of those contacts that are with susceptible people (Susceptible/Total Population). It moves people from the susceptible stock to the infected stock and can never be negative.

variables.name: Recovery Rate
variables.documentation: The number of people per day who stop being contagious. Modeled as a first-order draining process: on average each infected person stays sick for the average duration of illness, so a constant fraction of the infected stock recovers each day. It moves people from infected to recovered and can never be negative.

variables.name: Contact Rate
variables.documentation: The average number of other people each infected person comes into potentially disease-transmitting contact with per day. It represents the social mixing intensity of the population and is one of the two levers (with infectivity) that determine how fast contagion spreads.

variables.name: Infectivity
variables.documentation: The probability that a single contact between an infected person and a susceptible person actually transmits the disease. It captures the biological transmissibility of the pathogen, separate from how often people meet.

variables.name: Average Duration of Illness
variables.documentation: The average length of time a person remains infectious. It sets how long an infected person can keep spreading the disease before moving into the recovered stock; longer durations mean more onward transmission per case.

variables.name: Total Population
variables.documentation: The whole population at risk, computed as the simple sum of the three stocks. It is an auxiliary (an algebraic sum), not a stock, because it does not accumulate through flows of its own. It is used to work out what fraction of an infected person's contacts are with people who are still susceptible.

variables.name: Initial Population
variables.documentation: The size of the community at the start of the outbreak. It is used to initialize the susceptible stock and sets the scale of the epidemic.

variables.name: Initial Infected
variables.documentation: The number of index cases that seed the outbreak. It initializes the infected stock and is subtracted from the initial population to initialize the susceptible stock, so no one is double counted.

testParams.name: Software Project Rework variable documentation
testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete stock-and-flow model of software project rework. Make sure that every variable in the model is clearly documented, describing what it represents and its role within the system.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand why software projects run late even when the team works hard, and how undiscovered errors and schedule pressure feed on each other over the life of a project.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A software project has a fixed scope of work. Tasks begin in a backlog of work still to be done and move to a pool of completed work as the team finishes them at a work rate. The work rate depends on the number of developers and their productivity. Not all completed work is actually correct: a fraction contains defects and becomes undiscovered rework instead of being truly finished. Undiscovered rework is not visible to the team until it is found during testing, after a discovery delay, at which point it flows back into the backlog of work to be done. As the deadline approaches with work remaining, schedule pressure rises. Higher schedule pressure pushes developers to work faster, raising the work rate, but it also raises the fraction of work done incorrectly (haste makes waste), which generates still more undiscovered rework and further delays the project. Sustained overtime also erodes productivity as developers fatigue.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand why software projects run late even when the team works hard, and how undiscovered errors and schedule pressure feed on each other over the life of a project.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure built

Three core stocks form the classic rework cycle:

  • Work to Do — the visible backlog, drained by the work rate and refilled by discovered rework.
  • Work Done — only work completed correctly accumulates here, so it is the honest measure of progress.
  • Undiscovered Rework — work believed finished but defective, invisible until testing surfaces it after a discovery delay.

The work rate is a single outflow from the backlog; it is then split into a correct completion flow (into Work Done) and a defect generation flow (into Undiscovered Rework). No flow ever appears as both an inflow and an outflow of the same stock.

Why projects run late despite hard work — the feedback loops captured:

  1. Rework loop (reinforcing): Defects → Undiscovered Rework → discovery → backlog grows → less time per task → more pressure → more defects. Because the hidden pool is invisible, the visible backlog looks like it is shrinking on schedule, then work reappears late in the project — the "90% done for 90% of the time" signature.
  2. Haste makes waste (reinforcing): Schedule pressure raises the error multiplier, which raises the defect fraction, which feeds the rework loop. Working faster buys short-term throughput and pays for it with long-term rework.
  3. Overtime/fatigue erosion (reinforcing): Pressure raises work intensity; a smoothed Sustained Work Intensity stock accumulates that intensity so that only prolonged overtime causes fatigue, which cuts productivity, which slows the work rate and raises pressure again.
  4. Balancing: Pressure genuinely does increase intensity and throughput — but the effect saturates, so the reinforcing loops eventually dominate. This is a Fixes that Fail / Growth and Underinvestment pattern: the quick fix (push harder) undermines the very capability it needs.

Formulation choices:

  • Total Work Remaining and Fraction Complete are auxiliaries (simple sums/ratios), not stocks.
  • Fatigue is handled by a smoothing stock rather than a delay, since delays shift time without averaging.
  • All numeric parameters are named variables (scope, developers, normal productivity, deadline, normal defect fraction, discovery delay, fatigue adjustment time, minimum task time, minimum time remaining) — no constants are buried inside equations.
  • Time remaining is floored so pressure stays finite past the deadline, and the work rate is capped by available backlog so it can never go negative or overshoot.
  • All three graphical functions pass through (1, 1) so that normal input gives normal behaviour and deviations read directly as multipliers.

The deadline is set tighter than the scope-at-normal-pace requires, so the model starts under mild pressure and lets the loops generate the late-project slippage endogenously.
supportingInfo.title: Rework Cycle Drives Software Project Slippage

variables.name: Work to Do
variables.documentation: The backlog of tasks the team still believes it must complete. It starts at the full project scope, is drained as developers complete tasks, and is refilled when defective work is discovered in testing and must be redone. This stock is the visible measure of remaining work that drives schedule pressure.

variables.name: Work Done
variables.documentation: Tasks that have been completed correctly and will never need to be redone. Only genuinely correct work accumulates here, so the project is truly finished when this stock reaches the total project scope.

variables.name: Undiscovered Rework
variables.documentation: Work that the team believes is finished but actually contains defects. It is invisible to the team and therefore does not reduce perceived remaining work, which is the core reason projects appear on track and then slip late. It empties only when testing reveals the defects.

variables.name: Sustained Work Intensity
variables.documentation: A smoothed measure of how hard the team has been working relative to normal over recent weeks. Fatigue is caused by sustained rather than momentary overtime, so this accumulating index (not the instantaneous intensity) drives the erosion of productivity.

variables.name: Work Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which tasks are being processed by the team. It equals the team's potential output unless there is not enough work left in the backlog to keep everyone busy, in which case it is limited by the available work.

variables.name: Correct Completion Rate
variables.documentation: The portion of processed work that is actually done right and therefore permanently adds to completed work. It is the work rate multiplied by the share of work done correctly.

variables.name: Defect Generation Rate
variables.documentation: The portion of processed work that contains defects and silently becomes undiscovered rework. It is the work rate multiplied by the fraction of work done incorrectly, so haste directly manufactures hidden future work.

variables.name: Rework Discovery Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which hidden defects are found during testing and returned to the backlog. Modeled as a simple draining of the hidden rework pool over the average discovery delay, representing the fact that errors surface only gradually.

variables.name: Change in Sustained Work Intensity
variables.documentation: Adjusts the sustained work intensity index toward the current work intensity over the fatigue adjustment time. It is bidirectional because intensity can build up during crunch periods and decay again when pressure eases.

variables.name: Total Project Scope
variables.documentation: The fixed amount of work the project must deliver, in tasks. It sets the initial backlog and the benchmark against which completion is measured.

variables.name: Developers
variables.documentation: The number of developers assigned to the project, held constant here so that the dynamics come from rework and pressure rather than from staffing changes.

variables.name: Normal Productivity
variables.documentation: Tasks a rested developer completes per week under normal working conditions. It is the reference level against which fatigue effects are measured.

variables.name: Productivity
variables.documentation: Actual output per developer per week after accounting for fatigue from sustained overtime. It shows how working long hours for long periods erodes the value of each hour worked.

variables.name: Potential Work Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which the team could process tasks given its size, current productivity, and how intensely it is working in response to schedule pressure.

variables.name: Normal Work Rate
variables.documentation: The output the team would produce working normal hours at normal productivity. It is the reference throughput used to judge whether the required pace is reasonable.

variables.name: Deadline
variables.documentation: The committed delivery date measured in weeks from project start. It is deliberately shorter than the time the work would take at normal pace, which is what creates schedule pressure.

variables.name: Minimum Time Remaining
variables.documentation: A floor on the time remaining used so that pressure stays finite once the deadline passes. It represents the shortest horizon management will ever plan against.

variables.name: Time Remaining
variables.documentation: Time left until the deadline, floored at a minimum value so it never reaches zero or turns negative. Shrinking time remaining with work still outstanding is what drives pressure upward.

variables.name: Required Work Rate
variables.documentation: The pace the team would have to sustain to clear the visible backlog by the deadline. Note it uses only visible work, so hidden rework is ignored until discovered.

variables.name: Schedule Pressure
variables.documentation: The ratio of the pace required to the pace normally sustainable. A value of one means the schedule is comfortable; values above one mean the team is behind and must accelerate.

variables.name: Effect of Schedule Pressure on Work Intensity
variables.documentation: How hard the team works relative to normal as a function of schedule pressure. Normal pressure of one gives normal intensity of one; higher pressure raises intensity through overtime, but the gain saturates because there is a limit to how many hours people can work.

variables.name: Effect of Fatigue on Productivity

variables.name: Fatigue Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: How long it takes the sustained work intensity index to catch up with current working conditions. It captures the fact that fatigue builds and dissipates over weeks, not instantly.

variables.name: Normal Defect Fraction
variables.documentation: The share of work done incorrectly when the team is working at a normal, unpressured pace. It represents the baseline error rate of the development process.

variables.name: Effect of Schedule Pressure on Defects
variables.documentation: Multiplier on the error rate caused by working under pressure. At normal pressure it equals one; as pressure rises, corner cutting, skipped reviews and fatigue sharply increase the share of work done wrong. This is the haste makes waste link.

variables.name: Fraction Incorrect
variables.documentation: The share of currently processed work that contains defects, equal to the baseline error rate amplified by schedule pressure and capped at one. It splits the work rate between genuine completion and hidden rework.

variables.name: Discovery Delay
