variables.name: Minimum Task Time
variables.documentation: The shortest time in which a task in the backlog can physically be pushed through. It prevents the backlog from being emptied faster than work can flow, keeping the work rate finite and non negative.

variables.name: Total Work Remaining
variables.documentation: The true amount of work still to be completed, including defects the team does not yet know about. Comparing this with the visible backlog reveals the gap between perceived and real progress.

variables.name: Fraction Complete
variables.documentation: Share of the project that is genuinely finished. It is the key indicator of real progress and reaches one only when all work has been done correctly.

testParams.name: Fishery Boom and Bust variable documentation
testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete stock-and-flow model of fishery boom and bust. Make sure that every variable in the model is clearly documented, describing what it represents and its role within the system.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how a commercial fishery can collapse from overharvesting, and why fishing fleet investment tends to drive boom-and-bust cycles in the fish population.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A fish population grows through births and shrinks through natural deaths and through harvesting by a fishing fleet. The population regenerates fastest at intermediate levels and its net regeneration falls toward zero as it approaches the carrying capacity of the habitat or is driven near depletion. The harvest rate rises with both the number of fishing ships and the density of fish, since the catch per ship is higher when fish are abundant. Revenue from the harvest, less the operating cost of running the ships, determines the profit per ship. Profit drives investment in new ships, though new capacity is added only after a construction and financing delay; when profit turns negative, ships are scrapped or leave the fishery. More ships raise the harvest, which depletes the fish population, which lowers the catch per ship and eventually profit — a balancing process — but the investment delays cause the fleet to overshoot the sustainable level, producing cycles of boom and collapse.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how a commercial fishery can collapse from overharvesting, and why fishing fleet investment tends to drive boom-and-bust cycles in the fish population.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure built

Three stocks create the boom-and-bust dynamic

  1. Fish population — accumulates births and is drained by natural deaths and harvesting. Births are density-limited (they shut off as the stock nears carrying capacity) while natural deaths are a fixed fraction, so net regeneration peaks at intermediate stock levels and goes to zero both near carrying capacity and near depletion, exactly as described.
  2. Ships under construction — an explicit pipeline stock that embodies the construction and financing delay. This is the key structure: capital committed during the profitable boom keeps arriving after the fish have already begun to decline.
  3. Fishing fleet — accumulates completed ships and loses ships to retirement and forced exit.

The balancing loop (resource feedback): more ships → higher harvest → smaller fish population → lower fish density → lower catch per ship (via a saturating catchability curve) → lower revenue and profit → fewer orders and more scrapping → fewer ships. Because two long delays (construction pipeline plus the slow turnover of the fleet stock) sit inside this loop, correction arrives late and the fleet overshoots — the classic overshoot-and-collapse archetype acting on a tragedy of the commons resource.

The reinforcing loop (investment): profit → orders → more ships → more harvest → more revenue while fish are still abundant. This drives the boom.

Formulation choices

  • Catchability uses a graphical function of fish density normalized to pass through (1,1); it saturates at high abundance (limited hold and time at sea) and falls to zero at depletion, which is what ultimately kills profitability.
  • Investment and exit are driven by a dimensionless profit ratio (profit relative to operating cost) through two normalized graphical functions: ordering collapses to zero when profit is negative, and exit accelerates sharply when losses appear.
  • Fleet profit is reported as an indicator only, with no feedback of its own.
  • The harvest flow is capped by the physically available stock so the population can never be driven negative; all one-directional flows (births, deaths, harvest, orders, completions, exits) are constrained to be non-negative.
  • No aggregation was represented as a stock, and no delay function was used where an averaging behavior was intended; the only delay in the model is a genuine material pipeline (ships being built), correctly represented as a stock with an inflow and outflow.

Key leverage to explore: shortening the construction delay, lowering the maximum order fraction, or raising operating cost (a proxy for licence fees) all damp the oscillation; a long delay with aggressive investment drives the fish stock past the point where regeneration can recover, producing collapse.
supportingInfo.title: Fishery Overshoot and Collapse Stock Flow Model

variables.name: fish population
variables.documentation: The biomass (number) of fish in the fishery. It is the central renewable resource stock: it accumulates births and is drained by natural mortality and by harvesting. It is modeled as a stock because fish can only change through the biological and fishing flows that add to or remove from it.

variables.name: initial fish population
variables.documentation: The starting size of the fish stock, set at the unfished natural equilibrium where births exactly balance natural deaths. Used so the simulation begins with a healthy, virgin fishery.

variables.name: fish births
variables.documentation: Recruitment of new fish per year. Proportional to the existing spawning stock but reduced by crowding: as the population approaches carrying capacity, the fraction of the habitat still available (1 minus density) falls to zero and reproduction stops. This density dependence, combined with a constant natural death fraction, produces the classic logistic pattern in which net regeneration is fastest at intermediate population levels and approaches zero both near depletion and near carrying capacity.

variables.name: maximum birth rate fraction
variables.documentation: The maximum fractional rate at which fish reproduce per year when the habitat is essentially empty and there is no crowding. It sets the biological speed with which a depleted stock can rebuild.

variables.name: fish deaths
variables.documentation: Natural (non-fishing) mortality per year, a constant fraction of the standing population. Together with density-limited births it defines the net regeneration curve of the resource.

variables.name: natural death rate fraction
variables.documentation: The fraction of the fish population that dies each year from natural causes such as predation, disease and old age.

variables.name: carrying capacity
variables.documentation: The maximum fish population the habitat could support in the absence of mortality pressure. It is the reference against which crowding (density) is measured and is the limit that shuts down reproduction.

variables.name: fish density ratio
variables.documentation: Fish abundance expressed as a fraction of habitat carrying capacity. It is the dimensionless signal used both by the biology (crowding suppresses births) and by the economics (dense fish are easier to catch, raising catch per ship).

variables.name: harvest rate
variables.documentation: Total fish removed by the fleet each year. It is the number of ships multiplied by what each ship can catch, so it rises with both fleet size and fish density. The MIN term is a physical safeguard preventing the fleet from removing more fish than actually exist in a given period.

variables.name: minimum harvest time
variables.documentation: The shortest time in which the entire remaining fish stock could physically be taken. It caps the harvest flow so the population can never be driven negative.

variables.name: normal catch per ship
variables.documentation: The annual catch a single ship would land when fish density equals the reference level (density ratio of one). It represents the technical fishing power of a vessel.

variables.name: effect of density on catch
variables.documentation: Multiplier capturing how the ease of fishing depends on how abundant the fish are. It is normalized to one at the reference density, falls to zero when the stock is depleted, and saturates when fish are plentiful because a ship's hold and time at sea are limited. This is the link that lets a shrinking fish stock eventually undermine fleet profitability.

variables.name: catch per ship
variables.documentation: Actual annual catch landed by an average ship, equal to its technical capacity scaled by the abundance of fish. It is the productivity signal that drives revenue and therefore investment.

variables.name: fish price
variables.documentation: Market price received per fish landed, assumed constant so that the dynamics come from the resource and the fleet rather than from price swings.

variables.name: revenue per ship
variables.documentation: Annual gross income earned by an average vessel, the product of what it catches and what the catch sells for.

variables.name: operating cost per ship
variables.documentation: Annual cost of crewing, fuelling, maintaining and financing one vessel. It is the break-even hurdle: when catches fall so far that revenue drops below this cost, the fishery becomes unprofitable.

variables.name: profit per ship
variables.documentation: Annual operating profit of an average vessel. It can be negative when fish are scarce, which is what triggers scrapping and exit from the fishery.

variables.name: profit ratio
variables.documentation: Profit expressed relative to operating cost, giving a dimensionless measure of return on running a ship. Investors and owners react to this relative attractiveness rather than to absolute dollars, so it drives both ordering and exit decisions.

variables.name: effect of profit on orders
variables.documentation: Multiplier describing how eagerly owners order new vessels as a function of relative profitability. Normalized to one at the reference profit ratio, it falls to zero when the fishery loses money and saturates when profits are very high because shipyards and finance are limited.

variables.name: maximum order fraction
variables.documentation: The fractional rate at which the existing fleet is expanded per year under reference profitability. It sets the aggressiveness of the reinforcing investment loop.

variables.name: ship orders
variables.documentation: New vessels commissioned each year. It is proportional to the current fleet (success breeds imitation and reinvestment) and scaled by profitability. This is the reinforcing growth engine of the boom phase.

variables.name: ships under construction
variables.documentation: Vessels ordered and financed but not yet fishing. This stock is the explicit representation of the construction and financing delay: capacity committed during a profitable boom keeps arriving even after the resource has begun to crash, which is the main cause of fleet overshoot.

variables.name: construction delay
variables.documentation: Average time between ordering a ship and having it fishing. The longer this delay, the more severely the fleet overshoots the sustainable level and the more violent the boom-and-bust cycle.

variables.name: ship completions
variables.documentation: Rate at which new vessels are delivered into the active fleet, modeled as the pipeline stock drained over the average construction time.

variables.name: initial fishing fleet
variables.documentation: The small starting fleet that begins exploiting the virgin fishery, allowing the growth phase of the cycle to be observed.

variables.name: fishing fleet
variables.documentation: The number of active fishing vessels. It accumulates completed ships and loses ships that are scrapped or leave the fishery. Being a stock, capital cannot adjust instantly to changing profitability, which is the second source of inertia behind the cycles.

variables.name: normal retirement fraction
variables.documentation: The fraction of the fleet retired each year under normal profitability, reflecting the average economic lifetime of a vessel.

variables.name: effect of profit on exit
variables.documentation: Multiplier on the retirement rate reflecting economic pressure. Normalized to one at reference profitability, it rises sharply when profits go negative (owners lay up, scrap or sell vessels out of the fishery) and falls when profits are high and owners keep ageing boats working.

variables.name: ship exit rate
variables.documentation: Vessels leaving the fishery each year through scrapping, laying up or relocation. It combines normal wear-out with accelerated exit when the fishery loses money, producing the bust phase of the cycle.

variables.name: fleet profit
variables.documentation: Total annual profit of the whole fishery, reported as an indicator of the economic boom and bust that accompanies the resource cycle. It has no feedback effect of its own.

testParams.name: Market Growth and Capacity variable documentation
testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete stock-and-flow model of market growth and capacity. Make sure that every variable in the model is clearly documented, describing what it represents and its role within the system.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand why a fast-growing company's sales can stall or oscillate as it struggles to expand production capacity quickly enough to meet demand.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A company's installed base of customers grows as the sales force wins new customers and shrinks as existing customers are lost. Customers place orders, and orders that cannot be filled immediately accumulate in a backlog. Production capacity limits how quickly the backlog can be filled, so the delivery delay experienced by customers is the backlog divided by the available capacity. A longer delivery delay reduces the company's attractiveness, which lowers the order rate and slows customer acquisition — a balancing loop that constrains growth. Revenue from filled orders funds investment in both the sales force and additional production capacity, but new capacity comes online only after a construction delay. A larger sales force wins customers faster, creating a reinforcing growth loop, while the capacity and delivery-delay dynamics push back against that growth and can cause sales to overshoot and oscillate.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand why a fast-growing company's sales can stall or oscillate as it struggles to expand production capacity quickly enough to meet demand.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure built

Four real accumulations, plus a supply line. Only genuine accumulations are stocks: Installed Base (won and lost customers), Backlog (orders in, shipments out), Sales Force (hiring in, attrition out), Production Capacity (completions in, depreciation out), and Capacity Under Construction — the supply-line stock that holds ordered-but-not-yet-operational capacity. All aggregations and ratios (revenue, budgets, desired levels, delivery delay) are auxiliaries computed algebraically, not stocks. No flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow of the same stock.

Reinforcing growth engine. Revenue → sales budget → affordable sales force → hiring → sales force → customer acquisition → installed base → orders → shipments → revenue. This is the growth loop that makes the firm expand quickly at first.

Balancing loop through delivery delay. Backlog divided by capacity gives the delivery delay customers actually experience. Compared to the delay customers regard as normal, this produces a dimensionless Relative Delivery Delay that feeds a nonlinear table function, Effect of Delivery Delay on Attractiveness, normalized to pass through (1, 1): normal service gives normal behavior, better service boosts demand modestly, and long delays cut attractiveness sharply. That multiplier reduces both the order rate and salesperson effectiveness, so poor delivery performance both suppresses demand and slows customer acquisition — the classic growth and underinvestment archetype.

Why oscillation and stall emerge. Capacity investment is driven by the gap between capacity indicated by the backlog and capacity already installed or on order, closed over an adjustment time, but is also capped by what revenue can fund. Ordered capacity must then pass through a twelve-month construction pipeline before it can ship anything. This long delay between recognizing a shortfall and having usable capacity is what makes the firm chronically behind demand, lets delivery delay blow out, and produces overshoot and oscillation in sales rather than smooth growth.

Formulation safeguards. Physically one-directional flows (acquisition, losses, hiring, attrition, orders, shipments, completions, depreciation, capacity ordering) are marked as non-negative. Divisions that could face a zero denominator (delivery delay, desired capacity, desired sales force, affordable expansion, relative delay) use protected division. Shipments take the smaller of capacity and the fastest the existing backlog can physically be processed. No arbitrary constants are buried in equations — every parameter (churn fraction, construction delay, investment shares, target delay, unit costs) is an explicitly named and documented variable so policies can be tested one at a time. Averaging via delay functions was avoided entirely; delays appear only where real physical pipelines exist.

variables.name: Installed Base
variables.documentation: The accumulation of active customers the company serves. It grows only through customer acquisition by the sales force and shrinks only through customer losses, so it is a true stock. It is the source of the order rate and therefore the engine of revenue.

variables.name: Customer Acquisition Rate
variables.documentation: New customers won per month. Equals the number of salespeople times how many customers each can win per month. This is the inflow that drives the reinforcing growth loop (more revenue leads to a bigger sales force which wins more customers).

variables.name: Customer Loss Rate
variables.documentation: Customers lost per month, modeled as a constant fraction of the installed base decaying each month. This creates the balancing loop that requires continuous acquisition just to hold the customer base steady.

variables.name: Customer Loss Fraction
variables.documentation: The fraction of the installed base lost each month (average customer relationship lasts the reciprocal of this value). Kept as a named constant so the churn assumption is explicit and testable.

variables.name: Sales Effectiveness
variables.documentation: Customers each salesperson can win per month, given how attractive the company currently is. Normal effectiveness is scaled by the delivery-delay effect, so poor delivery performance makes selling harder.

variables.name: Normal Sales Effectiveness
variables.documentation: Reference productivity of a salesperson when delivery delay is normal. Provides the baseline against which the attractiveness effect is applied.

variables.name: Sales Force
variables.documentation: The number of salespeople employed. It accumulates hiring and loses people to attrition, so it is a stock. Its size determines how fast new customers are won, making it the central lever of the growth loop.

variables.name: Sales Force Hiring Rate
variables.documentation: People hired per month to close the gap between the sales force the budget can afford and the sales force on hand, spread over a hiring adjustment time. Constrained to be non-negative because hiring cannot be negative; downsizing occurs through attrition.

variables.name: Sales Force Attrition Rate
variables.documentation: Salespeople leaving per month as a constant fraction of the sales force. Represents normal turnover that must be replaced by hiring.

variables.name: Sales Force Attrition Fraction
variables.documentation: Fraction of salespeople who leave each month. Named constant capturing the turnover assumption.

variables.name: Sales Force Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: Average time to recruit and place a salesperson. This delay slows the reinforcing growth loop and contributes to overshoot behavior.

variables.name: Desired Sales Force
variables.documentation: The number of salespeople the company can afford, found by dividing the sales budget by the cost of one salesperson. Uses safe division so a zero salary assumption cannot break the model.

variables.name: Sales Budget
variables.documentation: Money allocated to the sales force each month, a fixed share of revenue. This is the link that makes sales-force growth self-funding and therefore reinforcing.

variables.name: Fraction of Revenue to Sales
variables.documentation: Share of revenue devoted to the sales force. A key policy parameter governing how aggressively the firm pursues growth.

variables.name: Salary per Salesperson
variables.documentation: Fully loaded monthly cost of employing one salesperson. Converts budget dollars into headcount.

variables.name: Revenue
variables.documentation: Money earned per month from orders actually filled. Because revenue depends on shipments rather than orders, capacity limits directly starve the budgets for both sales and capacity expansion.

variables.name: Price per Unit
variables.documentation: Average revenue earned per unit shipped. Held constant so attention stays on capacity and delivery dynamics rather than pricing.

variables.name: Backlog
variables.documentation: Unfilled orders waiting to be produced and shipped. It accumulates incoming orders and is drained by shipments, so it is a stock. Its size relative to capacity defines the delivery delay customers experience.

variables.name: Order Rate
variables.documentation: Orders placed per month. Proportional to the installed base and modulated by attractiveness, so long delivery delays cause existing customers to order less as well as deterring new ones.

variables.name: Normal Order Rate per Customer
variables.documentation: Units ordered per customer per month when delivery performance is normal. Baseline demand intensity per customer.

variables.name: Shipment Rate
variables.documentation: Units shipped per month. Limited either by production capacity or by how fast the existing backlog can physically be processed, whichever is smaller. This is where the capacity constraint bites and where revenue is generated.

variables.name: Minimum Order Processing Time
variables.documentation: Shortest possible time to process and ship an order even with ample capacity. Prevents the backlog from emptying instantaneously and sets the floor on delivery delay.

variables.name: Production Capacity
variables.documentation: Maximum units the company can produce per month. It rises only as construction projects are completed and falls as plant wears out, making it a slow-moving stock that cannot respond quickly to demand surges.

variables.name: Capacity Under Construction
variables.documentation: Capacity that has been ordered but is not yet operational. This supply-line stock creates the construction delay that is the main source of overshoot and oscillation in the system.

variables.name: Capacity Ordering Rate
variables.documentation: New capacity started per month, limited by both what the backlog indicates is needed and what revenue can pay for. Taking the smaller of the two captures the fact that a cash-constrained firm cannot build all the capacity it wants.

variables.name: Capacity Completion Rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which projects under construction become usable capacity, modeled as the supply line divided by the average construction time. It moves capacity from the pipeline into operation.

variables.name: Capacity Construction Delay
variables.documentation: Average time from ordering capacity to it becoming operational. The longer this delay, the more the firm overbuilds and the more sales oscillate.

variables.name: Capacity Depreciation Rate
variables.documentation: Capacity lost per month to wear-out and obsolescence, a constant fraction of installed capacity. Requires ongoing investment simply to maintain the current production level.

variables.name: Capacity Depreciation Fraction
variables.documentation: Fraction of production capacity that retires each month (reciprocal of average asset life). Named constant making the replacement burden explicit.

variables.name: Desired Capacity Expansion Rate
variables.documentation: How fast managers would like to add capacity: the shortfall between desired capacity and capacity already installed or on order, closed over an adjustment time. Counting the supply line prevents endless reordering of capacity already in the pipeline.

variables.name: Capacity Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: Time over which managers aim to close a perceived capacity shortfall. Shorter times mean more aggressive, potentially more oscillatory, investment behavior.

variables.name: Desired Capacity
variables.documentation: The capacity that would deliver the current backlog within the target delivery time. This is the goal that drives capacity investment, tying expansion decisions to observed order backlog.

variables.name: Target Delivery Delay
variables.documentation: The delivery delay management is trying to achieve. It converts backlog into a capacity goal and represents the firm's service-level ambition.

variables.name: Affordable Capacity Expansion Rate
variables.documentation: Capacity the firm can start building each month with the funds available, found by dividing the capacity budget by the cost of a unit of capacity. This is the financial ceiling on expansion.

variables.name: Capacity Budget
variables.documentation: Money allocated each month to building production capacity, a fixed share of revenue. Because revenue depends on shipments, capacity shortfalls limit the money available to fix them.

variables.name: Fraction of Revenue to Capacity
variables.documentation: Share of revenue reinvested in capacity. Together with the sales share it defines how the firm splits its growth investment between demand generation and supply.

variables.name: Cost per Unit of Capacity
variables.documentation: Capital cost of adding one unit per month of sustained production capability. Translates investment dollars into physical capacity.

variables.name: Delivery Delay
variables.documentation: Time customers wait for their orders, computed as backlog divided by available capacity (Little's Law). Safe division guards against zero capacity. This is the key service signal customers react to.

variables.name: Relative Delivery Delay
variables.documentation: Delivery delay expressed as a ratio to the delay customers consider normal. Normalizing makes the attractiveness relationship dimensionless and centered on a value of one.

variables.name: Normal Delivery Delay
variables.documentation: The delivery delay customers regard as acceptable or typical for the industry. It is the reference point for judging the company's service performance.

variables.name: Effect of Delivery Delay on Attractiveness
variables.documentation: A nonlinear table function translating relative delivery delay into a multiplier on company attractiveness. It passes through the point (1,1) so that normal delivery performance yields normal ordering and normal selling effectiveness; better-than-normal service boosts attractiveness while long delays sharply reduce it. This variable is the hinge of the balancing loops that stall growth.

testParams.name: Population Growth simulates to completion
testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete, simulatable quantitative stock-and-flow model of population growth. Every stock must have a numeric initial value, every flow and auxiliary must have a well-defined equation, and the model must include simulation specifications (start time, stop time, time step, and time units) covering the full horizon described. The model must be able to run to completion in a system dynamics simulator without errors.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to project how a population changes over time given its birth and death processes.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A single population is a stock of individuals. It increases through births and decreases through deaths. Births each year equal the current population multiplied by a fractional birth rate, and deaths each year equal the current population multiplied by a fractional death rate. Use an initial population of 1000 individuals, a fractional birth rate of 0.03 per year, and a fractional death rate of 0.015 per year. Simulate from year 0 to year 100 with a time step of 0.25 years, using years as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to project how a population changes over time given its birth and death processes.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

  • Population is the single stock, initialized numerically at 1000 individuals. It changes only through its two flows.
  • births is an inflow equal to Population * fractional_birth_rate; deaths is an outflow equal to Population * fractional_death_rate. Each flow appears in exactly one direction on the stock, never both.
  • fractional birth rate (0.03/year) and fractional death rate (0.015/year) are isolated as named constant auxiliaries rather than being buried inside the flow equations, so the assumptions are explicit and easy to test.

Feedback interpretation

The model contains two classic loops sharing the same stock: a reinforcing loop (Population → births → Population) that drives exponential growth, and a balancing loop (Population → deaths → Population) that drains it. Because the fractional birth rate exceeds the fractional death rate, the reinforcing loop dominates and the population grows exponentially at a net 1.5% per year, reaching roughly 4,480 individuals by year 100.

Formulation checks applied

  • Both flows are marked one-directional, since negative births or negative deaths are physically impossible.
  • No total/aggregate variable was created as a stock; the only stock is a genuine accumulation.
  • No conditional logic, no hard-coded values inside equations, and no delay functions used for averaging.
  • Simulation specs cover the full horizon: 0 to 100 years, time step 0.25 years, Euler integration.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how the balance of a savings account evolves as it earns interest and money is added and withdrawn.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A savings account has a single stock: its balance, in dollars. The balance grows through an inflow made up of interest earned plus regular deposits, and shrinks through an outflow of regular withdrawals. Interest earned each year equals the current balance multiplied by an annual interest rate. Use an initial balance of 5000 dollars, an annual interest rate of 0.03 per year, deposits of 2400 dollars per year, and withdrawals of 1200 dollars per year. Simulate from year 0 to year 30 with a time step of 0.25 years, using years as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how the balance of a savings account evolves as it earns interest and money is added and withdrawn.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

  • Balance is the single stock, initialized at 5000 dollars. It changes only through its flows, as required.
  • Interest and Deposits is the single inflow, equal to Interest_Earned + Deposit_Rate, combining compounding interest with the regular annual contribution. Marked as one-directional since money added can never be negative here.
  • Withdrawals is the single outflow, driven by a constant Withdrawal Rate, also one-directional.

Auxiliaries

  • Interest Earned = Balance * Annual Interest Rate — an auxiliary (algebraic calculation), not a stock, since it is computed instantaneously from the balance.
  • Annual Interest Rate (0.03/year), Deposit Rate (2400 $/yr) and Withdrawal Rate (1200 $/yr) are separate named constants rather than numbers buried inside equations, so each assumption can be inspected and changed.

Dynamics

The loop Balance → Interest Earned → Inflow → Balance is a reinforcing (compounding growth) loop: the larger the balance, the more interest it earns, which grows the balance further. Net contributions of 1200 dollars per year (2400 in, 1200 out) push the balance steadily upward, so the account exhibits exponential growth on top of a linear savings trend over the 30-year horizon.

Simulation settings: 0 to 30 years, time step 0.25 years, Euler integration — matching the specification.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how an infectious disease moves through a fixed population during an outbreak.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Use the classic SIR structure with three stocks: susceptible people, infected people, and recovered people. Susceptible people become infected and flow into the infected stock; infected people recover and flow into the recovered stock. The infection rate equals the contact rate times the infectivity times the number of infected people times the fraction of the total population that is still susceptible (susceptible divided by total population). The recovery rate equals the infected population divided by the average duration of illness. Use a total population of 10000, with 9990 initially susceptible, 10 initially infected, and 0 recovered. Use a contact rate of 6 contacts per person per day, an infectivity of 0.05, and an average duration of illness of 5 days. Simulate from day 0 to day 100 with a time step of 0.5 days, using days as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how an infectious disease moves through a fixed population during an outbreak.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

The model is the classic SIR epidemic, built as a chain of three stocks connected by two flows:

  • Susceptible Population (9990) drained by Infection Rate
  • Infected Population (10) filled by Infection Rate, drained by Recovery Rate
  • Recovered Population (0) filled by Recovery Rate

Each flow appears as an outflow of one stock and an inflow of the next, never both on the same stock, so the 10000 people are conserved.

Equations

  • Infection Rate = Contact Rate × Infectivity × Infected Population × (Susceptible Population / Total Population). This is the number of contacts infectious people make per day, times the share of those contacts that are with susceptibles, times the chance a contact transmits. Marked as one-directional since infections cannot be negative.
  • Recovery Rate = Infected Population / Average Duration of Illness — a first-order drain, also one-directional.
  • All parameters (contact rate 6, infectivity 0.05, illness duration 5 days, total population 10000) are separate named constants rather than numbers buried in equations, so they can be varied in experiments.

Feedback structure

Two loops drive the outbreak's characteristic S-shaped/bell-shaped behavior:

  1. A reinforcing contagion loop: more infected people → more infections → still more infected people. This drives the early exponential takeoff.
  2. A balancing depletion loop: infections deplete the susceptible pool → the susceptible fraction falls → fewer new infections. Together with recovery draining the infected stock, this loop eventually halts the epidemic — a limits-to-growth pattern where the constraint is the finite stock of susceptibles.

Simulation settings

Days 0 to 100 with a time step of 0.5 days, Euler integration, matching the specified horizon.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how a store's inventory responds when it continuously reorders stock toward a target level.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A store holds a single stock of inventory, in units. Inventory rises through a production/delivery inflow and falls through a shipment outflow. Shipments equal customer demand, which is a constant 100 units per week. The store wants to keep inventory at a desired level equal to a target coverage of expected sales: desired inventory equals demand multiplied by a desired coverage of 4 weeks. The production rate equals demand plus a correction that closes the gap between desired inventory and current inventory over an inventory adjustment time of 8 weeks (that is, production equals demand plus (desired inventory minus inventory) divided by the adjustment time). Start with an initial inventory of 200 units, which is below the desired level, so the correction loop is active. Simulate from week 0 to week 52 with a time step of 0.25 weeks, using weeks as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how a store's inventory responds when it continuously reorders stock toward a target level.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

One stock: Inventory, initialized at a numeric 200 units, changed only by its two flows.

  • Inflow — Production = Customer_Demand + Inventory_Correction. Marked uniflow (production cannot run backwards).
  • Outflow — Shipments = Customer_Demand, also uniflow.

Target and correction chain (auxiliaries, not stocks):

  • Customer_Demand = 100 units/week (constant)
  • Desired_Coverage = 4 weeks
  • Desired_Inventory = demand × coverage = 400 units
  • Inventory_Gap = desired − actual
  • Inventory_Adjustment_Time = 8 weeks
  • Inventory_Correction = gap ÷ adjustment time

Every arbitrary number (demand, coverage, adjustment time) is abstracted into its own named constant rather than buried inside a formula, so each equation reads in plain language.

Feedback behavior

The loop Inventory → Inventory Gap → Inventory Correction → Production → Inventory is a balancing (negative) feedback loop — a classic stock-adjustment / goal-seeking structure. Starting 200 units below target, the correction begins at 25 units/week on top of the 100 units/week replacement, and production is 125 units/week. As inventory closes the gap, the correction shrinks, so inventory approaches 400 units along a smooth exponential path with a time constant of 8 weeks — roughly 96% of the way there by week 26 and effectively at target well before week 52. No overshoot or oscillation occurs because there is no delay in the correction; this is why Euler integration is adequate.

Formulation checks applied

  • Aggregations/targets (Desired_Inventory, Inventory_Gap, Inventory_Correction) are algebraic auxiliaries, not stocks, since they are computed instantly rather than accumulated.
  • No flow appears as both an inflow and an outflow of the stock.
  • No conditionals, no INTEG in the stock equation (only its numeric initial value), and all variable references use underscores.

Simulation specs

Weeks 0 to 52, dt = 0.25 weeks, Euler — matching the described horizon exactly.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how the populations of a predator and its prey rise and fall together over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Use the classic Lotka-Volterra structure with two stocks: a prey population and a predator population. The prey population grows through prey births and shrinks through prey deaths caused by predation. Prey births equal a prey birth rate coefficient times the prey population. Prey deaths equal a predation coefficient times the prey population times the predator population. The predator population grows through predator births and shrinks through predator deaths. Predator births equal a predator efficiency coefficient times the prey population times the predator population. Predator deaths equal a predator death rate coefficient times the predator population. Use an initial prey population of 100 and an initial predator population of 20. Use a prey birth rate coefficient of 0.5, a predation coefficient of 0.02, a predator efficiency coefficient of 0.01, and a predator death rate coefficient of 0.4 (all per appropriate time unit). Because this system oscillates, use a small time step for numerical stability: simulate from time 0 to time 50 with a time step of 0.03125, using months as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how the populations of a predator and its prey rise and fall together over time.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

The model is the classic Lotka-Volterra predator-prey system, built from two stocks and four flows.

  • Prey population (initial 100): grows via prey births (reinforcing loop — more prey make more prey) and drains via prey deaths from predation.
  • Predator population (initial 20): grows via predator births fed by prey consumption, and drains via predator deaths (balancing loop — an exponential decay in the absence of food).

Coupling

The two mass-action terms (prey × predator) create the coupling that generates oscillation:

  • Prey deaths = predation coefficient × prey × predators — a balancing loop on prey.
  • Predator births = predator efficiency coefficient × prey × predators — a reinforcing loop on predators fueled by prey.

Together these form a delayed balancing structure: predators rise only after prey are abundant, then overshoot and crash the prey, which then starves the predators, allowing prey to recover. This delay is what produces the characteristic out-of-phase cycles.

Parameters and specs

All coefficients are separate named auxiliaries (no hard-coded numbers buried in the flow equations): prey birth rate 0.5, predation 0.02, predator efficiency 0.01, predator death rate 0.4 per month.

Simulation runs from month 0 to month 50 with a time step of 0.03125 months. Because Lotka-Volterra systems are neutrally stable, Euler integration with a coarse step artificially amplifies the cycles; RK4 is used together with the small step to keep the orbits closed and numerically faithful.

All four flows are marked one-directional, so births and deaths can never run backwards.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand why a software project takes longer than planned once undiscovered rework is taken into account.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Model a fixed-scope software project with three stocks, all measured in tasks: work to be done, undiscovered rework, and work truly done. The team completes tasks at a work rate that flows out of work to be done. The work rate equals the number of developers times their productivity. A fraction of completed work is done correctly and flows into work truly done; the remaining fraction contains defects and flows into undiscovered rework instead. Undiscovered rework is not visible immediately: it is detected and flows back into work to be done at a rework discovery rate equal to the undiscovered rework stock divided by an average discovery delay. Use an initial work to be done of 500 tasks, an initial undiscovered rework of 0 tasks, and an initial work truly done of 0 tasks. Use 10 developers, a productivity of 0.4 tasks per developer per week, a fraction correct of 0.85 (so 0.15 of completed work becomes undiscovered rework), and an average discovery delay of 4 weeks. To avoid completed work continuing to be generated once the backlog is empty, the work rate should not exceed the amount of work remaining to be done. Simulate from week 0 to week 200 with a time step of 0.25 weeks, using weeks as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand why a software project takes longer than planned once undiscovered rework is taken into account.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Three stocks in tasks: Work to be Done (500), Undiscovered Rework (0), and Work Truly Done (0).

  • work rate drains the backlog and equals the team's potential output (developers × productivity), capped by the remaining backlog so no phantom work is generated once the queue empties.
  • The executed work splits into two flows: correct completion rate (fraction correct × work rate) into Work Truly Done, and rework generation rate ((1 − fraction correct) × work rate) into Undiscovered Rework. These are separate flows rather than one flow feeding two stocks, which is required for a valid stock-and-flow formulation.
  • rework discovery rate is a first-order drain of the hidden rework stock over the average discovery delay, and returns those tasks to the backlog.

Why the project runs late

The model contains a balancing loop (work executed reduces the backlog) plus a reinforcing "rework cycle": every task executed silently manufactures a fraction of defective work, which after a detection delay reappears as new backlog and is itself subject to the same defect fraction. With 15% defects the effective work is 500/0.85 ≈ 588 tasks rather than 500, and the 4-week discovery delay means the backlog appears to empty before the hidden defects surface — producing the classic "90% done" plateau and a tail of late rework that extends the finish date well beyond the nominal 125 weeks.

All constants (developers, productivity, fraction correct, discovery delay) are named auxiliaries rather than numbers buried in equations, and simulation runs 0–200 weeks at a 0.25-week step.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Modular restructuring

The predator-prey system was split into two modules, hare and lynx, with each module owning the stock, flows, and parameters for its own species. Names inside each module drop the animal prefix as instructed (for example, hares killed per lynx becomes hare.killed per lynx, lynx births becomes lynx.births), while the two population stocks are hare.hares and lynx.lynx, and the ecosystem area becomes hare.area.

Closing the two coupling loops with ghosts

The predator-prey structure only works if each module can see one signal from the other. Two cross-level ghosts were added, the minimum necessary:

  • hare.lynx — a ghost of lynx.lynx, used in the hare death (predation) flow. Without it the balancing predation loop would be broken.
  • lynx.hare density — a ghost of hare.density, used to set the lynx starvation mortality fraction. Without it the lynx would have no food-driven feedback.

All equations inside a module reference only its own local variables and its ghosts, never the source variable in the other module.

Preserved structure

Every original equation, initial value, and graphical function was carried over unchanged: the hare reinforcing birth loop, the balancing predation loop (more lynx → more hare deaths → lower hare density → fewer kills per lynx), the lynx reinforcing birth loop, and the balancing starvation loop (lower hare density → higher lynx death fraction → fewer lynx). Both birth and death flows are marked one-directional so they can never run backwards. No additional variables beyond the two required ghosts were introduced.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Flattening the modular predator-prey model

Modules removed. The Hares and Lynx modules were dissolved and every variable was renamed by simply dropping its module prefix (for example Hares.hare density became hare density, Lynx.lynx death fraction became lynx death fraction).

Ghost variables eliminated. The two cross-level ghosts (Hares.Lynx and Lynx.hare density) existed only to carry information across module boundaries. In a single flat model they are redundant, so they were deleted and the equations that used them now point straight at the originals:

  • hare deaths reads the Lynx stock directly.
  • lynx death fraction reads hare density directly.

Causal structure preserved exactly. All stocks, flows, constants, and both graphical functions (kills per lynx as a function of hare density, and lynx mortality as a function of hare density) are unchanged, including the original initial values (hares at 50,000; lynx at 1250 - 400) and simulation settings (0–100 years, dt = 1/32).

Feedback loops that remain closed:

  • Reinforcing hare growth: Hares → hare births → Hares.
  • Reinforcing lynx growth: Lynx → lynx births → Lynx.
  • Balancing predation loop: Hares → hare density → kills per lynx → hare deaths → Hares.
  • The classic predator-prey coupling: Hares → hare density → lynx death fraction (negative) → lynx deaths → Lynx → hare deaths → Hares, which produces the characteristic oscillations of this archetype.

No new variables were introduced, since every loop in the source model is already fully closed once the module boundaries and their ghosts are removed.

Flattening the model

All three modules (Population, Housing, Commerce) were merged into a single flat model. Each variable kept its name with only the module prefix removed (for example, Population.target housing per person became target housing per person).

The four cross-level ghost variables (Population.Housing Stock, Population.total jobs, Housing.Population, Commerce.Population) were deleted, since in a flat model the equations can reference the originals directly. Their placeholder equations (including one that still held a literal placeholder string) are gone, so the housing, jobs and population links are now genuine live connections rather than constants.

Loops that are now explicitly closed

With the ghosts removed the following loops run in a single structure:

  • Housing balancing loop: more people → more crowding → more construction → more housing → less crowding.
  • Housing attraction reinforcing loop: more housing → better housing availability → more attractive city → more in-migration → more people.
  • Migration/crowding balancing loop: more people → less housing and fewer jobs per person → lower attractiveness → less in-migration.
  • Commerce reinforcing loop: more people → more labor per business → more business starts → more jobs → better job availability → more in-migration.
  • Commerce balancing loop: more businesses → labor spread thinner → fewer new business starts.

New structure added to close a missing loop

The source model let housing and business stocks grow without any physical limit, so the growth loops had no counterweight — a classic limits to growth situation with the limit missing. I added the land sector that closes it:

land area, land per housing unit, land per business structure → occupied land → fraction land occupied → relative land availability (normalized by normal vacant land fraction) → land availability multiplier, which now throttles both construction and business starts.

This creates two new balancing loops (building fills land, which slows further building) and couples the housing and commercial sectors: as one sector consumes land, the other's expansion slows too. The multiplier is normalized so that normal vacancy (input of 1) gives normal building (output of 1), and zero vacant land halts building entirely.
supportingInfo.title: Flattened urban model with land constraint loop

additionalParameters.problemStatement:
I've created this modular model simulating a predator-prey ecosystem.
            Please add a third module called 'cougars', representing cougars.
            
            As an apex predator, cougars are not hunted by any animal, and hunt lynxes to survive. 
            Cougars do not have any direct interactions with hares.

            Use the following component names in each module where appropriate:
            [animals], 
            [animal] births, [animal] deaths, 
            [animals] killed per [animal], [animal] density,
            [animal] birth fraction, [animal] death fraction
            - Note: [animal] is either "hare", "lynx", or "cougar"
            - Note: [animals] is either "hares", "lynx", or "cougars" (note the plural of "lynx" is "lynx")
            
            When ghosting, preserve the same variable name as in the source module. For instance, a ghost of "Hares.Hares"
            should be named "Lynx.Hares" in the "Lynx" module.

            You may add any necessary components, using appropriate names (as listed above) whenever possible.
            Do not modify or remove any existing causal relationships between lynxes and hares.

supportingInfo.explanation:
What was added

New Cougars module (apex predator). It mirrors the structure of the Lynx module: a Cougars stock with a compounding cougar births inflow (population times cougar birth fraction) and a draining cougar deaths outflow (population times cougar death fraction). Because nothing hunts cougars, starvation-driven mortality is their only loss. The cougar death fraction is a graphical function of lynx density — when prey is scarce, more cougars die — exactly parallel to how lynx mortality depends on hare density.

New predation link from cougars to lynx. Rather than altering the existing lynx deaths flow (which represents starvation driven by hare density), a separate outflow lynx deaths from cougars was added to the lynx stock. It equals the cougar population times lynx killed per cougar, a saturating graphical function of lynx density that passes through (1,1) and returns zero when there are no lynx. This leaves every existing hare–lynx relationship untouched.

Supporting variables. lynx density (lynx divided by area) was added in the Lynx module so the cougar–lynx pair uses the same density-based predation logic as the lynx–hare pair.

Ghosts (all keeping their source names).

  • Lynx.Cougars → ghost of Cougars.Cougars (lets lynx feel predation)
  • Lynx.area → ghost of Hares.area (needed to compute lynx density)
  • Cougars.lynx density → ghost of Lynx.lynx density (food signal for cougars)

Feedback loops closed

  • Cougar–lynx balancing loop: more cougars → more lynx killed → fewer lynx → lower lynx density → higher cougar death fraction → fewer cougars. This is a classic predator–prey balancing structure and will damp or oscillate rather than explode.
  • Cougar–lynx reinforcing (growth) loop: more cougars → more cougar births → more cougars, checked by the balancing loop above.
  • Indirect trophic cascade: cougars suppress lynx, which relieves predation pressure on hares, which raises hare density and lowers the lynx starvation fraction — coupling all three populations through the existing hare–lynx loops.

Parameters were chosen so the cougar population is small and slow-reproducing relative to lynx, keeping the added predation pressure a modest perturbation on the existing oscillation.
supportingInfo.title: Added cougar apex predator module with feedback

additionalParameters.problemStatement:
I've created this modular model simulating the urban dynamics in a city.
            However, I no longer need to simulate commerce dynamics. Please remove the 'Commerce' module from my model.

            Please do not add any variables or modify any processes or relationships unrelated to commerce.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Removal of the Commerce module

Deleted the entire Commerce module and everything it owned: the Business Structures stock, business starts, business closures, base start fraction, closure fraction, target labor per business, relative labor availability, start multiplier, jobs per structure, total jobs, and the Population ghost inside Commerce. All causal links among those elements were removed as well.

Cleaned up the dangling cross-module links. Because the Population module consumed commerce output through a ghost of total jobs, the following now-orphaned job-related elements were also removed from the Population module (they existed only to carry the commerce signal): the total jobs ghost, target jobs per person, relative job availability, and attractiveness from jobs.

Repaired the one equation that referenced removed structure. Net migration previously averaged housing attractiveness and job attractiveness. It now depends on housing attractiveness alone, so no reference points at deleted variables. No new variables or parameters were introduced.

Feedback structure that remains intact

The surviving model keeps the core urban balancing structure:

  • Population reinforcing loop: more people leads to more births leads to more people.
  • Housing-attractiveness balancing loop: more people lowers housing per person, which lowers attractiveness, which slows in-migration.
  • Construction balancing loop: more people per house raises relative housing demand, which raises the construction multiplier and adds housing, which relieves the crowding that triggered it.

These loops are closed through the two remaining cross-module ghosts: housing stock is visible to the Population module, and population is visible to the Housing module.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.


            At a certain business, employees are sorted in a three-role hierarchy.
            New hirees start with the "rookie" status.
            Rookies that perform well are promoted to associates.
            Associates that perform well are promoted to partners.
            To keep the hierarchy stable, the business promotes a strict percentage of each role every year.
            Some employees may also leave the company, whether due to personal reasons or exceptionally poor performance.
            A stable percentage of employees at each level of the company leave the company each year.
            The business also onboards a constant number of new hirees every year.

            Use the following component names as appropriate:
            rookies, associates, partners, promotion_rate, departure_rate, hire_rate,
            rookie_promotions, associate_promotions, rookie_hires,
            rookie_departures, associate_departures, partner_departures

            Do not create any modules in this model.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

The firm is represented as a three-stage aging chain: rookies → associates → partners. Each level is a stock of people, and people can only change level through explicit flows.

  • Entry: rookie_hires is set by the constant hire_rate, the only external source of people. It is a uniflow (you cannot hire a negative number of people).
  • Advancement: rookie_promotions and associate_promotions are each a strict fraction (promotion_rate) of the pool at that level. Each promotion flow drains one stock and fills the next, which is what keeps the hierarchy's shape stable rather than letting it drift.
  • Exit: rookie_departures, associate_departures, and partner_departures each remove a stable fraction (departure_rate) of their level, covering both voluntary exits and performance-based separations.

Key causal mechanism

Every level is a draining stock with a first-order outflow: the bigger the pool, the more people leave it per year (through promotion or departure). That negative feedback from each stock back onto its own outflows is a balancing loop, so each level self-equilibrates toward a level where inflow equals outflow. With constant hiring, rookies settle at hire rate divided by the sum of the promotion and departure fractions; associates and partners then settle at levels driven by the flow arriving from below. Because it is a chain of three first-order stocks, a change in hiring or in either fraction propagates upward with a cumulative delay — partners respond last and most slowly, which is the characteristic behavior of a promotion pipeline.

total employees is included as an auxiliary sum (not a stock), since it accumulates nothing of its own and is purely an algebraic aggregation of the three levels.
supportingInfo.title: Three Level Promotion Chain With Attrition

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.


            In a certain ecosystem, there are two animal populations: foxes and chickens.
            Initially, chickens significantly outnumber foxes.
            The chickens reproduce at a steady percentage rate per day.
            The foxes depend on the chickens for food. Each fox eats one chicken per day.
            Foxes also reproduce at a steady percentage rate per day, but slower than the chickens.
            
            Use the following component names as appropriate:
            fox_reproductionRate, fox_count, fox_reproduction,
            chicken_reproductionRate, chicken_count, chicken_reproduction, chicken_predation
            
            Do not create any modules in this model.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Two accumulations drive the behavior:

  • chicken_count grows through chicken_reproduction (a fixed percentage of the flock — a reinforcing loop producing exponential growth) and is drained by chicken_predation.
  • fox_count grows through fox_reproduction (also a fixed percentage of the fox population, another reinforcing loop, but with a smaller fractional rate).

chicken_predation is the single coupling between the two populations: because each fox eats exactly one chicken per day, predation equals the fox population times chickens_eaten_per_fox (a named constant of 1 so no bare number sits inside the equation). This creates a balancing pressure on the chickens that grows as the foxes multiply.

Expected behavior

Early on, chickens vastly outnumber foxes, so the reinforcing chicken loop dominates and chickens grow exponentially. Meanwhile foxes compound quietly in the background. Since predation is proportional to fox numbers only (not limited by chicken availability), once the fox population becomes large enough its linear appetite overtakes the chicken flock's growth and the chicken stock collapses — a classic case of exponential growth colliding with a limit that was invisible while it was small.

Note that, as described, fox births do not depend on food availability and there is no fox mortality, so foxes grow without limit; this faithfully reflects the stated assumptions and is exactly what makes the chicken collapse inevitable.

Choices

  • Both population totals are stocks; all rates are flows; the rates and per-fox appetite are auxiliaries.
  • Both flows into and out of populations are marked one-directional, since births and predation cannot run backwards.
  • No modules and no arrays were introduced, as requested.
supportingInfo.title: Fox and chicken predation growth model

testParams.prompt:

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.


            In a certain ecosystem, there are two animal populations: foxes and chickens.
            Initially, chickens significantly outnumber foxes.
            The chickens reproduce at a steady percentage rate per day.
            The foxes depend on the chickens for food. Each fox eats one chicken per day.
            Foxes also reproduce at a steady percentage rate per day, but slower than the chickens.
            
            Please create a model with two modules, 'foxes' and 'chickens'.

            Use the following component names within each module as appropriate:
            reproduction rate, count, reproduction, predation

            When creating a ghost component, preserve the name of the original component, including the module prefix (separated by a space rather than a period).
            So, a ghost of "module1.component" in module2 should be named "module2.module1 component".

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

The model is built as two modules, mirroring the two populations.

chickens module

  • count is a stock of chickens, initialized well above the fox population.
  • reproduction is an inflow equal to count * reproduction rate, giving compounding (reinforcing) growth.
  • predation is an outflow equal to the number of foxes times predation per fox, which is set to one chicken per fox per day exactly as described. The per-fox appetite is abstracted into its own named component rather than buried as a number in the equation.
  • foxes count is a cross-level ghost of the fox stock so the chickens module never reaches directly into the foxes module.

foxes module

  • count is a stock of foxes, starting small.
  • reproduction is an inflow equal to count * reproduction rate, with the rate set lower than the chickens' rate, again a reinforcing growth loop.

Key causal mechanisms

Two reinforcing (exponential growth) loops operate simultaneously — one per population — plus a one-way coupling from foxes to chickens through predation. Because foxes remove chickens in proportion to fox numbers, while chicken births grow in proportion to chicken numbers, the balance between the two exponentials determines behavior: chickens can grow at first, but the fox-driven drain also compounds, so predation losses eventually catch up with and can overtake chicken births. This is the classic "growth of a burden" pattern: the resource grows exponentially, but so does the claim on it.

Both flows are one-directional (births and predation cannot run backwards), so they are constrained to be non-negative.

Units are chickens, foxes, and per-day rates; the simulation runs over days with a small time step so the compounding dynamics resolve smoothly.

testParams.prompt:
Please give me a quantitative model that captures the key causal processes described in the background information.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.


            In a certain city, a population depends on a nonrenewable resource.
            The population reproduces and dies off at steady rates proportional to the total population.
            The resource starts with a large initial quantity, but cannot be refilled.
            Over time, the resource diminishes at a rate proportional to the population.
            Define the "resource density" as the ratio of resource quantity to the population.
            If the resource density drops below a fixed threshold, then members of the population migrate away at
            a rate proportional to the total population and the difference between the resource density 
            and the minimum threshold.

            Please create a model with two modules, 'population' and 'resource'.

            Use the following component names within each module as appropriate:
            count, birth rate, births, death rate, deaths, usage rate, usage, density, density threshold, migrations

            All "rate" variables should be constant percentages.
            Please compute the resource density inside the 'resource' module, not the 'population' module.
            (The resource density threshold should be in the 'population' module, however.)
            Do not create any intermediate variables when calculating population migrations.

            When creating a ghost component, preserve the name of the original component, including the module prefix (separated by a space rather than a period).
            So, a ghost of "module1.component" in module2 should be named "module2.module1 component".

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Two modules only: population and resource.

Population module

  • count is a stock of people, initialized at 1000, with births as its only inflow and deaths and migrations as outflows.
  • births = count × birth rate and deaths = count × death rate, both constant fractional (percentage) rates, producing the classic exponential growth/decay reinforcing and balancing loops.
  • migrations is computed directly, with no intermediate variables: it is proportional to the population and to the shortfall of resource density below density threshold, expressed relative to the threshold so the shortfall converts into a per-year fraction of people leaving. MAX(0, …) plus a uniflow setting guarantees no in-migration occurs when the resource is plentiful.
  • population.resource density is a cross-level ghost of resource.density.

Resource module

  • count is the nonrenewable stock (initial 100,000) with usage as its only outflow — no inflow, since it cannot be refilled.
  • usage = population × usage rate, so depletion is proportional to the number of people.
  • density = resource count ÷ population (safe division), computed here as requested.
  • resource.population count is a cross-level ghost of population.count.

Causal behavior

This is an overshoot and collapse archetype. The population grows exponentially (reinforcing loop through births) while consuming a fixed resource pool. As the stock drains and the population grows, resource density falls on two counts. Once density crosses the threshold, the migration outflow activates a strong balancing loop that pushes the population back down — but the resource cannot recover, so the city's population overshoots its resource base and then declines.

Ghosting convention

Ghost names preserve the original module prefix with a space: population.resource density (ghost of resource.density) and resource.population count (ghost of population.count). All equations in each module reference only the local ghost, never the source directly.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.


            At a certain business, employees are sorted in a three-role hierarchy.
            New hirees start with the "rookie" status.
            Rookies that perform well are promoted to associates.
            Associates that perform well are promoted to partners.
            To keep the hierarchy stable, the business promotes a strict percentage of each role every year.
            Some employees may also leave the company, whether due to personal reasons or exceptionally poor performance.
            A stable percentage of employees at each level of the company leave the company each year.
            The business also onboards a constant number of new hirees every year.

            Create a model with three modules named 'rookies', 'associates', and 'partners'.
            
            Use the following component names within each module as appropriate:        
            count, 
            promotions, departures, hires,
            promotion_rate, departure_rate, hire_rate
            
            When creating a ghost component, preserve the name of the original component, including the module prefix (separated by a space rather than a period).
            So, a ghost of "module1.component" in module2 should be named "module2.module1 component".

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

The workforce is modeled as an aging chain (a cascade of three stocks) with one module per role:

  • rookies: count accumulates a constant hires inflow (set by hire_rate) and is drained by two outflows — promotions (count * promotion_rate) and departures (count * departure_rate).
  • associates: count is fed by hires, which equals the rookie promotion flow brought in through the ghost rookies promotions. It drains through its own promotions to partner and departures.
  • partners: count is fed by hires, equal to the associate promotion flow via the ghost associates promotions. Being the top role, it has no promotions — only departures.

Key causal mechanisms

  • Every outflow is proportional to the stock it drains, so each role is a first-order draining process with a balancing loop: a bigger pool creates more promotions and departures, which shrink the pool back. This is what makes each level settle at an equilibrium rather than grow without bound.
  • The only exogenous driver is the constant hire rate; each level's steady-state size equals the flow arriving from below divided by that level's total exit fraction (promotion plus departure). Thus rookie hiring propagates upward with a lag set by the residence time at each level (1 / total exit fraction).
  • Because partners can only exit through attrition, their equilibrium size is the most sensitive to changes anywhere upstream, and their stock responds most slowly.

Modeling choices

  • Promotion and departure fractions are represented as named constants (promotion_rate, departure_rate) so no arbitrary numbers appear inside equations.
  • All flows are one-directional (uniflows) since hiring, promotion, and attrition cannot run backwards.
  • Cross-module links use ghost components named with the source module prefix, so no module references another module's variables directly.
supportingInfo.title: Three level promotion chain with attrition

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.


            In a certain ecosystem, there are three animal populations: lions, foxes, and chickens.
            
            All species reproduce and naturally die out at specific, stable percentage rates.
            Furthermore, the chicken population is predated at a rate proportional to the fox population,
            and the fox population is predated at a rate proportional to the lion population.
            
            Create a model with three modules named 'lions', 'foxes', and 'chickens'.
            
            Use the following component names within each module as appropriate:
            count, birth rate, death rate, births, deaths, predation rate

            In particular, "[animal].predation rate" should refer to the number of [animal]s that die off due to that animal's predator.

            When creating a ghost component, preserve the name of the original component, including the module prefix (separated by a space rather than a period).
            So, a ghost of "module1.component" in module2 should be named "module2.module1 component".

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Three modules — lions, foxes, chickens — each built around a count stock driven by flows.

  • Reinforcing loop (growth): in every module, count → births → count. Births equal count * birth rate, so each population compounds on itself.
  • Balancing loop (natural mortality): in every module, count → deaths → count, with deaths equal to count * death rate. These are the "stable percentage rates" described.
  • Predation chain: chickens.predation rate is an additional outflow from the chicken stock equal to the predation coefficient times the fox population times the chicken population — i.e., the per-chicken loss rate is proportional to fox numbers, exactly as described. Likewise foxes.predation rate drains the fox stock in proportion to the lion population. Lions, being the apex predator, have no predation outflow.

Cross-module links (ghosts)

  • foxes.lions count is a ghost of lions.count, used only to compute fox predation losses.
  • chickens.foxes count is a ghost of foxes.count, used only to compute chicken predation losses.

All predation equations reference the ghost, never the source directly, so each module stays self-contained.

Behavior to expect

Because births depend only on a species' own numbers (no prey-to-predator feedback was specified), the causal influence runs strictly top-down: lions set the mortality pressure on foxes, and foxes set the mortality pressure on chickens. The net growth of each population is birth rate minus death rate minus predation pressure, so a rising predator stock can flip its prey from exponential growth to exponential collapse — a one-way cascade rather than the closed oscillating predator-prey loop.

Parameters

Coefficients are illustrative and separated into named variables (birth rate, death rate, predation fraction per predator) so they can be adjusted without touching the equation structure.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure identified

The description contains a single object (frimbulators) and one reinforcing feedback loop.

  • Created module Frimbulators for the object, following the pluralized naming convention.
  • Frimbulators.count is a stock (an accumulation of inventory) with initial value 20, matching the stated baseline.
  • Frimbulators.growth is an inflow, marked one-directional since inventory gains cannot be negative here.
  • Frimbulators.growth rate isolates the 2%-per-day constant rather than hard-coding it inside the flow equation.

Causal relationships extracted

  1. Inventory count → growth (+): growth is explicitly relative to current size.
  2. Growth rate → growth (+): the fractional rate scales the gain.
  3. Growth → inventory count (+): the inflow accumulates in the stock.

Together these form a classic reinforcing (exponential growth) loop: more inventory produces more daily gain, which produces still more inventory. No ghost variables were needed because only one component exists and there are no cross-module references.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In my business, our records indicate one hundred frimbulators. Every week, this inventory benefits from 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each week the stock decreases by a constant five frimbulators.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure created

  • A single module, frimbulators, holds the whole component, following the requested naming convention with the quantity stored in frimbulators.count.
  • count is a stock initialized at 100 frimbulators, because inventory is an accumulation that changes only through its flows.

Causal relationships extracted

  1. Proportional growth (reinforcing loop): growth = count × growth fraction, with the fraction abstracted into its own named constant (0.05 per week) rather than hard-coded in the equation. Because the inflow depends on the stock itself, this forms a classic reinforcing (exponential growth) loop.
  2. Constant drain: removal = removal rate, a named constant of five frimbulators per week. This outflow does not depend on the stock, so it is a simple exogenous drain rather than a balancing loop.

Notes

  • Both flows are marked one-directional, since additions and removals of physical units cannot be negative.
  • No ghost variables were needed: there is only one component, and all references stay inside its module.
  • Net behavior: since 5% of 100 (five per week) exactly offsets the constant removal at the start, the inventory sits at an unstable equilibrium — any upward nudge triggers runaway growth, and any downward nudge triggers collapse.
