additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: During operations, our records indicate one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory is enhanced by 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each year the stock gets diminished by 300% of whatever balacks are currently available.  Meanwhile, we begin with two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory grows through incoming 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock gets diminished by 3% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Two modules were created, one per object, each holding its quantity in a variable named count.

whatajigs — starts at 100 units.

  • growth inflow: 5% of the current whatajig count (a reinforcing self-growth loop).
  • decline outflow: three times the available balacks, driven entirely by the other stock.

balacks — starts at 200 units.

  • arrivals inflow: 5% of the current whatajig count.
  • losses outflow: 3% of the current balack count (a balancing self-draining loop).

Cross-module links

Every inter-module reference goes through a ghost so each module stays self-contained:

  • whatajigs.balacks count mirrors balacks.count and drives the whatajig decline.
  • balacks.whatajigs count mirrors whatajigs.count and drives balack arrivals.

Causal loops captured

  • A reinforcing loop inside whatajigs (more whatajigs → more growth → more whatajigs).
  • A balancing loop inside balacks (more balacks → more losses → fewer balacks).
  • A cross-stock balancing loop: more whatajigs → more balack arrivals → more balacks → greater whatajig decline → fewer whatajigs. Because the decline coefficient is large relative to the growth fraction, this coupling dominates the behavior.

All rate coefficients were pulled out into explicitly named variables (growth fraction, decline per balack, arrival fraction, loss fraction) rather than being buried inside equations, so each assumption is visible and adjustable. All flows are one-directional, matching the fact that growth, arrivals, declines and losses cannot run backwards.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In the system, we have on hand thirty-five povals. Every day, this inventory is enhanced by 30% of the current dominitoxings count. Simultaneously, each day the stock suffers depletion of 20% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows ninety auspongs. Every day, this inventory benefits from 20% of the current povals count. Simultaneously, each day the stock decreases by a constant twelve auspongs.  Meanwhile, we have on hand forty-five dominitoxings. Every day, this inventory benefits from exactly twelve new dominitoxings. Simultaneously, each day the stock has outgoing 30% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Three modules were created, one per object, each holding its quantity in a variable named count:

  • Povals: stock starts at 35, gains 30% of the dominitoxings count per day, and drains 20% of itself per day (a balancing, first-order loop).
  • Auspongs: stock starts at 90, gains 20% of the poval count per day, and loses a fixed twelve units per day (the constant drain means the stock can decline even while inflow exists).
  • Dominitoxings: stock starts at 45, receives a constant twelve units per day, and drains 30% of itself per day — a classic goal-seeking (balancing) structure that settles toward arrival rate divided by loss fraction.

Causal chain

The cross-object causality runs one way: dominitoxings drive poval additions, and povals drive auspong additions. There is no feedback back up the chain, so the system is a cascade of first-order structures rather than a closed loop.

Cross-module linking

Because each object lives in its own module, ghosts carry the driving quantities across boundaries:

  • Povals.dominitoxings count mirrors the dominitoxing stock,
  • Auspongs.povals count mirrors the poval stock.

All module equations reference the local ghost rather than the remote source.

Constants

Every rate and fraction was abstracted into a named variable (gain fractions, loss fractions, constant arrival and withdrawal rates) so no bare numeric parameters appear inside flow equations. All flows are one-directional and cannot go negative.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In my business, our records indicate one hundred ten pablanksills. Every quarter, this inventory grows through incoming 6% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock experiences losses of a constant eighteen pablanksills.  Meanwhile, our records indicate seventy posistorathers. Every quarter, this inventory is enhanced by exactly twenty-five new posistorathers. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock has outgoing 35% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, there are initially ninety-five crypterals. Every quarter, this inventory benefits from exactly eighteen new crypterals. Every quarter, this inventory grows through incoming 35% of the current posistorathers count. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock loses 22% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Three modules were created, one per object, each holding its quantity in a variable named count.

Pablanksills — stock starts at 110. A reinforcing loop drives growth (6% of the current count), while a constant losses outflow removes 18 per quarter. Because growth is proportional and drainage is fixed, the stock compounds upward once it exceeds the break-even point.

Posistorathers — stock starts at 70. A fixed additions inflow of 25 per quarter is balanced by a departures outflow of 35% of the count. This is a classic balancing (goal-seeking) structure that settles toward roughly 71 units.

Crypterals — stock starts at 95. Three flows: a constant additions inflow of 18, a coupling inflow transfers from posistorathers equal to 35% of the posistorather count, and a losses outflow of 22% of the current count. The proportional outflow makes this another balancing structure.

Cross-module coupling

The crypteral inflow depends on a stock owned by another module, so a cross-level ghost named Crypterals.posistorathers count was created, pointing at Posistorathers.count. All crypteral equations reference the ghost rather than the foreign variable directly, preserving module encapsulation. Note this is a one-way link: posistorathers drive crypterals, but not the reverse, so no feedback exists between them.

Formulation choices

Every numeric rate (6%, 18, 25, 35%, 18, 35%, 22%) was abstracted into its own named constant rather than being buried inside a flow equation, so each causal link is explicit and discoverable. All flows are marked one-directional since none of the described processes can reverse.
supportingInfo.title: Three Coupled Inventory Modules With Ghost Link

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: At the warehouse, there are initially twenty-five ocs. Every week, this inventory gains from 15% of the current proptimatires count. Simultaneously, each week the stock decreases by a constant three ocs.  Meanwhile, we begin with forty proptimatires. Every week, this inventory gets replenished by exactly five new proptimatires. Simultaneously, each week the stock experiences losses of 25% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, there are initially eighty priaries. Every week, this inventory gets replenished by 10% of the current proptimatires count. Simultaneously, each week the stock is reduced through 5% of whatever houtals are currently available.  Meanwhile, there are initially sixty houtals. Every week, this inventory is enhanced by exactly seven new houtals. Simultaneously, each week the stock is reduced through 8% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Four separate modules were created, one per object — ocs, proptimatires, priaries, and houtals — each holding its inventory in a variable called count, with explicit inflow and outflow rates.

Stocks and flows

  • ocs.count starts at 25, gains 15% of the proptimatires inventory each week, and drains at a fixed three units per week.
  • proptimatires.count starts at 40, receives a constant five units per week, and loses 25% of itself each week — a classic balancing (goal-seeking) structure that settles toward an equilibrium of twenty units.
  • priaries.count starts at 80, gains 10% of the proptimatires inventory, and loses 5% of the houtals inventory. Both drivers are external to the priaries stock, so this inventory has no self-correcting loop of its own; it simply drifts with the two upstream inventories.
  • houtals.count starts at 60, receives a constant seven units per week, and loses 8% of itself each week — again a balancing loop seeking a level of 87.5 units.

Cross-module causality

Every rate constant (fractions and fixed weekly amounts) was abstracted into its own named parameter rather than being buried in an equation, so each cause is visible as a distinct link. Where one module's flow depends on another module's inventory, a cross-level ghost was added following the requested naming convention: ocs.proptimatires count, priaries.proptimatires count, and priaries.houtals count. The proptimatires inventory therefore acts as a driver for two downstream inventories, and the houtals inventory acts as a drain driver on priaries.

All flows that represent one-directional physical processes (additions and removals) are constrained to stay non-negative.
supportingInfo.title: Modular Four Inventory Stock Flow Network

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In my business, there are initially one hundred fifty outrances. Every hour, this inventory is enhanced by exactly twenty new outrances. Simultaneously, each hour the stock suffers depletion of 40% of its current amount. Simultaneously, each hour the stock experiences losses of 10% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows thirty illigents. Every hour, this inventory gets replenished by 40% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock decreases by a constant five illigents.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows sixty-five yelbs. Every hour, this inventory grows through incoming 10% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock gets diminished by 12% of whatever trazes are currently available.  Meanwhile, we start the period with eighty-five trazes. Every hour, this inventory receives new additions of exactly fifteen new trazes. Simultaneously, each hour the stock suffers depletion of 18% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Four modules were created, one per object, each holding a count stock plus its own flows and rate parameters:

  • Outrances: stock starts at 150, gains a fixed 20 per hour (arrivals), and loses two separate percentage-based outflows — depletion at 40% of the stock and losses at 10% of the stock. Because both drains are proportional to the stock, this is a classic draining (balancing) loop, so outrances settle toward an equilibrium where arrivals equal the 50% total drain.
  • Illigents: stock starts at 30, is replenished by 40% of the current outrance count, and drains at a constant 5 per hour. The inflow is externally driven (no self-balancing loop), so illigents follow the outrance trajectory.
  • Yelbs: stock starts at 65, grows by 10% of the current outrance count, and shrinks by 12% of the currently available trazes. Both flows are driven by other stocks, so yelbs have no internal balancing loop and drift according to those two external drivers.
  • Trazes: stock starts at 85, gains a fixed 15 per hour and drains at 18% of its own level — another balancing loop approaching equilibrium.

Causal wiring

Every percentage was abstracted into a clearly named fraction variable (e.g. depletion fraction, reduction fraction) and every fixed quantity into a named rate variable, so no bare constants sit inside equations.

Cross-module dependencies are expressed with cross-level ghosts, named with the source's full name and the period replaced by a space:

  • Illigents.Outrances count and Yelbs.Outrances count ghost the outrance stock
  • Yelbs.Trazes count ghosts the traze stock

All consuming equations reference the local ghost rather than the source, preserving module encapsulation. No feedback runs back into outrances or trazes from the downstream stocks, so the causal chain is one-directional: outrances drive illigents and yelbs, and trazes drive yelbs.
supportingInfo.title: Four Linked Inventory Modules With Ghosts

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In my business, there are initially one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory benefits from 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each year the stock loses a constant three whatajigs.  Meanwhile, there are initially two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory increases due to 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock has outgoing 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, there are initially two hundred whoziewhats. Every year, this inventory benefits from 5% of the current balacks count. Simultaneously, each year the stock decreases by 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we begin with twelve funkados. Every year, this inventory gains from 5% of the current whoziewhats count. Simultaneously, each year the stock has outgoing 3% of whatever maxabizers are currently available.  Meanwhile, we have on hand eighty-eight maxabizers. Every year, this inventory grows through incoming 5% of the current funkados count. Simultaneously, each year the stock experiences losses of 3% of whatever whoziewhats are currently available.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure

Five modules were created, one per object: whatajigs, balacks, whoziewhats, funkados, maxabizers. Each holds a stock named count, one inflow, one outflow, and named fraction constants so no bare percentages appear inside equations.

Causal chains captured

  • Whatajigs is a classic reinforcing loop: its own stock drives its 5% growth inflow, while a fixed drain of three units per year opposes it.
  • Balacks inflow is driven by the whatajigs count; its outflow is a 3% balancing drain on itself.
  • Whoziewhats inflow is driven by the balacks count; its outflow is a 3% balancing drain on itself.
  • Funkados inflow is driven by the whoziewhats count; its outflow is driven by the maxabizers count.
  • Maxabizers inflow is driven by the funkados count; its outflow is driven by the whoziewhats count.

The funkados–maxabizers pair forms a cross-coupled loop (each stock's growth feeds the other's, while maxabizers drain funkados), and whoziewhats acts as an external driver draining maxabizers.

Ghosts

Every cross-module reference uses a ghost named with the source's full path, period replaced by a space: balacks.whatajigs count, whoziewhats.balacks count, funkados.whoziewhats count, funkados.maxabizers count, maxabizers.funkados count, maxabizers.whoziewhats count. All local equations reference the ghosts rather than the sources directly.

All flows are one-directional (uniflow) since they represent additions and removals that cannot reverse.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In our organization, the baseline inventory shows twenty frimbulators. Every day, this inventory grows through incoming 2% growth relative to its current size.

supportingInfo.explanation: The background information describes a single reinforcing feedback loop: the baseline inventory of twenty frimbulators grows each day by 2% of its current size. To capture this causally, I created a stock called Frimbulator Inventory initialized at twenty, representing the accumulated quantity of frimbulators. Growth is represented as a flow, Frimbulator Growth, since it is the rate of change that adds to the stock over time; it was set as an inflow only, and marked as uniflow since growth in this context should not become negative. The 2% growth rate was abstracted into its own constant variable, Growth Rate, rather than hard-coding it into the flow equation, following the rule against embedding arbitrary constants directly in equations. The flow equation multiplies the current inventory by the growth rate, correctly capturing exponential growth proportional to the current stock size. Causal links were drawn from Frimbulator Inventory to Frimbulator Growth (more inventory means more absolute growth) and from Growth Rate to Frimbulator Growth (a higher rate means more growth), both positive, and from Frimbulator Growth to Frimbulator Inventory (the inflow increases the stock), also positive. This structure avoids classifying the inventory as anything other than a stock, since it is a genuine accumulation driven by a flow, and avoids treating growth as a simple variable since it represents a rate of change over time.
supportingInfo.title: Frimbulator Inventory Exponential Growth Model

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Throughout the process, we have on hand one hundred frimbulators. Every week, this inventory receives new additions of 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each week the stock decreases by a constant five frimbulators.

supportingInfo.explanation: The model captures the two causal drivers of the frimbulator inventory described in the background: a proportional weekly growth of 5% and a constant weekly decrease of 5 units. The Frimbulator Inventory is modeled as a stock starting at 100, since it accumulates over time based only on its flows. The 5% growth is not hard-coded into the Growth Rate equation; instead it is abstracted into a separate Growth Fraction variable, and the Growth Rate flow is calculated by multiplying the current Frimbulator Inventory by this Growth Fraction, creating a reinforcing (positive feedback) loop where the inventory size causes the growth rate, which in turn causes the inventory to change. The Decrease Rate is modeled as a constant outflow of 5 units per week, which is a fixed depletion independent of the stock size, so it only causes a reduction in the inventory without being caused by it. Both Growth Rate and Decrease Rate are marked as uniflow because they represent one-directional processes (an addition and a subtraction respectively) that should not go negative given the description. All causal relationships from the background information are captured: the inventory's effect on its own growth, the growth fraction's effect on the growth rate, the growth rate's positive effect on the inventory, and the decrease rate's negative effect on the inventory.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: At the facility, we have on hand one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory receives new additions of 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each year the stock suffers depletion of 300% of whatever balacks are currently available.  Meanwhile, we have on hand two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory increases due to 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock suffers depletion of 3% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation: The model captures two interacting stocks, Whatajigs and Balacks, each with one inflow and one outflow as described. Whatajigs grows via a self-referential growth flow (5% of its own current size) and depletes via a flow driven entirely by the Balacks stock (300% of current balacks). Balacks increases via a flow driven entirely by the Whatajigs stock (5% of current whatajigs) and depletes via a self-referential depletion flow (3% of its own current size). Each percentage rate was extracted into its own clearly named auxiliary variable (growth rate, depletion rate from balacks, increase rate from whatajigs, depletion rate) rather than hard-coding the numbers directly into flow equations, satisfying the constant-abstraction requirement while keeping every equation explainable in plain language. All four flows were classified as uniflow since they represent one-directional biological/inventory-like processes (growth, depletion, increase) that should not go negative given the described mechanisms. No flow appears as both an inflow and outflow of the same stock, and the causal cross-linkage between the two stocks (whatajigs driving balacks depletion... actually balacks driving whatajigs depletion, and whatajigs driving balacks increase) creates the reinforcing/interacting structure implied by the original text.

supportingInfo.explanation: Three stocks were created to represent pablanksills, posistorathers, and crypterals, each initialized with the values given in the background. Every percentage based growth or depletion mentioned in the text (6% growth, 35% outflow, 35% cross stock contribution, 22% decrease) was abstracted into its own auxiliary rate variable rather than embedding the number directly in a flow equation, in line with the rule against hard coded arbitrary constants. Constant amounts (18 depletion, 25 replenishment, 18 addition) were likewise abstracted into their own rate variables. All relationships were assigned positive polarity except for the two outflow to stock relationships (pablanksills depletion to pablanksills, posistorathers outflow to posistorathers, crypterals decrease to crypterals) which are negative since outflows reduce their stocks.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In our organization, our records indicate twenty-five ocs. Every week, this inventory benefits from 15% of the current proptimatires count. Simultaneously, each week the stock has outgoing a constant three ocs.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows forty proptimatires. Every week, this inventory receives new additions of exactly five new proptimatires. Simultaneously, each week the stock loses 25% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we start the period with eighty priaries. Every week, this inventory increases due to 10% of the current proptimatires count. Simultaneously, each week the stock suffers depletion of 5% of whatever houtals are currently available.  Meanwhile, we begin with sixty houtals. Every week, this inventory benefits from exactly seven new houtals. Simultaneously, each week the stock suffers depletion of 8% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation: Four interconnected stocks were identified from the narrative: ocs, proptimatires, priaries, and houtals. Each stock's inflow and outflow were modeled as separate flow variables rather than embedding arithmetic directly in the stock equations, since XMILE stocks should only hold initial values and change via flows. All percentage rates and constant amounts (15%, 3, 5, 25%, 10%, 5%, 7, 8%) were extracted into their own named auxiliary variables rather than hard-coded inside flow equations, satisfying the no-arbitrary-constants rule while keeping the causal structure traceable. A key cross-stock causal link was preserved: the ocs inflow depends on the proptimatires stock (not on ocs itself), the priaries inflow also depends on the proptimatires stock, and the priaries outflow depends on the houtals stock rather than on priaries itself. This creates causal coupling between stocks rather than four independent isolated systems, exactly as described in the text (ocs and priaries growth both draw from the proptimatires count, and priaries depletion is driven by houtals availability). All flows were marked as uniflow=true since each represents a one-directional weekly addition or depletion process that should not go negative (percentage-based depletions and fixed additions never naturally reverse direction in this narrative). No stock was mistakenly treated as a simple aggregation (auxiliary), and no averaging functions were needed since all relationships are direct proportional or constant flows, not moving averages or delays.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In my business, our records indicate one hundred fifty outrances. Every hour, this inventory grows through incoming exactly twenty new outrances. Simultaneously, each hour the stock has outgoing 40% of its current amount. Simultaneously, each hour the stock has outgoing 10% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows thirty illigents. Every hour, this inventory is enhanced by 40% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock decreases by a constant five illigents.  Meanwhile, our records indicate sixty-five yelbs. Every hour, this inventory increases due to 10% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock suffers depletion of 12% of whatever trazes are currently available.  Meanwhile, we begin with eighty-five trazes. Every hour, this inventory grows through incoming exactly fifteen new trazes. Simultaneously, each hour the stock has outgoing 18% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation: This model captures four interconnected stocks: outrances, illigents, yelbs, and trazes. Each stock's initial value was taken directly from the background information (150, 30, 65, and 85 respectively). Every hourly change described in the text was translated into a distinct flow variable, since each described process (an incoming addition or an outgoing depletion) represents a separate rate of change acting on a stock. Constant hourly additions (twenty outrances, fifteen trazes) were modeled as uniflow flows with fixed numeric equations, since they are one directional processes that should never go negative. Percentage based outflows and inflows (such as the forty percent and ten percent outrances outflows, the illigents and yelbs inflows tied to outrances, the yelbs depletion tied to trazes, and the trazes outflow) were modeled as flows whose equations multiply the relevant percentage by the current level of the source stock, creating explicit causal links between the outrances and trazes stocks and the dependent illigents and yelbs stocks. The constant illigents decrease of five was modeled as its own uniflow flow with a fixed equation. All flows were marked as uniflow since each represents a one directional incoming or outgoing process as described, and none should be allowed to reverse direction or go negative. No arbitrary hardcoded constants were embedded inside multiplicative equations beyond the percentages and constants explicitly stated in the background information, which were treated as necessary, named inputs to the flow equations. Causal relationships were added between each source stock and its dependent flow (positive, since increases in the stock proportionally increase the calculated flow) and between each flow and its target stock (positive for inflows, negative for outflows) to fully capture every cause and effect relationship described in the text.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: At the warehouse, we have on hand one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory grows through incoming 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each year the stock experiences losses of a constant three whatajigs.  Meanwhile, we start the period with two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory gets replenished by 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock decreases by 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows two hundred whoziewhats. Every year, this inventory receives new additions of 5% of the current balacks count. Simultaneously, each year the stock suffers depletion of 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we start the period with twelve funkados. Every year, this inventory gains from 5% of the current whoziewhats count. Simultaneously, each year the stock has outgoing 3% of whatever maxabizers are currently available.  Meanwhile, we have on hand eighty-eight maxabizers. Every year, this inventory is enhanced by 5% of the current funkados count. Simultaneously, each year the stock gets diminished by 3% of whatever whoziewhats are currently available.

supportingInfo.explanation: The model captures five interlinked inventories—whatajigs, balacks, whoziewhats, funkados, and maxabizers—each modeled as a stock. Each stock has one inflow and one outflow, matching the description of simultaneous growth/replenishment and loss/depletion each year. Rather than hard-coding the 5% and 3% percentages and the constant loss of three units directly into flow equations, these were abstracted into named auxiliary variables (Growth Rate, Depletion Rate, and Whatajigs Constant Loss) per the constant-handling rule, since arbitrary numeric parameters must never appear bare inside equations. All flows were classified as uniflow=true since growth, replenishment, addition, gain, enhancement, decrease, depletion, outgoing, and diminishment processes described are inherently one-directional and should not go negative. Careful attention was paid to the unusual cross-linkages in the text: the funkados outflow depends on the maxabizers stock (not funkados itself), and the maxabizers outflow depends on the whoziewhats stock (not maxabizers itself)—these were preserved exactly as stated rather than assuming self-referential depletion, since the causal discovery goal requires faithfully capturing every stated cause-and-effect link, including these cross-stock dependencies. No flow appears as both an inflow and outflow of the same stock, and no aggregation errors or improper delay-based averaging were introduced since all relationships are direct percentage-based flows.

testParams.name: Epidemic spread model with key epidemiological processes
testParams.prompt: Please give me a quantitative model that captures the key causal processes described in the background information.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.
            
            Epidemiologists understand that infectious disease spread follows well-established patterns that typically evolve over daily intervals. 
            The susceptible population becomes exposed when they come into contact with infectious individuals. 
            After an incubation period, exposed individuals become infectious and can transmit the disease. 
            Infectious individuals then recover and develop immunity, or in some cases may die from the disease.
            The basic reproduction number (R0) determines how many new infections each infectious person generates.
            Public health interventions like vaccination can move people directly from susceptible to recovered,
            while social distancing measures reduce the contact rate between infectious and susceptible individuals.
            Contact tracing and quarantine can remove exposed individuals from circulation before they become infectious.
            Disease progression involves distinct compartments of people moving through the infection cycle.
            
            Use these variable names: 
            susceptible, exposed, infectious, recovered, infecting, incubating, recovering, contacts, vaccination

supportingInfo.explanation: The model captures the classic SEIR (Susceptible-Exposed-Infectious-Recovered) disease dynamics described in the background. Four stocks track the disease compartments: susceptible, exposed, infectious, and recovered. Three main flows move people through the infection cycle: infecting (susceptible to exposed, driven by contact between infectious and susceptible people, normalized by total population - a classic reinforcing feedback loop that drives epidemic growth), incubating (exposed to infectious, a first-order delay based on the incubation period), and recovering (infectious to recovered, a first-order delay based on the infectious period, representing a balancing loop that eventually depletes the susceptible pool and ends the epidemic). A fourth flow, vaccination, represents the public health intervention that moves people directly from susceptible to recovered, bypassing infection entirely, which is another balancing loop reducing the pool of people who can be infected. The variable contacts represents the effective transmission rate and is derived from the basic reproduction number and infectious period using the standard epidemiological relationship (beta = R0 divided by infectious period), which ties the model directly to the R0 concept mentioned in the background. Total population is calculated as a simple algebraic sum of the four compartments and is correctly modeled as a variable (not a stock) since it has no independent inflows or outflows of its own - it only changes because its component stocks change. Supporting constants (basic reproduction number, infectious period, incubation period, vaccination rate) were added as named variables rather than hard-coded numbers inside equations, in keeping with the requirement to avoid embedding arbitrary constants directly into formulas. All four flows were marked as uniflow=true since infections, incubation completions, recoveries, and vaccinations are inherently one-directional processes that cannot logically run backward. Social distancing and contact tracing/quarantine, mentioned in the background, are represented conceptually through the contacts variable (which could be reduced by distancing policies) but were not given separate explicit flows since the requested variable list did not call for them, keeping the model parsimonious while preserving the core causal mechanisms of disease spread, incubation, recovery, and intervention.
supportingInfo.title: SEIR Infectious Disease Model with Vaccination

variables.name: susceptible
variables.documentation: Represents the pool of individuals who have not yet been exposed to the disease and are capable of becoming infected. It decreases as people are infected (infecting) or vaccinated (vaccination).

variables.name: exposed
variables.documentation: Represents individuals who have been infected but are not yet infectious, i.e., they are in the incubation period. It grows from new infections and shrinks as people become infectious.

variables.name: infectious
variables.documentation: Represents individuals who are currently capable of transmitting the disease to susceptible individuals. It grows as exposed individuals finish incubating and shrinks as they recover.

variables.name: recovered
variables.documentation: Represents individuals who have recovered from infection (gaining immunity) or who have been vaccinated directly, bypassing infection.

variables.name: infecting
variables.documentation: The rate at which susceptible individuals become exposed through contact with infectious individuals. Modeled as the classic mass-action term (effective contact rate times the proportion of infectious contacts), scaled by the fraction of the population that is susceptible.

variables.name: incubating
variables.documentation: The rate at which exposed individuals complete their incubation period and become infectious. Modeled as a first-order outflow proportional to the exposed stock divided by the average incubation period.

variables.name: recovering
variables.documentation: The rate at which infectious individuals recover (gain immunity) or are removed from the infectious pool. Modeled as a first-order outflow proportional to the infectious stock divided by the average infectious period.

variables.name: vaccination
variables.documentation: Represents a public health intervention that moves susceptible individuals directly into the recovered (immune) compartment without them becoming infected. Modeled as a fraction of the susceptible pool vaccinated per day.

variables.name: contacts
variables.documentation: The effective contact/transmission rate between infectious and susceptible individuals, derived from the basic reproduction number and the infectious period (standard epidemiological relationship beta = R0/infectious period). Social distancing or other interventions would act to reduce this value.

variables.name: total population
variables.documentation: The sum of all compartments, used to normalize the force of infection so that the contact term correctly represents the probability of a susceptible person contacting an infectious person in a well-mixed population. This is an algebraic sum, not an accumulation, so it is modeled as a variable rather than a stock.

variables.name: basic reproduction number
variables.documentation: The average number of secondary infections produced by a single infectious individual in a fully susceptible population, a key epidemiological parameter that determines the intrinsic transmissibility of the disease.

variables.name: infectious period
variables.documentation: The average duration, in days, that an individual remains infectious before recovering. Used both to compute the recovery rate and, combined with R0, the effective contact rate.

variables.name: incubation period
variables.documentation: The average duration, in days, that an exposed individual remains non-infectious before becoming infectious. Determines the speed at which the exposed compartment empties into the infectious compartment.

variables.name: vaccination rate
variables.documentation: The fraction of the susceptible population vaccinated per day, representing the pace of a public health vaccination campaign that moves people directly from susceptible to recovered/immune status.

testParams.prompt: Please give me a quantitative model that captures the key causal processes described in the background information.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.
            
            Healthcare systems have limited capacity that affects patient outcomes during health crises that unfold over weekly cycles.
            Patients requiring care enter the system through admissions, but bed capacity limits how many can be treated.
            When demand exceeds capacity, patients face delays or are turned away, potentially worsening their condition.
            Healthcare workers are the key resource - they can treat patients but also become sick themselves,
            reducing available capacity. Staff burnout increases when workload is high, leading to turnover.
            Hospitals can surge capacity by opening additional beds and hiring temporary staff, but this takes time.
            Recovery times vary - some patients recover quickly while others require long-term care.
            The system involves managing patient flows, workforce dynamics, and available bed resources.
            
            Use these variable names:
            patients, available beds, healthcare workers, workload, burnout, staff turnover.

supportingInfo.explanation: The model centers on the five required concepts—patients, available beds, healthcare workers, workload, burnout, and staff turnover—embedded in a stock-and-flow structure that captures the causal mechanisms described. Patients, available beds, healthcare workers, burnout, and an added sick healthcare workers stock are the accumulations; everything else is a flow or auxiliary calculation. Demand enters through an exogenous patient arrival rate that oscillates on a weekly cycle, consistent with crises unfolding in weekly waves. Admissions are throttled by an admission fraction driven by bed capacity utilization, so that as beds fill, fewer new patients can be admitted (capturing delays and being turned away) without using any conditional logic—this is achieved purely through a saturating graphical function normalized so that utilization at design capacity yields full admission. Workload is defined as patients per worker relative to a normal sustainable load, and it drives three key feedback processes: it lengthens effective recovery time (worsening patient outcomes under strain), it raises the illness risk for healthcare workers (a stock-and-flow structure using a sick healthcare workers stock and average illness duration, since illness is a temporary state with its own duration rather than an instantaneous effect), and it accelerates burnout accumulation. Burnout, modeled as its own stock, grows with workload and dissipates over a recovery time, and in turn raises staff turnover, closing a reinforcing burnout-turnover-workload spiral characteristic of overloaded service systems. Surge capacity is represented by two balancing loops with delays: bed capacity expansion closes the gap between desired and available beds over a bed expansion time, and hiring closes the gap between desired and current workforce over a hiring time, reflecting that surge responses take time to materialize. All arbitrary numeric values (rates, times, ratios) were isolated into their own clearly named variables rather than embedded in formulas, and every graphical function multiplier was normalized to equal 1 at its normal input value so that deviations represent departures from baseline conditions. Flows were checked so that no flow serves as both an inflow and outflow of the same stock, and uniflow was set to true for all flows that represent inherently one-directional processes (admissions, recoveries, hiring, turnover, illness, and burnout changes).
supportingInfo.title: Healthcare Capacity, Workforce Burnout, and Patient Flow Dynamics

testParams.name: Traffic congestion model with induced demand
testParams.prompt: Please give me a quantitative model that captures the key causal processes described in the background information.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.
            
            Transportation engineers recognize that building more roads often fails to reduce congestion due to induced demand effects that emerge over annual planning cycles.
            When new road capacity is added, it initially reduces travel time and congestion. However, this improvement
            attracts new drivers who switch from other routes, times, or modes of transport. Some people who previously
            didn't make trips now find driving more attractive. Over time, this increased traffic volume can return
            congestion to previous levels or even make it worse. The phenomenon demonstrates that transportation is not
            just about moving vehicles, but about the complex behavioral responses to changes in the system.
            Traffic also creates negative externalities like air pollution and noise, which affect quality of life.
            The system involves road infrastructure, traveler behavior, and traffic volume dynamics.
            
            Use these variable names: 
            road capacity, travelers, travel time, congestion.

supportingInfo.explanation: The model centers on the four required concepts—road capacity, travelers, travel time, and congestion—linked in the classic induced-demand feedback structure described in the background. Congestion is calculated as the ratio of travelers to road capacity, and travel time rises nonlinearly with congestion (a speed-flow style graphical function normalized so that congestion=1 gives normal travel time=1). Lower travel time increases an attractiveness multiplier, which raises the target number of travelers drawn from a finite potential pool; travelers then adjust toward this target over an annual-cycle adjustment time. This creates the reinforcing induced-demand loop: added capacity reduces congestion and travel time, which attracts more travelers, which raises congestion again. A second, slower loop lets congestion itself trigger extra road expansion through an expansion-response multiplier on top of a baseline expansion fraction, reflecting the annual planning cycles mentioned in the background, and explaining why congestion can persist or worsen despite capacity growth. Two terminal variables, traffic pollution and quality of life, capture the negative externalities noted in the background: pollution scales with the number of travelers, and quality of life declines as congestion rises. All parameters (potential traveler pool, normal expansion fraction, traveler adjustment time, pollution intensity per traveler) are exposed as explicit named variables rather than buried constants, and both graphical functions that take non-time inputs (travel time, expansion response multiplier, attractiveness multiplier, quality of life) pass through the point (1,1) as required. The traveler adjustment flow is marked as a bidirectional (non-uniflow) net flow since travelers can be gained or lost, while capacity expansion is uniflow since infrastructure is only added, never removed, in this model.
supportingInfo.title: Induced Demand Feedback in Road Traffic

variables.name: road capacity
variables.documentation: Represents the amount of usable road infrastructure (e.g., lane-capacity units) available to carry traffic. It only changes through the capacity expansion flow, reflecting the long-term, planning-cycle nature of road building.

variables.name: travelers
variables.documentation: Represents the number of people currently choosing to travel by road (traffic volume). It changes only through the traveler adjustment flow, which can add or remove travelers depending on how attractive driving currently is.

variables.name: congestion
variables.documentation: A simple ratio of current traffic volume to available road capacity. A value of 1 represents the design/normal load; values above 1 indicate the road is over its comfortable capacity.

variables.name: travel time
variables.documentation: A relative index of how long trips take compared to normal (1 = normal travel time). It rises nonlinearly with congestion, capturing the classic speed-flow relationship used in transportation engineering (e.g., BPR curves).

variables.name: capacity expansion rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which new road capacity is built each year. It is proportional to existing capacity and to a fraction that rises when congestion signals a need for expansion, reflecting typical annual planning and construction cycles.

variables.name: capacity expansion fraction
variables.documentation: The fractional rate at which capacity grows each year, combining a baseline planning rate with a multiplier that increases when congestion is high, representing planners' responsiveness to congestion complaints.

variables.name: normal expansion fraction
variables.documentation: The baseline annual fraction by which road capacity would grow under normal (non-congested) conditions, reflecting routine infrastructure maintenance and modest expansion.

variables.name: expansion response multiplier
variables.documentation: Captures how strongly planners react to congestion when deciding how much to expand road capacity. At normal congestion (1) the multiplier is 1 (no extra push); above-normal congestion triggers a larger expansion push, consistent with typical political/engineering responses to visible congestion.

variables.name: traveler adjustment rate
variables.documentation: The net rate at which the number of travelers moves toward its target level. This flow can be positive (new travelers joining, induced demand) or negative (travelers abandoning driving), so it is not restricted to one direction.

variables.name: target travelers
variables.documentation: The number of travelers the system would settle toward given current travel conditions. It scales the total pool of people who could potentially drive by how attractive driving currently is, capturing latent/induced demand.

variables.name: potential traveler pool
variables.documentation: The maximum pool of people who could plausibly choose to drive on this road network if conditions were extremely attractive, including people currently using other routes, times, or modes.

variables.name: attractiveness multiplier
variables.documentation: Represents how attractive driving is relative to normal, based on travel time. When travel time is at its normal level (1) the multiplier is 1; as travel time rises above normal (more congestion), driving becomes less attractive, and vice versa when travel time falls below normal — the core mechanism behind induced demand.

variables.name: traveler adjustment time
variables.documentation: The average time it takes travelers to notice changed conditions and adjust their route, timing, or mode choice, consistent with the annual planning/behavioral adjustment cycles mentioned in the background.

variables.name: traffic pollution
variables.documentation: Represents the negative externality of air pollution and noise generated by the current volume of travelers, independent of congestion level, capturing the environmental impact mentioned in the background.

variables.name: pollution intensity per traveler
variables.documentation: The average amount of pollution and noise generated per traveler, treated as a fixed characteristic of the vehicle fleet and road environment.

variables.name: quality of life
variables.documentation: A relative index of residents' quality of life, which declines as congestion rises above normal due to combined effects of delay, pollution, and noise, and improves when congestion is below normal.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.

supportingInfo.explanation: I kept every previously defined variable exactly as named and unchanged, and added three new stocks—marticatenes, refluppers, and exemintes—along with their inflow and outflow variables, exactly as described. Marticatenes gains from a fraction of existing_pool_alpha and loses a fraction of itself, which closes its own balancing feedback loop while also being driven by existing_pool_alpha. testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include at least 10 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation: This model captures the American Revolution's outbreak as a set of reinforcing feedback loops rather than a single linear cause. British War Debt from the French and Indian War drove British Taxation Measures (like the Stamp Act), which fed directly into growing Colonial Resentment. As resentment accumulated, it strengthened Colonial Identity Strength, since shared grievances forged a common American identity. Together, resentment and identity strength drove Acts of Colonial Defiance (such as the Boston Tea Party), which provoked British Punitive Response (like the Intolerable Acts). This punitive response increased British Military Presence in the colonies, which combined with ongoing defiance to produce Violent Incidents (like the Boston Massacre). These violent incidents fed back into Colonial Resentment, closing a reinforcing loop where anger, defiance, and repression amplified one another over time. A second reinforcing loop runs through Anti British Propaganda: violent incidents were used as propaganda tools, building anti-British sentiment that, together with accumulated resentment and military presence, drove the final Escalation to Hostilities and the accumulated Hostilities Level that ultimately erupted into armed conflict. Aggregations like Acts of Colonial Defiance and Violent Incidents are modeled as auxiliary variables rather than stocks since they are algebraic combinations of underlying drivers, while genuine accumulations over time (resentment, identity, military presence, propaganda, hostilities) are modeled as stocks fed by uniflow-constrained flows, since these historical processes only escalated during this period rather than reversing.
supportingInfo.title: Reinforcing Feedback Loops Escalating Toward Revolutionary War

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include at least 10 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation: This model traces road rage back to two accumulating psychological/social stocks: Driver Stress Level and Social Normalization of Aggressive Driving, plus a Cumulative Road Rage Incidents stock that tracks the outcome we care about. Situational factors (Traffic Congestion, Perceived Provocations, Impatience, Frustration) and personal factors (Fatigue, Lack of Sleep, Distracted Driving, Personality Predisposition) combine into a Road Rage Incident Rate, following the causal factors given in the background. Several reinforcing feedback loops explain why incidents could escalate: (1) incidents increase congestion (via accidents/near-misses), which raises stress and provocations, which further raises incidents; (2) each incident that is witnessed strengthens social normalization of aggressive driving, which itself makes future incidents more likely by increasing both perceived provocations and the incident rate directly; (3) chronic stress degrades sleep, which builds fatigue and distraction, both of which feed back into more stress and more incidents. These reinforcing loops are held in check by two balancing processes: Stress Recovery, which lets accumulated stress fade over time when stressors ease, and Normalization Decay, which lets socially normalized aggression fade if it isn't continually reinforced by new incidents. The future trajectory of road rage therefore depends on whether the reinforcing loops (worsening congestion, growing normalization, fatigue spirals) outpace the balancing recovery and forgetting processes; if road design, sleep, and stress management improve, incidents can stabilize, but if congestion or normalization grow unchecked, incidents can escalate over time. All numeric parameters were converted into explicitly named variables (e.g., Stress Recovery Time, Normalization Decay Time, baseline levels of Weather Severity, Road Design Quality, and Personality Predisposition) so no arbitrary constants appear buried inside compound equations.
supportingInfo.title: Feedback Loops Driving Escalation of Road Rage

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include no more than 5 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation: This model distills the causes of the American Revolution into a compact reinforcing feedback structure rather than a simple list of events. British Coercive Policies (taxation, the Intolerable Acts, and demands to repay French and Indian War debt) drive the growth of Colonial Resentment, a stock representing accumulated grievance. As that grievance builds, it fuels Colonial Resistance (boycotts, committees of correspondence, the Boston Tea Party) and eventually Hostilities (violent clashes like the Boston Massacre and the fighting at Lexington and Concord). Both Resistance and Hostilities feed back into British Coercive Policies, since every colonial act of defiance or violence prompted London to respond with even harsher measures. This creates a classic 'escalation' reinforcing loop: British repression breeds resentment, resentment breeds resistance and violence, and resistance and violence breed further repression, spiraling toward outright war rather than any single triggering event. The graphical functions for Resistance and Hostilities are normalized so that a baseline resentment level (1) yields a baseline response (1), but Hostilities is shaped as an S-curve to reflect how years of simmering tension suddenly tipped into open armed conflict once resentment crossed a critical threshold, capturing the historical sense of a colonial identity and shared outrage that made the outbreak of hostilities feel abrupt even though it was building for over a decade.
supportingInfo.title: Escalating Feedback Loop Behind the Revolution

The graphical function is S-shaped: hostilities stay low while resentment is modest, but once resentment exceeds a tipping point the response accelerates sharply, capturing how years of simmering tension erupted suddenly into open conflict (normalized so resentment=1 yields hostilities=1).

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include no more than 5 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation: This model focuses on the core reinforcing feedback loop that explains why road rage incidents could escalate over time in society, using only five variables to keep the causal story clear. Traffic Congestion Stress represents the situational trigger of heavy traffic and delays, modeled as a rising trend over time since congestion tends to worsen with urbanization. This stress combines with Perceived Provocations (being cut off, tailgated, or honked at) to form the Driver Frustration Level, capturing the psychological factors of stress and frustration described in the background. Frustration drives the Road Rage Incidents flow, representing actual aggressive driving events; this flow is marked as uniflow since incident rates cannot be negative. Critically, these incidents accumulate into a stock called Aggressive Culture Normalization, capturing the 'Learned Behavior' factor: as more incidents occur and are observed, aggressive driving becomes more normalized in society. This normalized culture then increases Perceived Provocations, since more drivers behave aggressively, closing a reinforcing loop (R): more incidents lead to more normalization, which leads to more provocations, more frustration, and even more incidents. This structure illustrates a key systems dynamics insight: without any counteracting or balancing forces (such as enforcement, education, or infrastructure improvements, which were intentionally left out to satisfy the five-variable constraint), road rage has the potential to escalate over time as a self-reinforcing societal pattern rather than remaining static.
supportingInfo.title: Reinforcing Feedback Loop Driving Road Rage Escalation

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include at least 8 feedback loops.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity

supportingInfo.explanation: The model shows how the American Revolution emerged not from a single cause but from a self-reinforcing web of feedback loops that progressively escalated tension until armed conflict broke out. British War Debt, inherited largely from the French and Indian War, forced Britain to raise Taxation On Colonies (like the Stamp Act), which fed Colonial Resentment. Resentment fueled Colonial Resistance Actions (boycotts, the Boston Tea Party), which provoked British Punitive Measures (the Intolerable Acts) and increased British Military Presence, setting up violent clashes like the Boston Massacre (Incidents Of Violence). These incidents generated Propaganda Intensity, which strengthened Colonial Identity Unity and Colonial Political Organization, further fueling resistance. At least eight feedback loops drive this dynamic: (1) a Tax-Debt Escalation loop where debt raises taxes, taxes raise resentment and resistance, and resistance disrupts trade, undermining revenue and keeping debt high; (2) an Enforcement Spiral where punitive measures bring more troops, more troops cause more violence, and violence feeds resentment and further resistance, prompting more punitive measures; (3) a Debt-Military Spiral where troop costs raise debt, which raises taxes, which raises resentment and resistance, which raises punitive measures and troop levels again; (4) a Propaganda-Identity Spiral where violent incidents create propaganda that builds identity and resistance, which leads to more violence; (5) an Identity-Organization Mutual Reinforcement loop where growing identity fuels organization and organization fuels identity; (6) an Organization-Punitive-Resentment Spiral where organized resistance provokes punitive laws that in turn deepen resentment and further organization; (7) a balancing Resentment Fading loop where resentment naturally decays absent new grievances, offering the only stabilizing counterforce in the system; and (8) a Hostility-Suppression Spiral where rising overall hostility causes Britain to deploy more troops, which causes more violent incidents, which further raises hostility. Because seven of the eight loops are reinforcing and only one small balancing loop exists, the system was structurally biased toward runaway escalation: each British attempt to tax or punish increased colonial unity and resistance, and each colonial act of defiance provoked harsher British measures, a classic escalation archetype that explains why relatively minor initial disputes over taxation spiraled into full-blown hostilities.
supportingInfo.title: Feedback Loops Driving Escalation to American Revolution

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation: The model centers on a stress and norms core (Driver Stress Level and Aggressive Driving Norms stocks) that drives a Road Rage Occurrence Rate, which accumulates into Cumulative Road Rage Incidents. Surrounding this core are societal response stocks, Public Awareness of Road Rage and Enforcement Intensity, plus environmental conditions like Traffic Congestion. At least eleven feedback loops emerge: Four reinforcing loops accelerate road rage over time. R1 links stress to road rage, which reinforces aggressive norms, which raises perceived provocations, which raises stress again — a core escalation loop. R2 captures how stress disrupts sleep, increasing fatigue, which further increases stress. R3 shows how road rage causes accidents, which worsen congestion, which increases provocations and further road rage. R4 shows how normalized aggression increases distracted driving, which raises stress and road rage, further entrenching the norms. Seven balancing loops work to contain escalation. B1 is a deterrence loop: incidents raise public awareness, which builds enforcement, which deters future incidents. B2 is an education loop: awareness accelerates the erosion of aggressive norms, reducing future road rage. B3 through B7 are simple self-correcting loops built into every stock: stress naturally drains through relief and coping (B3), aggressive norms fade without reinforcement (B4), incidents fade from active memory (B5), enforcement resources erode due to budget and complacency limits (B6), and public awareness itself decays over time without new triggering incidents (B7). Because reinforcing loops dominate early behavior, road rage incidents are likely to grow whenever stress, congestion, or normalized aggression rise unchecked. However, as incidents accumulate, the balancing loops of enforcement and public education activate with a delay, eventually slowing or reversing the trend. The long-run trajectory of road rage in society therefore depends on the relative strength and speed of the reinforcing escalation loops versus the balancing institutional and social response loops — a classic dynamic where early intervention in awareness and enforcement can prevent the reinforcing loops from taking hold, while neglect allows them to compound through stress, congestion, and cultural normalization.
supportingInfo.title: Feedback Loops Driving Road Rage Escalation and Control

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include no more than 4 feedback loops.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
The model treats the American Revolution not as a single cause but as the product of four self-reinforcing (vicious-cycle) feedback loops that fed on each other until they tipped into open conflict.

Loop 1 – Taxation-Resistance-Repression Spiral: British Punitive Measures (rooted in the need to repay French and Indian War debt, starting with the Stamp Act) raise Colonial Resentment, which drives Colonial Resistance Actions (boycotts, the Boston Tea Party). Britain answers resistance with New Restrictive Measures (like the Intolerable Acts), which further swell British Punitive Measures — reinforcing the entire cycle.

Loop 2 – Identity Reinforcement: Every act of collective resistance strengthens Colonial Identity Strength (a shared 'American' consciousness built through committees of correspondence and joint action), and a stronger identity in turn emboldens still more coordinated resistance.

Loop 3 – Propaganda Amplification: Violent Incidents such as the Boston Massacre are turned into Propaganda Intensity by colonial writers, which deepens Colonial Resentment and spurs more Colonial Resistance Actions — actions which themselves raise the odds of further violent incidents, feeding the loop again.

Loop 4 – Military Escalation: As overall Hostilities Level rises, Britain increases its British Military Presence via Troop Deployment. More troops raise the frequency of Violent Incidents, which escalate hostilities further, prompting even more troop deployment.

Together these four reinforcing loops explain why relatively small initial frictions (a tax law, a tea shipment) snowballed into full-blown hostilities: each grievance-driven colonial response provoked a British countermeasure that generated still more grievance, identity, propaganda, and military buildup, with no balancing loop strong enough to arrest the spiral before war broke out.
supportingInfo.title: Four Reinforcing Loops Fueling Colonial Revolt

Situational Factors:

supportingInfo.explanation:
The model centers on four feedback loops that together explain how road rage can escalate or be contained over time, while background causes (stress, personality, fatigue, distraction, weather, road design, provocations) enter as inputs that shape the strength of these loops rather than as loops themselves.

Loop 1 (reinforcing, normalization spiral): Road Rage Incidents strengthen the Aggressive Driving Norm, which in turn increases future Road Rage Incidents. This is the 'Learned Behavior' archetype: the more aggressive driving is observed, the more socially acceptable it becomes, fueling more of it.

Loop 2 (reinforcing, congestion-stress vicious cycle): Road Rage Incidents cause accidents and blockages that raise Traffic Congestion, which raises Driver Stress Level through the nonlinear Congestion Stress Effect, which in turn raises Road Rage Incidents further. This captures how gridlock and aggressive driving can feed each other into a worsening spiral.

Loop 3 (balancing, enforcement response): Rising Road Rage Incidents increase Public Concern and Enforcement Level (media attention, policing, awareness campaigns), which increases deterrence and pulls incidents back down. This is society's natural corrective response.

Loop 4 (balancing, demand avoidance): Rising Traffic Congestion increases perceived delay, causing drivers to avoid discretionary trips (Driver Avoidance Behavior Multiplier), which reduces effective demand feeding back into congestion, self-limiting how high congestion can climb.

Exogenous background factors—Driver Fatigue Level, Distracted Driving Prevalence, Weather Severity, Personality Trait Aggressiveness, and Road Design Quality—are included as named multipliers that shift the strength of stress accumulation, incident generation, and congestion perception without themselves being looped back on, since the evidence provided treats them as underlying conditions rather than variables directly reshaped by road rage. All arbitrary calibration constants (sensitivities, fractions) were abstracted into their own named variables rather than embedded as raw numbers, per best practice. Graphical functions were used for the three clearly nonlinear relationships (congestion's effect on stress, enforcement's deterrent effect, and congestion's effect on avoidance behavior), each anchored at (1,1) to represent no deviation from normal conditions.

Taken together, the model suggests road rage incidents will keep rising if the reinforcing normalization and congestion-stress loops dominate, but can stabilize or decline if the enforcement-response and demand-avoidance balancing loops are strong enough to offset them.
