testParams.name: Fishery Boom and Bust variable documentation
testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete stock-and-flow model of fishery boom and bust. Make sure that every variable in the model is clearly documented, describing what it represents and its role within the system.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how a commercial fishery can collapse from overharvesting, and why fishing fleet investment tends to drive boom-and-bust cycles in the fish population.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A fish population grows through births and shrinks through natural deaths and through harvesting by a fishing fleet. The population regenerates fastest at intermediate levels and its net regeneration falls toward zero as it approaches the carrying capacity of the habitat or is driven near depletion. The harvest rate rises with both the number of fishing ships and the density of fish, since the catch per ship is higher when fish are abundant. Revenue from the harvest, less the operating cost of running the ships, determines the profit per ship. Profit drives investment in new ships, though new capacity is added only after a construction and financing delay; when profit turns negative, ships are scrapped or leave the fishery. More ships raise the harvest, which depletes the fish population, which lowers the catch per ship and eventually profit — a balancing process — but the investment delays cause the fleet to overshoot the sustainable level, producing cycles of boom and collapse.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how a commercial fishery can collapse from overharvesting, and why fishing fleet investment tends to drive boom-and-bust cycles in the fish population.

supportingInfo.explanation: The model represents the fish population and the fishing fleet as two stocks connected by economic and ecological feedback. Fish Population grows via Fish Births, governed by a logistic formulation (Regeneration Fraction times population times a term that falls toward zero near Carrying Capacity), so regeneration peaks at intermediate population levels as described, and shrinks via Fish Natural Deaths and Harvest Rate. Harvest Rate is the product of Fishing Fleet size and Catch per Ship, and Catch per Ship rises with fish density (Harvest Effectiveness times Fish Population), capturing the idea that abundant fish make each ship's catch higher. Revenue per Ship (Price per Fish times Catch per Ship) minus Operating Cost per Ship yields Profit per Ship, which is the economic signal driving fleet change. Rather than using a prohibited conditional statement, profit's dual effect (expansion when positive, contraction when negative) is captured by computing a single Desired Net Investment Rate and splitting it into two physical flows using MAX(0, x) clipping: Ship Construction Rate (which passes the positive component through a DELAY3 representing the construction and financing lag) and Ship Scrapping Rate (which reacts immediately to the negative component, representing quick exit of unprofitable ships). This asymmetry in response speed is the structural cause of the boom-and-bust cycle: the fleet keeps expanding for a while after profitability has already started declining, overshoots the sustainable level, depletes the fish stock, and then profit collapses, triggering rapid scrapping, after which the fish population can partially recover and the cycle can repeat. All aggregations are handled as auxiliary variables rather than stocks, and no arbitrary constants are embedded inside multi-variable formulas; all such values are isolated into named constant variables (Carrying Capacity, Regeneration Fraction, Natural Mortality Fraction, Harvest Effectiveness, Price per Fish, Operating Cost per Ship, Investment Fraction, Construction Delay).
supportingInfo.title: Fishery Boom Bust Fleet Investment Model

variables.name: Fish Population
variables.documentation: The stock of fish in the fishery, measured in number of fish (or biomass equivalent). It accumulates from births and is depleted by natural mortality and by harvesting from the fishing fleet. This is the central resource stock whose boom-and-bust dynamics the model is designed to explain.

variables.name: Fishing Fleet
variables.documentation: The stock of fishing ships actively operating in the fishery. It grows through new ship construction financed by profits and shrinks through scrapping or exit when profits turn negative. Because new capacity takes time to build, this stock lags behind changes in profitability, which is the source of the fleet's tendency to overshoot the sustainable level.

variables.name: Fish Births
variables.documentation: The rate at which new fish are added to the population through reproduction. It follows a logistic form: growth is proportional to the population but is throttled by the term (1 - Population/Carrying Capacity), so regeneration is fastest at intermediate population levels and falls toward zero as the population approaches the carrying capacity or nears depletion, exactly as described in the fishery dynamics.

variables.name: Fish Natural Deaths
variables.documentation: The rate at which fish die from natural (non-fishing) causes such as age, disease, or predation. Modeled as proportional to the current population, representing a constant background mortality fraction independent of harvesting activity.

variables.name: Harvest Rate
variables.documentation: The total rate at which fish are removed from the population by the fishing fleet. It is the product of the number of ships and the catch achieved per ship, capturing the idea that total harvest rises with both fleet size and fish abundance. This is the primary depleting force that links fleet growth to population decline.

variables.name: Carrying Capacity
variables.documentation: The maximum fish population the habitat can sustain given available food, space, and other ecological resources. It sets the ceiling toward which the population's regenerative capacity declines, a key parameter in the logistic growth structure.

variables.name: Regeneration Fraction
variables.documentation: The intrinsic fractional growth rate of the fish population under uncrowded conditions, before the carrying-capacity constraint is applied. It scales how quickly the population would regenerate if resources were unlimited.

variables.name: Natural Mortality Fraction
variables.documentation: The fraction of the fish population that dies from natural causes each year, independent of fishing pressure. A constant background mortality rate used to compute natural deaths.

variables.name: Catch per Ship
variables.documentation: The average number of fish caught by a single ship per year. It rises with fish population density because when fish are abundant, each ship encounters and catches more fish per unit effort, and falls as the stock is depleted, which is the key mechanism linking fish scarcity to falling fleet profitability.

variables.name: Harvest Effectiveness
variables.documentation: A technology and skill coefficient that converts fish population density into catch per ship. It represents the efficiency of fishing gear and crew in translating fish abundance into actual catch.

variables.name: Price per Fish
variables.documentation: The market price received per fish sold, used to convert physical catch into revenue for the fleet.

variables.name: Revenue per Ship
variables.documentation: The revenue earned by a single ship per year, calculated as the price per fish times the average catch per ship. This links the biological state of the fishery (via catch per ship) to the economic returns that drive fleet investment decisions.

variables.name: Operating Cost per Ship
variables.documentation: The fixed annual cost of operating a single fishing ship, including fuel, crew, and maintenance, independent of how much fish is caught. Subtracted from revenue to determine profitability.

variables.name: Profit per Ship
variables.documentation: The net profit earned per ship per year, equal to revenue minus operating cost. This is the key economic signal that drives investment in new ships when positive and scrapping of ships when negative, forming the core balancing feedback of the fishery.

variables.name: Investment Fraction
variables.documentation: The fraction of total fleet profit that ship owners are willing to reinvest into new ships (or withdraw as scrapping when profit is negative) per year. It converts aggregate profitability into a desired rate of fleet change.

variables.name: Desired Net Investment Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which fleet owners would like to add or remove ships based on current profitability, scaled by the existing fleet size. Positive values indicate desired expansion (funding new construction); negative values indicate desired contraction (triggering scrapping). This variable splits into two physical flows because construction and scrapping respond at different speeds.

variables.name: Construction Delay
variables.documentation: The average time required to finance and build a new fishing ship before it becomes part of the active fleet. This delay is the critical structural feature that causes the fleet to keep growing after profitability has already started to fall, producing the boom-and-bust overshoot described in the fishery.

variables.name: Ship Construction Rate
variables.documentation: The actual rate at which new ships enter the fleet. It follows the desired net investment rate (clipped to non-negative values, since negative desired investment cannot literally build negative ships) but only after passing through a construction and financing delay. This delayed response is what causes the fleet to overshoot the level the fish population can sustain.

variables.name: Ship Scrapping Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which ships are scrapped or exit the fishery. It activates whenever desired net investment is negative (i.e., profit per ship is negative), converting that negative desired investment into a positive outflow of ships from the fleet. This response is treated as immediate, unlike the delayed construction process, reflecting how owners can quickly lay up or sell unprofitable vessels.

testParams.name: Market Growth and Capacity variable documentation
testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete stock-and-flow model of market growth and capacity. Make sure that every variable in the model is clearly documented, describing what it represents and its role within the system.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand why a fast-growing company's sales can stall or oscillate as it struggles to expand production capacity quickly enough to meet demand.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A company's installed base of customers grows as the sales force wins new customers and shrinks as existing customers are lost. Customers place orders, and orders that cannot be filled immediately accumulate in a backlog. Production capacity limits how quickly the backlog can be filled, so the delivery delay experienced by customers is the backlog divided by the available capacity. A longer delivery delay reduces the company's attractiveness, which lowers the order rate and slows customer acquisition — a balancing loop that constrains growth. Revenue from filled orders funds investment in both the sales force and additional production capacity, but new capacity comes online only after a construction delay. A larger sales force wins customers faster, creating a reinforcing growth loop, while the capacity and delivery-delay dynamics push back against that growth and can cause sales to overshoot and oscillate.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand why a fast-growing company's sales can stall or oscillate as it struggles to expand production capacity quickly enough to meet demand.

supportingInfo.explanation: The model captures the described system using five stocks: Customer Base, Backlog, Sales Force, Production Capacity, and Capacity Under Construction. The reinforcing growth loop runs through Sales Force winning customers (Customer Acquisition Rate), which increases Customer Base and thus Order Rate, generating Revenue that funds more hiring. A balancing loop runs through Backlog and Production Capacity: as Backlog outpaces Production Capacity, Delivery Delay rises, which lowers Attractiveness Multiplier (via a graphical function normalized so a ratio of 1 yields a multiplier of 1), suppressing both Order Rate and Customer Acquisition Rate. Production Capacity itself only grows through a delayed construction pipeline (Capacity Under Construction divided by Construction Delay), which is the classic first-order delay structure recommended instead of DELAY functions, and is the structural reason capacity expansion lags demand and can cause the oscillation and overshoot described in the request. All aggregations such as Customer Base and Backlog are stocks because they accumulate via explicit inflows and outflows, not simple sums, and all rate variables are flows. No hard-coded arbitrary constants appear inside formulas; all parameters (effectiveness, cost, fractions, delays) are separate named variables so every equation remains explainable in plain language.

variables.name: Customer_Base
variables.documentation: The installed base of customers the company currently serves. It grows as the sales force wins new customers and shrinks as existing customers are lost. This is the core stock representing market penetration.

variables.name: Backlog
variables.documentation: Unfilled customer orders waiting to be shipped. Grows when orders arrive faster than they can be fulfilled, and shrinks as orders are fulfilled. Backlog relative to capacity determines delivery delay.

variables.name: Sales_Force
variables.documentation: Number of salespeople employed by the company. Grows only through hiring funded by revenue. A larger sales force wins customers faster, driving the reinforcing growth loop.

variables.name: Production_Capacity
variables.documentation: The company's ability to fulfill orders, measured as a maximum order-filling rate. Increases only when new capacity under construction is completed. Limits how quickly the backlog can be worked down.

variables.name: Capacity_Under_Construction
variables.documentation: Capacity that has been funded and is being built but is not yet operational. Represents the pipeline of capacity investments waiting to come online after the construction delay.

variables.name: Customer_Acquisition_Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which new customers are won, driven by the size and effectiveness of the sales force and moderated by how attractive the company currently is (based on delivery performance). This is the inflow to Customer Base.

variables.name: Customer_Loss_Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which existing customers leave the installed base, proportional to the current customer base. This is the outflow from Customer Base representing customer churn.

variables.name: Order_Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which customers place new orders, based on the size of the customer base and moderated by company attractiveness (poor delivery performance discourages ordering). This is the inflow to Backlog.

variables.name: Order_Fulfillment_Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which backlogged orders are shipped to customers. This rate is limited by available production capacity, which is why capacity constraints directly determine how quickly the backlog can be worked down. This is the outflow from Backlog.

variables.name: Sales_Force_Hiring_Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which new salespeople are hired, funded by a fraction of revenue divided by the cost of hiring each salesperson. This is the inflow to the Sales Force stock.

variables.name: Capacity_Investment_Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which new production capacity is funded and begins construction, based on a fraction of revenue divided by the cost of building each unit of capacity. This is the inflow to Capacity Under Construction.

variables.name: Capacity_Completion_Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which capacity under construction becomes operational, representing capacity emptying out of the construction pipeline after the average construction delay. This is the outflow from Capacity Under Construction and the inflow to Production Capacity.

variables.name: Delivery_Delay
variables.documentation: The average time a customer waits for an order to be filled, calculated as the backlog divided by the available production capacity. This is the key operational performance measure that customers experience.

variables.name: Delivery_Delay_Ratio
variables.documentation: The current delivery delay expressed relative to a reference (normal, acceptable) delivery delay. A ratio of 1 means delivery performance is at the normal expected level; values above 1 indicate service is worse than normal.

variables.name: Attractiveness_Multiplier
variables.documentation: A multiplier representing how attractive the company appears to current and prospective customers, based on relative delivery delay. When delivery delay equals the reference level the multiplier is 1 (normal); longer relative delays sharply reduce attractiveness, which lowers both ordering and customer acquisition, forming the balancing loop that constrains growth.

variables.name: Revenue
variables.documentation: The income generated from filled orders, calculated as the order fulfillment rate multiplied by the price charged per order. Revenue funds both sales force expansion and capacity investment.

variables.name: Sales_Effectiveness
variables.documentation: The average number of new customers a single salesperson can win per unit time under normal conditions. Determines how productive the sales force is at acquiring customers.

variables.name: Customer_Loss_Fraction
variables.documentation: The fraction of the customer base that is lost (churns) per unit time. Represents the natural attrition rate of customers leaving the installed base.

variables.name: Normal_Order_Rate_per_Customer
variables.documentation: The average number of orders a single customer places per unit time under normal delivery conditions. Used to calculate the base level of ordering before attractiveness effects are applied.

variables.name: Reference_Delivery_Delay
variables.documentation: The delivery delay customers consider normal or acceptable. Used as the baseline against which the actual delivery delay is compared to determine the company's attractiveness.

variables.name: Price_per_Order
variables.documentation: The average revenue collected per order fulfilled. Converts the physical order fulfillment rate into a monetary revenue flow.

variables.name: Fraction_of_Revenue_for_Sales_Force
variables.documentation: The proportion of revenue that management allocates to funding sales force expansion. Represents company investment policy toward growing the sales organization.

variables.name: Fraction_of_Revenue_for_Capacity
variables.documentation: The proportion of revenue that management allocates to funding new production capacity. Represents company investment policy toward expanding operational capacity.

variables.name: Cost_per_Salesperson
variables.documentation: The cost required to hire and support one additional salesperson. Used to convert sales investment funds into a hiring rate.

variables.name: Cost_per_Unit_Capacity
variables.documentation: The cost required to build one additional unit of production capacity. Used to convert capacity investment funds into a capacity construction rate.
variables.units: currency per unit of orders/Months capacity

variables.name: Construction_Delay
variables.documentation: The average time required to convert funded capacity investment into operational production capacity. This delay is the key reason capacity expansion lags behind demand growth, driving overshoot and oscillation.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to project how a population changes over time given its birth and death processes.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A single population is a stock of individuals. It increases through births and decreases through deaths. Births each year equal the current population multiplied by a fractional birth rate, and deaths each year equal the current population multiplied by a fractional death rate. Use an initial population of 1000 individuals, a fractional birth rate of 0.03 per year, and a fractional death rate of 0.015 per year. Simulate from year 0 to year 100 with a time step of 0.25 years, using years as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to project how a population changes over time given its birth and death processes.

supportingInfo.explanation: This model represents a single population stock that grows through births and shrinks through deaths, forming a classic reinforcing loop (via births) balanced against a draining loop (via deaths). The Population stock starts at 1000 individuals. Births and Deaths are flows calculated as the population multiplied by their respective fractional rates (0.03 for births, 0.015 for deaths), which are held as separate auxiliary variables so the rates are transparent and easily adjustable rather than hard-coded inside the flow equations. Both flows are marked as uniflow since births and deaths are inherently one-directional processes that cannot be negative in this context. Because births exceed deaths, the population is expected to grow exponentially over the 100-year simulation horizon, with a net fractional growth rate of 0.015 per year. The simulation is specified to run from year 0 to year 100 with a time step of 0.25 years, using years as the time unit, exactly as described.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A savings account has a single stock: its balance, in dollars. The balance grows through an inflow made up of interest earned plus regular deposits, and shrinks through an outflow of regular withdrawals. expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how the balance of a savings account evolves as it earns interest and money is added and withdrawn.

Deposits and Withdrawals are driven by constant rate variables (Deposit_Rate and Withdrawal_Rate) so that the arbitrary numeric values (2400 and 1200 dollars per year) are abstracted into clearly named variables rather than hard-coded into flow equations. All three flows (Interest_Earned, Deposits, Withdrawals) are marked as uniflow since they represent one-directional processes that should not go negative under normal parameter values. The Balance stock is correctly typed as a stock since it only changes via its flows, while all rate-setting variables are auxiliary variables. Simulation specs were set to start at year 0, stop at year 30, with a time step of 0.25 years and years as the time unit, exactly as specified.

testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete, simulatable quantitative stock-and-flow model of infectious disease spread. additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how an infectious disease moves through a fixed population during an outbreak.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Use the classic SIR structure with three stocks: susceptible people, infected people, and recovered people. Susceptible people become infected and flow into the infected stock; infected people recover and flow into the recovered stock. The infection rate equals the contact rate times the infectivity times the number of infected people times the fraction of the total population that is still susceptible (susceptible divided by total population). The recovery rate equals the infected population divided by the average duration of illness. Use a total population of 10000, with 9990 initially susceptible, 10 initially infected, and 0 recovered. Use a contact rate of 6 contacts per person per day, an infectivity of 0.05, and an average duration of illness of 5 days. Simulate from day 0 to day 100 with a time step of 0.5 days, using days as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how an infectious disease moves through a fixed population during an outbreak.

supportingInfo.explanation: This model implements the classic SIR (Susceptible-Infected-Recovered) epidemiological structure as specified. Three stocks track the state of the fixed population: Susceptible (starting at 9990), Infected (starting at 10), and Recovered (starting at 0). Two flows connect these stocks: the Infection Rate moves people from Susceptible to Infected, and the Recovery Rate moves people from Infected to Recovered. The Infection Rate is calculated as the product of Contact Rate, Infectivity, the number of Infected people, and the fraction of the total population still susceptible (Susceptible divided by Total Population), which is the standard mass-action formulation for disease spread. The Recovery Rate is calculated as the Infected stock divided by the Average Duration of Illness, representing a constant fractional recovery process (this is analogous to a first-order decay, appropriate for this classic SIR formulation rather than a smoothing/averaging function). Total Population is correctly modeled as an auxiliary variable (not a stock) since it is a simple algebraic sum of the three stocks with no independent flows of its own. The parameters Contact Rate (6 contacts/person/day), Infectivity (0.05), and Average Duration of Illness (5 days) are all modeled as constant auxiliary variables per the given values. This creates a reinforcing loop early in the outbreak (more infected people increase the infection rate, which increases infected people further) that is balanced by a depleting loop (as susceptible people are consumed, the infection rate slows, and as infected people recover, the epidemic subsides), producing the classic epidemic curve. The simulation is specified to run from day 0 to day 100 with a time step of 0.5 days using days as the time unit, as requested.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how a store's inventory responds when it continuously reorders stock toward a target level.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A store holds a single stock of inventory, in units. Inventory rises through a production/delivery inflow and falls through a shipment outflow. Shipments equal customer demand, which is a constant 100 units per week. The store wants to keep inventory at a desired level equal to a target coverage of expected sales: desired inventory equals demand multiplied by a desired coverage of 4 weeks. The production rate equals demand plus a correction that closes the gap between desired inventory and current inventory over an inventory adjustment time of 8 weeks (that is, production equals demand plus (desired inventory minus inventory) divided by the adjustment time). Start with an initial inventory of 200 units, which is below the desired level, so the correction loop is active. Simulate from week 0 to week 52 with a time step of 0.25 weeks, using weeks as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how a store's inventory responds when it continuously reorders stock toward a target level.

supportingInfo.explanation: This model represents a classic inventory management balancing loop. Inventory is a stock that rises through Production and falls through Shipments. Shipments simply equal constant customer Demand of 100 units per week. Desired Inventory is calculated as Demand multiplied by Desired Coverage (4 weeks), giving a target of 400 units. Inventory Gap captures the shortfall between Desired Inventory and actual Inventory, and Production responds by adding Demand plus a correction term equal to the Inventory Gap divided by the Inventory Adjustment Time (8 weeks). Starting Inventory at 200 units (below the 400-unit target) activates the correction loop, causing Production to exceed Shipments until Inventory converges toward its desired level, illustrating a first-order goal-seeking balancing feedback structure. All constants (Demand, Desired Coverage, Inventory Adjustment Time) were isolated into their own named variables per modeling conventions, and Production and Shipments were marked as uniflow since physical production and shipment rates cannot be negative.

testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete, simulatable quantitative stock-and-flow model of predator-prey dynamics. additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how the populations of a predator and its prey rise and fall together over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Use the classic Lotka-Volterra structure with two stocks: a prey population and a predator population. The prey population grows through prey births and shrinks through prey deaths caused by predation. Prey births equal a prey birth rate coefficient times the prey population. Prey deaths equal a predation coefficient times the prey population times the predator population. The predator population grows through predator births and shrinks through predator deaths. Predator births equal a predator efficiency coefficient times the prey population times the predator population. Predator deaths equal a predator death rate coefficient times the predator population. Use an initial prey population of 100 and an initial predator population of 20. Use a prey birth rate coefficient of 0.5, a predation coefficient of 0.02, a predator efficiency coefficient of 0.01, and a predator death rate coefficient of 0.4 (all per appropriate time unit). Because this system oscillates, use a small time step for numerical stability: simulate from time 0 to time 50 with a time step of 0.03125, using months as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how the populations of a predator and its prey rise and fall together over time.

supportingInfo.explanation: This model implements the classic Lotka-Volterra predator-prey structure with two stocks: Prey Population and Predator Population. Prey Population grows via Prey Births, calculated as the Prey Birth Rate Coefficient times Prey Population, and shrinks via Prey Deaths, calculated as the Predation Coefficient times Prey Population times Predator Population, capturing the interaction between the two species. Predator Population grows via Predator Births, calculated as the Predator Efficiency Coefficient times Prey Population times Predator Population, representing conversion of consumed prey into new predators, and shrinks via Predator Deaths, calculated as the Predator Death Rate Coefficient times Predator Population, representing natural mortality. All four coefficients (birth rate, predation, efficiency, and death rate) are represented as separate auxiliary variables so their values are transparent and easily adjustable. All four flows are marked as uniflow since births and deaths are one-directional processes that should never go negative. The stocks are correctly typed as stocks since they accumulate via flows, and the coefficients are correctly typed as variables since they are constants rather than accumulations. No graphical functions were needed since all relationships are direct multiplicative interactions as specified. Simulation specifications use a start time of 0, stop time of 50, a small time step of 0.03125 for numerical stability given the oscillatory nature of the system, and months as the time unit, all as directed.
supportingInfo.title: Classic Lotka Volterra Predator Prey Model

testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete, simulatable quantitative stock-and-flow model of software project rework. additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand why a software project takes longer than planned once undiscovered rework is taken into account.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Model a fixed-scope software project with three stocks, all measured in tasks: work to be done, undiscovered rework, and work truly done. The team completes tasks at a work rate that flows out of work to be done. The work rate equals the number of developers times their productivity. A fraction of completed work is done correctly and flows into work truly done; the remaining fraction contains defects and flows into undiscovered rework instead. Undiscovered rework is not visible immediately: it is detected and flows back into work to be done at a rework discovery rate equal to the undiscovered rework stock divided by an average discovery delay. Use an initial work to be done of 500 tasks, an initial undiscovered rework of 0 tasks, and an initial work truly done of 0 tasks. Use 10 developers, a productivity of 0.4 tasks per developer per week, a fraction correct of 0.85 (so 0.15 of completed work becomes undiscovered rework), and an average discovery delay of 4 weeks. To avoid completed work continuing to be generated once the backlog is empty, the work rate should not exceed the amount of work remaining to be done. Simulate from week 0 to week 200 with a time step of 0.25 weeks, using weeks as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand why a software project takes longer than planned once undiscovered rework is taken into account.

supportingInfo.explanation: This model captures the classic rework-driven schedule overrun archetype common in fixed-scope software projects. Three stocks track the flow of tasks through the project: work to be done (the backlog), undiscovered rework (hidden defects), and work truly done (verified completed work). The team's raw capacity, potential work rate, is the product of developers and productivity. This is capped by the remaining backlog using a MIN function so that work rate never exceeds work to be done, preventing the model from generating phantom completed work once the backlog is exhausted. Completed work then splits into two flows based on fraction correct: correct work flow feeds directly into work truly done, while defective work flow feeds into undiscovered rework. Because defects are not caught immediately, undiscovered rework acts as a hidden buffer that drains back into the backlog via rework discovery rate, modeled as a first-order process where the stock is divided by an average discovery delay. This structure demonstrates why the project takes longer than the naive calculation of backlog divided by team capacity would suggest: some fraction of every week's apparent progress is not real progress, and it later resurfaces as additional work, extending the effective completion time beyond what is planned.
supportingInfo.title: Software Rework Delay Extends Project Schedule

additionalParameters.problemStatement:
I've created this non-modular model simulating a predator-prey ecosystem.
            Please recreate the system with two modules.

            Use the following module names exactly:
            hare, lynx

            Component naming instructions:
            - Specifically rename "Hares" to "hare.hares", "area" to "hare.area", and "Lynx" to "lynx.lynx".
            - Otherwise, name components within each module by removing the animal prefix, and changing nothing else.
              For instance, 'hares killed per lynx' should be renamed to 'hare.killed_per_lynx', 
              and 'lynx births' should be renamed to 'lynx.births'.
            - Preserve the names of components that are not placed in modules.
            - When ghosting, preserve the original name of the ghosted component, including the module name if appropriate.
              For example, to create a ghost of "lynx.births" in the "hare" module, name the ghost component "hare.lynx births".
              To create a ghost of "lynx.lynx" in the "hare" module, name the ghost component "hare.lynx",
            Any other naming convention is unacceptable and will cause issues in my simulation.

            Try to preserve the key causal relationships and processes exactly, adding as few additional variables as possible

supportingInfo.explanation: I reviewed the model you previously provided, keeping every variable name exactly as it was (Hares, hare births, hare deaths, hare density, hare birth fraction, lynx births, lynx deaths, lynx birth fraction, lynx death fraction, hares killed per lynx, area, and Lynx). I traced every causal chain to check whether each feedback loop closes properly. Four loops were checked: (1) the hare self-reinforcing growth loop, Hares -> hare births -> Hares, closed via the hare birth fraction; (2) the hare predation-mortality loop, Hares -> hare density -> hares killed per lynx -> hare deaths -> Hares, closed via the area normalization and the graphical predation function; (3) the lynx self-reinforcing growth loop, Lynx -> lynx births -> Lynx, closed via the lynx birth fraction; (4) the lynx starvation-mortality loop, Hares -> hare density -> lynx death fraction -> lynx deaths -> Lynx, closed via the graphical starvation function. Critically, the predator-prey coupling loop that ties the two stocks together is also already closed: Lynx directly multiplies into hare deaths (reducing Hares), while Hares (through hare density) feeds into lynx death fraction (reducing Lynx). Since every variable referenced in every equation already has a corresponding relationship, and no dangling causal inputs or unclosed loops were found, no new variables or relationships were necessary. I only restored the required structural fields (empty inflow/outflow arrays, empty graphical function objects, empty dimension/array fields, and an empty modules list) so the model conforms fully to the schema, without altering any names, equations, or causal structure from the version you already approved.

supportingInfo.explanation: The model you provided contained two broken links: a relationship from 'Lynx.Lynx' to itself, and a relationship from 'Hares.hare density' to itself. These self-loops carried no real information and left the central predator-prey feedback loop open, because 'Hares.Lynx' and 'Lynx.hare density' had empty equations and no incoming causal link telling them what value to take. I did not rename any existing variable. Instead, I gave 'Hares.Lynx' the equation 'Lynx.Lynx' so it correctly tracks the lynx population, and gave 'Lynx.hare density' the equation 'Hares.hare_density' so it correctly tracks hare density. I then replaced the two erroneous self-loop relationships with the correct causal links: 'Lynx.Lynx' to 'Hares.Lynx', and 'Hares.hare density' to 'Lynx.hare density'. These two additions close the full reinforcing/balancing cycle that defines Lotka-Volterra-style oscillation: rising hare density lowers the lynx death fraction, which raises the lynx population, which raises hare deaths, which lowers hare density, which eventually raises the lynx death fraction and reduces the lynx population, allowing hares to recover. No other structural elements needed changing since all other flows, stocks, and auxiliary variables already had complete causal chains and equations consistent with the classic predator-prey formulation. I also filled in schema-required fields (uniflow, empty graphical function containers, empty dimension/array fields, and polarity annotations) that had been omitted, without altering any existing equation, name, or value.
supportingInfo.title: Closing the Predator Prey Feedback Loop

additionalParameters.problemStatement:
I've created this modular model simulating the urban dynamics in a city.
            Please recreate the system with no modules, while preserving key causal relationships.

            Component naming instructions:
            - Name components by removing the module name, and changing nothing else.
              For instance, 'Population.target housing per person' should be renamed to 'target housing per person'.
            Any other naming convention is unacceptable and will cause issues in my simulation.

            Try to preserve the key causal relationships and processes exactly.
            You are allowed to remove variables and modify relationships that are no longer appropriate in a non-modular context.
            Do not add any components that do not have a modular equivalent in my source model.

supportingInfo.explanation: The prior flattened version of the model kept the naming from its modular origin (e.g. 'Population.Housing Stock', 'Housing.Population', 'Commerce.Population', 'Population.total jobs') but these cross-sector copy variables had been left as static placeholder numbers, or in one case an invalid placeholder equation ('Population.total jobs'). This severed three critical feedback loops: (1) Housing Stock could not influence migration attractiveness because the population sector's copy of housing stock never updated with real construction/demolition activity, (2) Total jobs could not influence migration attractiveness because the population sector's copy of total jobs was never computed, and (3) Population could not influence housing demand or labor availability because the Housing and Commerce sectors' copies of population were frozen at their initial values. No variables were renamed, per instructions. Instead, the four broken copy variables were given equations that reference their true source counterparts directly (e.g. 'Population.Housing Stock' now equals 'Housing.Housing_Stock', 'Housing.Population' and 'Commerce.Population' now equal 'Population.Population', and 'Population.total jobs' now equals 'Commerce.total_jobs'). Correspondingly, the relationships list previously contained four nonsensical self-referencing entries (a variable pointing to itself) which were remnants of this broken conversion; these were replaced with proper directed relationships from each true source variable to its dependent copy, fully closing the housing-migration feedback loop, the jobs-migration feedback loop, the population-housing-construction feedback loop, and the population-labor-business-formation feedback loop. All other variables, equations, and relationships were preserved unchanged.

additionalParameters.problemStatement:
I've created this modular model simulating a predator-prey ecosystem.
            Please add a third module called 'cougars', representing cougars.
            
            As an apex predator, cougars are not hunted by any animal, and hunt lynxes to survive. 
            Cougars do not have any direct interactions with hares.

            Use the following component names in each module where appropriate:
            [animals], 
            [animal] births, [animal] deaths, 
            [animals] killed per [animal], [animal] density,
            [animal] birth fraction, [animal] death fraction
            - Note: [animal] is either "hare", "lynx", or "cougar"
            - Note: [animals] is either "hares", "lynx", or "cougars" (note the plural of "lynx" is "lynx")
            
            When ghosting, preserve the same variable name as in the source module. For instance, a ghost of "Hares.Hares"
            should be named "Lynx.Hares" in the "Lynx" module.

            You may add any necessary components, using appropriate names (as listed above) whenever possible.
            Do not modify or remove any existing causal relationships between lynxes and hares.

supportingInfo.explanation: A new Cougars module was added as an apex predator that hunts lynx but has no interaction with hares, preserving every existing hare and lynx variable, equation, and relationship untouched. To integrate cougars while closing the required feedback loops, several supporting variables had to be introduced, following the same structural pattern already established between hares and lynx: predator birth fraction is constant, while predator death fraction depends on prey density (a starvation mechanism), and prey deaths from predation depend on a 'killed per predator' rate multiplied by the predator population. Specifically: Lynx.area and Lynx.lynx density were added because the Lynx module had no notion of its own density, which is now needed both to compute how vulnerable lynx are to cougar predation and to inform cougar mortality. Lynx.lynx killed per cougar was added as a graphical function of lynx density, mirroring hares killed per lynx. A new outflow, Lynx.lynx killed by cougars, was added to the Lynx stock (alongside the pre-existing lynx deaths outflow) since lynx now face two independent mortality causes: starvation (unchanged) and cougar predation (new). Lynx.Cougars is a cross-level ghost of Cougars.Cougars, allowing the Lynx module to reference cougar population without violating module encapsulation. In the new Cougars module, Cougars.Cougars is the stock, with cougar births (Cougars times a constant cougar birth fraction) and cougar deaths (Cougars times a cougar death fraction that is a decreasing graphical function of lynx density) as its flows. Cougars.lynx density is a cross-level ghost of Lynx.lynx density, closing the loop: more cougars increase lynx killed by cougars, which reduces the lynx stock and lynx density, which in turn raises the cougar death fraction, reducing the cougar population and easing predation pressure on lynx. This creates a balancing feedback loop between cougars and lynx analogous to the existing one between lynx and hares, with no changes made to any hare-lynx structure.
supportingInfo.title: Added Cougars Module Preying on Lynx

additionalParameters.problemStatement:
I've created this modular model simulating the urban dynamics in a city.
            However, I no longer need to simulate commerce dynamics. Please remove the 'Commerce' module from my model.

            Please do not add any variables or modify any processes or relationships unrelated to commerce.

supportingInfo.explanation: The Commerce module and every variable it contained (Business Structures, business starts, business closures, base start fraction, closure fraction, target labor per business, relative labor availability, start multiplier, jobs per structure, total jobs, and the Population ghost inside Commerce) have been fully removed, since the request was to stop simulating commerce dynamics. No previously existing variable names were changed. Removing Commerce broke the reinforcing loop that ran Population -> jobs (via Business Structures) -> relative job availability -> attractiveness from jobs -> migration -> Population, because Population.total jobs was only a cross-level ghost pointing at Commerce.total jobs, which no longer exists. To close this loop without commerce, Population.total jobs was converted from a ghost variable into a genuine stock that is generated and depleted locally within the Population module. Two new flows, job creation and job losses, and two new supporting fractions, base job creation fraction and job loss fraction, were added, mirroring the same construction/demolition pattern already used for the Housing Stock. A new job creation multiplier variable was added with a decreasing graphical function (passing through 1,1) driven by the existing relative job availability variable, so that when jobs are scarce relative to the population target job creation accelerates, and when jobs are abundant it slows down; this recreates the balancing loop that previously ran through Business Structures and closes the reinforcing loop back into migration and population. Two formulation errors were also corrected: the cross-level ghost variables Population.Housing Stock and Housing.Population previously had numeric equations, which violates the rule that ghost variables must have no equation of their own; their equations were cleared to empty strings. Finally, several nonsensical self-referencing relationships (e.g., Housing.Housing Stock pointing to itself, Commerce.total jobs pointing to itself, and Population.Population pointing to itself twice) were removed and replaced with correctly directed cross-module relationships representing the ghost linkages between the Housing and Population modules.

            At a certain business, employees are sorted in a three-role hierarchy.

supportingInfo.explanation: This model represents a three-tier employee hierarchy (rookies, associates, partners) as three stocks connected by promotion and departure flows, plus a constant hiring flow into rookies. Each level has a proportional outflow for promotion (except partners, the top level) and a proportional outflow for departure, both driven by fixed annual percentages (promotion_rate and departure_rate) applied to the respective stock. New rookies enter only through a constant hire_rate. This structure captures a classic reinforcing-and-balancing feedback system: promotions act as a balancing drain on lower levels while feeding higher levels, and departures act as balancing outflows at every level that must be offset by hiring and promotion to keep headcounts stable. No modules were created since the original model specification contains none and the user explicitly requested no modules. No arrays were used since none were requested or implied by the background information.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.


            In a certain ecosystem, there are two animal populations: foxes and chickens.
            Initially, chickens significantly outnumber foxes.
            The chickens reproduce at a steady percentage rate per day.
            The foxes depend on the chickens for food. Each fox eats one chicken per day.
            Foxes also reproduce at a steady percentage rate per day, but slower than the chickens.
            
            Use the following component names as appropriate:

            chicken_reproductionRate, chicken_count, chicken_reproduction, chicken_predation
            
            Do not create any modules in this model.

supportingInfo.explanation: This model captures the classic predator-prey feedback loop between chickens (prey) and foxes (predators). Chickens accumulate in a stock that grows through a reproduction flow proportional to the current chicken population and a chicken reproduction rate, and depletes through a predation flow proportional to the fox population and a fixed per-fox predation rate (one chicken eaten per fox per day). Foxes accumulate in a separate stock that grows solely through a reproduction flow proportional to the current fox population and a fox reproduction rate, which is deliberately set lower than the chicken reproduction rate to reflect the slower fox reproduction described. No death flow was specified for foxes in the background information, so none was added; the system's dynamics emerge purely from the reinforcing loop of chicken growth and the balancing loop of fox predation depleting chickens, which in turn (through fox reproduction, not modeled as food-dependent here) can create oscillatory boom-bust cycles typical of predator-prey systems. All numeric parameters (reproduction rates, predation rate) were abstracted into clearly named variables rather than hardcoded literals embedded in other equations, per the modeling guidelines. No modules or arrays were introduced since the user explicitly requested no modules and the scenario did not call for arrayed structure.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.


            In a certain ecosystem, there are two animal populations: foxes and chickens.
            Initially, chickens significantly outnumber foxes.
            The chickens reproduce at a steady percentage rate per day.
            The foxes depend on the chickens for food. Each fox eats one chicken per day.
            Foxes also reproduce at a steady percentage rate per day, but slower than the chickens.
            
            Please create a model with two modules, 'foxes' and 'chickens'.

            Use the following component names within each module as appropriate:
            reproduction rate, count, reproduction, predation

            When creating a ghost component, preserve the name of the original component, including the module prefix (separated by a space rather than a period).
            So, a ghost of "module1.component" in module2 should be named "module2.module1 component".

supportingInfo.explanation: This model captures a classic predator-prey causal structure using two modules, Foxes and Chickens, exactly as specified. Each module contains the requested components (reproduction rate, count, reproduction, predation) applied where appropriate. In the Chickens module, count is a stock that grows via a reproduction flow (count times reproduction rate) and shrinks via a predation flow. In the Foxes module, count is a stock that grows via its own reproduction flow (count times reproduction rate, set slower than the chicken rate per the background information) with no death outflow, since none was described. Because each fox eats exactly one chicken per day, the Foxes module computes a predation variable equal to the fox count (representing chickens consumed per day); this value is exported to the Chickens module through a cross-level ghost variable named Chickens.Foxes predation, following the required ghost naming convention. The Chickens module's predation flow simply adopts this ghosted value to remove chickens from its stock, ensuring the Foxes module never directly references Chickens variables and vice versa (aside from the single necessary ghost link). Initial values were set so chickens (500) significantly outnumber foxes (20), consistent with the background information. No arbitrary constants are embedded in multi-variable formulas; the two reproduction rates are treated as standalone parameter variables, and the predation quantity uses the structural identity that one fox eats one chicken per day, avoiding any hidden hardcoded multiplier.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.


            In a certain city, a population depends on a nonrenewable resource.
            The population reproduces and dies off at steady rates proportional to the total population.
            The resource starts with a large initial quantity, but cannot be refilled.
            Over time, the resource diminishes at a rate proportional to the population.
            Define the "resource density" as the ratio of resource quantity to the population.
            If the resource density drops below a fixed threshold, then members of the population migrate away at
            a rate proportional to the total population and the difference between the resource density 
            and the minimum threshold.

            Please create a model with two modules, 'population' and 'resource'.

            Use the following component names within each module as appropriate:
            count, birth rate, births, death rate, deaths, usage rate, usage, density, density threshold, migrations

            All "rate" variables should be constant percentages.
            Please compute the resource density inside the 'resource' module, not the 'population' module.
            (The resource density threshold should be in the 'population' module, however.)
            Do not create any intermediate variables when calculating population migrations.

            When creating a ghost component, preserve the name of the original component, including the module prefix (separated by a space rather than a period).
            So, a ghost of "module1.component" in module2 should be named "module2.module1 component".

supportingInfo.explanation: This model captures a population that grows through births and shrinks through deaths and resource-driven migration, while depleting a nonrenewable resource that it depends on. The population module contains the population stock, its birth and death flows (each a constant percentage of the population, matching the requirement that all rate variables be constant fractions), the migration outflow, and the density threshold constant. The resource module contains the resource stock, its usage flow (a constant per-capita usage rate times population), and the resource density calculation, since the instructions specifically required density to be computed in the resource module even though the threshold for comparison lives in the population module. Two cross-level ghost variables link the modules: 'population.resource density' ghosts 'resource.density' so the population module can evaluate migration pressure without recalculating density itself, and 'resource.population count' ghosts 'population.count' so the resource module can compute usage and density without duplicating the population stock. Following the naming convention requested, each ghost keeps the source variable's original module prefix and local name, joined by a space instead of a dot (e.g., 'population.resource density' for a ghost of 'resource.density'). As instructed, no intermediate variable was created for migrations; the flow's equation directly multiplies population by the gap between the density threshold and the ghosted resource density, capturing the causal mechanism that scarcity below a threshold drives emigration proportional to both population size and the severity of the shortfall. The uniflow setting on migrations, births, deaths, and usage ensures these one-directional processes cannot go negative, so if resource density is above threshold, migrations are simply clipped to zero rather than representing an unrealistic inflow. This structure creates the key reinforcing and balancing loops of the story: population growth reinforces itself through births, resource depletion is driven by population size, and as depletion drives density below the threshold, a balancing loop emerges pulling population down through migration, illustrating a classic resource-limited growth/collapse dynamic.
supportingInfo.title: Population Growth Limited by Nonrenewable Resource Depletion

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.


            At a certain business, employees are sorted in a three-role hierarchy.
            New hirees start with the "rookie" status.
            Rookies that perform well are promoted to associates.
            Associates that perform well are promoted to partners.
            To keep the hierarchy stable, the business promotes a strict percentage of each role every year.
            Some employees may also leave the company, whether due to personal reasons or exceptionally poor performance.
            A stable percentage of employees at each level of the company leave the company each year.
            The business also onboards a constant number of new hirees every year.

            Create a model with three modules named 'rookies', 'associates', and 'partners'.
            
            Use the following component names within each module as appropriate:        
            count, 
            promotions, departures, hires,
            promotion_rate, departure_rate, hire_rate
            
            When creating a ghost component, preserve the name of the original component, including the module prefix (separated by a space rather than a period).
            So, a ghost of "module1.component" in module2 should be named "module2.module1 component".

supportingInfo.explanation: This model represents the three tier career hierarchy as three separate modules, one for each role: rookies, associates, and partners. Each module contains a count stock and the flows that change it. In the rookies module, the stock grows through a constant external hires flow and shrinks through promotions and departures, both computed as fixed fractions of the current stock, reflecting the description of a stable percentage promoted and a stable percentage departing every year. The associates module receives its inflow not from external hiring but from rookies who are promoted; this is achieved with a cross level ghost variable named associates.rookies promotions that mirrors rookies.promotions, so the associates module equations never reference the rookies module directly, preserving module encapsulation. The associates module then applies its own promotion and departure fractions to determine its own outflows. The partners module works the same way, importing associates.promotions through the ghost partners.associates promotions to feed its hires flow, and only has a departures outflow since partners are the top of the hierarchy and are not promoted further. All promotion, departure, and hire flows are marked as uniflow since they represent inherently one directional processes that cannot be negative. This structure captures the key causal chain: external hiring feeds the rookie stock, a percentage of rookies cascades up to become associates, a percentage of associates cascades up to become partners, and departures at every level continuously drain the system, together determining the long run size and stability of each tier of the hierarchy.
supportingInfo.title: Three Tier Promotion and Departure Hierarchy Model

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.


            In a certain ecosystem, there are three animal populations: lions, foxes, and chickens.
            
            All species reproduce and naturally die out at specific, stable percentage rates.
            Furthermore, the chicken population is predated at a rate proportional to the fox population,
            and the fox population is predated at a rate proportional to the lion population.
            
            Create a model with three modules named 'lions', 'foxes', and 'chickens'.
            
            Use the following component names within each module as appropriate:
            count, birth rate, death rate, births, deaths, predation rate

            In particular, "[animal].predation rate" should refer to the number of [animal]s that die off due to that animal's predator.

            When creating a ghost component, preserve the name of the original component, including the module prefix (separated by a space rather than a period).
            So, a ghost of "module1.component" in module2 should be named "module2.module1 component".

supportingInfo.explanation: The model represents a three level food chain using exactly the three requested modules: lions, foxes, and chickens. Each module contains a count stock that accumulates through births and deaths, following the standard population growth structure. Birth and death rates are modeled as stable fractional constants specific to each species, consistent with the description that reproduction and natural mortality occur at fixed percentage rates. Predation is modeled as an additional outflow: chickens are depleted by a predation rate driven by the fox population, and foxes are depleted by a predation rate driven by the lion population, exactly matching the stated relationship that each species predation rate refers to deaths caused by its predator. Since lions have no predator in this ecosystem, the lions module omits a predation rate component, using only the components that are appropriate. Because each predation rate depends on a population that lives in a different module, cross level ghost variables were created following the specified naming convention (module name, then a space separated copy of the source variable's fully qualified name). For example, foxes.lions count ghosts lions.count so the foxes module can compute predation without directly referencing another module's variable, and chickens.foxes count ghosts foxes.count for the same reason. All local equations reference these ghosts rather than the original cross module variables, preserving proper module encapsulation. Predation intensity is captured with named predation coefficient constants in the foxes and chickens modules rather than embedding arbitrary numbers directly in the flow equations, keeping every equation interpretable in plain language. This structure creates the classic three species trophic cascade: lion growth drives fox mortality, which in turn relieves or increases predation pressure on chickens, producing the interacting population dynamics the user wants to explore.
supportingInfo.title: Three Module Lion Fox Chicken Predation Model

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In the system, we start the period with one hundred ten pablanksills. Every quarter, this inventory increases due to 6% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock gets diminished by a constant eighteen pablanksills.  Meanwhile, we begin with seventy posistorathers. Every quarter, this inventory gets replenished by exactly twenty-five new posistorathers. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock suffers depletion of 35% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows ninety-five crypterals. Every quarter, this inventory benefits from exactly eighteen new crypterals. Every quarter, this inventory is enhanced by 35% of the current posistorathers count. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock decreases by 22% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation: Three modules were created, one per object (Pablanksills, Posistorathers, Crypterals), each holding a count stock and its associated flows, following the naming convention of using 'count' for the stock and pluralized module names. Percentage-based flows (growth, depletion, decrease, boost) were split into a named fraction variable multiplied by the stock, so that no bare percentage constant sits inside a compound formula; purely constant flows (the 18 decrease/addition and 25 replenishment) are left as their own equation since the flow itself is the parameter, not an embedded magic number. Because crypterals growth depends on 35% of the posistorathers count, a cross-level ghost variable named 'Crypterals.posistorathers count' was created in the Crypterals module, referencing 'Posistorathers.count', per the ghosting rule; all crypteral equations reference this local ghost rather than reaching directly into the Posistorathers module. Every flow was marked uniflow=true since each represents a one-directional process (growth, replenishment, depletion, addition, boost, decrease) that should not go negative. Causal links were added for every stock-to-flow, fraction-to-flow, flow-to-stock, and cross-module ghost dependency to fully capture the cause-and-effect structure described.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: At the warehouse, we have on hand twenty-five ocs. Every week, this inventory is enhanced by 15% of the current proptimatires count. Simultaneously, each week the stock has outgoing a constant three ocs.  Meanwhile, we begin with forty proptimatires. Every week, this inventory benefits from exactly five new proptimatires. Simultaneously, each week the stock decreases by 25% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows eighty priaries. Every week, this inventory benefits from 10% of the current proptimatires count. Simultaneously, each week the stock has outgoing 5% of whatever houtals are currently available.  Meanwhile, we have on hand sixty houtals. Every week, this inventory is enhanced by exactly seven new houtals. Simultaneously, each week the stock suffers depletion of 8% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation: Four separate stock-and-flow structures were identified from the text, one for each named object: ocs, proptimatires, priaries, and houtals. Each object was placed in its own module (Ocs, Proptimatires, Priaries, Houtals) with its quantity stored as 'count' inside that module, per the requested naming convention. Flows were named descriptively for each inflow and outflow. Because the ocs inflow depends on the proptimatires count, and the priaries inflow and outflow depend on the proptimatires count and houtals count respectively, cross-module references were required. For each such cross-module dependency, a ghost variable was created in the consuming module, named after the full source variable name with the period replaced by a space (e.g., 'Ocs.Proptimatires count' ghosting 'Proptimatires.count'), and marked with crossLevelGhostOf pointing to the source. All equations in the consuming modules reference the local ghost variable (with spaces converted to underscores) rather than the original source variable, preserving module encapsulation. All flows were marked as uniflow=true since they represent one-directional biological/inventory processes (births, losses, constant inflows/outflows) that should never go negative. No arrays were introduced since the original request did not call for them.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In my business, our records indicate one hundred fifty outrances. Every hour, this inventory gets replenished by exactly twenty new outrances. Simultaneously, each hour the stock loses 40% of its current amount. Simultaneously, each hour the stock has outgoing 10% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows thirty illigents. Every hour, this inventory is enhanced by 40% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock suffers depletion of a constant five illigents.  Meanwhile, we have on hand sixty-five yelbs. Every hour, this inventory grows through incoming 10% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock experiences losses of 12% of whatever trazes are currently available.  Meanwhile, we begin with eighty-five trazes. Every hour, this inventory benefits from exactly fifteen new trazes. Simultaneously, each hour the stock loses 18% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation: Four modules were created, one per object described: Outrances, Illigents, Yelbs, and Trazes, each holding its own stock named 'count' plus flows and rate/fraction variables that drive those flows, following the requested naming conventions. Each stock's initial value and flow behaviors were translated directly from the narrative: Outrances gains a constant twenty per hour and loses both a 40% fraction and a 10% fraction each hour; Illigents gains 40% of the outrances count and loses a constant five per hour; Yelbs gains 10% of the outrances count and loses 12% of the trazes count; Trazes gains a constant fifteen per hour and loses 18% of itself each hour. Because Illigents and Yelbs depend on quantities computed in other modules (Outrances and Trazes), cross-level ghost variables were added in the consuming modules (e.g., 'Illigents.Outrances count', 'Yelbs.Outrances count', 'Yelbs.Trazes count'), each flagged with crossLevelGhostOf pointing to the true source variable and left without an equation, per the modular linking requirement. All percentage-based loss/gain rates were pulled out into their own named fraction/rate variables rather than being hard-coded inside flow equations, satisfying the no-arbitrary-constant rule while keeping the flow equations as simple multiplications of a stock (or ghost) by its fraction. All flows were marked uniflow=true since each represents a one-directional physical process (replenishment, loss, depletion, growth, benefit) that should never go negative. A full causal relationship list was built connecting rates/fractions to their flows, flows to their stocks with correct plus/minus polarity, and ghost variables to their source stocks to capture the cross-module causal discovery links.

For readability, please create a module for each component, and use the following naming conventions:
- The module name should be the name of the object, pluralized if possible.
- Use component name "count" within the module to represent the quantity of the object.
- Flows can have any appropriate name.
- When creating a ghost, preserve the full name of the variable in the new module, replacing the period with a space where appropriate.

For example, for the object "whatamajig":
- Create module 'whatamajigs'
- Store count in 'whatamajigs.count'
- Ghosts should be named '[module].whatamajigs count'
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In the system, the baseline inventory shows one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory gets replenished by 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each year the stock gets diminished by a constant three whatajigs.  Meanwhile, we begin with two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory gains from 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock suffers depletion of 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows two hundred whoziewhats. Every year, this inventory grows through incoming 5% of the current balacks count. Simultaneously, each year the stock decreases by 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we begin with twelve funkados. Every year, this inventory is enhanced by 5% of the current whoziewhats count. Simultaneously, each year the stock experiences losses of 3% of whatever maxabizers are currently available.  Meanwhile, we begin with eighty-eight maxabizers. Every year, this inventory benefits from 5% of the current funkados count. Simultaneously, each year the stock decreases by 3% of whatever whoziewhats are currently available.

supportingInfo.explanation: Five interconnected stocks (whatajigs, balacks, whoziewhats, funkados, maxabizers) were each placed in their own module per the naming convention, with a 'count' stock, growth and depletion flows, and named fractional or constant rate variables (avoiding any bare hard-coded percentages inside equations). Cross-module dependencies are handled with cross-level ghost variables: for example, balacks growth depends on whatajigs count, so a ghost named 'Balacks.whatajigs count' was created in the Balacks module pointing to 'Whatajigs.count', and the balacks growth equation references the ghost rather than the original variable. This pattern repeats for whoziewhats (depends on balacks), funkados (depends on whoziewhats for growth and maxabizers for depletion), and maxabizers (depends on funkados for growth and whoziewhats for depletion), each with their own appropriately named ghost variables. All growth and depletion flows are marked uniflow since they represent one-directional accumulation or loss processes. Relationships were drawn to capture every causal link described: each stock's own level influencing percentage-based flows, each rate/fraction variable influencing its flow, each flow influencing its stock with correct polarity (positive for inflows, negative for outflows), and each ghost variable influencing the flow that consumes it.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model structure and units check out — no fabricated warnings to report since I haven't seen any yet; let me confirm via get_current_model's warnings field explicitly and then run the model.

Model built and validated. Here's the summary:

Structure (Stock Flow Diagram):

  • Stock — Frimbulators (units: frimbulators): initial value 20. Represents the on-hand inventory of frimbulators.
  • Flow — Frimbulator_Growth (units: frimbulators/day), inflow to Frimbulators: equation Frimbulators * Frimbulator_Growth_Rate.
  • Variable — Frimbulator_Growth_Rate (units: 1/day): equation 0.02, the 2% daily fractional growth rate (kept as a named parameter rather than a hard-coded constant in the flow equation).

Causal relationships captured:

  • Frimbulators → Frimbulator_Growth (more frimbulators on hand → more daily growth in absolute terms)
  • Frimbulator_Growth_Rate → Frimbulator_Growth (the 2% rate scales the growth)
  • Frimbulator_Growth → Frimbulators (the inflow accumulates into the stock)

This captures every cause-effect relationship stated in your background: the initial inventory of twenty frimbulators, and the daily addition of new frimbulators equal to 2% of the current inventory size.

Validation performed:

  • get_current_model showed no errors or warnings, and no unitWarnings were reported by the engine — units are consistent as-is.
  • Frimbulator_Growth is set uniflow (cannot go negative), and since it's proportional to the stock itself, Frimbulators cannot go negative — no artificial clamping needed.
  • Ran the simulation (100 days, dt = 0.25): Frimbulators rises smoothly from 20 to ~147 by day 100, with Frimbulator_Growth rising in lockstep from 0.4 to ~2.94 frimbulators/day — consistent with compounding 2%/day growth, no anomalies.

I have not run feedback-loop analysis in this session, so I'm not describing any loop structure — just the stock/flow/variable composition above.

What would you like to do next — inspect a longer time horizon, visualize the growth curve, or add other structure (e.g., outflows, capacity constraints)?
