errorExplanations.name: recovery_without_symptoms
errorExplanations.problem: Should use DELAY3 with the 'Asymptomatic incubation' flow as input, not the 'Asymptomatic infectious' stock divided by a time constant.

supportingInfo.explanation:
All stocks stay non-negative, exhibit a plausible SEIR-style epidemic curve (susceptible depletion, infection peak ~week 15-16, recovered rising, deaths accumulating and saturating), and Recovery_without_symptoms now tracks the same shape as the other pipeline-delay outflows (Asymptomatic_infectious rises and falls in sync). Behavior looks structurally sound. Model re-validated with no structural errors remaining.

Formulation Error Report

I inspected every stock, flow, and auxiliary equation in the model and cross-checked them against the delay-formulation style you've used consistently elsewhere. I found one formulation error, which the engine's own unit checker also flagged.

Error: Recovery_without_symptoms — incorrect delay formulation

Original equation:

DELAY3(Asymptomatic_infectious/Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections/Days_per_week,
       Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections/Days_per_week)

Why this is wrong:

  1. Structural inconsistency with the model's own style. Every other multi-stage residence-time outflow in this model — Total_incubation (Exposed stage), Developing_symptoms (Presymptomatic stage), Total_exiting_symptomatic_infectious (Symptomatic stage) — is formulated as a third-order pipeline delay applied to the upstream flow entering the stock: DELAY3(inflow, residence_time). Recovery_without_symptoms was the only outflow that instead divided the stock itself by its residence time (Asymptomatic_infectious/Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections, i.e., a first-order exponential-decay outflow) and then additionally wrapped that already-computed rate in a DELAY3 using the same time constant again. This double-applies the delay: once implicitly (stock/time is itself a rate with an inherent first-order lag) and once explicitly via DELAY3.
  2. It produces a dimensional inconsistency, which the engine's unit checker confirmed: "Recovery without symptoms" has units: "Person/Week (People/Weeks)" but the equation suggests units: "People*Weeks/Days^2". Dividing the stock (Person) by the residence time (Day) and again by Days_per_week (Day/Week) before feeding it into DELAY3 produces units of Person·Week/Day², not Person/Week.

Fix applied:

DELAY3(Asymptomatic_incubation, Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections/Days_per_week)

This delays the actual inflow to the Asymptomatic_infectious stock (Asymptomatic_incubation, already in Person/Week) by the residence time converted from Days to Weeks — exactly the same pattern used for the other three staged delays in the model. This is dimensionally consistent (Person/Week in, Person/Week out) and structurally consistent (single, correctly-parameterized third-order pipeline delay per stock stage).

I did not add, rename, or remove any variables or relationships — only the equation (and documentation) of the existing Recovery_without_symptoms flow was changed.

Everything else checked and found consistent

  • All other DELAY3 calls (Total_incubation, Developing_symptoms, Total_exiting_symptomatic_infectious, Losing_immunity) correctly delay an upstream flow by a residence time expressed in Weeks (converting from Days via Days_per_week where the parameter is stated in Days, and using the raw parameter directly where it's already stated in Weeks, e.g. Average_immunity_period, Average_length_of_symptomatic_period).
  • Infection, Incubation, Asymptomatic_incubation, Recovery, Dying_of_COVID are all dimensionally consistent (Person/Week) and use fraction-splitting off a shared upstream delay output, consistent with the SEIR-with-asymptomatic-branch structure.
  • Stock non-negativity is structurally guaranteed: every stock's outflows are ultimately driven by non-negative DELAY3 outputs of non-negative inflows, so no MIN/MAX clamps are needed.
  • Population conservation holds: Total_population sums the six living-population stocks and only shrinks through the Dying_of_COVID outflow, which is separately tracked in Cumulative_COVID_deaths.

I re-ran the model after the fix: all stocks remain non-negative, Recovery_without_symptoms now tracks the same rise-and-fall shape as Asymptomatic_infectious, and the epidemic curve (infection peak, recovery buildup, death accumulation and saturation) behaves as expected for this SEIR-style structure.

Note on the unit checker: after applying the fix, get_current_model continued to echo the original unitWarnings message verbatim, including when I temporarily changed the variable's declared units to something else entirely as a test — the message text didn't change. That indicates this field is not being live-recomputed in this session after edits, so I'm reporting it here for transparency but treating my own dimensional analysis (Person/Week in, Person/Week out) as the basis for the fix, consistent with how the other three pipeline delays in this model are dimensioned.

errorExplanations.problem: The graphical function should use TIME as an input, not DT (DT).

supportingInfo.explanation:
No errors or warnings surfaced — no unitWarnings field present, so the engine reports no dimensional-consistency problems. Let me run the model to confirm behavior is now sensible.

Formulation Review — COVID-19 SEIR-type Model

I reviewed all 34 variables and equations against SD best practice (delay structure consistency, unit handling, split-fraction conservation, and non-negativity safeguards), and inspected the unitWarnings field via get_current_model (empty — the engine reports no dimensional-consistency problems, so none are claimed here).

Error found and fixed

Variable: Influx_of_presymptomatic_infectious_people_from_abroad (flow)

  • What was wrong: Its equation was DT (the integration time-step constant, ≈0.0078 weeks) instead of TIME. This flow carries an attached graphical function whose x-axis runs from 0 to 104 — clearly indexed on simulation week number, not on the step size. With DT as the lookup input, the function was evaluated at a fixed x ≈ 0.0078 for the entire 60-week run, near the (0,0) anchor point of the table — so this exogenous "imported cases" pulse would never actually fire as the calibrated timeline (rising to 2,000/week around week 8, a second smaller bump around weeks 26–35, tapering to 0) intended.
  • Why it's an error: For a variable that owns a graphical function, the equation must be the algebraic expression of the function's input. The sibling variable Social_distancing_measures in this same model demonstrates the correct, working pattern for exactly this situation — a time-indexed graphical function driven by equation: "TIME". Using DT instead of TIME is a copy/formulation slip that breaks the intended exogenous time-profile.
  • Fix applied: Changed the equation from DT to TIME, matching the style already established by Social_distancing_measures elsewhere in the model. No variables, relationships, or names were added or changed — only this equation's right-hand side.

Other formulation aspects checked — no errors found

  • Delay style consistency: Every stock-outflow delay (Total_incubation, Developing_symptoms, Recovery_without_symptoms, Total_exiting_symptomatic_infectious, Losing_immunity) uses DELAY3 — a consistent third-order material delay throughout, with no stray first-order or SMTH delays mixed in.
  • Day/Week unit conversions: Delay times specified in Day units (Average_COVID_incubation_time, Presymptomatic_period, Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections) are each divided by Days_per_week before use in DELAY3, correctly converting to the model's native Week time unit. Delay times already specified in Week (Average_immunity_period, Average_length_of_symptomatic_period) are used directly with no spurious conversion. This is applied consistently.
  • Split-after-delay conservation: Both split points (Total_incubation → Incubation/Asymptomatic_incubation via Share_of_asymptomatic_infections; Total_exiting_symptomatic_infectious → Recovery/Dying_of_COVID via Case_fatality_rate_of_COVID_patients) use complementary fractions that sum to 1, so the split flows always reconstitute the delayed total — mass is conserved into and out of each stock.
  • Non-negativity: Infection is proportional to Susceptible_population (via Chance_of_contact_with_an_susceptible_person = Susceptible_population/Total_population), giving it a natural first-order control that drives the outflow toward zero as the stock is depleted — no clamping needed. The delay-based outflows elsewhere are conservative transformations of their own inflows (DELAY3), which cannot emit more than has accumulated, so no stock can be structurally driven negative.
  • Total_population accounting: Correctly excludes Cumulative_COVID_deaths, so the living population total appropriately declines as Dying_of_COVID removes people — consistent with a conservation-of-people check.

Since get_current_model shows no remaining errors or warnings after the fix, I did not need to make further changes.

Next steps: I'd suggest running the model (already done to confirm no structural break) and, if you'd like, using get_feedback_information + Seldon to walk through why the corrected import pulse now shapes early outbreak seeding, or requesting a chart of Influx_of_presymptomatic_infectious_people_from_abroad and Presymptomatic_infectious to visually confirm the corrected exogenous timing lines up with your intended reference mode.

Formulation Review — COVID-19 SEIR-style SFD Model

I inspected every stock, flow, and delay structure in the model (get_current_model / read_model_section), ran it, and checked the resulting time series. I found one real formulation error, which had two symptoms, plus one robustness gap. Everything else in the model — the DELAY3 pipeline-delay chains, the fractional splits (symptomatic/asymptomatic, recovery/death), and the Day→Week unit conversions on delay times — is internally consistent and mass-conserving, so I left those untouched.

Error found

Total_population / Total_population_net_flow — flow equation was a level, not a rate

  • Total_population was modeled as a stock, fed by an inflow called Total_population_net_flow (units Person/Week).
  • But Total_population_net_flow's equation was simply Susceptible_population + Exposed_population + Asymptomatic_infectious + Presymptomatic_infectious + Symptomatic_infectious + Recovered_population — i.e., it just re-summed the compartment levels (units Person) and called the result a flow. This is exactly the dimensional inconsistency the simulation engine's unit checker flagged: "Total population net flow" has units: "Person/Week" but the equation suggests units: "Person".
  • This had a second, worse consequence: Total_population's own stock equation (its initial value) was hard-coded to 0, unlike every other compartment, whose initial values correctly encode the starting epidemic state (e.g., Susceptible_population starts at Initial_Susceptible_population). Since Chance_of_contact_with_an_susceptible_person = Susceptible_population / Total_population, this meant the model divided by zero at t=0.

Why this is a genuine formulation error, not just a units label mismatch: Total_population is not something that independently accumulates — it is definitionally the sum of the six living compartments at every instant. Modeling it as an integrated stock driven by a "flow" that recomputes the sum every step duplicates the state and breaks both dimensional consistency and the initial condition, while adding nothing the six stocks don't already provide.

Fix applied (no variables added, no variables renamed, no new causal relationships — I kept exactly the same six inputs that were already feeding this quantity):

  • Removed the erroneous Total_population_net_flow flow.
  • Converted Total_population from a stock to a plain auxiliary variable, with its equation unchanged in substance (Susceptible_population + Exposed_population + Asymptomatic_infectious + Presymptomatic_infectious + Symptomatic_infectious + Recovered_population, units Person). This resolves the unit mismatch and the divide-by-zero at t=0 simultaneously, since the auxiliary is instantaneously correct at every step rather than being integrated from a bad initial condition.

Robustness hardening (same relationship, no new links)

Chance_of_contact_with_an_susceptible_person = Susceptible_population / Total_population

Ordinary division. Under extreme-condition stress-testing (e.g., very high case-fatality rate over a long horizon), Total_population could in principle approach zero, which would crash the simulation. I changed the operator to safe division (Susceptible_population // Total_population), per the modeling guidance to guard any denominator that can plausibly reach zero. This changes no variable names and no causal structure — only the division operator.

Verification

  • Re-ran get_current_model: no structural errors. (Note: the tool's cached issues field kept echoing the old Total_population_net_flow unit warning after I removed that variable; I confirmed via read_model_section that the variable, and every relationship/equation referencing it, is actually gone — this is a stale cache echo, not a live issue.)
  • Ran the simulation: Total_population now starts at 17,000,000 (matching Initial_Susceptible_population), declines smoothly to ~16.93M as Cumulative_COVID_deaths rises to ~69,450 (the decline in population matches cumulative deaths, confirming conservation is intact), and Chance_of_contact_with_an_susceptible_person stays a well-behaved fraction between 0 and 1 throughout — no NaNs, no crash at t=0.
  • All other stocks (Susceptible, Exposed, Presymptomatic, Symptomatic, Asymptomatic, Recovered, Cumulative deaths) remain non-negative across the 60-week run, consistent with the DELAY3 pipeline structure conserving mass through each compartment (verified the inflow/outflow pairing for every stock nets out exactly against the corresponding Total_incubation / Total_exiting_symptomatic_infectious delay splits).

No other formulation errors were identified. I did not touch the model beyond these two equation-level fixes and one variable-type change — no variables were added or renamed, and no new causal relationships were introduced.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I reviewed the full model (variables, relationships, specs) and cross-checked equation logic and units against the engine's authoritative unit-warning output. Here's what I found and the fix I'm applying.

Formulation error found

Infectious_population_net_flow (the flow into stock Infectious_population) is defined as:

Symptomatic_infectious + Presymptomatic_infectious + Asymptomatic_infectious

This is why the engine's unit checker flags: "Infectious population net flow" has units "Person/Week" but the equation suggests units "Person".

Why this is wrong: A flow must be a rate (Person/Week) — the derivative of its stock. This equation instead sums three levels (Person). Integrating a level as if it were a rate is dimensionally invalid, and structurally it double-accounts population that is already tracked by the Presymptomatic_infectious, Symptomatic_infectious, and Asymptomatic_infectious stocks themselves (via their own DELAY3-based pipeline delays for Developing_symptoms, Recovery, Recovery_without_symptoms, Dying_of_COVID, etc.). The model already has the correct pattern for exactly this kind of computation — Total_population is a plain auxiliary variable that directly sums stock levels, with no spurious stock/flow pair. Infectious_population needed to follow that same style instead of being integrated through a flow.

The fix: Convert Infectious_population from a stock into a plain variable (matching the Total_population pattern), with its equation set directly to the sum of the three infectious stocks (the same quantity Infectious_population_net_flow was computing). Then remove the now-redundant Infectious_population_net_flow flow. This does not add any new variable, rename anything, or add any new causal relationship — it only removes the intermediate flow (and the relationship-cleanup that removal triggers automatically), leaving the causal structure feeding Infection (Infectious_population → Infection) exactly as it was.

Applying this now.

Now removing the now-redundant flow variable:

Good — the variable is confirmed removed, and Infectious_population is now a plain sum variable. The issues field on get_current_model appears to be a stale/cached warning message (referencing a variable that no longer exists in the model). Let me confirm by running the model, which will force fresh validation.

The variable and all its relationships are confirmed gone from the model. The issues field text is a stale cache artifact from the tool wrapper (it's echoing the original warning message text rather than re-deriving it), not a live re-check — the actual model state, confirmed by direct section reads, no longer contains Infectious_population_net_flow at all. No unit warnings apply to the current model.

Now let's check stock behavior per the SFD validation workflow (physical stocks shouldn't go negative):

The model has been re-validated and simulated successfully. Non-negativity check passed for all population stocks (Susceptible, Exposed, Presymptomatic, Symptomatic, Asymptomatic, Recovered, Cumulative deaths), and Infectious_population now correctly tracks the sum of the three infectious-stage stocks at every timestep (verified numerically, e.g. at t≈12.2: Presymptomatic 14,001 + Symptomatic 18,472 + Asymptomatic 23,241 = 55,714, matching Infectious_population = 55,714.6). Behavior shows a plausible epidemic wave — infection rises, peaks, and is suppressed by the social-distancing policy input, with cumulative deaths asymptoting — consistent with the SEIR-with-waning-immunity reference mode this model is built for.

Summary of formulation review

Reviewed: all 35 variables, their equations, units, and the delay/pipeline formulation style used throughout (DELAY3 for stage-progression delays: Total_incubation, Developing_symptoms, Recovery_without_symptoms, Total_exiting_symptomatic_infectious, Losing_immunity). That family of formulations is internally consistent — each delay time is correctly unit-converted to Weeks (dividing Day-valued parameters by Days_per_week, or using parameters already specified in Weeks) — and required no changes.

One error found and fixed:

  • What: Infectious_population_net_flow (the sole inflow to stock Infectious_population) was defined as Symptomatic_infectious + Presymptomatic_infectious + Asymptomatic_infectious — a sum of stock levels (Person) assigned to a variable typed as a flow (which must be Person/Week).
  • Why it's an error: A flow must be a rate of change; this equation instead computed an instantaneous total and then integrated it again into Infectious_population, which is dimensionally invalid. This is exactly what the engine's unit checker flagged: "Infectious population net flow" has units "Person/Week" but the equation suggests units "Person". It also silently double-accounted population already tracked by the three infectious stocks via their own pipeline delays.
  • How I fixed it: The model already has the correct pattern for this exact kind of computation — Total_population, a plain variable that directly sums stock levels with no intervening flow. I converted Infectious_population from a stock into a plain variable with the equation Symptomatic_infectious + Presymptomatic_infectious + Asymptomatic_infectious (mirroring Total_population's style), and removed the now-unneeded Infectious_population_net_flow. No variables were added or renamed, and no new causal relationships were introduced — only the redundant flow and its associated arrows were removed; Infectious_population's connection into the Infection equation is unchanged. The unit warning is now resolved.

Everything else in the model — the force-of-infection formulation (Infection = Infectious_population × Contacts_per_person_per_week × Infection_rate_per_contact × Chance_of_contact_with_an_susceptible_person), the incubation/asymptomatic split, the case-fatality split, and the population-conservation logic in Total_population (correctly excluding Cumulative_COVID_deaths) — checked out as structurally and dimensionally sound.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a model that exhibits exponential growth behavior in the 'output' variable.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Exponential growth occurs when the rate of increase is proportional to the current value. This creates a reinforcing feedback loop where larger values grow faster. Examples include compound interest, viral spread, and unconstrained population growth. A classic example would be compound interest or unconstrained population growth where the rate of growth is proportional to the current value.

supportingInfo.explanation:
No errors or warnings reported. Structure check: stock output (initial value 1, units), inflow growth = output * fractional_growth_rate, no outflow — this is exactly the proportional-growth formulation requested, with a reinforcing loop (output → growth → output). No hard-coded constants embedded in equations (the 0.1 rate is its own named parameter, not inlined). No unit warnings were returned, so none exist to report.

Let me run it and check the output data before reporting.

Model built, validated, and simulated successfully.

Structure

  • Stock output (units: units): initial value 1, single inflow growth, no outflows.
  • Flow growth (units: units/time): equation output * fractional_growth_rate — the rate of increase is directly proportional to the current value of output.
  • Variable fractional_growth_rate (units: 1/time): constant, set to 0.1.

No errors or warnings came back from get_current_model, and no unit inconsistencies were flagged.

Behavior check (run over t=0–50, dt=0.25): output rises from 1 at t=0 to ~139.6 at t=50, with growth tracking it proportionally the whole way (growth/output ratio stays fixed at 0.1 throughout, confirming the proportional-rate mechanism is working exactly as intended). The curve accelerates monotonically — value roughly doubles every ~7 time units, consistent with the ln(2)/0.1 ≈ 6.9 doubling time implied by the 0.1 fractional rate. This is the textbook unconstrained-exponential-growth signature: no inflection, no saturation, ever-increasing absolute growth.

Structural/behavioral critique

  • Loop polarity: output → growth → output is a single reinforcing loop by construction (growth increases output, more output increases growth) — this is the sole mechanism driving the curve, and it's the correct one for the stated reference mode.
  • No balancing structure exists (no carrying capacity, no depletion term) — that's intentional per your request for unconstrained growth, but it also means this model is only valid over the range where no limiting factor would realistically apply. If you ever want a more realistic long-run reference mode (e.g., S-shaped growth), a limiting term would need to be added later.
  • Conservation: not applicable here in the mass-balance sense — output is a single accumulating quantity with one source term, which is appropriate for compound-growth-type stocks (e.g., capital, population) rather than a conserved physical quantity split across compartments.
  • No hard-coded constants are buried in equations; the only numeric parameter (0.1) is isolated in its own named, documented variable (fractional_growth_rate), as required.

Model type is SFD for this session, as established.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a model that exhibits exponential decay behavior in the 'output' variable.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Exponential decay occurs when the rate of decrease is proportional to the current value. This creates a negative feedback loop where the value decreases rapidly at first, then more slowly as it approaches zero. Examples include radioactive decay, drug elimination from the body, and temperature cooling. The output should show rapid decrease that slows over time, asymptotically approaching zero.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model structure is clean: no errors/warnings surfaced in variables, and it's exactly the minimal first-order decay loop. Let's check for any errors/warnings via get_current_model's full payload — it didn't include an errors field, implying none. Proceeding to run and verify behavior.

Behavior confirmed: output falls from 100 toward 0 with rapid initial decline that slows over time, never going negative — textbook exponential decay.

Model built: Simple First-Order Exponential Decay

Structure (3 variables):

  • output (stock, units: units) — initial value 100, depletes via outflow decay_rate. This is the variable you asked to show decay behavior.
  • decay_time (parameter, units: time) — value 10, the characteristic time constant.
  • decay_rate (flow, units: units/time) — equation output/decay_time, marked uniflow (one-directional depletion, cannot reverse).

This is the minimal negative-feedback structure needed for exponential decay: the outflow is proportional to the stock itself, so as output shrinks, decay_rate shrinks proportionally — producing fast initial decline that asymptotically flattens toward zero.

Validation performed:

  • Checked variables/specs — no errors or warnings surfaced.
  • No hard-coded constants inside equations; the only numeric literals are the stock's initial value (100) and decay_time (10), both are named-variable values, not embedded in formulas.
  • decay_rate is uniflow-constrained so it can't reverse into an inflow — physically appropriate for a depleting quantity.
  • Ran the simulation (startTime 0, stopTime 50, dt 0.25): output goes 100 → 90.4 → 81.7 → ... → 0.63 at t=50, and decay_rate falls in lockstep (10 → 0.063), confirming the proportional relationship holds throughout. output stays strictly positive and trends toward zero without oscillation or overshoot — matches the requested reference mode exactly.

Structural/behavioral critique:

  • This is intentionally the simplest possible molecule for the request — a single first-order negative feedback loop. There's no other stock, no conservation-law partner (e.g., decayed material isn't accumulating anywhere), which is fine if you only care about output's trajectory, but if the physical interpretation matters (e.g., mass conservation for radioactive decay into a daughter product), that outflow currently just disappears rather than accumulating elsewhere.
  • decay_time = 10 and initial output = 100 are reasonable illustrative defaults but arbitrary — let me know if you have specific values or units (e.g., days, becquerels, mg/L, degrees) tied to your actual application.

What would you like to do next — adjust parameters/units to match a specific real-world case (radioactive isotope, drug half-life, cooling process), add a conserving "sink" stock, or visualize the run?

relationships.polarityReasoning: As output increases, the decay_rate increases proportionally (since decay_rate = output/decay_time); as output decreases, decay_rate decreases proportionally. This is a positive relationship because both variables move in the same direction.

relationships.reasoning: The time constant parameter determines how quickly output is depleted; it is used as the divisor in the decay_rate calculation.
relationships.polarityReasoning: As decay_time increases (a longer characteristic time constant), decay_rate decreases because output is divided by a larger number, resulting in slower depletion. As decay_time decreases, decay_rate increases because output is divided by a smaller number, resulting in faster depletion. This inverse relationship is negative polarity.

relationships.reasoning: The decay_rate is the outflow that removes quantity from the output stock over time, directly reducing its accumulated value.
relationships.polarityReasoning: As decay_rate increases, output decreases faster (more is being removed); as decay_rate decreases, output decreases more slowly. Since the outflow removes from the stock, an increase in the outflow causes a decrease in the stock, making this a negative relationship. This also closes the negative feedback loop: higher output leads to higher decay_rate, which in turn reduces output, driving the exponential decay pattern.

variables.name: output
variables.documentation: The stock representing the quantity undergoing exponential decay, such as a radioactive substance, drug concentration, or temperature difference. It starts at an initial value and depletes over time via the decay_rate outflow, which is proportional to its current value, creating the classic negative feedback loop of first-order exponential decay.

variables.name: decay_time
variables.documentation: The characteristic time constant of the decay process. It represents how quickly output decays: a larger decay_time means slower decay, while a smaller decay_time means faster decay. This is analogous to the half-life concept in radioactive decay or the elimination rate constant in pharmacokinetics.

variables.name: decay_rate
variables.documentation: The outflow that depletes the output stock. It is calculated as output divided by decay_time, making the rate of decrease directly proportional to the current value of output. This proportionality is what creates the negative feedback loop responsible for exponential decay: as output shrinks, the absolute rate of decrease also shrinks, producing rapid initial decline that slows asymptotically toward zero.

testParams.name: Logistic Decay Pattern
testParams.prompt: Please create a model that demonstrates logistic decay (inverse S-curve) behavior. The model must include a variable named 'output' that shows this behavior over time.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a model that exhibits logistic decay (inverse S-curve) behavior in the 'output' variable.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Logistic decay follows an S-shaped (sigmoid) decline and is the mirror image of logistic growth. The output starts high and declines only slowly at first while it is near its initial level. The decline then accelerates, reaching its maximum rate around the midpoint between the starting value and the floor, before slowing again as balancing feedback becomes dominant near the floor, until the system stabilizes at a lower equilibrium. Because the decline is slow at both the top and the bottom and fastest in the middle, the curve has an inflection point (it is NOT exponential decay, which declines fastest at the very start). A natural structure is an outflow proportional to both the distance still remaining above the floor and the distance already fallen from the initial value (for example, rate proportional to (initial - output) * (output - floor)), which is near zero at both ends and largest in between. Examples include the decline phase of a product life cycle and the abandonment of a technology following an inverse S-curve. The output should start high and nearly flat, decline most steeply through the middle, and then level off as it approaches a minimum sustainable level or floor.

supportingInfo.explanation:

The model now clearly exhibits the requested inverse S-curve: nearly flat near 99, accelerating decline peaking around month 19.5 (decline_rate ≈ 4.8/month), then decelerating as output approaches the floor, settling near 20 by month 50.

Model summary

Structure (single-stock SFD):

  • output (stock, units) — starts at initial_output minus a small perturbation (initial_decline_trigger_fraction × (initial_output − output_floor)), so it isn't parked exactly on the unstable equilibrium where decline would never start. Its only outflow is decline_rate.
  • initial_output = 100 units — the starting/reference level.
  • output_floor = 20 units — the minimum sustainable level output approaches but never crosses.
  • initial_decline_trigger_fraction = 0.01 (dimensionless) — small nudge off the unstable fixed point at t=0.
  • decline_rate_coefficient = 0.003 (1/(units·units·Months)) — governs decay speed; tuned so the full curve plays out within the 50-month horizon.
  • gap_below_initial = initial_output − output — how far output has already fallen.
  • gap_above_floor = output − output_floor — how far output still is above the floor.
  • decline_rate (outflow) = decline_rate_coefficient × gap_below_initial × gap_above_floor — near zero at both extremes, maximal near the midpoint, producing the inflection point.

No errors or unit warnings were reported by the engine after any edit.

Validation performed:

  1. First build had a structural bug — output started exactly at initial_output, making gap_below_initial = 0 and decline_rate = 0 for all time (an unstable equilibrium under Euler integration), so output never moved. Fixed by adding the trigger-fraction perturbation to output's initial condition.
  2. Second run showed correct S-shaped decline but hadn't reached the leveling-off phase by t=50 (still accelerating, only down to 72). Retuned decline_rate_coefficient from 0.001 to 0.003 so the full slow-steep-slow curve, including flattening near the floor, is visible within the existing 50-month window.
  3. Final run (verified via get_variable_data): output goes 99.2 → 98.7 → ... slow decline early, drops steeply through the 60s–40s range (decline_rate peaks ~4.8 units/month near t≈19.5), then decelerates smoothly to ~20.04 by t=50 — never crossing the floor. Conservation/boundary behavior checks out: output stays positive and bounded above the floor throughout.

Next steps you might want: I can run feedback loop analysis (Loops That Matter) to explain the mechanism driving this behavior, generate a time-series visualization, or run a sensitivity analysis on decline_rate_coefficient / output_floor. Let me know which you'd like.

variables.name: output
variables.documentation: The central stock representing the quantity undergoing logistic decay (e.g., product sales, technology adoption level). Its initial value is set slightly below initial_output using the small initial_decline_trigger_fraction parameter (scaled by the full range initial_output - output_floor) so that gap_below_initial is not exactly zero at time zero. Without this nudge, output = initial_output is an exact fixed point of the ODE (decline_rate = 0), and under Euler integration the stock would remain flat forever instead of beginning its S-shaped decline. From this slightly perturbed starting point, output declines toward output_floor, with the decline being most rapid through the middle of the range and leveling off at both extremes because its only outflow, decline_rate, is proportional to the product of the remaining distance above the floor and the remaining distance below the initial value. Structure unchanged from the prior model.

variables.name: initial_output
variables.documentation: Parameter representing the starting (high) value of output before decline begins. Used to set the stock's initial condition (net of the small trigger perturbation) and as the upper reference point in the decline-rate formula. Unchanged from the prior model.

variables.name: output_floor
variables.documentation: Parameter representing the minimum sustainable level that output approaches but never falls below. Used as the lower reference point in the decline-rate formula and, together with initial_output, defines the full range that the trigger-fraction parameter scales to perturb output's initial condition. Unchanged from the prior model.

variables.name: initial_decline_trigger_fraction
variables.documentation: Small dimensionless fraction (e.g., 0.01, i.e., 1% of the full range) representing that the decline process has already been nudged slightly away from the unstable equilibrium at the start of the simulation. It multiplies the full range (initial_output - output_floor) and is subtracted from initial_output to set output's initial value just barely below initial_output. This structural fix is necessary because output = initial_output is an exact fixed point of the logistic decay ODE (gap_below_initial = 0 there), so without this small perturbation an Euler integrator would leave output flat forever with decline_rate stuck at zero. Unchanged from the prior model.

variables.name: decline_rate_coefficient
variables.documentation: Parameter governing how fast the decay proceeds. Multiplies the product of the two gap terms to produce the actual decline rate; larger values produce a faster, steeper S-shaped decline. RETUNED from 0.001 to 0.003 (roughly 3x increase) because at 0.001 the decline was still accelerating at t=50 and had only reached about 72 units, far short of the leveling-off phase near output_floor=20. At 0.003 the decline proceeds fast enough that by t=50 the curve has clearly passed through its inflection point (where gap_below_initial and gap_above_floor are roughly equal) and is visibly flattening as output approaches output_floor, making the full slow-steep-slow inverse-S-curve observable within the existing 50-month, dt=0.25 simulation window. No other structural or numeric changes were made.

variables.name: gap_below_initial
variables.documentation: Represents how far output has already fallen from its initial value. Thanks to the initial_decline_trigger_fraction perturbation applied to output's initial condition, this term is slightly above zero at time zero rather than exactly zero, allowing the decline process to actually start. It continues to grow as output declines further, contributing a reinforcing push to the decline rate, before its contribution to the product term is outweighed by the shrinking gap_above_floor term as output nears the floor. Unchanged from the prior model.

variables.name: gap_above_floor
variables.documentation: Represents how far output still is above the floor. This term starts near its maximum (close to the full range) since output begins just barely below initial_output, and shrinks as output declines, contributing a balancing pull that slows the decline rate as output approaches the floor. Unchanged from the prior model.

variables.name: decline_rate
variables.documentation: Outflow from output equal to decline_rate_coefficient times the product of gap_below_initial and gap_above_floor. Because output's initial condition is perturbed slightly below initial_output via initial_decline_trigger_fraction, gap_below_initial is nonzero at time zero, so decline_rate starts slightly positive instead of being stuck at exactly zero forever. This product remains near zero when output is near either extreme and is maximal near the midpoint, producing the characteristic inflection point of logistic (S-shaped) decay rather than exponential decay. With decline_rate_coefficient retuned to 0.003, this reinforcing-then-balancing feedback loop (output feeds gap_below_initial and gap_above_floor, which together set decline_rate, which drains output) now completes its full transit through slow, steep, and leveling-off phases within the 50-month window. Marked as uniflow since output can only decline, never spontaneously regenerate.

testParams.name: Standing Oscillation Pattern
testParams.prompt: Please create a model that demonstrates sustained oscillation behavior. The model must include a variable named 'output' that shows this behavior over time.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a model that exhibits sustained oscillation behavior in the 'output' variable.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Standing oscillations occur in systems with delays and feedback loops that create periodic behavior. The system oscillates around an equilibrium point with relatively constant amplitude. Examples include predator-prey models (Lotka-Volterra), inventory management with ordering delays, economic business cycles, and many engineering control systems. The oscillation is sustained rather than dampening out. The output should oscillate periodically with relatively constant amplitude over time.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Now let's inspect the built model and validate it.

The initial Lotka‑Volterra formulation is exhibiting amplitude drift (each cycle's peak growing: ~104 → 110 → 117 → 121 → ...125→131→133→143→155) rather than the "relatively constant amplitude" required — this is the classic numerical-drift problem with a conservative center (marginally stable orbit, non-self-correcting). I'll rebuild using a self-correcting stable limit-cycle oscillator (Van der Pol-type structure), which is inherently robust to this problem.

No errors reported. Now run and inspect the simulation to confirm constant-amplitude sustained oscillation.

Model built, validated, and simulated successfully. Here is a summary.

Structure (SFD, 7 variables):

  • Stocks
    • output (units) — the tracked oscillating signal. Initial value 1 (a small perturbation off the unstable equilibrium at zero). Inflow: output_change.
    • output_velocity (units/Time) — the rate of change of output. Initial value 0. Inflow: output_velocity_change.
  • Flows
    • output_change = output_velocity — definitional link (derivative of output).
    • output_velocity_change = damping_coefficient * (1 - (output/reference_amplitude)^2) * output_velocity - (natural_frequency^2) * output — nonlinear self-correcting damping term plus a linear restoring term.
  • Constants
    • damping_coefficient (1/Time) = 1 — strength of the amplitude-correcting nonlinearity
    • reference_amplitude (units) = 2 — sets the target oscillation amplitude
    • natural_frequency (1/Time) = 1 — sets the oscillation's angular frequency

Simulation specs: RK4 integration, dt = 0.02, stopTime = 100.

Why this structure: This is a self-sustained (Van der Pol type) limit-cycle oscillator. The nonlinear term in output_velocity_change injects energy into the system while |output| is below reference_amplitude and removes energy once it exceeds that threshold — this is a self-correcting mechanism, so the amplitude locks onto a fixed value rather than drifting. (I initially tried a conservative Lotka-Volterra-style two-stock structure, but on inspecting get_variable_data I found its peak amplitude was growing cycle over cycle — 104 → 110 → 117 → 121 → 125 → 131 → 143 → 155 — a neutrally-stable center is prone to numerical drift over long runs and doesn't satisfy "relatively constant amplitude." I rebuilt with the self-correcting structure above instead.)

Validation performed:

  • get_current_model after each build: no errors or warnings returned.
  • run_model + get_variable_data: after an initial transient (roughly the first 2 cycles), output settles into a clean sustained oscillation with peak values consistently around ±4.0–4.1 (matching the theoretical ~2×reference_amplitude) for the remainder of the 100-time-unit simulation — confirming constant amplitude, not damping or growing.
  • Note: output is a deviation-type signal (like a control-system output deviation or oscillator displacement) by design, so it legitimately swings both positive and negative — this is not a physical stock like inventory/population that requires a non-negativity constraint.

Structural/behavioral critique:

  • Structurally, the two coupled first-order stocks correctly reduce the second-order Van der Pol dynamics; the nonlinear damping term is the key self-limiting mechanism and is essential — without it the system would either damp to zero or grow unbounded.
  • Behaviorally, the reference-mode fit is good: sustained, constant-amplitude, periodic oscillation as required, with a clear settling transient consistent with a limit-cycle attractor.
  • Limitation to flag: amplitude and frequency are governed by reference_amplitude and natural_frequency, which are illustrative placeholder values (2 and 1) rather than calibrated to any specific real-world system — reasonable if the goal is purely to demonstrate the oscillation mechanism.

What would you like to do next — adjust the parameters (e.g., amplitude, frequency, or damping strength), run a feedback loop (LTM) analysis to see the loop dynamics behind this behavior, or visualize the results?

variables.name: output
variables.documentation: The tracked oscillating signal, a deviation-type quantity (analogous to a control system output deviation or oscillator displacement) that swings both above and below zero as part of its normal sustained oscillation. Retained from the prior model but restructured: it is now the position variable of a Van der Pol oscillator instead of a Lotka-Volterra prey stock. Initialized at a small nonzero value (1 unit) so the system starts off the unstable equilibrium at the origin and spirals outward onto its stable limit cycle, avoiding the flat trivial solution.

variables.name: output_velocity
variables.documentation: The rate of change of output, i.e. its velocity. This is the second state variable required to turn the single output stock into a genuine second-order (Van der Pol) oscillator. Initialized at 0 because at time zero output is only slightly perturbed and not yet moving. Its net inflow is nonlinear and can be positive or negative, so it is not constrained to be non-negative.

variables.name: output_change
variables.documentation: Purely definitional link stating that the rate of change of output equals output_velocity. This is the standard first-order reduction used to convert a second-order differential equation (Van der Pol equation) into two coupled first-order stocks. Not constrained to be non-negative because output_velocity itself legitimately swings positive and negative as the oscillator moves back and forth through its cycle.

variables.name: output_velocity_change
variables.documentation: The net rate of change of output_velocity, implementing the Van der Pol equation. It has two structural pieces: a nonlinear damping term, damping_coefficient*(1-(output/reference_amplitude)^2)*output_velocity, which injects energy when |output| is below reference_amplitude and removes energy when |output| exceeds it, and a linear restoring term, -(natural_frequency^2)*output, which pulls output back toward zero and sets the base oscillation frequency. This self-correcting nonlinear damping is exactly what makes the resulting cycle a stable limit cycle rather than a neutrally stable conservative orbit, so amplitude does not drift over long simulations. Not constrained to be non-negative because this net rate legitimately alternates sign throughout each oscillation cycle.

variables.name: damping_coefficient
variables.documentation: Named constant controlling how strongly the nonlinear damping term pushes the trajectory toward the limit cycle. Larger values cause faster convergence to the limit cycle and a more strongly nonlinear (relaxation-oscillator-like) waveform; smaller values give a more sinusoidal waveform that converges to the limit cycle more slowly. Kept as an explicit named variable rather than a literal inside the flow equation so it can be tuned without editing equations.

variables.name: reference_amplitude
variables.documentation: Named constant that sets the size of the sustained oscillation: the stable limit cycle of output settles to a peak-to-peak swing of roughly twice this value. It appears in the denominator of the squared ratio inside the nonlinear damping term, defining the boundary between energy injection (|output| below this value) and energy dissipation (|output| above this value), which is the self-correcting mechanism that fixes the amplitude.

variables.name: natural_frequency
variables.documentation: Named constant that sets the angular frequency of the sustained oscillation via the linear restoring term -(natural_frequency^2)*output. Combined with damping_coefficient, it determines how many oscillation cycles occur over the simulated time horizon; a value of 1 with the chosen stopTime and dt gives several full cycles for observation.

testParams.name: Simple Pendulum
testParams.prompt: Create a System Dynamics model of a simple pendulum with a small initial displacement. The model must include variables named 'angle' (angular position in radians), 'angular_velocity' (angular velocity in radians/second), and 'angular_acceleration' (angular acceleration in radians/second²). The model should obey Newton's laws of motion.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a pendulum model that accurately represents a simple pendulum with a small initial displacement and follows Newton's laws.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A simple pendulum consists of a mass suspended from a fixed point by a massless string. For small angles, the motion approximates simple harmonic motion. Newton's second law for rotational motion states: τ = I*α, where τ is torque, I is moment of inertia, and α is angular acceleration. For a simple pendulum: α = -(g/L)*sin(θ), where g is gravitational acceleration (9.8 m/s²), L is length, and θ is angle. For small angles, sin(θ) ≈ θ, giving α ≈ -(g/L)*θ. The angular velocity ω = dθ/dt, and angular acceleration α = dω/dt. Energy is conserved: E = (1/2)*I*ω² + mgh, where potential energy depends on height h = L*(1-cos(θ)).

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structure matches the specification exactly: two stocks (angle, angular_velocity), two flows implementing the kinematic definitions, and an auxiliary computing the small-angle restoring acceleration from named constants (gravitational_acceleration, pendulum_length). No unit warnings or errors were reported, and no hard-coded constants appear except as the defining values of the two named constants. Simulation specs: 0–20 s, dt=0.01, RK4 — appropriate for resolving oscillatory dynamics without numerical damping.

Now let me run it and verify the behavior (oscillation without unbounded growth, correct period).

The initial run shows a concerning result: energy is not staying constant. Let me verify conservation quantitatively before reporting, and test whether tightening the time step resolves it (this distinguishes genuine RK4 truncation error from a deeper issue).

I found a genuine behavioral problem: energy is growing (not conserved) at a rate consistent with a first-order integration error, not RK4's expected near-zero drift. Let me verify by tightening the time step to see how the error scales — this diagnoses whether it's a real integration issue before I decide how to fix it.

Model delivered: Simple Pendulum (Small-Angle Approximation)

Structure (verified via get_current_model / read_model_section, not assumed):

Variable Type Equation Units
angle stock init 0.1, inflow angle_change radians
angular_velocity stock init 0, inflow angular_velocity_change radians/second
angle_change flow angular_velocity radians/second
angular_velocity_change flow angular_acceleration radians/second²
angular_acceleration variable -(gravitational_acceleration/pendulum_length)*angle radians/second²
gravitational_acceleration constant 9.8 m/s²
pendulum_length constant 1 m

This is the direct stock-flow encoding of Newton's second law for rotational motion under the small-angle approximation: d(theta)/dt = omega, d(omega)/dt = alpha, alpha ≈ -(g/L)theta. No mass, energy, torque, or moment-of-inertia variables were introduced — none are needed at this level of abstraction, and none were requested. No hard-coded constants appear except as the defining values of the two named parameters. get_current_model reported no errors, no warnings, and no unitWarnings.

Structural critique:

  • Both stock outflows correctly omitted (angle/velocity legitimately swing negative — no artificial non-negativity constraint, which would be wrong here since angular displacement/velocity are signed, not physical-quantity stocks like mass or population).
  • The single balancing loop (angle → acceleration → velocity → angle, restoring sign) is the only causal path — appropriate for an idealized, undamped small-angle pendulum with no external driving or friction.

Behavioral critique — a real issue I found and want to flag: I tested conservation of mechanical energy (should be exactly constant in this undamped, undriven system) by tracking angle² + (angular_velocity/ω₀)², which is invariant for true simple harmonic motion. At dt=0.01 (RK4), this quantity grew 7x over 20 seconds — the amplitude visibly crept outward each cycle, which is not physical for a lossless pendulum. I refined dt to 0.001, keeping RK4, and re-ran: the drift shrank substantially (22% growth over 20 s instead of ~600%), confirming the growth is a numerical-integration artifact, not a structural equation error — the equations themselves are dimensionally and causally correct. However, the drift scales closer to first-order than to RK4's expected near-zero error, suggesting the simulation engine's effective numerical behavior here is less accurate than nominal RK4 for this stiffness. I've kept dt=0.001 (RK4, 0–20 s) as the delivered configuration since it materially reduces the artifact, but you should be aware some slow amplitude creep remains and isn't a defect in the causal structure.

Next steps you could ask for: shrink dt further to test whether drift keeps shrinking proportionally (isolating engine-side integration accuracy), plot angle vs. time to see the oscillation and residual drift, or extend the model beyond small-angle (replacing angle with SIN(angle) in the acceleration equation) to compare against the linear approximation.

testParams.name: Damped Pendulum
testParams.prompt: Create a System Dynamics model of a damped pendulum with friction. The model must include variables named 'angle' (angular position in radians), 'angular_velocity' (angular velocity in radians/second), and 'angular_acceleration' (angular acceleration in radians/second²). The model should obey Newton's laws of motion.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a pendulum model that accurately represents a damped pendulum with friction and follows Newton's laws.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A damped pendulum experiences a resistive force proportional to velocity. The equation of motion becomes: α = -(g/L)*sin(θ) - (b/I)*ω, where b is the damping coefficient. Newton's second law still applies: τ_total = τ_gravity + τ_damping = I*α. The system loses energy over time due to friction, causing oscillation amplitude to decrease exponentially. Angular acceleration must still be the derivative of angular velocity, and angular velocity the derivative of angle.

Damped Pendulum Model — Built and Validated

Structure (Stock Flow Diagram, Newtonian torque formulation):

Variable Type Equation Units
angle stock init 0.5, inflow d_angle_dt radians
angular_velocity stock init 0, inflow d_angular_velocity_dt radians/second
d_angle_dt flow angular_velocity radians/second
d_angular_velocity_dt flow angular_acceleration radians/second²
angular_acceleration converter torque_total / moment_of_inertia radians/second²
torque_gravity converter -mass*gravitational_acceleration*pendulum_length*SIN(angle) newton·meter
torque_damping converter -damping_coefficient*angular_velocity newton·meter
torque_total converter torque_gravity + torque_damping newton·meter
moment_of_inertia converter mass*pendulum_length^2 kilogram·meter²
mass, pendulum_length, gravitational_acceleration, damping_coefficient constants 1, 1, 9.81, 0.2 kg, m, m/s², N·m·s

This directly implements τ_total = τ_gravity + τ_damping = I·α, with α integrated to ω (angular_velocity) and ω integrated to θ (angle) — Newton's second law for rotation, closed as a proper stock-flow chain. Neither stock is clamped non-negative, since both angle and angular velocity are legitimately signed, oscillating quantities. No hard-coded constants appear inside equations; every physical parameter is a named variable. get_current_model reports no errors and no unit warnings.

Behavioral critique — I caught a real numerical artifact, not a structural flaw: At the initial time step (dt=0.02s, RK4 nominally), simulated amplitude decayed only from 0.5 to ~0.37 rad over 60s. I cross-checked this against an independent reference integration of the identical ODE (same equations, parameters) and found the true physical decay should reach ~0.001 rad by t=60s given damping_coefficient=0.2 and moment_of_inertia=1 (decay time constant ≈ 10s). The coarse time step was injecting spurious numerical energy into this lightly-damped oscillator (period ≈ 2s, so only ~100 steps/cycle), masking the real friction-driven decay. I regenerated the model with the same structure but dt reduced to 0.005s. Re-running confirms the fix: amplitude now decays smoothly and monotonically from 0.5 rad to ~0.003 rad over 60s, consistent with the expected exponential envelope — the friction term is now behaving credibly.

Extreme-condition sanity check implicit in the run: with damping_coefficient > 0 and no external torque, energy strictly declines and the pendulum settles toward θ=0, ω=0 — consistent with conservation/dissipation expectations for a frictional system with no forcing.

Next steps you could take: run feedback loop analysis (LTM) to see how the gravity-restoring and damping loops trade off dominance across the decay; visualize angle and angular_velocity time series or a phase portrait (θ vs ω, which should spiral inward); or test sensitivity of decay rate to damping_coefficient. testParams.name: Pendulum with Moderate Initial Angle
testParams.prompt: Create a System Dynamics model of a simple pendulum with a moderate initial displacement (30 degrees). The model must include variables named 'angle' (angular position in radians), 'angular_velocity' (angular velocity in radians/second), and 'angular_acceleration' (angular acceleration in radians/second²). The model should obey Newton's laws of motion.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a pendulum model that accurately represents a simple pendulum with a moderate initial displacement (30 degrees) and follows Newton's laws.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: For larger angles, the small-angle approximation breaks down and we must use the full equation: α = -(g/L)*sin(θ). This introduces non-linearity, making the period slightly longer than predicted by the small-angle approximation. Newton's laws still govern the motion: the restoring torque is τ = -m*g*L*sin(θ), and τ = I*α. Energy conservation still holds (in the absence of damping): KE + PE = constant, where PE = m*g*L*(1-cos(θ)). The motion is still periodic but not exactly sinusoidal due to the nonlinear restoring force.

The nonlinear pendulum model is built and validated. Here's what's in place:

Structure (SFD, Newton's laws, full nonlinear formulation — no small-angle approximation):

  • Stock angle (radians) — angular position θ, initial value = initial_angle_radians (30° converted to radians ≈ 0.5236 rad), integrated from angular_velocity.
  • Stock angular_velocity (radians/second) — dθ/dt, initial value 0 (released from rest), integrated from angular_acceleration.
  • Converter angular_acceleration (radians/second²) = restoring_torque / moment_of_inertia — this is Newton's second law for rotation, τ = Iα, applied directly.
  • Converter restoring_torque (newton·meter) = -pendulum_mass * gravitational_acceleration * pendulum_length * SIN(angle) — the exact nonlinear restoring torque, using SIN(angle) rather than the small-angle linearization.
  • Converter moment_of_inertia (kilogram·meter²) = pendulum_mass * pendulum_length^2.
  • Constants: pendulum_mass (1 kg), pendulum_length (1 m), gravitational_acceleration (9.81 m/s²), initial_angle_degrees (30°), with initial_angle_radians converting degrees to radians.
  • Diagnostic converters potential_energy = m·g·L·(1−cos θ), kinetic_energy = 0.5·I·ω², and total_mechanical_energy = PE + KE, included specifically to check energy conservation.

Validation performed:

  • No errors or unit warnings reported by the engine.
  • Ran the simulation and inspected angle, angular_velocity, and total_mechanical_energy numerically (not just names). The first attempt (dt=0.01, RK4) showed serious non-physical energy growth — I caught this by actually reading the output data rather than assuming RK4 with a "small" dt would behave. I iteratively tightened the timestep (0.01 → 0.001 → 0.0002s, still RK4) until total_mechanical_energy stayed nearly flat: it now drifts only about 4% over 20 seconds/roughly 10 oscillation periods (1.3143 J → 1.3646 J), versus growing over 5x in the original attempt. This is a numerical-integration accuracy issue (timestep resolution vs. the model's oscillation frequency), not a structural error in the physics.
  • With the refined timestep, angle oscillates in a bounded, non-sinusoidal pattern (roughly between −0.44 and +0.53 rad) consistent with a large-angle pendulum released from rest at 30° — it does not blow up or grow in amplitude cycle to cycle.

Current simulation specs: startTime=0, stopTime=20s, dt=0.0002s, RK4 integration.

variables.name: angle
variables.documentation: The angular position theta of the pendulum bob measured from the vertical equilibrium. This is the primary state variable of the nonlinear pendulum. It starts at the moderate 30-degree displacement (converted to radians) and evolves according to its own rate of change, angular_velocity, via the connecting flow angular_velocity_flow.

variables.name: angular_velocity
variables.documentation: The rate of change of angle (dtheta/dt). Modeled as a stock because it accumulates the effect of angular acceleration over time. Starts at zero because the pendulum is released from rest. Feeds the angle stock through the connecting flow angular_velocity_flow, closing the core nonlinear feedback loop: angle -> restoring_torque -> angular_acceleration -> angular_velocity -> angle.

variables.name: angular_velocity_flow
variables.documentation: This flow carries the current value of the angular_velocity stock into the angle stock, implementing the definition dtheta/dt = angular_velocity. A distinct flow object is required structurally to connect one stock's value as the rate feeding another stock. It is bidirectional (not uniflow) since angular velocity can be positive or negative as the pendulum swings both directions.

variables.name: angular_acceleration_flow
variables.documentation: This flow carries the current value of the angular_acceleration converter into the angular_velocity stock, implementing d(angular_velocity)/dt = angular_acceleration. It is bidirectional because the nonlinear restoring torque changes sign as the pendulum swings through its equilibrium, completing the closed nonlinear feedback loop that produces oscillation.

variables.name: angular_acceleration
variables.documentation: Computed directly from Newton's second law for rotation (tau = I*alpha, so alpha = tau/I). Uses the exact nonlinear restoring torque, not a linearized approximation, so the resulting motion captures the true nonlinear pendulum dynamics.

variables.name: restoring_torque
variables.documentation: The exact nonlinear gravitational restoring torque on the pendulum bob, tau = -m*g*L*sin(theta). Using SIN(angle) instead of the small-angle approximation (angle) is what makes this model capture true nonlinear pendulum behavior, especially important at the moderate 30-degree initial displacement.

variables.name: moment_of_inertia
variables.documentation: Moment of inertia of a point-mass bob on a massless rigid rod, I = m*L^2. This determines how much angular acceleration results from a given restoring torque.

variables.name: pendulum_mass
variables.documentation: The mass of the pendulum bob, held fixed for this experiment. A reasonable representative value of 1 kilogram is used; since torque and moment of inertia are both proportional to mass, it cancels out of the angular acceleration equation, but is retained for physical completeness and for the energy calculations.

variables.name: pendulum_length
variables.documentation: The length of the rigid pendulum rod, held fixed at a representative value of 1 meter. This directly determines the natural period of oscillation and the magnitude of the restoring torque.

variables.name: gravitational_acceleration
variables.documentation: Standard gravitational acceleration near Earth's surface, the driving force behind the pendulum's restoring torque.

variables.name: initial_angle_degrees
variables.documentation: The moderate initial displacement angle in degrees at which the pendulum is released from rest. 30 degrees is large enough that the small-angle approximation noticeably breaks down, which is the central phenomenon this model is designed to explore.

variables.name: initial_angle_radians
variables.documentation: Converts the initial angle from degrees to radians using the standard mathematical conversion factor pi/180, since the pendulum's equations of motion require angle in radians.

variables.name: potential_energy
variables.documentation: Gravitational potential energy of the pendulum bob relative to its lowest point, PE = m*g*L*(1-cos(theta)). This exact nonlinear form (rather than a small-angle quadratic approximation) is required for consistent energy conservation checks.

variables.name: kinetic_energy
variables.documentation: Rotational kinetic energy of the pendulum bob, KE = 0.5*I*omega^2. Used together with potential_energy to verify that total mechanical energy is conserved in this undamped model.

variables.name: total_mechanical_energy
variables.documentation: Sum of potential and kinetic energy. In the absence of damping, this quantity should remain essentially constant throughout the simulation. The physical equations (exact nonlinear restoring torque, no small-angle approximation, no damping) were already correct; the previously observed 20% upward energy drift over 20 seconds at dt=0.001s with RK4 was a purely numerical integration-error artifact, not a structural or causal-loop deficiency. Reducing the timestep further to dt=0.0002s (a 5x refinement) while keeping RK4 integration reduces the local truncation error per step by roughly two more orders of magnitude, pushing the residual numerical energy injection down to well under 5% drift over the full 20-second run. No new variables or feedback paths were needed to fix this because the issue was numerical resolution, not missing causality.

testParams.name: Simple Spring-Mass System
testParams.prompt: Create a System Dynamics model of a simple spring-mass system with a small initial displacement. The model must include variables named 'position' (displacement from equilibrium in meters), 'velocity' (velocity in meters/second), and 'acceleration' (acceleration in meters/second²). The model should obey Hooke's law and Newton's second law.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a spring-mass system model that accurately represents a simple spring-mass system with a small initial displacement and follows physical laws.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A spring-mass system consists of a mass attached to a spring. Hooke's law states that the force exerted by a spring is F = -kx, where k is the spring constant and x is displacement. Newton's second law: F = ma, so ma = -kx, giving a = -(k/m)*x. This produces simple harmonic motion with angular frequency ω = sqrt(k/m). The velocity v = dx/dt, and acceleration a = dv/dt. Energy is conserved: E = (1/2)*m*v² + (1/2)*k*x², where kinetic energy KE = (1/2)*m*v² and potential energy PE = (1/2)*k*x².

supportingInfo.explanation:
No errors or warnings reported. Let me verify the specs actually changed and re-run to check energy conservation.

Spring-Mass System Model — Complete

Structure (Stock Flow Diagram):

Variable Type Equation Units
position stock init = 0.05 (inflow: position_rate) meters
velocity stock init = 0 (inflow: acceleration_flow) meters/second
position_rate flow velocity meters/second
acceleration_flow flow acceleration meters/second^2
acceleration variable spring_force / mass meters/second^2
spring_force variable -1 * spring_constant * position newtons
spring_constant variable 2 (constant) newtons/meter
mass variable 0.5 (constant) kilograms
kinetic_energy variable 0.5 * mass * velocity^2 joules
potential_energy variable 0.5 * spring_constant * position^2 joules
total_mechanical_energy variable kinetic_energy + potential_energy joules

This directly implements the required physics: spring_force is Hooke's law (F = -kx), acceleration is Newton's second law rearranged (a = F/m), and the two stocks form the coupled system dx/dt = v, dv/dt = a, which is the standard SFD representation of simple harmonic motion.

Validation performed:

  • get_current_model returned no errors, no warnings (including no unitWarnings), and no missing-units fields.
  • Initial run at dt=0.01 (RK4) showed total_mechanical_energy drifting upward substantially (~230% growth over 30 s) — a numerical-integration artifact, not a structural flaw (equations/loop closure were already correct). testParams.prompt: Create a System Dynamics model of a spring-mass system with damping (friction). The model must include variables named 'position' (displacement from equilibrium in meters), 'velocity' (velocity in meters/second), and 'acceleration' (acceleration in meters/second²). The model should obey Hooke's law and Newton's second law.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a spring-mass system model that accurately represents a spring-mass system with damping (friction) and follows physical laws.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A damped spring-mass system experiences both spring force and damping force. The total force is F = -kx - bv, where k is spring constant, b is damping coefficient, and v is velocity. Newton's second law gives: ma = -kx - bv, or a = -(k/m)*x - (b/m)*v. The system loses energy over time due to damping, causing oscillation amplitude to decrease exponentially. Acceleration must still be the derivative of velocity, and velocity the derivative of position.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Now let me validate the generated structure and check for errors/warnings.

Damped Spring-Mass Model — Built and Validated

Structure (SFD):

Variable Type Equation Units
position stock ∫velocity, init = 1 meters
velocity stock ∫acceleration, init = 0 meters/second
acceleration variable -(spring_constant/mass)*position - (damping_coefficient/mass)*velocity meters/second²
mass constant 1 kilograms
spring_constant constant 2 N/m
damping_coefficient constant 0.3 N·s/m
position_flow flow (net, into position) = velocity meters/second
velocity_flow flow (net, into velocity) = acceleration meters/second²

Simulation specs: t = 0–25 s, dt = 0.02 s, RK4 integration.

Structural critique:

  • Each stock uses a single net (bidirectional) flow rather than separate inflow/outflow pairs — correct here because both position and velocity must legitimately swing positive and negative as the mass oscillates through equilibrium; forcing non-negativity would break the physics.
  • acceleration is correctly a converter (instantaneous algebraic function of state), not a stock — it has no memory of its own, consistent with Newton's second law being an algebraic force balance at each instant.
  • Hooke's law term (-spring_constant/mass * position) and the damping term (-damping_coefficient/mass * velocity) are additive per F = -kx - bv, ma = F.
  • No hard-coded constants appear inside the acceleration equation — k, b, and m are all isolated as named parameters.
  • No unit warnings were returned by the engine.

Behavioral validation (run eval-run-1):

  • t=0: position = 1 m, velocity = 0, acceleration = -2 m/s² (= -(2/1)·1 - (0.3/1)·0), matching Hooke's law exactly at the initial condition.
  • Over 0–25 s, position and velocity oscillate through zero with visibly shrinking peak magnitude (position peaks: 1 → -0.72 → 0.55 → -0.42 → 0.29 → ... → decaying toward 0), consistent with underdamped exponential decay of amplitude — the expected reference-mode behavior for a spring-mass-damper system.
  • Velocity and acceleration show the same decaying-oscillation pattern, phase-shifted relative to position as expected for this second-order system.
  • No physically-impossible values: position/velocity are legitimately allowed to go negative (displacement/direction), and nothing diverges or blows up.

The model reproduces the expected physics: oscillation with exponentially decaying amplitude driven by the damping term. Let me know if you'd like a time-series visualization, sensitivity analysis on damping_coefficient/spring_constant, or a feedback-loop (LTM) explanation of the oscillation/decay mechanism.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a spring-mass system model that accurately represents a spring-mass system with a large initial displacement and follows physical laws.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Good, dt reduced to 0.001s (RK4, ~4443 steps/period). Let's rerun and verify energy conservation now.

I built and validated the spring-mass model. Here's what's in it and how it behaves.

Structure (SFD, all variables named exactly as required):

Stocks:

  • position (m) — initial value 5 m (large displacement), inflow position_rate
  • velocity (m/second) — initial value 0 m/s, inflow velocity_rate

Flows:

  • position_rate = velocity (defines velocity as dPosition/dt)
  • velocity_rate = acceleration (defines acceleration as dVelocity/dt)

Converters:

  • acceleration = -(spring_constant/mass)*position — Hooke's law (F=-kx) combined with Newton's second law (F=ma)
  • spring_constant = 2 N/m, mass = 1 kg (fixed parameters)
  • kinetic_energy = 0.5*massvelocityvelocity (joule)
  • potential_energy = 0.5*spring_constantpositionposition (joule)
  • total_energy = kinetic_energy + potential_energy (joule), included specifically to let you check energy conservation

Specs: RK4 integration, dt = 0.001 s, 0–20 s.

Validation performed:

  1. Model check: no errors or warnings on the current model.
  2. Structural check: position and velocity are legitimately signed quantities that oscillate through zero (unlike population/inventory stocks), so no non-negativity constraint applies — clamping would misrepresent the physics. The 0.5 coefficients in the energy formulas are the standard kinetic/potential-energy identities, not arbitrary constants, so they're left inline per the no-hardcoded-constants rule.
  3. Ran the simulation and inspected position, velocity, acceleration, and total_energy numerically (not just by variable name):
    • At t=0: position=5, velocity=0, acceleration=-10 = -(2/1)*5, confirming Hooke's law/Newton's law are correctly wired.
    • position and velocity oscillate smoothly between roughly ±5 and ±7-10 respectively, with velocity peaking near equilibrium and position peaking at the turning points — matching the expected SHM reference mode.
    • total_energy starts at 25 J and drifts to about 26.0 J by t=20 s (~4% growth). This is a numerical integration artifact (RK4 truncation error accumulating over ~4.5 oscillation periods), not a structural flaw — I confirmed this by first running at dt=0.02 s, where energy drifted to more than double its initial value, then cutting dt to 0.001 s, which reduced the drift by roughly 25x. There is no tool available in this session to hand-tune dt further without regenerating the model, so ~4% drift over 20 s is the current numerical fidelity; it can be tightened further by shrinking dt if better precision is needed.

Assessment: structurally sound (correct restoring-force formulation, dimensionally sensible per the engine's own unit checks — no unit warnings were reported), and behaviorally credible (large-amplitude SHM with slow, well-controlled numerical energy drift rather than runaway or divergent behavior).
