relationships.polarityReasoning: An increase in Population leads to an increase in Births because Births = Population * Fractional_Birth_Rate, a direct multiplicative relationship.

relationships.reasoning: The fractional birth rate determines what proportion of the population is added as new births each year.
relationships.polarityReasoning: An increase in the Fractional_Birth_Rate leads to an increase in Births since Births is directly proportional to this rate.

relationships.reasoning: A larger population results in more deaths since deaths are calculated as a proportion of the existing population.
relationships.polarityReasoning: An increase in Population leads to an increase in Deaths because Deaths = Population * Fractional_Death_Rate, a direct multiplicative relationship.

relationships.reasoning: The fractional death rate determines what proportion of the population is lost to death each year.
relationships.polarityReasoning: An increase in the Fractional_Death_Rate leads to an increase in Deaths since Deaths is directly proportional to this rate.

relationships.reasoning: Births add new individuals directly into the population stock, increasing its size.
relationships.polarityReasoning: An increase in Births leads to an increase in Population since Births is an inflow that accumulates into the stock.

relationships.reasoning: Deaths remove individuals directly from the population stock, decreasing its size.
relationships.polarityReasoning: An increase in Deaths leads to a decrease in Population since Deaths is an outflow that depletes the stock.

variables.name: Population
variables.documentation: The stock of individuals in the population. It starts at 1000 individuals and changes only through births (inflow) and deaths (outflow). This represents the accumulation of people over time.

variables.name: Births
variables.documentation: The flow of new individuals added to the population each year, calculated as the current population multiplied by the fractional birth rate. Births are a one-directional process that cannot be negative, so uniflow is set to true.

variables.name: Deaths
variables.documentation: The flow of individuals removed from the population each year, calculated as the current population multiplied by the fractional death rate. Deaths are a one-directional process that cannot be negative, so uniflow is set to true.

variables.name: Fractional_Birth_Rate
variables.documentation: The constant fractional rate at which new individuals are born relative to the current population, set at 0.03 per year (3% annually).

variables.name: Fractional_Death_Rate
variables.documentation: The constant fractional rate at which individuals die relative to the current population, set at 0.015 per year (1.5% annually).

testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete, simulatable quantitative stock-and-flow model of savings account. additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how the balance of a savings account evolves as it earns interest and money is added and withdrawn.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A savings account has a single stock: its balance, in dollars. The balance grows through an inflow made up of interest earned plus regular deposits, and shrinks through an outflow of regular withdrawals. Interest earned each year equals the current balance multiplied by an annual interest rate. Use an initial balance of 5000 dollars, an annual interest rate of 0.03 per year, deposits of 2400 dollars per year, and withdrawals of 1200 dollars per year. Simulate from year 0 to year 30 with a time step of 0.25 years, using years as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how the balance of a savings account evolves as it earns interest and money is added and withdrawn.

supportingInfo.explanation:
The model is built, validated, and simulated successfully. Here's what's in place:

Structure

  • Balance (stock, dollars) — initial value 5000
    • Inflow: Total_Inflow = Interest_Earned + Deposits
    • Outflow: Withdrawals = 1200 dollars/year (constant)
  • Interest_Earned (auxiliary, dollars/year) = Balance × Interest_Rate
  • Interest_Rate (auxiliary, 1/year) = 0.03
  • Deposits (auxiliary, dollars/year) = 2400

Simulation specs: start 0, stop 30, dt 0.25, time units years — matches exactly what you specified.

Validation

  • get_current_model returned no errors or warnings.
  • Ran the simulation (runId eval-run-1): Balance grows monotonically from 5000 to about 70,311 dollars at year 30, never approaching zero (net inflow is always positive since interest + deposits of 2550/year initially exceeds the constant 1200/year withdrawal, and the gap widens as interest compounds on a growing balance). No negative-stock risk exists here — there's no first-order control needed because deposits and withdrawals are exogenous constants, not balance-dependent, and the growing interest term only pushes the balance up further.
  • Total_Inflow correctly tracks Interest_Earned + Deposits at every timestep, and Withdrawals stays flat at 1200 as specified.

The model runs cleanly end-to-end with no structural or unit issues.

What would you like to do next — inspect the feedback-loop structure behind this growth, run a sensitivity analysis on the interest rate or deposit/withdrawal levels, or visualize the balance trajectory?

relationships.reasoning: A larger balance generates more interest since interest is calculated as a fraction of the balance.
relationships.polarityReasoning: An increase in Balance leads to an increase in Interest Earned because they move in the same direction (both increase or both decrease together).

relationships.reasoning: A higher annual interest rate produces more interest earned on the same balance.
relationships.polarityReasoning: An increase in Interest Rate leads to an increase in Interest Earned, so they move together, which is positive polarity.

relationships.reasoning: Interest earned is one of the two components that make up the total inflow to the balance.
relationships.polarityReasoning: An increase in Interest Earned directly increases Total Inflow since Total Inflow is the sum of Interest Earned and Deposits.

relationships.reasoning: Deposits are the other component that makes up the total inflow to the balance.
relationships.polarityReasoning: An increase in Deposits directly increases Total Inflow since Total Inflow is the sum of Interest Earned and Deposits.

relationships.polarityReasoning: An increase in Total Inflow leads to an increase in Balance because inflows add to a stock, moving in the same direction.

relationships.reasoning: Withdrawals remove money from the balance each period, decreasing the stock.
relationships.polarityReasoning: An increase in Withdrawals leads to a decrease in Balance because outflows subtract from a stock, moving in opposite directions.

variables.name: Balance
variables.documentation: The savings account balance in dollars. It is the central accumulation in this model, increasing from interest earned and deposits, and decreasing from withdrawals. Modeled as a stock because it only changes through its inflow and outflow.

variables.name: Interest Rate
variables.documentation: The annual interest rate applied to the balance, expressed as a fraction per year. Held constant at 0.03 per year as specified.

variables.name: Interest Earned
variables.documentation: The dollar amount of interest generated each year, calculated as the current balance multiplied by the annual interest rate. This is an auxiliary calculation, not a stock, because it is simply the product of two other variables and does not accumulate on its own.

variables.name: Deposits
variables.documentation: The regular annual deposit amount added to the savings account, held constant at 2400 dollars per year.

variables.name: Total Inflow
variables.documentation: The combined inflow to the balance, summing interest earned and deposits. Marked as uniflow because under normal conditions (positive balance and rate) this represents money being added to the account and should not go negative.

variables.name: Withdrawals
variables.documentation: The regular annual withdrawal amount subtracted from the savings account, held constant at 1200 dollars per year. Marked as uniflow because withdrawals represent a one-directional removal of money and should not be negative.

testParams.name: Infectious Disease Spread simulates to completion
testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete, simulatable quantitative stock-and-flow model of infectious disease spread. Every stock must have a numeric initial value, every flow and auxiliary must have a well-defined equation, and the model must include simulation specifications (start time, stop time, time step, and time units) covering the full horizon described. The model must be able to run to completion in a system dynamics simulator without errors.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how an infectious disease moves through a fixed population during an outbreak.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Use the classic SIR structure with three stocks: susceptible people, infected people, and recovered people. Susceptible people become infected and flow into the infected stock; infected people recover and flow into the recovered stock. The infection rate equals the contact rate times the infectivity times the number of infected people times the fraction of the total population that is still susceptible (susceptible divided by total population). The recovery rate equals the infected population divided by the average duration of illness. Use a total population of 10000, with 9990 initially susceptible, 10 initially infected, and 0 recovered. Use a contact rate of 6 contacts per person per day, an infectivity of 0.05, and an average duration of illness of 5 days. Simulate from day 0 to day 100 with a time step of 0.5 days, using days as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how an infectious disease moves through a fixed population during an outbreak.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I built the classic SIR model exactly per your specification. Here's what was generated and validated.

Stocks (all with numeric initial values, units in people):

  • Susceptible_People = 9990
  • Infected_People = 10
  • Recovered_People = 0

Flows:

  • Infection_Rate (people/day) = Contact_Rate * Infectivity * Infected_People * (Susceptible_People / Total_Population) — outflow of Susceptible, inflow to Infected
  • Recovery_Rate (people/day) = Infected_People / Average_Duration_of_Illness — outflow of Infected, inflow to Recovered

Auxiliaries/constants:

  • Total_Population = 10000 (people)
  • Contact_Rate = 6 (contacts/person/day)
  • Infectivity = 0.05 (dimensionless)
  • Average_Duration_of_Illness = 5 (days)

Simulation specs: start = 0, stop = 100, dt = 0.5, time units = days, Euler integration.

Validation performed:

  • Reviewed the full variable list via read_model_section — no errors, no missing equations, no unit warnings reported by the engine.
  • Ran the simulation successfully (runId: eval-run-1).
  • Inspected Susceptible_People, Infected_People, Recovered_People time series numerically:
    • Susceptible declines monotonically from 9990 toward ~4263 by day 100, never negative.
    • Infected rises from 10, peaks near day 55–57 (~645 people), then declines toward ~78.5 by day 100 — never negative.
    • Recovered rises monotonically from 0 to ~5659 by day 100.
    • At every time point the three stocks sum to 10000, confirming population conservation (no leaks, no fabricated growth).
  • Behavior matches the expected SIR reference mode: an epidemic wave that grows, peaks, and burns out as the susceptible pool depletes, with no need for any negative-value clamping (the structural depletion of Susceptible_People naturally throttles Infection_Rate since it's proportional to susceptible fraction).

The model is complete, dimensionally sound per the engine, and runs cleanly end-to-end.

What would you like to do next — inspect feedback loop structure and dominance shifts over the outbreak, visualize the time series, run a sensitivity analysis on contact rate or infectivity, or something else?

relationships.reasoning: The number of susceptible people directly determines how many people are available to become infected.
relationships.polarityReasoning: As the susceptible pool increases (holding other factors constant), the pool of people who can become infected increases, raising the infection rate. Both move in the same direction, so the relationship is positive.

relationships.reasoning: The number of currently infected people determines how many potential transmission events can occur since infected people are the source of transmission.
relationships.polarityReasoning: More infected people means more opportunities to transmit the disease to susceptibles, increasing the infection rate. Both move in the same direction, so the relationship is positive.

relationships.reasoning: Total Population appears in the denominator when calculating the fraction of the population that is susceptible, so it dilutes the infection rate.
relationships.polarityReasoning: Holding the number of susceptible people constant, a larger total population reduces the susceptible fraction, which decreases the infection rate. This is an inverse relationship, so the polarity is negative.

relationships.reasoning: The contact rate is a direct multiplicative factor in the infection rate equation, representing how many contacts occur per person per day.
relationships.polarityReasoning: An increase in the number of contacts per person increases the number of opportunities for transmission, increasing the infection rate. Both move in the same direction, so the relationship is positive.

relationships.reasoning: Infectivity is a direct multiplicative factor in the infection rate equation, representing the probability that a contact results in transmission.
relationships.polarityReasoning: A higher infectivity means a greater fraction of contacts result in transmission, increasing the infection rate. Both move in the same direction, so the relationship is positive.

relationships.reasoning: The Infection Rate is the outflow from the Susceptible People stock, so it depletes the susceptible population as people become infected.
relationships.polarityReasoning: An increase in the infection rate causes a faster depletion of the susceptible stock, so susceptible people decreases as the outflow increases. This is an inverse relationship, so the polarity is negative.

relationships.reasoning: The Infection Rate is the inflow to the Infected People stock, so it directly increases the infected population as people transition from susceptible to infected.
relationships.polarityReasoning: An increase in the infection rate directly adds more people to the infected stock, so both move in the same direction. The polarity is positive.

relationships.reasoning: The number of infected people directly determines how many people are available to recover, since the recovery rate is calculated as infected people divided by the average duration of illness.

variables.name: Susceptible_People
variables.documentation: Initial pool of people who can become infected. Starts at 9990 out of a total population of 10000, with 10 already infected.

variables.name: Infected_People
variables.documentation: People currently infected and infectious. Increases via the Infection Rate as susceptibles become infected, and decreases via the Recovery Rate as infected individuals recover.

variables.name: Recovered_People
variables.documentation: People who have recovered from the illness and are assumed immune, accumulated from the Recovery Rate.

variables.name: Infection_Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which susceptible people become infected. Depends on the number of contacts each person has per day, the probability a contact results in transmission (infectivity), the number of currently infected people who can transmit the disease, and the fraction of the population that is still susceptible. This is the classic mass-action mixing formulation used in SIR models. Marked as uniflow since new infections cannot be negative.

variables.name: Recovery_Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which infected people recover, calculated as the infected population divided by the average duration of illness (implying an exponential recovery process with mean duration equal to Average Duration of Illness). variables.name: Total_Population
variables.documentation: Fixed total population size, equal to the sum of the initial values of Susceptible, Infected, and Recovered People. Used to normalize the susceptible fraction in the infection rate calculation. Held constant since no births, deaths, or migration are modeled.

variables.name: Contact_Rate
variables.documentation: Average number of contacts each person has per day. A key driver of how quickly the disease can spread through the population.

variables.name: Infectivity
variables.documentation: The probability that a contact between a susceptible and an infected person results in transmission of the disease. A dimensionless fraction between 0 and 1.

variables.name: Average_Duration_of_Illness
variables.documentation: The average number of days a person remains infected before recovering. Used to calculate the recovery rate as Infected People divided by this duration, representing an exponential recovery process.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how a store's inventory responds when it continuously reorders stock toward a target level.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A store holds a single stock of inventory, in units. Inventory rises through a production/delivery inflow and falls through a shipment outflow. Shipments equal customer demand, which is a constant 100 units per week. The store wants to keep inventory at a desired level equal to a target coverage of expected sales: desired inventory equals demand multiplied by a desired coverage of 4 weeks. The production rate equals demand plus a correction that closes the gap between desired inventory and current inventory over an inventory adjustment time of 8 weeks (that is, production equals demand plus (desired inventory minus inventory) divided by the adjustment time). Start with an initial inventory of 200 units, which is below the desired level, so the correction loop is active. Simulate from week 0 to week 52 with a time step of 0.25 weeks, using weeks as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how a store's inventory responds when it continuously reorders stock toward a target level.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Now let me verify the actual built model.

Model matches spec exactly, no errors/warnings reported. Structural check: Inventory stock, Production/Shipments flows, all auxiliaries correctly defined with named constants (no embedded hard-coded numbers in equations). Let's run it and inspect behavior.

Model behaves exactly as expected: Inventory rises smoothly and monotonically from 200 units toward the desired level of 400 units (Demand 100 × Desired Coverage 4), asymptotically closing the gap via first-order exponential adjustment, reaching ~399.7 by week 52. Shipments stay constant at 100 (=Demand), Production starts at 125 (100 + (400-200)/8) and decays back toward 100 as the gap closes. No negative values, no oscillation — consistent with a single balancing (goal-seeking) loop with adjustment time 8 weeks.

Summary

Model built (SFD, weeks 0–52, dt=0.25, Weeks):

Variable Type Equation Units
Inventory stock init 200 units
Production inflow Demand + (Desired_Inventory − Inventory) / Inventory_Adjustment_Time units/Week
Shipments outflow Demand units/Week
Demand constant 100 units/Week
Desired_Inventory auxiliary Demand × Desired_Coverage units
Desired_Coverage constant 4 Weeks
Inventory_Adjustment_Time constant 8 Weeks

Validation:

  • get_current_model shows no errors or unit warnings; every stock/flow/auxiliary has an equation, units, and documentation.
  • No hard-coded constants sit inside equations — Demand, Desired_Coverage, and Inventory_Adjustment_Time are all named variables.
  • Ran to completion (0–52 weeks, dt 0.25) without error.
  • Extreme-condition/behavior check: Inventory starts at 200 (below the 400-unit desired level), rises monotonically and smoothly toward 400 with no overshoot, oscillation, or negative excursions — consistent with a single first-order balancing correction loop with an 8-week adjustment time. Shipments stay pinned at Demand (100) throughout; Production starts elevated (125) and relaxes back to 100 as the gap closes. Conservation holds: all inflow to Inventory comes only from Production, all outflow only from Shipments.

The model has earned structural and behavioral credibility for this simple goal-seeking replenishment structure.

Next steps — let me know if you'd like to visualize Inventory vs. Desired_Inventory over time, inspect the feedback loop structure (via Loops That Matter), test sensitivity to the adjustment time or desired coverage, or extend the model (e.g., add backlog/stockouts, delivery delay, or demand variability).

variables.name: Inventory
variables.documentation: The store's accumulated stock of units on hand. It rises with Production (inflow) and falls with Shipments (outflow). Initialized below the desired level (200 vs 400) to illustrate how the system corrects a gap over time.

variables.name: Production
variables.documentation: Production/delivery inflow to inventory. Set equal to Demand plus a correction term that closes the gap between Desired Inventory and actual Inventory over the Inventory Adjustment Time. variables.name: Shipments

variables.name: Demand
variables.documentation: Constant customer demand rate of 100 units per week. Drives both Shipments (directly) and Desired Inventory (via Desired Coverage), and is also the baseline term in the Production equation.

variables.name: Desired Inventory
variables.documentation: Target inventory level the store aims to hold, calculated as Demand multiplied by Desired Coverage (in weeks of supply). This target is used by Production to determine how much extra to produce/order when actual Inventory is below or above this goal.

variables.name: Desired Coverage
variables.documentation: Constant policy parameter specifying how many weeks of demand the store wants to hold in inventory as a buffer. Multiplied by Demand to compute Desired Inventory.

variables.name: Inventory Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: Constant time parameter representing how quickly the store attempts to close the gap between Desired Inventory and actual Inventory through adjustments to Production. A longer adjustment time means slower correction of inventory imbalances.

testParams.name: Predator-Prey Dynamics simulates to completion
testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete, simulatable quantitative stock-and-flow model of predator-prey dynamics. Every stock must have a numeric initial value, every flow and auxiliary must have a well-defined equation, and the model must include simulation specifications (start time, stop time, time step, and time units) covering the full horizon described. The model must be able to run to completion in a system dynamics simulator without errors.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how the populations of a predator and its prey rise and fall together over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Use the classic Lotka-Volterra structure with two stocks: a prey population and a predator population. The prey population grows through prey births and shrinks through prey deaths caused by predation. Prey births equal a prey birth rate coefficient times the prey population. Prey deaths equal a predation coefficient times the prey population times the predator population. The predator population grows through predator births and shrinks through predator deaths. Predator births equal a predator efficiency coefficient times the prey population times the predator population. Predator deaths equal a predator death rate coefficient times the predator population. Use an initial prey population of 100 and an initial predator population of 20. Use a prey birth rate coefficient of 0.5, a predation coefficient of 0.02, a predator efficiency coefficient of 0.01, and a predator death rate coefficient of 0.4 (all per appropriate time unit). Because this system oscillates, use a small time step for numerical stability: simulate from time 0 to time 50 with a time step of 0.03125, using months as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how the populations of a predator and its prey rise and fall together over time.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model matches spec exactly: variable names, initial values, equations, units, and simulation specs (0–50 months, dt=0.03125, Euler) all correct. No errors/warnings surfaced. Stocks are structurally protected from going negative — Prey_Population and Predator_Population are net-nonlinear stocks whose outflows (Prey_Deaths, Predator_Deaths) scale down naturally as population approaches zero (no clamping needed, consistent with the specified formulation). Now let's run it to confirm behavior.

The model is built and validated. Summary:

Structure (stock-and-flow, exact names as specified):

  • Stocks: Prey_Population (initial 100, units: animals), Predator_Population (initial 20, units: animals)
  • Flows: Prey_Births = prey_birth_rate_coefficient × Prey_Population; Prey_Deaths = predation_coefficient × Prey_Population × Predator_Population; Predator_Births = predator_efficiency_coefficient × Prey_Population × Predator_Population; Predator_Deaths = predator_death_rate_coefficient × Predator_Population. All flows are uniflows (non-negative), consistent with births/deaths never running backward.
  • Parameters: prey_birth_rate_coefficient = 0.5/month, predation_coefficient = 0.02 1/(animals·month), predator_efficiency_coefficient = 0.01 1/(animals·month), predator_death_rate_coefficient = 0.4/month.
  • Sim specs: start 0, stop 50, dt = 0.03125, units = months, Euler integration.

Validation:

  • get_current_model showed no errors or warnings; no unit-consistency issues were reported by the engine.
  • Ran the model (eval-run-1) and inspected Prey_Population and Predator_Population time series directly: both oscillate with the expected phase lag (predator peaks trail prey peaks), amplitude grows somewhat over the 50-month horizon (typical of Euler-integrated Lotka-Volterra with this dt), and neither stock goes negative at any point — consistent with the fact that outflows are proportional to the stock itself (or its product with the other stock), so both naturally approach but don't cross zero.
  • No hard-coded arbitrary constants in equations — all four coefficients are named variables, and the only literal numbers appearing are the two stocks' initial values (100 and 20), which are the specified initial conditions, not embedded constants.

The model runs cleanly end-to-end with no structural fixes needed. Since it's a textbook Lotka-Volterra formulation, the stocks are guaranteed non-negative by construction (multiplicative outflows), so no additional first-order control structure was needed beyond what's already there.

What would you like to do next — visualize the prey/predator time series, examine feedback loop dominance (LTM), or explore parameter sensitivity?

testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete, simulatable quantitative stock-and-flow model of software project rework. Every stock must have a numeric initial value, every flow and auxiliary must have a well-defined equation, and the model must include simulation specifications (start time, stop time, time step, and time units) covering the full horizon described. additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand why a software project takes longer than planned once undiscovered rework is taken into account.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Model a fixed-scope software project with three stocks, all measured in tasks: work to be done, undiscovered rework, and work truly done. The team completes tasks at a work rate that flows out of work to be done. The work rate equals the number of developers times their productivity. A fraction of completed work is done correctly and flows into work truly done; the remaining fraction contains defects and flows into undiscovered rework instead. Undiscovered rework is not visible immediately: it is detected and flows back into work to be done at a rework discovery rate equal to the undiscovered rework stock divided by an average discovery delay. Use an initial work to be done of 500 tasks, an initial undiscovered rework of 0 tasks, and an initial work truly done of 0 tasks. Use 10 developers, a productivity of 0.4 tasks per developer per week, a fraction correct of 0.85 (so 0.15 of completed work becomes undiscovered rework), and an average discovery delay of 4 weeks. To avoid completed work continuing to be generated once the backlog is empty, the work rate should not exceed the amount of work remaining to be done. Simulate from week 0 to week 200 with a time step of 0.25 weeks, using weeks as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand why a software project takes longer than planned once undiscovered rework is taken into account.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model structure and specs check out — all matches the spec. Now let's check for errors/warnings via get_current_model and confirm no unit warnings.

No errors or warnings reported. The model structure is exactly as specified — three stocks (Work_To_Be_Done, Undiscovered_Rework, Work_Truly_Done), four flows, four parameters, all in tasks/weeks as required. Now let's run it to verify behavior.

Good, equation updated. Now let's run the model and verify.

The model itself is built correctly, but the simulation run is consistently failing to produce output (three attempts, all returning empty data with run IDs literally named "eval-run-failed-1/2/3"). I won't fabricate results. Here's an honest status report:

Model built — structure confirmed correct

Stocks (all in tasks):

  • Work_To_Be_Done — initial 500, inflow: Rework Discovery Rate, outflow: Work Rate
  • Undiscovered_Rework — initial 0, inflow: Defective Work Rate, outflow: Rework Discovery Rate
  • Work_Truly_Done — initial 0, inflow: Correct Work Rate

Flows:

  • Work_Rate = MIN(Developers*Productivity, Work_To_Be_Done/TIME STEP) — tasks/week
  • Correct_Work_Rate = Work_Rate * Fraction_Correct — tasks/week
  • Defective_Work_Rate = Work_Rate * (1 - Fraction_Correct) — tasks/week
  • Rework_Discovery_Rate = Undiscovered_Rework / Average_Discovery_Delay — tasks/week

Parameters: Developers=10 (developers), Productivity=0.4 (tasks/developer/week), Fraction_Correct=0.85 (dimensionless), Average_Discovery_Delay=4 (weeks)

Specs: start=0, stop=200, dt=0.25, units=weeks, Euler integration.

get_current_model reports no errors and no unit warnings on this structure — it matches your specification exactly, and I corrected an initial equation issue (an undefined dt reference in the Work Rate cap) by switching to the proper XMILE TIME STEP builtin.

Simulation issue — unresolved

I called run_model three times. Each time it reports success: true but returns a run (eval-run-failed-1, -2, -3) with zero variables — get_variable_data for the stocks and Work_Rate comes back empty every time. I have not been able to produce an actual simulated time series, so I cannot yet confirm the model's dynamic behavior (e.g., that Work_Rate correctly tapers as the backlog is exhausted, or that Work_Truly_Done asymptotes above 500 tasks due to rework).

variables.name: Work_To_Be_Done
variables.documentation: Represents the total backlog of tasks that still need to be completed for the fixed-scope project. It starts at 500 tasks and is drawn down by the Work Rate (developers completing tasks) but replenished by the Rework Discovery Rate (previously completed defective work that must be redone). This stock captures why the project can take longer than planned: even as developers work, discovered rework flows back in, keeping the backlog from shrinking as fast as expected.

variables.name: Undiscovered_Rework
variables.documentation: Represents the hidden pool of defective work that has been completed but not yet identified as needing rework. It grows via the Defective Work Rate (the fraction of completed work that is faulty) and shrinks via the Rework Discovery Rate (the rate at which this hidden defective work is found and sent back to Work To Be Done). This stock is the core of the 'invisible backlog' that causes schedule slippage in software projects.

variables.name: Work_Truly_Done
variables.documentation: Represents the cumulative amount of work that has been completed correctly and will never need to be redone. It only increases via the Correct Work Rate, the fraction of total Work Rate that is done correctly. This is the true measure of project completion, distinct from work that merely appears finished but may still contain undiscovered defects.

variables.name: Developers
variables.documentation: The fixed number of developers assigned to the project. This determines the raw capacity for completing tasks each week, combined with individual Productivity to determine the Work Rate.

variables.name: Productivity
variables.documentation: The average number of tasks a single developer can complete per week, whether the task is done correctly or not. Multiplied by Developers to determine the maximum potential Work Rate.

variables.name: Fraction_Correct
variables.documentation: The fraction of completed work (Work Rate) that is done correctly and will not require rework. The remaining fraction (1 - Fraction Correct) becomes undiscovered defective work. This parameter drives the split between Correct Work Rate and Defective Work Rate.

variables.name: Average_Discovery_Delay
variables.documentation: The average time it takes for defective work sitting in Undiscovered Rework to be discovered (e.g., through testing, review, or usage) and sent back into the Work To Be Done backlog for correction. A longer delay means defects linger longer before being caught, extending the overall project timeline.

variables.name: Work_Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which developers complete tasks, whether correct or defective, determined by Developers multiplied by Productivity. This rate is capped so it cannot draw Work To Be Done below zero within a single time step, using the built-in XMILE TIME STEP keyword (the simulation time step) as the limiting divisor rather than a hardcoded constant or a custom variable. This flow depletes Work To Be Done and feeds into both Correct Work Rate and Defective Work Rate.

variables.name: Correct_Work_Rate
variables.documentation: The portion of Work Rate that is completed correctly, calculated by multiplying Work Rate by Fraction Correct. This flow feeds into Work Truly Done, representing genuine, permanent project progress.

variables.name: Defective_Work_Rate
variables.documentation: The portion of Work Rate that is completed with defects, calculated as Work Rate multiplied by the complement of Fraction Correct (1 - Fraction Correct). This flow feeds into Undiscovered Rework, representing work that appears done but will later need to be redone once discovered.

variables.name: Rework_Discovery_Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which hidden defective work is discovered and sent back to the Work To Be Done backlog for correction, calculated as Undiscovered Rework divided by the Average Discovery Delay. This flow is central to explaining schedule overruns: it depletes Undiscovered Rework but replenishes Work To Be Done, effectively adding extra work that was not visible in the original plan.

I've created this non-modular model simulating a predator-prey ecosystem.
            Please recreate the system with two modules.

            Use the following module names exactly:
            hare, lynx

            Component naming instructions:
            - Specifically rename "Hares" to "hare.hares", "area" to "hare.area", and "Lynx" to "lynx.lynx".
            - Otherwise, name components within each module by removing the animal prefix, and changing nothing else.
              For instance, 'hares killed per lynx' should be renamed to 'hare.killed_per_lynx', 
              and 'lynx births' should be renamed to 'lynx.births'.
            - Preserve the names of components that are not placed in modules.
            - When ghosting, preserve the original name of the ghosted component, including the module name if appropriate.
              For example, to create a ghost of "lynx.births" in the "hare" module, name the ghost component "hare.lynx births".
              To create a ghost of "lynx.lynx" in the "hare" module, name the ghost component "hare.lynx",
            Any other naming convention is unacceptable and will cause issues in my simulation.

            Try to preserve the key causal relationships and processes exactly, adding as few additional variables as possible
            and only when strictly necessary.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Now updating the two equations to route through the ghosts instead of directly across modules:

Now rebuilding the relationships to use the new module-qualified names and route cross-module links through the ghosts:

Now validating the full model:

The predator-prey model has been rebuilt as a two-module system. Here's a summary of what was done and the resulting structure.

Modules created: hare, lynx (both top-level, no nesting)

Renaming applied (equations auto-rewritten by the rename operation):

Original New name Module
area hare.area hare
Hares hare.hares hare
hare_births hare.births hare
hare_deaths hare.deaths hare
hare_density hare.density hare
hare_birth_fraction hare.birth_fraction hare
hares_killed_per_lynx hare.killed_per_lynx hare
Lynx lynx.lynx lynx
lynx_births lynx.births lynx
lynx_deaths lynx.deaths lynx
lynx_birth_fraction lynx.birth_fraction lynx
lynx_death_fraction lynx.death_fraction lynx

Cross-module links required two ghosts (the only new components added, since the two stocks each drive a process in the other module):

  • hare.lynx — ghost of lynx.lynx, used in hare.deaths = hare.lynx * hare.killed_per_lynx
  • lynx.hare_density — ghost of hare.density, used in lynx.death_fraction's graphical function (input: hare density)

All other equations and the two graphical functions (hare kills-per-lynx vs. density, lynx death fraction vs. density) are untouched — only names changed. Relationships were rebuilt to match the new names, with the two cross-module arrows now routed through their respective ghosts (lynx.lynx → hare.lynx → hare.deaths, and hare.density → lynx.hare_density → lynx.death_fraction).

get_current_model reports no errors or warnings after these changes — the module split preserved dimensional consistency and structure.

Note on simulation: I ran the model, but get_variable_data returned no data for this run (even for a constant like hare.area), which appears to be an environment/tooling issue in this session rather than a model defect — the model validated cleanly and the equations are structurally identical to the original, just re-scoped into modules. I was not able to independently confirm time-series behavior (e.g., non-negativity of the stocks) beyond the pre-existing formulation, which itself was unchanged.

What would you like to do next — retry the simulation, or something else?

Now cleaning up the relationships to use flat names, dropping the stale qualified/self-loop entries and re-adding the causal links that the cross-module ghosts used to carry:

Now let's validate the full model — check for errors/warnings, then run the simulation and inspect stock behavior.

Structure is clean, all 16 causal links preserved with correct flat names and no module prefixes. Modules array is empty. Let me confirm variable definitions one final time before reporting.

The de-modularization is complete and structurally valid. Here's the summary:

What changed

I removed the Hares and Lynx module boundaries and flattened all 12 variables per your naming rule (strip the module prefix, change nothing else):

Original (modular) Flattened
Hares.Hares Hares (stock)
Hares.hare_births hare_births (flow)
Hares.hare_deaths hare_deaths (flow)
Hares.hare_density hare_density
Hares.hare_birth_fraction hare_birth_fraction
Hares.area area
Hares.hares_killed_per_lynx hares_killed_per_lynx
Lynx.Lynx Lynx (stock)
Lynx.lynx_births lynx_births (flow)
Lynx.lynx_deaths lynx_deaths (flow)
Lynx.lynx_birth_fraction lynx_birth_fraction
Lynx.lynx_death_fraction lynx_death_fraction

Two variables removed — these had no modular equivalent worth preserving standalone; they were cross-module ghost placeholders that only existed to pipe a value across the module boundary:

  • Hares.Lynx (a ghost of Lynx.Lynx, used only so hare_deaths could reference the lynx population from inside the Hares module)
  • Lynx.hare_density (a ghost of Hares.hare_density, used only so lynx_death_fraction could reference hare density from inside the Lynx module)

Since both real variables (Lynx the stock, hare_density) now live in the same flat namespace, hare_deaths and lynx_death_fraction reference them directly — no equation text needed to change, since the ghosts shared the same base names as the real variables.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Now update the Lynx stock to add the new predation outflow, and add the required relationship arrows.

Now let's validate the model — check for errors/warnings and inspect the full structure.

Structure looks correct. No errors or warnings surfaced. Now let's run the simulation and check the stocks for negative values / plausible behavior.

New "Cougars" module added. Summary of what was actually built (verified via get_current_model / read_model_section):

Cougars module (new)

  • Cougars (stock) — initial value 50 cougars; inflow cougar births, outflow cougar deaths
  • cougar_births (flow) = Cougars * cougar_birth_fraction
  • cougar_deaths (flow) = Cougars * cougar_death_fraction — this is the only death process for cougars, consistent with them being an apex predator with no hunter of their own
  • cougar_birth_fraction = 0.1/year (constant)
  • cougar_death_fraction — graphical function of lynx density (ghosted from Lynx module): low lynx density → high cougar starvation/death fraction, same structural pattern as Lynx.lynx_death_fraction vs. hare density
  • cougar_density = Cougars / area
  • area — ghost of Hares.area (same 1000-acre ecosystem)
  • lynx_density — ghost of the new Lynx.lynx_density

Lynx module (extended, existing hare/lynx structure untouched)

  • Added lynx_density = Lynx / area (new area ghost of Hares.area added to this module)
  • Added lynx_killed_per_cougar — graphical function of lynx_density, mirroring the hares_killed_per_lynx pattern (0 kills at 0 density, saturating at high density)
  • Added Cougars ghost (of Cougars.Cougars)
  • Added a second outflow on the Lynx stock, lynx_deaths_by_cougars = Cougars * lynx_killed_per_cougar, alongside the pre-existing lynx_deaths (density-dependent starvation) outflow

I did not touch Hares.*, Lynx.lynx_deaths, Lynx.lynx_death_fraction, or any hare↔lynx relationship — cougars have no direct link to hares, as specified.

  • get_current_model shows no errors or warnings after these edits.

I've created this modular model simulating the urban dynamics in a city.
            However, I no longer need to simulate commerce dynamics. Please remove the 'Commerce' module from my model.

            Please do not add any variables or modify any processes or relationships unrelated to commerce.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Now update the migration equation to drop the jobs-attractiveness term (which no longer exists) and rely on housing attractiveness alone:

Clean. All Commerce variables and their relationships are gone, and the remaining Population and Housing modules are intact and self-consistent. Now let's run the model to confirm behavior remains valid.

No leftover references. Model structure looks clean. Let's retry running the model to rule out a transient issue.

Commerce module removed

What I did:

  1. Deleted the entire Commerce module — all 11 variables: Business_Structures (stock), its flows business_starts/business_closures, and supporting variables base_start_fraction, closure_fraction, target_labor_per_business, relative_labor_availability, start_multiplier, jobs_per_structure, total_jobs, plus its cross-level ghost of Population.Population. Removing these variables automatically cleared all causal relationships attached to them.

  2. Cleaned up the one cross-module dependency. Population.relative_job_availability (and its downstream attractiveness_from_jobs, and the target_jobs_per_person parameter and total_jobs ghost that fed it) existed only to pull Commerce.total_jobs into the migration calculation. Since their sole purpose was piping in a Commerce output, I removed them along with the Commerce module rather than leaving dangling references.

  3. Adjusted Population.migration's equation from Population*base_migration_fraction*((attractiveness_from_housing+attractiveness_from_jobs)/2) to Population*base_migration_fraction*attractiveness_from_housing so migration is now driven by housing attractiveness alone. This is the minimal change needed to keep the equation dimensionally and structurally valid once the jobs-availability term no longer exists — I did not touch anything else in the Housing or Population modules, nor any of their other processes (births, deaths, construction, demolition, housing-driven migration all remain exactly as they were).

Resulting model: two modules — Population (stock: Population; flows: births, deaths, migration) and Housing (stock: Housing_Stock; flows: construction, demolition) — linked only via their existing cross-level ghosts of each other's stocks. No orphaned equations or references to Commerce remain (verified via a full variable/relationship scan).

Validation status: edit_variables/edit_relationships reported no errors or warnings after each edit, and a fresh scan of all variables and relationships shows no dangling references to any removed Commerce or jobs-related variable. I did attempt to run the simulation to reconfirm numeric behavior, but the run returned no time-series data in this session (empty result for both attempts) — so I can't show you fresh output values right now. The structural/equation validation is clean, but if you want the behavioral check (housing-driven migration dynamics, stock trajectories) confirmed numerically, let me know and I'll retry the run.

What would you like to do next — retry the simulation, inspect the updated model structure, or something else?

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.


            At a certain business, employees are sorted in a three-role hierarchy.
            New hirees start with the "rookie" status.
            Rookies that perform well are promoted to associates.
            Associates that perform well are promoted to partners.
            To keep the hierarchy stable, the business promotes a strict percentage of each role every year.
            Some employees may also leave the company, whether due to personal reasons or exceptionally poor performance.
            A stable percentage of employees at each level of the company leave the company each year.
            The business also onboards a constant number of new hirees every year.

            Use the following component names as appropriate:
            rookies, associates, partners, promotion_rate, departure_rate, hire_rate,
            rookie_promotions, associate_promotions, rookie_hires,
            rookie_departures, associate_departures, partner_departures

            Do not create any modules in this model.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Now let's inspect the actual model built.

The model matches the spec exactly: no modules, correct component names, sensible equations. Structure looks correct — all stocks have first-order proportional outflows (safe from going negative), no hard-coded arbitrary constants embedded in equations (rates are separate named variables). Let's check for errors/warnings via get_current_model's full output (it only returned a message above, likely because content was too large — but no errors/warnings field was shown, which usually means none). Let me confirm by checking again, and then run the model.

The model is built, validated, and simulated. Here's what's actually there:

Structure (3 stocks, 6 flows, 3 constants — no modules, as specified):

  • Stocks: rookies (init 50), associates (init 30), partners (init 10) — all in units of people
  • Flows:
    • rookie_hires = hire_rate → inflow to rookies
    • rookie_promotions = rookies * promotion_rate → outflow from rookies, inflow to associates
    • associate_promotions = associates * promotion_rate → outflow from associates, inflow to partners
    • rookie_departures = rookies * departure_rate → outflow from rookies
    • associate_departures = associates * departure_rate → outflow from associates
    • partner_departures = partners * departure_rate → outflow from partners
  • Constants: hire_rate = 20 people/year, promotion_rate = 0.2 fraction/year, departure_rate = 0.1 fraction/year — applied uniformly at every role, matching the "strict/stable percentage at each level" language in the background

All flows are marked uniflow (can't go negative), and every stock has a first-order proportional outflow, so none of the three stocks can go negative regardless of parameter values. No unit warnings or errors were reported by the engine, and no arbitrary numeric constants are embedded directly in equations — every parameter is a named variable.

Simulation check (50 years, dt=0.25): Starting from (50, 30, 10), the system settles into equilibrium: rookies → 66.67, associates → 44.44, partners → 88.89 (partners keep accumulating longest since they have no promotion outflow, only the departure drain). At equilibrium, total departures (6.67 + 4.44 + 8.89 = 20) exactly balance hire_rate = 20, confirming the headcount conserves correctly and the hierarchy reaches a stable size rather than growing or collapsing — consistent with the reference mode implied by "keep the hierarchy stable."

Model has passed structural review (no negative-stock risk, no hardcoded constants, dimensionally sound per the engine) and behavioral review (smooth convergence to a self-consistent equilibrium, conservation of headcount holds).

What would you like to do next — adjust the rate assumptions, inspect feedback-loop dominance behind this convergence, or something else?

supportingInfo.explanation:
I've built the quantitative model per the exact background information and component list. Here is what was actually generated (verified via get_current_model/read_model_section, not assumed):

Stocks

  • chicken_count (chickens) — initial value 1000. Inflow: chicken_reproduction. Outflow: chicken_predation.
  • fox_count (foxes) — initial value 20. Inflow: fox_reproduction. No outflow (the background gives no fox death or attrition mechanism, so none was added).

Flows

  • chicken_reproduction = chicken_count * chicken_reproductionRate (chickens/day), uniflow (births only).
  • chicken_predation = fox_count * chicken_predationRate (chickens/day), uniflow (consumption only).
  • fox_reproduction = fox_count * fox_reproductionRate (foxes/day), uniflow (births only).

Auxiliaries

  • chicken_reproductionRate = 0.1 (1/day)
  • fox_reproductionRate = 0.03 (1/day) — set slower than the chicken rate, per the background.
  • chicken_predationRate = 1 (chickens/fox/day) — this one variable was added beyond your list, solely to avoid hard-coding the "one chicken per fox per day" literal directly into the chicken_predation equation.

No modules were created. get_current_model reports no errors and no unit warnings.

Simulation check (365 days, dt = 0.125): Both chicken_count and fox_count grow monotonically and explosively over the run — chickens go from 1,000 to roughly 4×10^15, foxes from 20 to roughly 1.1×10^6 — with no decline in either population at any point.

Critique:

  • Structural: This is the literal, minimal reading of your background — chickens only reproduce and get eaten, foxes only reproduce and eat. Because there is no fox death/mortality term and no carrying-capacity limit on chicken reproduction, nothing in the stated mechanisms can ever push either population down. The result is unbounded exponential growth of both stocks rather than a bounded oscillation. If a cyclical predator-prey pattern (the classic reference mode) is what you expect to see, the background as given doesn't supply the mechanism for it (e.g., a fox death rate, or a chicken carrying capacity) — I have not added one since it wasn't specified.
  • Behavioral/conservation: In this parameter regime, chicken_count stays far larger than fox_count throughout, so chicken_predation never approaches chicken_count's available stock and it never goes negative. However, structurally, chicken_predation is not limited by chicken availability — if fox_count ever grew large enough relative to chicken_count, chicken_count could be driven negative, since predation is not clamped by the food supply. This is a latent structural risk under other parameter values, worth flagging even though it didn't manifest in this run.

What would you like to do next — adjust parameters, add a mortality/limiting mechanism, or proceed as-is to further analysis (e.g., sensitivity testing)?

Model Built: Fox–Chicken Predator-Prey (SFD, two modules)

Modules: chickens, foxes — exactly as specified, no additional modules.

chickens module

Component Type Equation Units Notes
count stock init = 1000 chickens Prey stock, initialized far larger than foxes per background
reproduction rate variable 0.10 1/day Steady fractional growth rate
reproduction flow (inflow, uniflow) count * reproduction_rate chickens/day Births proportional to current population
predation rate variable 1 chickens/fox/day Named constant for "one chicken per fox per day"
predation flow (outflow, uniflow) chickens_foxes_count * predation_rate chickens/day Chickens removed by fox consumption
chickens foxes count ghost = foxes.count foxes Ghost of foxes.count, imported so predation can reference fox population without direct cross-module coupling

foxes module

Component Type Equation Units Notes
count stock init = 20 foxes Predator stock, initialized far smaller than chickens
reproduction rate variable 0.03 1/day Slower than chickens' rate, per background
reproduction flow (inflow, uniflow) count * reproduction_rate foxes/day Births proportional to fox population; foxes grow only via reproduction, not via predation success (background specifies a steady reproduction rate independent of feeding)

No unit warnings were reported by the engine, and no bare numeric constants appear inside multi-term equations — reproduction_rate and predation_rate are named parameters rather than hardcoded numbers.

Structural critique (before trusting this model)

  • Loop structure: chickens grow chickens (self-reinforcing), foxes deplete chickens (chickens→foxes coupling via the ghost), and foxes grow foxes (self-reinforcing). I have not called the feedback-loop tool yet, so I'm not characterizing loop polarity or dominance here — that requires a successful run first.
  • Extreme-condition risk: predation is driven only by fox count and the fixed per-fox consumption rate — it is not scaled by chicken availability. This faithfully implements the literal background statement ("each fox eats one chicken per day"), but it means if the fox population is ever large relative to the chicken population, chickens.count could be driven below zero, which is physically impossible for a population stock. I did not add a MIN/MAX clamp (per guidance to fix structure, not mask it), and I did not deviate from the explicit background formulation either — flagging this as an open validity question for you rather than silently altering the specified mechanism.
  • Conservation: there is no shared mass/energy conservation constraint between the two populations (this is a pure count-based Lotka-Volterra formulation, not a biomass-conservation model) — consistent with the background, which describes counts, not biomass.

Simulation status — could not verify behavior

I ran the model (mcp__builtin__run_model) twice and both times the run reported success but returned no time-series data for chickens.count/foxes.count (get_variable_data came back empty, and get_run_info shows the runs with variables: []). Per the data-inspection rule, I will not claim or describe any simulated behavior (growth, oscillation, extremes) since I have not actually seen numbers — that would be fabrication. I also have not called the feedback-information tool, since it depends on a completed run with real output, so I'm making no claims about loop dominance or causal mechanisms behind behavior at this time.

Next steps, your call:

  1. Retry the run (may be a transient issue) so we can inspect actual chickens.count/foxes.count trajectories and confirm reference-mode fit (oscillatory or damped predator-prey cycles) and non-negativity.
  2. Once a run produces data, I can pull feedback-loop information and walk through the causal mechanisms driving the oscillation.
  3. Decide whether the "chickens can go structurally negative under extreme fox dominance" issue is acceptable for this exercise or whether you want the predation formulation revisited.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model Summary: Population–Resource Depletion (SFD, 2 modules)

I built the model exactly to spec, validated it via get_current_model, read_model_section, and get_feedback_information. No errors or unit warnings were reported by the engine.

Module: population

Variable Type Equation Units
count stock init = 1000; in: births; out: deaths, migrations people
birth rate constant 0.03 1/year
births flow count * birth rate people/year
death rate constant 0.02 1/year
deaths flow count * death rate people/year
density threshold constant 5 resource units/person
resource density (ghost of resource.density) ghost = resource.density resource units/person
migrations flow (outflow) count * MAX(0, density threshold − resource density) people/year

Module: resource

Variable Type Equation Units
count stock init = 100000; out: usage (no inflow — nonrenewable) resource units
usage rate constant 0.01 1/year
population count (ghost of population.count) ghost = population.count people
usage flow population count * usage rate resource units/year
density variable count / population count resource units/person

Migrations is computed directly from count and the ghosted resource density, with no intermediate variable — the MAX(0, ...) clip is a structural boundary condition (zero migration once density is at/above threshold), not a hidden constant. Ghosts follow the specified naming convention: resource.density ghosted into population as resource density; population.count ghosted into resource as population count.

  • get_current_model reports no errors, no warnings, and no unitWarnings — the engine finds the equations dimensionally consistent as written.
  • get_feedback_information (called this turn) returns exactly three loops, all local to the population module:

    • L2 (balancing): count → deaths → count
    • L3 (balancing): count → migrations → count No cross-module loop through resource depletion was returned by the tool — I'm reporting only what it actually returned, not inferring a resource-feedback loop myself.
  • I ran the simulation (run_model) twice and pulled get_variable_data for stocks, flows, and even a plain constant — all returned empty time series with no retrievable values. Per the data-inspection rule, I cannot and will not characterize numeric behavior (growth, overshoot, collapse, etc.) since I have no inspected data to back it up. This looks like a sandbox/run-execution limitation in this environment rather than a structural model defect (the model itself validates cleanly and loop detection, which is structural, works fine).

  • count (stock, initial 100 people) — inflow hires, outflows promotions, departures
  • hires = hire_rate (constant, 50 people/year) — the only exogenous entry point into the hierarchy
  • promotions = count * promotion_rate (promotion_rate = 0.2/year)
  • departures = count * departure_rate (departure_rate = 0.15/year)

associates module

  • count (stock, initial 60 people) — inflow is a ghost of rookies.promotions (named associates.rookies_promotions, crossLevelGhostOf: rookies.promotions), outflows promotions, departures
  • promotions = count * promotion_rate (0.15/year)
  • departures = count * departure_rate (0.1/year)

partners module

  • count (stock, initial 30 people) — inflow is a ghost of associates.promotions (named partners.associates_promotions), outflow departures only — correctly, no promotions component exists here since partner is the top of the hierarchy
  • departures = count * departure_rate (0.05/year)

One naming note: your spec calls for the ghost to be named with a literal space (e.g., "associates rookies promotions"). This environment's identifier syntax does not accept spaces in variable names, so the tool substituted an underscore (associates.rookies_promotions) while correctly preserving the crossLevelGhostOf link back to rookies.promotions. Functionally this is the ghost you asked for; only the separator character differs from the literal instruction.

Validation

  • mcp__builtin__get_current_model returned no errors and no unitWarnings — units (people, people/year, fraction/year) are dimensionally consistent throughout.
  • Structural check: every outflow is count * rate, so as any count approaches zero its outflows shrink proportionally — this is a self-limiting formulation with no risk of negative headcount, and no MIN/MAX clamp was needed.
  • hires, promotions, and departures are all marked uniflow, consistent with people not being "un-hired" or "un-departed."
  • I called mcp__builtin__run_model and then mcp__builtin__get_feedback_information — the structural loop scan found five loops (L1–L5), each a simple stock-to-its-own-outflow pair (e.g., associates.count -> associates.promotions -> associates.count, one for each module's promotions or departures outflow, all balancing polarity). No reinforcing or cross-module loops were found — consistent with the design, since a ghosted promotion inflow feeds the next module without any path back to influence the source module's own count.
  • I attempted to pull the numeric time series (mcp__builtin__get_variable_data) for count in each module, but the run in this environment returned no time-series values, only the structural feedback scan succeeded. Per the data-inspection rule, I won't assert specific numeric trajectories (e.g., "partners grows to X by year 20") without inspected values — I can only confirm the structure is sound. If you'd like, I can re-run and re-pull data to attempt to get actual numbers.

Critique

Structurally sound: each module is a first-order stock with two proportional balancing outflows, and only rookies has an exogenous inflow — this matches the description exactly (constant hiring at entry, strict percentage promotion and departure at each level). No missing feedback: the description doesn't call for promotion/departure rates to depend on anything besides each level's own count, and that's what's built. One limitation worth flagging: because promotion_rate and departure_rate are fixed constants rather than policy variables that respond to headcount targets, this model shows the hierarchy's response to a given policy, not a self-correcting hierarchy that adjusts rates to hit a target headcount — consistent with what you described ("the business promotes a strict percentage... to keep the hierarchy stable"), so no change needed unless you want that added.

Next steps: I can (a) re-run and pull actual time-series data to check reference-mode fit (e.g., whether partner headcount grows, shrinks, or reaches equilibrium), (b) run Seldon/LTM discussion once data is confirmed, or (c) adjust any rate constants if you have real target values in mind. Let me know which you'd like.

Please give me a quantitative model that captures the key causal processes described in the background information.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.


            In a certain ecosystem, there are three animal populations: lions, foxes, and chickens.
            
            All species reproduce and naturally die out at specific, stable percentage rates.
            Furthermore, the chicken population is predated at a rate proportional to the fox population,
            and the fox population is predated at a rate proportional to the lion population.
            
            Create a model with three modules named 'lions', 'foxes', and 'chickens'.
            
            Use the following component names within each module as appropriate:
            count, birth rate, death rate, births, deaths, predation rate

            In particular, "[animal].predation rate" should refer to the number of [animal]s that die off due to that animal's predator.

            When creating a ghost component, preserve the name of the original component, including the module prefix (separated by a space rather than a period).
            So, a ghost of "module1.component" in module2 should be named "module2.module1 component".

supportingInfo.explanation:
Now let me verify the actual structure matches the spec exactly.

Let's verify and actually run it.

Good, the diagnosis makes sense. Let's verify and actually run it.

Model built: three-module predator-prey food chain (lions, foxes, chickens)

I generated a quantitative SFD with exactly the three modules requested — lions, foxes, chickens — no others. Final structure (verified via get_current_model/read_model_section, not assumed):

lions module (no predator — top of the chain)

  • lions.count — stock, initial 20 lions. Inflow: lions.births. Outflow: lions.deaths.
  • lions.birth rate = 0.1 /year (constant)
  • lions.death rate = 0.1 /year (constant)
  • lions.births = count × birth rate (lions/year)
  • lions.deaths = count × death rate (lions/year)

foxes module

  • foxes.count — stock, initial 150 foxes. Inflow: foxes.births. Outflows: foxes.deaths, foxes.predation rate.
  • foxes.birth rate = 0.3 /year, foxes.death rate = 0.2 /year (constants)
  • foxes.births, foxes.deaths = count × respective rate
  • foxes.predation coefficient = 0.005 1/(lion·year) — added support constant (not in the required list, but needed to make predation proportional to lion population)
  • foxes.lions count — ghost of lions.count (crossLevelGhostOf = "lions.count"), per the ghosting convention (module.component → "thismodule component")
  • foxes.predation rate = count × predation coefficient × lions count — number of foxes lost per year to lion predation; this is strictly a loss from the fox stock, with no other effect (matches your definition of predation rate)

chickens module

  • chickens.count — stock, initial 800 chickens. Inflow: chickens.births. Outflows: chickens.deaths, chickens.predation rate.
  • chickens.birth rate = 0.9 /year, chickens.death rate = 0.5 /year (constants)
  • chickens.births, chickens.deaths = count × respective rate
  • chickens.predation coefficient ≈ 0.002667 1/(fox·year)
  • chickens.foxes count — ghost of foxes.count (crossLevelGhostOf = "foxes.count")
  • chickens.predation rate = count × predation coefficient × foxes count — chickens lost per year to fox predation, strictly a loss term

All 21 variables carry units and documentation; no unit warnings were reported by the engine. I deliberately kept births/deaths purely self-referential (count × own rate) with predation acting only as an outflow on the predated species — an earlier draft had erroneously added "growth from predation" feedback into the predators' stocks, which is not supported by your background and was removed.

Open issue — simulation run: run_model executed without a reported error, but the resulting run (eval-run-failed-3) returned no time-series data when I queried lions.count, foxes.count, chickens.count. I traced and fixed one real defect along the way (a ghost variable had a literal cross-module dotted reference baked into its equation instead of relying solely on crossLevelGhostOf), but after that fix the run still returns empty data, and get_current_model reports no structural errors or unit warnings to act on. I don't have a further lead to chase without more diagnostic visibility, so I'm flagging this rather than continuing to speculatively regenerate the model.

Since no run has produced valid output, I have not called feedback-loop or LTM analysis (that would require simulated behavior, and I won't speculate about loop structure or dynamics without it). Let me know if you'd like me to retry the run, adjust parameters, or proceed with a structural/behavioral discussion based on the equations as specified.

variables.documentation: The population of foxes, the mid-level predator that eats chickens and is preyed upon by lions. It grows via its own births and shrinks via natural deaths and predation by lions. Predation by foxes on chickens has no effect on this stock; only predation suffered by foxes (from lions) does. Starting value is set between lions (fewer) and chickens (more), reflecting typical trophic pyramid proportions.

variables.name: foxes.birth rate
variables.documentation: A constant fractional rate at which foxes reproduce each year, applied to the current fox count. This is the sole driver of fox births; predation on chickens does not contribute to fox growth in this model.

variables.name: foxes.death rate

variables.name: foxes.births

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model structure is clean, no errors. Now checking for warnings and running the simulation to confirm behavior.

I built the model and validated its structure, but want to flag one thing before summarizing: the simulation run itself did not produce usable output (empty data on two consecutive attempts), so I have not verified numeric behavior — I won't fabricate that.

Model structure built (verified via get_current_model/read_model_section, no errors or warnings reported):

Module: frimbulators

  • frimbulators.count (stock, initial value 20, units frimbulators) — the twenty frimbulators on record.
  • frimbulators.fractional_growth_rate (variable, equation 0.02, units 1/day) — the 2% daily growth rate, kept as a named parameter rather than hard-coded.
  • frimbulators.growth_flow (inflow to frimbulators.count, equation frimbulators.count * frimbulators.fractional_growth_rate, units frimbulators/day, uniflow) — the daily increase driven by growth proportional to current size.

Root-level ghost:

  • frimbulators.frimbulators_count — crossLevelGhostOf: "frimbulators.count", equation frimbulators.count, units frimbulators. (Note: the platform's variable-name validator does not permit literal spaces, so it rendered the space in "frimbulators count" as an underscore — frimbulators_count — despite two explicit attempts to force the literal space. This is the closest the tool will produce to your requested convention.)

Causal relationships captured (from read_model_section: relationships):

  • frimbulators.count → frimbulators.growth_flow (+): larger inventory produces a proportionally larger growth flow.
  • frimbulators.fractional_growth_rate → frimbulators.growth_flow (+): higher rate produces a larger flow for the same stock.
  • frimbulators.growth_flow → frimbulators.count (+): the flow accumulates into the stock.

Time specs: 0–30 days, dt 0.25, units "day".

Structural critique:

  • This is a plain reinforcing exponential-growth structure — count feeds growth_flow feeds count. No balancing loop is present because none was described in the background (no capacity limit, no depletion mechanism was mentioned).
  • Conservation is trivially satisfied: the only inflow is growth_flow; there is no outflow, consistent with the background statement ("increases due to... growth," nothing about decreases).
  • No unit warnings were reported by the engine, and no hard-coded arbitrary constants appear in the flow equation — the 2% rate is abstracted into frimbulators.fractional_growth_rate.

Outstanding issue: mcp__builtin__run_model returned run IDs (eval-run-failed-1, eval-run-failed-2) with no variable data on both attempts, so I cannot confirm simulated behavior (e.g., that frimbulators.count actually rises smoothly from 20 toward an exponential trajectory over 30 days). I did not fabricate a data-inspection result to fill this gap.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Now let's inspect what was actually built.

Let's verify the fix and check for errors/warnings.

Model Built: Four-Module SFD with Cross-Module Ghost Links

I extracted every stated cause-and-effect relationship into a Stock Flow Diagram organized as four modules — outrances, illigents, yelbs, trazes — each holding its entity's quantity in a stock named count.

Structure per module

outrances

  • outrances.count (stock, initial = 150 outrances)
  • outrances.inflow = inflow_rate (constant, = 20 outrances/hour) → causes outrances.count to rise
  • outrances.depletion = count * depletion_fraction (0.4 /hour) → causes outrances.count to fall
  • outrances.outgoing = count * outgoing_fraction (0.1 /hour) → causes outrances.count to fall

illigents

  • illigents.count (stock, initial = 30 illigents)
  • illigents.growth = outrances_count * growth_fraction (0.4 /hour), where outrances_count is a ghost of outrances.count → outrances.count causes illigents.count to rise
  • illigents.reduction = reduction_rate (constant, = 5 illigents/hour) → causes illigents.count to fall

yelbs

  • yelbs.count (stock, initial = 65 yelbs)
  • yelbs.growth = outrances_count * growth_fraction (0.1 /hour), ghost of outrances.count → outrances.count causes yelbs.count to rise
  • yelbs.reduction = trazes_count * reduction_fraction (0.12 /hour), ghost of trazes.count → trazes.count causes yelbs.count to fall

trazes

  • trazes.count (stock, initial = 85 trazes)
  • trazes.inflow = inflow_rate (constant, = 15 trazes/hour) → causes trazes.count to rise
  • trazes.reduction = count * reduction_fraction (0.18 /hour) → causes trazes.count to fall

Every percentage from the background is a named fraction parameter (e.g. outrances.depletion_fraction = 0.4) and every constant flow is a named rate parameter (e.g. outrances.inflow_rate = 20) — no bare numbers sit inside flow equations. get_current_model reports no errors and no unit warnings on this structure.

One naming caveat

I instructed the generator twice to name the ghost variables with a space in place of the source's period (e.g. illigents.outrances count), per your convention. The engine consistently stores the local ghost name with an underscore instead (illigents.outrances_count) — variable identifiers referenced inside equations appear not to support embedded spaces in this engine. Functionally these are exactly the ghost variables you specified (full source name preserved, just underscore instead of space as the separator); I flag the deviation rather than silently claim compliance.

Structural critique

  • outrances and trazes each have outflows proportional to their own stock plus a bounded constant inflow — these naturally settle to an equilibrium and cannot go negative.
  • illigents.reduction and (indirectly) yelbs are driven by a constant outflow (5 illigents/hour) against an inflow that depends on outrances.count. Because this outflow is not proportional to illigents.count itself, if the outrances-driven inflow ever falls persistently below 5/hour, illigents.count has no structural floor and could be driven negative. I have not altered this, since the background explicitly specifies a constant reduction and I'm holding strictly to the stated causal relationships for this causal-discovery exercise — flagging it as a credibility caveat rather than modifying unstated structure.

Simulation status

I ran the model to check behavior, but both run_model calls (eval-run-failed-1, eval-run-failed-2) returned runs with no variable data — get_variable_data came back empty both times. I'm not able to confirm runtime behavior (equilibrium values, extreme-condition checks) until a run actually produces data; I have not fabricated or inferred any numbers in place of it.

Next steps available: retry the simulation run, inspect feedback-loop structure (requires a successful run first), or visualize the four stocks' trajectories once data is available.
