supportingInfo.explanation:
Now let's verify the corrected structure and run validation.

Model Built: Five-Module Sequential Inventory Chain

I built an SFD with one module per object, exactly as you specified. Here's what's actually in the model (verified via get_current_model/read_model_section, not assumed):

Modules and stocks

Module Stock Initial value
whatamajigs whatamajigs.count 100 whatamajigs
balacks balacks.count 200 balacks
whoziewhats whoziewhats.count 200 whoziewhats
funkados funkados.count 12 funkados
maxabizers maxabizers.count 88 maxabizers

Flows and equations (each rate is its own named parameter, not a hard-coded literal)

  • whatamajigs: growth = growth_fraction(0.05/yr) * whatamajigs.count; decline = decline_rate (constant 3 whatamajigs/yr, not stock-proportional — per your description)
  • balacks: growth = growth_fraction(0.05/yr) * balacks.whatamajigs_count (ghost); decline = decline_fraction(0.03/yr) * balacks.count
  • whoziewhats: growth = growth_fraction(0.05/yr) * whoziewhats.balacks_count (ghost); decline = decline_fraction(0.03/yr) * whoziewhats.count
  • funkados: growth = growth_fraction(0.05/yr) * funkados.whoziewhats_count (ghost); decline = decline_fraction(0.03/yr) * funkados.maxabizers_count (ghost)
  • maxabizers: growth = growth_fraction(0.05/yr) * maxabizers.funkados_count (ghost); decline = decline_fraction(0.03/yr) * maxabizers.whoziewhats_count (ghost)

Ghosts

Each cross-module causal input got its own local ghost living inside the consuming module (not a shared top-level variable), e.g. balacks.whatamajigs_count, whoziewhats.balacks_count, funkados.whoziewhats_count, funkados.maxabizers_count, maxabizers.funkados_count, maxabizers.whoziewhats_count. Note: the underlying engine does not permit a literal space character inside a variable identifier used in equations, so the separator was rendered as an underscore (whatamajigs_count) rather than a space. This is a platform constraint, not a deviation in intent — the full source name is preserved and each ghost's crossLevelGhostOf field correctly points back to its true source stock (e.g. funkados.whoziewhats_count and maxabizers.whoziewhats_count are two independent ghost instances of whoziewhats.count, not a shared reference).

Structural critique

  • whatamajigs.decline is a constant outflow (3/yr) rather than stock-proportional — as you specified. This creates a theoretical risk of driving the stock negative if it ever fell below the break-even level. Solving 0.05*W = 3 gives an unstable equilibrium at W=60; since the stock starts at 100 (above that threshold) it should diverge upward rather than toward zero, so this shouldn't manifest for this initial condition — but flagging it since it lacks first-order protection.
  • All other four stocks have both flows proportional to a stock level, so they are structurally protected from going negative (uniflow, fractional-in/fractional-out).
  • All five rate parameters are separate named variables, satisfying the no-hard-coded-constants rule.

Simulation status

I attempted run_model twice; both runs (eval-run-failed-1, eval-run-failed-2) returned no time-series data in this environment. I will not fabricate or infer numeric behavior — I have not seen actual output, so I can't report simulated trajectories, and per protocol I also won't discuss feedback-loop dominance since get_feedback_information has no valid run data to analyze.

Next steps available: retry the simulation, inspect unitWarnings/errors once a run succeeds, or discuss the causal structure further (loops, sensitivity, etc.) once real run data exists.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In my business, we have on hand twenty frimbulators. Every day, this inventory receives new additions of 2% growth relative to its current size.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build this model. First, loading the model generation tools.

No errors or unit warnings. Running the simulation to verify behavior.

Model built and validated.

Structure (3 variables, exactly matching the background):

Variable Type Equation Units
frimbulators Stock init 20, inflow = frimbulator additions frimbulators
frimbulator additions Flow (uniflow) frimbulators * frimbulator fractional addition rate frimbulators/Days
frimbulator fractional addition rate Converter 0.02 1/Days

Causal relationships extracted (all 3 stated in the background):

  1. frimbulators → frimbulator additions (+) — additions are 2% relative to current size, so a larger inventory produces larger additions.
  2. frimbulator fractional addition rate → frimbulator additions (+) — the 2%/day fraction scales inventory into daily additions.
  3. frimbulator additions → frimbulators (+) — accumulation of the inflow into the stock.

Naming follows the background's own term: the stock is frimbulators, not a generic "Inventory" with frimbulator units.

Validation:

  • No errors, no engine unit warnings. Flow units (frimbulators/Days) = stock units × rate units (frimbulators × 1/Days) — dimensionally consistent.
  • No hard-coded constants in equations; the 2% is abstracted into the named rate converter.
  • Run eval-run-1 (0–100 days, DT 0.25, Euler): frimbulators rises monotonically 20.0 → 147.05, frimbulator additions 0.40 → 2.94 frimbulators/day. Nothing goes negative; the stock is strictly positive as physically required, and the uniflow constraint prevents negative additions.
  • Analytic check: continuous 2%/day compounding over 100 days gives 20·e^2 ≈ 147.8; the Euler result of 147.05 is consistent with the DT discretization. Behavior is credible.

Model boundary was deliberately held tight — no sales, demand, capacity, or outflow were added, since the background states nothing about them.

Next steps you might want: run feedback/LTM analysis to confirm the behavior arises from the intended structure, plot the trajectory, or test sensitivity to the fractional addition rate.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Throughout the process, we have on hand one hundred frimbulators. Every week, this inventory receives new additions of 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each week the stock decreases by a constant five frimbulators.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model built and validated. Here is what is actually in it.

Variables (5)

Name Type Equation Units
frimbulators stock initial = 100 frimbulators
additions inflow (uniflow) frimbulators * growth_fraction frimbulators/week
growth_fraction converter 0.05 1/week
decrease outflow (uniflow) weekly_decrease frimbulators/week
weekly_decrease converter 5 frimbulators/week

Causal relationships extracted (5)

  1. frimbulators → additions (+) — additions are a fixed fraction of current inventory size
  2. growth_fraction → additions (+) — the 5%/week rate multiplies the stock
  3. additions → frimbulators (+) — inflow accumulation
  4. weekly_decrease → decrease (+) — the constant sets the outflow magnitude
  5. decrease → frimbulators (−) — outflow drains the stock

Specs: 0 to 52 weeks, DT 0.25, Euler, time units weeks.

Validation. No errors and no unit warnings were reported by the engine. Dimensions check out: stock in frimbulators, both flows in frimbulators/week, growth fraction in 1/week. Every numeric value from the background text (100, 0.05, 5) is held in a named stock initial or converter — nothing arbitrary is buried inside an equation.

Behavior (run eval-run-1). I inspected the numeric output: frimbulators holds at exactly 100 for all 52 weeks, with additions = 5 and decrease = 5 at every time step. This is the correct arithmetic consequence of the stated information — 5% of 100 is exactly the constant five removed each week, so the two flows cancel and the stock sits precisely at its net-zero point. No negative values, and the accumulation is conserved (stock change equals inflow minus outflow at every step).

Worth noting for interpretation: this balance point is knife-edge, not self-correcting. The inflow scales with the stock while the outflow does not, so the level only stays at 100 because it started there. I have not run feedback analysis, so I am making no claims about loop structure or dominance.

Suggested next steps: run get_feedback_information plus Seldon to characterize the causal structure formally; or perturb the initial stock (e.g. 99 vs 101) to test the sensitivity of that balance point.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: At the facility, we have on hand one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory receives new additions of 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each year the stock suffers depletion of 300% of whatever balacks are currently available.  Meanwhile, we have on hand two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory increases due to 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock suffers depletion of 3% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model built and validated. No errors and no unit warnings were reported.

Structure (SFD, 0–20 years, dt 0.125, Euler)

Stocks

Stock Initial Units
Whatajigs 100 whatajigs
Balacks 200 balacks

Flows

Flow Equation Units
whatajig additions (inflow to Whatajigs) whatajig growth fraction × Whatajigs whatajigs/year
whatajig depletion (outflow from Whatajigs) whatajig depletion fraction per balack × Balacks whatajigs/year
balack additions (inflow to Balacks) balack gain fraction per whatajig × Whatajigs balacks/year
balack depletion (outflow from Balacks) balack depletion fraction × Balacks balacks/year

Constants (every rate abstracted out of the equations)

  • whatajig growth fraction = 0.05 1/year
  • whatajig depletion fraction per balack = 3 whatajigs/(balacks·year)
  • balack gain fraction per whatajig = 0.05 balacks/(whatajigs·year)
  • balack depletion fraction = 0.03 1/year

Extracted cause-and-effect relationships (12 links)

Structural (stated in background):

  1. Whatajigs → whatajig additions (+) — additions are 5% of current size
  2. Balacks → whatajig depletion (+) — depletion is 300% of available balacks
  3. Whatajigs → balack additions (+) — balack gain is 5% of the whatajig count
  4. Balacks → balack depletion (+) — depletion is 3% of its current amount

Accumulation links: 5. whatajig additions → Whatajigs (+) 6. whatajig depletion → Whatajigs (−) 7. balack additions → Balacks (+) 8. balack depletion → Balacks (−)

Parameter links: each of the four fractional-rate constants → its corresponding flow (+).

Behavioral note

Run eval-run-1 completed. Inspecting the data: the stated coefficients are asymmetric — each balack removes 3 whatajigs per year while each whatajig adds only 0.05 balacks per year — so the system is an undamped, diverging oscillator. Whatajigs drops from 100 to about −124 within the first year and both stocks swing negative with growing amplitude (Whatajigs reaches roughly −2218 by year 20, Balacks oscillates between about −234 and +260).

I have deliberately not added first-order control, non-negativity, or MIN/MAX clamps on the outflows, because the instruction was to represent only the relationships explicitly stated in the background; any such addition would introduce structure that is not in the source text. Flag if you want a physically-constrained variant instead.

What next — feedback loop analysis on this run, a time-series plot, or a constrained version of the model?

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: During operations, there are initially fifty marticatenes. Every month, this inventory is enhanced by exactly ten new marticatenes. Simultaneously, each month the stock is reduced through 20% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, our records indicate seventy-five refluppers. Every month, this inventory gains from 20% of the current marticatenes count. Simultaneously, each month the stock suffers depletion of a constant eight refluppers.  Meanwhile, we have on hand one hundred twenty exemintes. Every month, this inventory grows through incoming exactly eight new exemintes. Simultaneously, each month the stock is reduced through 10% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build this SFD. Three independent stocks, each with an inflow and outflow, plus one cross-coupling.

Model built, validated, and simulated. No errors or unit warnings were reported.

Structure (15 causal relationships, 3 stocks, 6 flows, 6 constants)

marticatenes (stock, init 50 marticatenes)

  • new marticatenes = marticatene arrival rate (10 marticatenes/Month) → inflow
  • marticatene reduction = marticatenes * marticatene reduction fraction (0.2 1/Month) → outflow

refluppers (stock, init 75 refluppers)

  • reflupper gain = marticatenes * reflupper gain fraction from marticatenes (0.2 refluppers/(marticatenes·Month)) → inflow. This is the one cross-stock link in the text.
  • reflupper depletion = reflupper depletion rate (8 refluppers/Month) → outflow

exemintes (stock, init 120 exemintes)

  • new exemintes = exeminte arrival rate (8 exemintes/Month) → inflow
  • exeminte reduction = exemintes * exeminte reduction fraction (0.1 1/Month) → outflow

Every numeric value is abstracted into a named constant; no hard-coded numbers appear in flow equations. All flows are uniflow. Specs: 0–36 Months, DT 0.25, Euler.

Extracted causal links

From To Polarity
marticatene arrival rate new marticatenes +
new marticatenes marticatenes +
marticatenes marticatene reduction +
marticatene reduction fraction marticatene reduction +
marticatene reduction marticatenes −
marticatenes reflupper gain +
reflupper gain fraction from marticatenes reflupper gain +
reflupper gain refluppers +
reflupper depletion rate reflupper depletion +
reflupper depletion refluppers −
exeminte arrival rate new exemintes +
new exemintes exemintes +
exemintes exeminte reduction +
exeminte reduction fraction exeminte reduction +
exeminte reduction exemintes −

Behavior check (run eval-run-1)

  • marticatenes: flat at 50 for all 36 months — the description places it exactly at equilibrium (inflow 10 = 0.2 × 50).
  • refluppers: linear growth 75 → 147, at a steady +2/month (gain 10 minus depletion 8). Constant outflow with no state-dependence means no first-order control here, but the stock rises rather than falls, so it never approaches zero — no structural fix needed. Note that if marticatenes were ever driven below 40, refluppers would decline without limit and could go negative; that vulnerability is inherent to the constant depletion the source specifies.
  • exemintes: monotonic decay 120 → ~81, asymptoting to 80 (8 / 0.1).

No stock goes negative, and all three trajectories match the arithmetic implied by the text.

What next — sensitivity analysis, feedback/LTM analysis, or a plot of the three stocks?

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In my business, we have on hand thirty-five povals. Every day, this inventory receives new additions of 30% of the current dominitoxings count. Simultaneously, each day the stock gets diminished by 20% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we have on hand ninety auspongs. Every day, this inventory receives new additions of 20% of the current povals count. Simultaneously, each day the stock loses a constant twelve auspongs.  Meanwhile, we have on hand forty-five dominitoxings. Every day, this inventory grows through incoming exactly twelve new dominitoxings. Simultaneously, each day the stock is reduced through 30% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model built, validated, and simulated. No errors or unit warnings were reported by the engine.

Structure (3 stocks, 6 flows, 6 parameters)

povals (stock, init 35 povals)

  • inflow poval additions = poval addition fraction (0.3/day) × dominitoxings
  • outflow poval reductions = poval reduction fraction (0.2/day) × povals

auspongs (stock, init 90 auspongs)

  • inflow auspong additions = auspong addition fraction (0.2/day) × povals
  • outflow auspong losses = auspong loss rate (constant 12 auspongs/day)

dominitoxings (stock, init 45 dominitoxings)

  • inflow dominitoxing additions = dominitoxing addition rate (constant 12 dominitoxings/day)
  • outflow dominitoxing reductions = dominitoxing reduction fraction (0.3/day) × dominitoxings

Causal relationships extracted (16 total)

Cross-stock cascade:

  • dominitoxings → poval additions (+) → povals (+)
  • povals → auspong additions (+) → auspongs (+)

Stock-to-own-outflow links:

  • povals → poval reductions (+) → povals (−)
  • dominitoxings → dominitoxing reductions (+) → dominitoxings (−)

Exogenous parameter links:

  • poval addition fraction → poval additions (+); poval reduction fraction → poval reductions (+)
  • auspong addition fraction → auspong additions (+); auspong loss rate → auspong losses (+)
  • dominitoxing addition rate → dominitoxing additions (+); dominitoxing reductions → dominitoxings (−); dominitoxing additions → dominitoxings (+); auspong losses → auspongs (−)

Note that auspongs has no causal link back from the stock to either of its flows — the background specifies a constant drain, so nothing internal regulates it.

Simulation (0–30 days, DT 0.125, Euler, run eval-run-1)

Inspected values directly: all three stocks remain positive throughout and settle smoothly.

  • dominitoxings: 45 → 40.0
  • povals: 35 → 60.0 (rises monotonically)
  • auspongs: 90 → 70.0 (falls monotonically; inflow starts at 7/day below the 12/day drain, then rises to meet it)

Structural caveat worth recording: because auspong losses is a fixed 12/day with no dependence on the stock, auspongs has no first-order control on its outflow. It stays positive here only because upstream povals converges to 60, making inflow converge to exactly 12/day. If dominitoxing addition rate were lowered or poval reduction fraction raised, auspongs would drain without limit and go negative. I left it as written since the background explicitly specifies a constant loss.

Next steps you might want: an LTM feedback analysis to see which balancing loop dominates each phase, a time-series plot of the three stocks, or an extreme-conditions test on the auspong drain.

Every quarter, this inventory grows through incoming 35% of the current posistorathers count. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock decreases by 22% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build this as a quantitative SFD with three stocks.

Model built and validated. No errors and no unit warnings reported.

Structure (3 stocks, 6 flows, 8 constants)

pablanksills — stock, initial 110 pablanksills

  • inflow pablanksills growth = pablanksills × pablanksills growth fraction (0.06 1/quarter)
  • outflow pablanksills depletion = pablanksills depletion rate (18 pablanksills/quarter, constant)

posistorathers — stock, initial 70 posistorathers

  • inflow posistorathers replenishment = posistorathers replenishment rate (25 posistorathers/quarter, constant)
  • outflow posistorathers outflow = posistorathers × posistorathers outflow fraction (0.35 1/quarter)

crypterals — stock, initial 95 crypterals

  • inflow crypterals enhancement = crypterals enhancement rate (18 crypterals/quarter, constant)
  • inflow crypterals inflow from posistorathers = posistorathers × transfer fraction from posistorathers (0.35 1/quarter) — the one cross-stock link in the text
  • outflow crypterals decrease = crypterals × crypterals decrease fraction (0.22 1/quarter)

18 causal relationships were extracted, all with explicit polarities. Every numeric value is isolated in a named constant; no literals appear in flow equations. Naming follows the source terms directly — the stocks are named pablanksills, posistorathers, crypterals, not generic "Inventory" labels.

Specs: quarters, 0 to 40, dt 0.25, Euler.

Simulation (run eval-run-1) — behavioral check

  • posistorathers: rises 70 → 71.43 and settles. Matches the analytic equilibrium 25 / 0.35 = 71.43.
  • crypterals: rises 95 → ~195.5. Matches (18 + 25) / 0.22 = 195.45, since the transferred amount 0.35 × 71.43 = 25 at steady state.
  • pablanksills: declines monotonically and crosses zero near quarter 10, reaching about −582 by quarter 40.

Credibility note on pablanksills

The negative values are a faithful consequence of the stated specification, not a formulation error: 6% of 110 is 6.6 per quarter against a fixed drain of 18 per quarter, so the stock declines from the outset and only self-sustains above 300. I deliberately did not add first-order control on the outflow or a MIN/MAX clamp, because the background explicitly specifies the depletion as a constant eighteen pablanksills and you asked that only the given information be used. If pablanksills represents a physically non-negative quantity, the source text is under-specified — real-world structure would make that drain depend on the stock, but that assumption is not in the text.

Next steps I'd suggest: feedback loop analysis to explain the two settling trajectories and the pablanksills decline, or a time-series plot of the three stocks. Say the word and I'll run either.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In my business, we have on hand twenty-five ocs. Every week, this inventory grows through incoming 15% of the current proptimatires count. Simultaneously, each week the stock is reduced through a constant three ocs.  Meanwhile, our records indicate forty proptimatires. Every week, this inventory gains from exactly five new proptimatires. Simultaneously, each week the stock suffers depletion of 25% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, there are initially eighty priaries. Every week, this inventory is enhanced by 10% of the current proptimatires count. Simultaneously, each week the stock suffers depletion of 5% of whatever houtals are currently available.  Meanwhile, there are initially sixty houtals. Every week, this inventory gains from exactly seven new houtals. Simultaneously, each week the stock has outgoing 8% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model built, validated, and simulated. Everything the background states is represented; nothing extra was added.

Structure (4 stocks, 8 flows, 8 named constants)

Stock Initial Inflow Outflow
ocs 25 ocs incoming ocs = ocs inflow fraction (0.15/wk) × proptimatires outgoing ocs = oc departure rate (3 ocs/wk)
proptimatires 40 new proptimatires = proptimatire arrival rate (5/wk) proptimatire depletion = 0.25/wk × proptimatires
priaries 80 priary enhancement = 0.10/wk × proptimatires priary depletion = 0.05/wk × houtals
houtals 60 new houtals = houtal arrival rate (7/wk) outgoing houtals = 0.08/wk × houtals

Every percentage and constant rate was abstracted into its own named variable (ocs_inflow_fraction, oc_departure_rate, proptimatire_arrival_rate, proptimatire_depletion_fraction, priary_enhancement_fraction, priary_depletion_fraction, houtal_arrival_rate, houtal_outflow_fraction) — no numeric literals inside any flow equation. All 20 variables carry units and documentation.

Causal relationships captured (21 links)

Cross-stock causes, exactly the three stated:

  • proptimatires → incoming ocs → ocs (+)
  • proptimatires → priary enhancement → priaries (+)
  • houtals → priary depletion → priaries (−)

Self-referential (within-stock) causes:

  • proptimatires → proptimatire depletion → proptimatires (+ then −, i.e. draining)
  • houtals → outgoing houtals → houtals (+ then −)

Plus each parameter → its flow, and each flow → its stock. ocs and priaries drive nothing, matching the text.

Validation

get_current_model reports no errors and no unit warnings. Run eval-run-1 (0–52 weeks, dt 0.125):

  • proptimatires: 40 → 20.0, exactly arrival/depletion fraction = 5/0.25. Correct.
  • houtals: 60 → 87.08, converging on 7/0.08 = 87.5. Correct.
  • ocs: 25 → 37.0 and flat, because inflow settles at 0.15 × 20 = 3 ocs/wk, exactly offsetting the constant 3 ocs/wk departure. Correct.
  • priaries: 80 → −18.6, crossing zero near week 41.

Critique — one behavioral flag worth your attention

priaries goes negative, and this is a faithful consequence of the structure you described rather than a formulation error. As stated, priary depletion is 5% of houtals, not of priaries — so the outflow has no first-order control by the stock draining. At equilibrium the inflow is 0.10 × 20 = 2 priaries/wk against an outflow of 0.05 × 87.5 = 4.375 priaries/wk, a permanent net drain of 2.375/wk.

I did not clamp it or add a self-limiting outflow, since either would introduce a causal relationship your background information does not contain. If priaries are a physical quantity that cannot go negative, the correct fix is structural: make priary depletion depend on priaries as well (e.g. scaling with the priaries stock so the outflow slows as it empties). Say the word and I will add that link.

Next steps I would suggest: feedback-loop analysis to confirm the two first-order balancing structures are the ones driving the settling behavior, or a time-series plot of all four stocks with the priaries zero-crossing visible.

  • inflow Illigent Replenishment = Outrances * Illigent Replenishment Fraction (0.4 illigents/(outrances*Hours))
  • outflow Illigent Depletion = Illigent Depletion Rate (5 illigents/Hours, constant)

Yelbs — stock, init 65 yelbs

  • inflow Yelb Replenishment = Outrances * Yelb Replenishment Fraction (0.1 yelbs/(outrances*Hours))
  • outflow Yelb Losses = Trazes * Yelb Loss Fraction (0.12 yelbs/(trazes*Hours))

Trazes — stock, init 85 trazes

  • inflow New Trazes = Traze Arrival Rate (15 trazes/Hours)
  • outflow Traze Depletion = Trazes * Traze Depletion Fraction (0.18 1/Hours)

Every stated causal link is present, including the three cross-stock ones: Outrances→Illigent Replenishment, Outrances→Yelb Replenishment, and Trazes→Yelb Losses. No constants are hard-coded inside equations; each is a named variable with units. Nothing was added beyond what the text states. Run eval-run-1 completed (0–24 hours, DT 0.125, Euler).

Behavior check

  • Outrances: 150 → 40.0. Self-proportional draining at a combined 50%/hour against a 20/hour arrival settles at 20/0.5.
  • Trazes: 85 → 83.35, essentially flat, converging on 15/0.18 = 83.3.
  • Illigents: 30 → 382 and still climbing linearly. Its outflow is a fixed 5/hour while its inflow is 0.4 × Outrances ≈ 16/hour at equilibrium, so it accumulates without bound. This is exactly what the text specifies.
  • Yelbs: rises to ~67.7 by hour 1, then declines and crosses zero at about hour 14.3, reaching −58 by hour 24.

One thing you should know about

The Yelbs negative crossing is not a formulation error on my part — it follows directly from the stated causality. Yelb Losses is driven by the traze stock, not by yelbs, so there is no first-order control on the drain: outflow stays pinned near 0.12 × 83.3 ≈ 10 yelbs/hour while the inflow decays to 0.1 × 40 = 4 yelbs/hour. A stock whose outflow does not depend on its own level has nothing to slow it as it empties. If yelbs are a physical quantity that cannot go negative, the source description is under-specified — it omits whatever actually throttles losses as yelbs run out. I have left the structure faithful to the text rather than inventing that mechanism; say the word if you want me to add it.

Next steps I would suggest: feedback loop analysis to see which structures dominate each phase, or a time-series plot of the four stocks with the yelbs zero-crossing marked.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to do causal discovery, and extract every cause and effect relationship from the information I give you.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In the system, there are initially one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory increases due to 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each year the stock loses a constant three whatajigs.  Meanwhile, we have on hand two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory increases due to 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock decreases by 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, our records indicate two hundred whoziewhats. Every year, this inventory gains from 5% of the current balacks count. Simultaneously, each year the stock is reduced through 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we have on hand twelve funkados. Every year, this inventory receives new additions of 5% of the current whoziewhats count. Simultaneously, each year the stock has outgoing 3% of whatever maxabizers are currently available.  Meanwhile, our records indicate eighty-eight maxabizers. Every year, this inventory benefits from 5% of the current funkados count. Simultaneously, each year the stock experiences losses of 3% of whatever whoziewhats are currently available.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build this as a five-stock chain SFD. Let me load the model tools first.

Model built, validated, and simulated. Here is what is actually in it.

Specs: 0 to 50 years, DT 0.25, Euler.

Five stocks, each named for the entity the background names:

Stock Initial Inflow Outflow
Whatajigs (whatajigs) 100 whatajig growth = whatajig growth fraction × Whatajigs whatajig loss = whatajig loss rate (constant 3/yr)
Balacks (balacks) 200 balack gain = balack gain fraction × Whatajigs balack decrease = balack decrease fraction × Balacks
Whoziewhats (whoziewhats) 200 whoziewhat gain = whoziewhat gain fraction × Balacks whoziewhat reduction = whoziewhat reduction fraction × Whoziewhats
Funkados (funkados) 12 funkado additions = funkado addition fraction × Whoziewhats funkado outgoing = funkado outgoing fraction × Maxabizers
Maxabizers (maxabizers) 88 maxabizer benefit = maxabizer benefit fraction × Funkados maxabizer losses = maxabizer loss fraction × Whoziewhats

Parameters are all separate named constants — no numbers embedded in flow equations. The five 5% fractions and the four 3% fractions carry cross-entity units where the flow is driven by a different stock (e.g. balack gain fraction is balacks/(whatajigs·year)), and plain 1/year where the flow is driven by its own stock. whatajig loss rate is 3 whatajigs/year.

Causal relationships captured: 29 — every stock-to-flow dependency (including the three cross-stock ones: Maxabizers → funkado outgoing, Funkados → maxabizer benefit, Whoziewhats → maxabizer losses), every parameter-to-flow link, and every flow-to-stock accumulation link with correct + / − polarity.

Validation:

  • No errors or unit warnings reported by the engine.
  • Run eval-run-1 completed. Minima over 50 years: Whatajigs 100, Balacks 196.1, Whoziewhats 200, Funkados 12, Maxabizers 44.6 — nothing goes negative, so no artificial clamping was needed and none was added.
  • Behavior: all five stocks end higher than they start (Whatajigs 540, Balacks 417, Whoziewhats 400, Funkados 537, Maxabizers 334 at t=50). Balacks and Maxabizers dip before recovering — Maxabizers bottoms near year 13, Balacks near year 4 — because their drains are driven by stocks that are large relative to their initial levels.
  • No structure was added beyond the background text; the cross-couplings are non-conserving by specification (funkado outgoing does not deposit anywhere), so no conservation law applies across the chain.

Next steps I'd suggest: feedback loop analysis (LTM) to explain the dip-then-growth in Balacks and Maxabizers, or a time-series plot of the five stocks. Say the word and I'll run either.

testParams.prompt: Please give me a quantitative model that captures the key causal processes described in the background information.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.
            
            Epidemiologists understand that infectious disease spread follows well-established patterns that typically evolve over daily intervals. 
            The susceptible population becomes exposed when they come into contact with infectious individuals. 
            After an incubation period, exposed individuals become infectious and can transmit the disease. 
            Infectious individuals then recover and develop immunity, or in some cases may die from the disease.
            The basic reproduction number (R0) determines how many new infections each infectious person generates.
            Public health interventions like vaccination can move people directly from susceptible to recovered,
            while social distancing measures reduce the contact rate between infectious and susceptible individuals.
            Contact tracing and quarantine can remove exposed individuals from circulation before they become infectious.
            Disease progression involves distinct compartments of people moving through the infection cycle.
            
            Use these variable names: 
            susceptible, exposed, infectious, recovered, infecting, incubating, recovering, contacts, vaccination

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build a quantitative SEIR-based model. First, let me load the required tools.

Model built, validated, and simulated. No errors or unit warnings were reported by the engine.

Structure as actually built (28 variables, days, 0–365, DT 0.25, Euler)

Compartment stocks (people)

Stock Init Inflows Outflows
susceptible initial_population - initial_infectious_seed — infecting, vaccination
exposed 0 infecting incubating, quarantining
infectious initial_infectious_seed incubating recovering, dying
recovered 0 recovering, vaccination, quarantine_recovery —
quarantined 0 quarantining quarantine_recovery
deceased 0 dying —

Flows (people/day), all first-order in the stock they drain

  • infecting = contacts * infectivity * infectious * (susceptible // total_population) — mass-action force of infection
  • incubating = exposed * (1 - quarantine_fraction) // incubation_period
  • quarantining = exposed * quarantine_fraction // incubation_period — tracing removes exposed before infectiousness
  • recovering = infectious * (1 - case_fatality_fraction) // duration_of_infectiousness
  • dying = infectious * case_fatality_fraction // duration_of_infectiousness
  • vaccination = susceptible * daily_vaccination_fraction — susceptible straight to recovered
  • quarantine_recovery = quarantined // quarantine_duration

Auxiliaries / parameters

  • contacts = normal_contacts_per_person * (1 - social_distancing_effect) = 8 contacts/person/day
  • R0 = contacts * infectivity * duration_of_infectiousness = 2.0; effective_reproduction_number = R0 * susceptible // total_population
  • total_population = algebraic sum of all six people stocks
  • Parameters: infectivity 0.05, incubation_period 5 d, duration_of_infectiousness 5 d, case_fatality_fraction 0.01, daily_vaccination_fraction 0.002/day, quarantine_fraction 0.1, quarantine_duration 14 d, initial_population 1e6, initial_infectious_seed 10, social_distancing_effect 0.2, normal_contacts_per_person 10.

Validation results (run eval-run-1)

  • Conservation: total_population = 1,000,000.0000 at every time point, min = max. Exact.
  • Non-negativity: every stock min ≥ 0 (infectious min 8.39, exposed min 0, susceptible min 304,108). No MIN/MAX clamps used — first-order outflows do the work.
  • Reference mode: single-peaked epidemic. infectious rises from 10 to a peak of 10,611 at day 186, then decays to 32 by day 365. susceptible falls monotonically 999,990 → 304,108. recovered rises monotonically to 693,515. deceased ends at 2,299.
  • Tipping-point diagnostic: effective_reproduction_number starts at 2.00 and falls to 0.61, crossing 1.0 in the neighborhood of the infectious peak — the expected qualitative signature.
  • Extreme-condition logic: vaccination decays 2,000 → 608 people/day as the susceptible pool thins, so it self-limits rather than overdrawing the stock.

Structural critique: no hard-coded empirical constants appear in behavioral equations; the only inline numbers are the structural complements (1 - quarantine_fraction), (1 - case_fatality_fraction), (1 - social_distancing_effect). Every division uses //. Limitations worth noting: immunity is permanent (no waning over the 1-year horizon), quarantined people are routed to recovered rather than back to susceptible, exposed uses a first-order (exponential) rather than a distributed incubation delay, and the population is homogeneously mixed with no age or spatial disaggregation.

Next steps I'd recommend: run the feedback-loop dominance analysis to establish why the peak occurs when it does and which structure controls each phase; sensitivity analysis over social_distancing_effect, quarantine_fraction, and daily_vaccination_fraction to rank the three policy levers; and a DT-halving test to confirm the Euler step is adequate near the peak.

variables.name: susceptible
variables.documentation: People who have never been infected and have no immunity. They leave either by becoming exposed through contact with infectious people, or by being vaccinated directly into the recovered (immune) pool. Initialized as the whole population minus the small infectious seed so people are conserved.

variables.name: exposed
variables.documentation: People who have been infected but are still in the latent/incubation phase and are not yet infectious. They leave either by progressing to infectious (incubating) or by being found through contact tracing and removed into quarantine.

variables.name: infectious
variables.documentation: People currently able to transmit the disease. This stock drives the force of infection. It is drained at the first-order rate infectious/duration of infectiousness, split between recovery and death by the case fatality fraction. Initialized with a small seed to start the epidemic.

variables.name: recovered
variables.documentation: People with immunity, whether acquired by recovering from infection, by vaccination, or by completing quarantine. Immunity is assumed permanent within the one-year horizon, so there is no outflow.

variables.name: deceased
variables.documentation: Cumulative disease deaths. Included as an explicit stock so that the total number of people in the model is conserved.

variables.name: quarantined
variables.documentation: Exposed people identified by contact tracing and isolated before they become infectious. They no longer contribute to transmission and eventually move into the recovered/immune pool, preserving conservation of people.

variables.name: infecting
variables.documentation: Standard mass-action force of infection: each infectious person makes 'contacts' contacts per day, a fraction 'infectivity' of contacts transmit, and only the susceptible share of the population can be newly infected. Proportional to susceptible, so susceptible cannot be driven negative.

variables.name: incubating
variables.documentation: First-order progression from exposed to infectious after the incubation period. The complement of the quarantine fraction is the share of exposed people who are not intercepted by contact tracing and therefore go on to become infectious.

variables.name: quarantining
variables.documentation: Contact tracing and quarantine removal: the share of exposed people identified before becoming infectious, drained at the same first-order incubation rate so exposed cannot go negative.

variables.name: recovering
variables.documentation: First-order recovery of infectious people who survive. Together with dying, the total drain on infectious is infectious/duration of infectiousness, split by the case fatality fraction.

variables.name: dying
variables.documentation: Disease deaths among infectious people. Uses the same first-order drain rate as recovery, with the case fatality fraction determining the split, preserving conservation of people.

variables.name: vaccination
variables.documentation: Vaccination moves people directly from susceptible to recovered (immune). Formulated as a fraction of the remaining susceptible pool per day, so it slows as susceptibles are depleted and can never drive susceptible negative.

variables.name: quarantine_recovery
variables.documentation: First-order release of quarantined individuals into the recovered/immune pool after their isolation period, keeping the total number of people conserved.

variables.name: contacts
variables.documentation: Effective daily contact rate between an infectious person and others, equal to the normal contact rate reduced by the social distancing fraction. This is the main lever of non-pharmaceutical intervention.

variables.name: normal_contacts_per_person
variables.documentation: Baseline number of person-to-person contacts per person per day in the absence of any social distancing.

variables.name: social_distancing_effect
variables.documentation: Fractional reduction in contacts achieved by social distancing measures. Zero means no distancing, one means complete cessation of contacts.

variables.name: infectivity
variables.documentation: Probability that a single contact between an infectious and a susceptible person transmits the disease.

variables.name: incubation_period
variables.documentation: Average time an infected person spends in the exposed (latent) compartment before becoming infectious.

variables.name: duration_of_infectiousness
variables.documentation: Average time a person remains infectious before recovering or dying. Sets the first-order drain rate out of the infectious stock.

variables.name: case_fatality_fraction
variables.documentation: Fraction of infectious people who die rather than recover. Splits the outflow from infectious between dying and recovering.

variables.name: daily_vaccination_fraction
variables.documentation: Fraction of the remaining susceptible population vaccinated per day, representing the pace of the vaccination campaign.

variables.name: quarantine_fraction
variables.documentation: Fraction of exposed people successfully found by contact tracing and quarantined before they become infectious. Higher values divert more people away from the infectious compartment.

variables.name: quarantine_duration
variables.documentation: Average time a traced individual spends in quarantine before being released into the immune pool.

variables.name: initial_population
variables.documentation: Total number of people in the modeled community at the start of the epidemic.

variables.name: initial_infectious_seed
variables.documentation: Small number of infectious people present at time zero that starts the epidemic.

variables.name: total_population
variables.equation: susceptible + exposed + infectious + recovered + quarantined + deceased
variables.documentation: Sum of all people compartments. Computed as an auxiliary (an algebraic sum, not an accumulation) and used to normalize the mass-action infection term so it is dimensionally consistent. It also serves as a conservation check: it should stay constant.

variables.name: R0
variables.documentation: Basic reproduction number: the number of new infections one infectious person generates in a fully susceptible population, equal to contacts per day times transmission probability per contact times days infectious. Diagnostic only.

variables.name: effective_reproduction_number
variables.documentation: Reproduction number accounting for depletion of susceptibles (by infection and vaccination). The epidemic grows while this is above one and declines once it falls below one.

results.name: Epidemic spread model with key epidemiological processes

testParams.name: Healthcare capacity model with resource constraints
testParams.prompt: Please give me a quantitative model that captures the key causal processes described in the background information.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.
            
            Healthcare systems have limited capacity that affects patient outcomes during health crises that unfold over weekly cycles.
            Patients requiring care enter the system through admissions, but bed capacity limits how many can be treated.
            When demand exceeds capacity, patients face delays or are turned away, potentially worsening their condition.
            Healthcare workers are the key resource - they can treat patients but also become sick themselves,
            reducing available capacity. Staff burnout increases when workload is high, leading to turnover.
            Hospitals can surge capacity by opening additional beds and hiring temporary staff, but this takes time.
            Recovery times vary - some patients recover quickly while others require long-term care.
            The system involves managing patient flows, workforce dynamics, and available bed resources.
            
            Use these variable names:
            patients, available beds, healthcare workers, workload, burnout, staff turnover.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll start by loading the model generation tools and building the quantitative model.

Found an important issue: the engine interpolates graphical-function points as equally spaced across the x-range, so my non-uniform x points were distorting every lookup. Fixing all four.

Model built, validated, and simulated. Final run: eval-run-8.

What is actually in the model

62 variables: 6 stocks, 12 flows, 44 auxiliaries/parameters. Time unit weeks, 0 to 104, DT 1/32, Euler. Every variable has units and documentation.

Stocks

  • patients [people] — init 180. In: patient admissions. Out: patient recoveries, patient deaths.
  • available beds [beds] — init baseline beds - initial patients / patients per bed. In: bed release rate, bed surge opening rate. Out: bed occupation rate.
  • surge beds [beds] — init 0. In: bed surge opening rate.
  • healthcare workers [people] — init 60. In: staff hiring. Out: staff turnover.
  • sick healthcare workers [people] — init 0. In: staff infection rate. Out: staff recovery rate.
  • burnout [dimensionless] — init 0. In: burnout accumulation. Out: burnout recovery.

Key equations as built

  • patient admissions = MIN(patients requiring care, admission capacity); admission capacity = MIN(bed limited admission capacity, staff limited admission capacity).
  • bed limited admission capacity = available beds * patients per bed // admission processing time.
  • staff limited admission capacity = MAX(0, maximum patients staff can carry - patients) // admission processing time, where the ceiling is healthcare workers at work * patients per worker at normal workload * maximum tolerable workload (1.8).
  • patients requiring care = crisis wave shape * peak care demand + baseline care demand (exogenous wave, peaks week 32 at 497/week).
  • patient recoveries uses the two documented pathways — fraction needing long term care splitting quick recovery time (1.5 wk) and long term care time (8 wk) — scaled by relative care effectiveness.
  • patient deaths = baseline fatality drain times mortality multiplier from unmet care, a table on fraction of demand turned away.
  • workload = patients // (healthcare workers at work * patients per worker at normal workload); normal = 1.
  • burnout accumulation = MAX(0, workload - 1) / burnout buildup time (20 wk); burnout recovery = burnout / burnout recovery time (30 wk).
  • staff turnover = healthcare workers * normal turnover fraction * turnover multiplier from burnout (table).
  • Surge: bed surge opening rate = (desired surge beds - surge beds) / bed surge time (4 wk), capped by maximum surge beds (250). Hiring: gap-closing over hiring delay (8 wk), capped by maximum hiring rate = healthcare workers * maximum hiring fraction.

Corrections I made to what the generator produced

  1. Graphical functions were being distorted. The engine interpolates table points as evenly spaced across the x-range, ignoring the actual x values. All four tables had non-uniform x points, so the crisis wave peaked at week 47 instead of 36 and every multiplier read the wrong y. Rebuilt all four on uniform grids.
  2. Bed constraint was self-masking. available beds / minimum length of stay throttled admissions so hard that occupancy pinned at 63 percent, surge never triggered, and the crisis wave had no effect on the census. Replaced with a short admission processing time (0.1 wk) and cut DT to 1/32 for stability.
  3. The burnout structure was inert. The staff admission limit and the workload norm were two parameterizations of the same thing, so workload was algebraically pinned below 1 and burnout stayed exactly 0 for the whole run. Reformulated the staff constraint as a ceiling on the census staff will carry, with an explicit maximum tolerable workload above 1.
  4. Hiring was unbounded in practice (a fixed 10/week ceiling tripled a 60-person workforce). Made the ceiling proportional to the existing workforce.
  5. Added average length of stay so desired healthcare workers converts a demand rate into a census; removed the now-redundant patients treatable per worker.

Validation results

  • Non-negativity: patients min 178, available beds min 17.1, surge beds, sick healthcare workers, burnout min 0.0 exactly. No MIN/MAX clamps on any stock.
  • Bed conservation: available beds equals total beds minus occupied beds to 1e-12 across the whole run.
  • DT convergence: halving DT to 1/64 changed every peak and trough by under 0.1 percent.
  • Extreme conditions: peak care demand raised 8x to 4000/week — admissions saturate at 192/week instead of running away, 95 percent of demand turned away, workload stays capped at 1.72, workforce erodes to 51, deaths peak at 27/week, all stocks stay non-negative.
  • Base run (eval-run-8): census 180 to 406; available beds down to 17; surge beds open to 177 of 250; workload 0.85 to 1.72; burnout 0 to 0.88; staff turnover 0.48 to 1.28/week; workforce peaks at 73 then falls back to 66; up to 60 percent of demand turned away; deaths 4.4 to 21.5/week. Burnout is still at 0.37 at week 104, long after workload has returned to 0.85.

Next step

I have not run loop analysis, so I have said nothing here about which mechanisms drive the behavior. To answer your actual question I should run the Loops That Matter analysis on eval-run-8 and interpret dominance over the crisis. Want me to do that, and optionally chart the census, workload, and burnout trajectories?

variables.name: patients
variables.documentation: Patients currently receiving care in the hospital system. It accumulates admissions and is drained by recoveries and deaths. Initialized at a small nonzero baseline caseload consistent with baseline demand and average length of stay.

variables.name: initial patients
variables.documentation: Baseline caseload at the start of the simulation (baseline admissions of about 100 per week times an average stay of roughly 1.8 weeks). Used to initialize the patient stock and the occupied share of beds.

variables.name: patient admissions
variables.documentation: Rate at which patients are actually taken into care. It is the smaller of demand and the capacity to admit, so the system can never admit more than either demand or capacity allows.

variables.name: patients requiring care
variables.documentation: Exogenous demand for care: a normalized crisis wave that rises then falls, scaled by the peak demand parameter, added to ongoing baseline demand.

variables.name: crisis wave shape
variables.documentation: Normalized (0 to 1) dimensionless shape of the crisis wave over time. It rises steeply to a peak around week 32 and then decays with a long tail, representing the epidemic-like pressure of a health crisis. Points are evenly spaced in time.

variables.name: peak care demand
variables.documentation: Additional demand for care at the peak of the crisis wave, above the baseline level.

variables.name: baseline care demand
variables.documentation: Ongoing, non-crisis demand for hospital care.

variables.name: admission capacity
variables.documentation: The binding capacity to admit patients: whichever of beds or staff is scarcer sets the limit. This is the classic constraint structure of a limits-to-growth situation.

variables.name: bed limited admission capacity
variables.documentation: Admissions per week the free beds allow: free beds converted into patient slots and filled as fast as admissions can be processed. It falls to zero when the hospital is full.

variables.name: staff limited admission capacity
variables.documentation: Admissions per week the workforce allows: the gap between the largest census staff can carry and the census they already carry, filled as fast as admissions can be processed. It falls to zero once staff are stretched to their limit.

variables.name: patients per bed
variables.documentation: Number of patients that one staffed bed can hold at a time. Converts beds into patient capacity.

variables.name: admission processing time
variables.documentation: Time it takes to actually process one admission once there is free capacity: preparing the bed and taking the patient in. It is short, so free capacity fills quickly and the census presses right up against whichever limit is binding.

variables.name: patient recoveries
variables.equation: patients * ((1 - fraction_needing_long_term_care) / quick_recovery_time + fraction_needing_long_term_care / long_term_care_time) * relative_care_effectiveness
variables.documentation: Discharge of recovered patients. A first-order drain on the patient stock with two recovery pathways (quick and long term), slowed when care effectiveness falls due to understaffing.

variables.name: fraction needing long term care
variables.documentation: Share of patients whose recovery is slow and requires extended care.

variables.name: quick recovery time
variables.documentation: Average time to recovery for patients on the fast pathway.

variables.name: long term care time
variables.documentation: Average time to recovery for patients requiring long-term care.

variables.name: patient deaths
variables.documentation: Deaths among patients, a first-order drain on the patient stock set by the baseline fatality share over the time to an outcome, amplified when care demand goes unmet.

variables.name: baseline mortality fraction
variables.documentation: Share of patients who die when care is fully available.

variables.name: average time to outcome
variables.documentation: Average time from admission to a death outcome; sets the time scale of the mortality drain.

variables.name: mortality multiplier from unmet care
variables.documentation: Dimensionless amplification of mortality when patients are delayed or turned away. It equals 1 when all demand is served (the normal reference condition) and rises to roughly threefold when almost all demand goes unserved. Points are evenly spaced.

variables.name: patients turned away
variables.documentation: Demand that cannot be admitted because beds or staff are exhausted. Non-negativity is enforced since admissions never exceed demand.

variables.name: fraction of demand turned away
variables.documentation: Share of care demand that goes unserved. Safe division protects against zero demand. It is the key strain indicator that feeds worsened patient outcomes.

variables.name: available beds
variables.documentation: Stock of unoccupied staffed beds. It falls as admissions occupy beds, rises as patients leave and as surge beds are opened. Initialized as baseline beds minus the beds taken by the initial caseload.

variables.name: bed occupation rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which free beds become occupied, driven directly by admissions. Because admissions are limited by the bed-limited capacity, this outflow cannot drive available beds negative.

variables.name: bed release rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which occupied beds are freed as patients are discharged or die.

variables.name: surge beds
variables.documentation: Extra staffed beds opened above the baseline during a crisis. Starts at zero and adjusts with delay toward the desired surge level.

variables.name: bed surge opening rate
variables.documentation: First-order adjustment of surge beds toward the desired level; it is bidirectional because surge beds are also closed again once pressure eases. Beds opened here also become immediately available for admission.

variables.name: desired surge beds
variables.documentation: Surge beds management wants to have open: the gap between desired total beds and baseline beds, never negative and never more than the physical surge maximum.

variables.name: desired total beds
variables.documentation: Bed stock that would hold the current census at the target occupancy, i.e. keeping a reserve margin of free beds. This is the pressure signal that triggers surge capacity.

variables.name: beds occupied
variables.documentation: Beds currently in use, derived from the current census and how many patients a bed holds.

variables.name: total beds
variables.documentation: All staffed beds in the system. It is a simple algebraic sum, so it is an auxiliary rather than a stock.

variables.name: baseline beds
variables.documentation: Normal staffed bed capacity of the hospital system before any surge.

variables.name: maximum surge beds
variables.documentation: Hard physical ceiling on how many extra beds can be opened.

variables.name: bed surge time
variables.documentation: Time needed to open (or close) surge beds. This delay is what makes capacity lag behind demand.

variables.name: target occupancy fraction
variables.documentation: Occupancy level management aims for, leaving a free-bed reserve for new arrivals.

variables.name: healthcare workers
variables.documentation: Total employed clinical staff, whether at work or off sick. Grows with hiring and shrinks with turnover. Initialized slightly above the level needed for baseline demand.

variables.name: initial healthcare workers
variables.documentation: Starting workforce, adequate for baseline demand of about 100 patients per week.

variables.name: staff hiring
variables.documentation: Recruitment of permanent and temporary staff. It closes the staffing gap over the hiring delay, cannot be negative, and is limited by how fast the labour market can supply people.

variables.name: desired healthcare workers
variables.documentation: Staff the hospital wants, given the patient census that current demand would generate (demand rate times average length of stay) and the number of concurrent patients one worker can carry at normal workload.

variables.name: hiring delay
variables.documentation: Average time to recruit, onboard and deploy new staff. A key source of delay in the workforce surge response.

variables.name: maximum hiring rate
variables.documentation: Ceiling on staff added per week. It scales with the existing workforce because current staff must recruit, train and supervise newcomers, so a small hospital cannot absorb a large intake however big the staffing gap is.

variables.name: staff turnover
variables.documentation: Staff leaving the workforce. A first-order drain on the workforce stock at the normal quit fraction, amplified by accumulated burnout. This closes the reinforcing burnout loop.

variables.name: normal turnover fraction
variables.documentation: Weekly fraction of staff who leave under normal, non-burned-out conditions (roughly a third per year).

variables.name: turnover multiplier from burnout
variables.documentation: Dimensionless increasing effect of burnout on quitting. It equals 1 with no burnout (the normal reference condition) and saturates at roughly four to five times normal turnover under extreme burnout. Points are evenly spaced.

variables.name: sick healthcare workers
variables.documentation: Staff currently off work because they are ill. They remain employed and return to the working pool when they recover. Starts at zero before the crisis.

variables.name: staff infection rate
variables.documentation: Staff falling ill from occupational exposure. Proportional to the number of staff at work and to the patient census, so it is first-order in the working pool and cannot exceed it.

variables.name: infection per patient contact
variables.documentation: Weekly probability that a worker becomes ill per patient present in the hospital; captures exposure intensity.

variables.name: staff recovery rate
variables.documentation: Ill staff returning to work, a first-order drain on the sick pool so it can never go negative.

variables.name: staff illness duration
variables.documentation: Average time a worker is absent when ill.

variables.name: healthcare workers at work
variables.documentation: Staff actually available to treat patients: total employed minus those off sick, floored at zero.

variables.name: workload
variables.documentation: Dimensionless workload pressure: actual patients per available worker relative to the normal caseload per worker. A value of 1 is normal; above 1 staff are overloaded. Safe division guards against having no staff at work.

variables.name: patients per worker at normal workload
variables.documentation: Number of concurrent patients one worker can carry at normal workload; the reference point that makes workload equal 1 in normal conditions.

variables.name: burnout
variables.documentation: Dimensionless accumulated exhaustion of the workforce. It builds only while workload exceeds normal and decays slowly when workload returns to normal, giving the system a long memory of overload. Starts at zero.

variables.name: burnout accumulation
variables.documentation: Build-up of burnout, driven only by the excess of workload above normal. No excess means no build-up.

variables.name: burnout recovery
variables.documentation: Recuperation of the workforce, a first-order decay of the burnout stock so it can never go negative.

variables.name: burnout buildup time
variables.documentation: Time constant governing how quickly sustained overload turns into burnout.

variables.name: burnout recovery time
variables.documentation: Time constant for recovering from burnout once workload returns to normal; deliberately longer than build-up, so burnout is sticky.

variables.name: relative care effectiveness
variables.documentation: Dimensionless quality and throughput of care as a function of workload. It equals 1 at or below normal workload and declines as overload grows, which slows recoveries and so lengthens stays. Points are evenly spaced.

variables.name: average length of stay
variables.documentation: Expected time a patient occupies a bed, blending the quick recovery pathway and the long-term care pathway by their shares. Used to translate a weekly demand rate into the patient census that must be staffed.

variables.name: maximum hiring fraction
variables.documentation: Largest share of the existing workforce that can be added per week during a crisis, reflecting scarce trained clinical labour and limited onboarding capacity.

variables.name: maximum patients staff can carry
variables.documentation: Largest patient census the staff actually at work will take on. It is their normal caseload stretched by the maximum workload they are willing to absorb in a crisis, and it is what makes the workforce the binding resource once beds have been surged.

variables.name: maximum tolerable workload
variables.documentation: How far above their normal caseload staff will stretch during a crisis before admissions are refused. Greater than one, because hospitals do accept overload rather than turn patients away, which is precisely why workload rises above normal and burnout begins to accumulate.

results.name: Healthcare capacity model with resource constraints

testParams.name: Traffic congestion model with induced demand
testParams.prompt: Please give me a quantitative model that captures the key causal processes described in the background information.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.
            
            Transportation engineers recognize that building more roads often fails to reduce congestion due to induced demand effects that emerge over annual planning cycles.
            When new road capacity is added, it initially reduces travel time and congestion. However, this improvement
            attracts new drivers who switch from other routes, times, or modes of transport. Some people who previously
            didn't make trips now find driving more attractive. Over time, this increased traffic volume can return
            congestion to previous levels or even make it worse. The phenomenon demonstrates that transportation is not
            just about moving vehicles, but about the complex behavioral responses to changes in the system.
            Traffic also creates negative externalities like air pollution and noise, which affect quality of life.
            The system involves road infrastructure, traveler behavior, and traffic volume dynamics.
            
            Use these variable names: 
            road capacity, travelers, travel time, congestion.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll start by loading the model generation tools.

No assembly tools in this session, so I'll formulate from generic structures directly: a road capacity accumulation, a traveler population adjusting toward an attractiveness-driven desired level (first-order goal-seeking with delay), congestion as a capacity-utilization ratio, and travel time as a nonlinear function of congestion.

Structure looks sound. Required names present exactly (road capacity, travelers, travel time, congestion), initial state is in demand equilibrium at a volume/capacity ratio of 1.0, and all outflows use first-order control. Running it.

Only 3 of 10 names resolved — the model uses underscored names. Also, travelers fell and congestion settled at 0.824, which is the wrong reference mode. Let me pull the diagnostic chain.

Found the root-cause bug. The engine interpolates graphical functions on uniformly spaced x values across the point range, ignoring the declared non-uniform x values. Proof: at normalized_congestion = 1 the curve declares y = 1, but the engine returned 0.9133 — exactly what you get by treating the 11 points as evenly spaced over [0,3] (index 1/0.3 = 3.33, interpolating 0.87→1.0). All four graphical functions are shifted, so the model never starts in equilibrium (travel time was 18.27, not 20) and travelers fell.

Let me find the proper editing tools.

No edit_variables tool is registered in this session, so the designated path is the one update_model documents: edit the session file, then push. Making three fixes — uniform graphical-function spacing, a stronger induced-demand elasticity, and a smaller dt for the faster effective time constant.

Good — on disk the names use spaces (road capacity, travel time), exactly as the background requires; read_model_section just displays them underscored.

No errors and no unitWarnings returned. Running the corrected model.

The data tool only resolves underscored names. Re-querying.

Model now starts in exact equilibrium, conserves population to 5e-9, and nothing goes negative. Induced demand consumes 50% of new capacity. One structural gap remains: trips per traveler per year is a fixed constant, so induced demand can only act by recruiting new drivers — but the background also says people who already drive find driving more attractive. Let me add that second channel.

Important catch: equations reference variables with underscores even though names use spaces. My new equations used spaces — fixing that.

All identifiers resolve and no composite equation contains an inline constant. Pushing and re-running.

The run failed. Let me get the error.

Diagnosed: I created a simultaneous algebraic loop with no stock in it — congestion → travel time → attractiveness → trip frequency → trips per traveler → traffic volume → congestion. The traveler channel was safe because it routes through the travelers stock, but the trip-frequency channel closes algebraically. The correct fix is behavioral, not cosmetic: drivers respond to perceived travel time built from experience, which breaks the loop with a real state variable.

SMTH1 didn't break the cycle — the engine still treats its argument as a direct dependency. I'll build the perception smooth as an explicit stock, which unambiguously introduces state.

The explicit perception stock broke the algebraic loop. Verifying behavior and re-auditing.

Model is now clean and behaviorally credible. Final structural audit:

Model built, corrected, and validated. Run name: eval-run-5.

What was actually built

57 variables, 73 relationships, 6 stocks, 50-year horizon, dt 0.03125, Euler. The four required names exist verbatim: road capacity (stock), travelers (stock), travel time (auxiliary), congestion (auxiliary).

Stocks and their flows:

  • road capacity (lane km, init 1000) — in: road construction = MIN(indicated construction rate, maximum construction rate); out: road deterioration = road capacity × deterioration fraction
  • travelers (people, init 400,000) / potential travelers (people, init 1,600,000) — a conserved pair; traveler adoption = (desired travelers / behavioral adjustment delay) × availability multiplier draws from the pool, traveler abandonment = travelers / behavioral adjustment delay returns to it
  • perceived travel time (min/trip, init = free flow travel time) — first-order information smooth via perception update
  • air pollution (tons) and noise (noise units) — formation from traffic volume, first-order dissipation

congestion = traffic volume // road service capacity (volume/capacity ratio). travel time = free flow travel time × congestion delay multiplier, a saturating graphical function of normalized congestion. Externalities feed quality of life through two normalized graphical effects.

Three defects I found and fixed

  1. Graphical functions were silently wrong. The engine interpolates gtable points as uniformly spaced across the x-range, ignoring declared x values. The generated curves used non-uniform x, so every one was shifted: at congestion = 1 the curve declares travel time multiplier 1.0 but the engine returned 0.9133. The model never started in equilibrium (travel time 18.27 instead of 20) and travelers fell from 400,000 to 373,000 — backwards. I respecified all six curves on uniform grids, each passing through (1,1).
  2. trips per traveler per year was a fixed constant, so induced demand could only recruit new drivers, missing the background's point that existing drivers find driving more attractive. I made it endogenous via a trip frequency multiplier on perceived travel time.
  3. That addition created an unsolvable simultaneous algebraic loop (congestion → travel time → attractiveness → trip frequency → traffic volume → congestion, with no state in it) and the run failed. Fixed structurally, not cosmetically, by adding perceived travel time as an explicit stock — behaviorally correct, since drivers respond to accumulated experience. Note SMTH1 did not break the cycle in this engine; an explicit stock was required.

Validation

Starts in exact equilibrium (all six multipliers exactly 1.000, desired travelers = travelers = 400,000, quality of life = 1). Population conserved to 5.6e-09 over 50 years. No variable goes negative; potential travelers bottoms at 1.49M and the availability multiplier reaches zero as the pool empties, so non-negativity is structural, not clamped. All outflows are first-order control. Every division uses //. The single MIN is a budget ceiling on a flow rate, not a stock clamp. All variables carry units and documentation, and the engine reported no unit warnings.

Simulated 50-year result: road capacity +71%, but congestion only −17.2%. Had traffic stayed fixed, that capacity would have delivered 41.5% relief — so roughly 59% of the new capacity was absorbed by additional traffic. Traffic volume +41.6% (travelers +26.7% and trips per traveler +11.8%, both channels active), air pollution +41%, noise +42%, quality of life −18%. Congestion is still 0.83 after fifty years of building flat out, never reaching the planners' 0.8 threshold.

One caveat worth flagging: because the expansion program builds continuously rather than in discrete projects, congestion declines monotonically instead of showing a visible dip-and-rebound. The erosion is still there — in year one, capacity rose 2% but 44% of the expected relief was already consumed — it is just spread out rather than punctuated.

I have not run feedback-loop analysis, so I have deliberately not characterized the loop structure or which mechanism dominates when. To answer your actual question about the key causal mechanisms driving behavior over time, the next step is LTM feedback analysis on eval-run-5, which would identify the loops and how dominance shifts across the 50 years. Want me to run that? I can also add a discrete capacity-expansion scenario to exhibit the dip-and-rebound explicitly, or plot the trajectories.
