variables.name: Road Rage Incidents
variables.documentation: The stock of active road rage incidents (aggressive driving behaviour caused by anger and frustration) currently occurring in the driving population. It accumulates newly triggered incidents and drains as incidents de-escalate.

variables.name: road rage incident onset
variables.documentation: Rate at which new road rage incidents begin. The exposed driving population times a baseline propensity, amplified or damped by the dimensionless aggression propensity that carries all of the driver-state feedbacks.

variables.name: road rage incident de escalation
variables.documentation: First-order drain of the incident stock: incidents cool down after an average duration. Formulating it as stock over a time constant guarantees the stock can never go negative.

variables.name: average road rage incident duration
variables.documentation: Average time an active road rage incident (episode of aggressive, angry driving) persists before it de-escalates.

variables.name: initial road rage incidents
variables.documentation: Initial number of active road rage incidents, chosen so the base run begins close to the pre-existing balance of onset and de-escalation.

variables.name: drivers at risk
variables.documentation: Size of the exposed driving population (vehicles on the road) that can potentially generate or witness aggressive driving.

variables.name: baseline incident propensity
variables.documentation: Fraction of the driving population per week that would start an aggressive-driving episode under normal (reference) driver-state conditions.

variables.name: incidents per aggressive driver
variables.documentation: Explicit unit-bridging conversion: each aggressive driver-trigger produces one road rage incident.

variables.name: aggression propensity
variables.documentation: Dimensionless multiplier on incident onset. It is the product of the psychological, situational and learned-behaviour effects, so it equals 1 when every driver-state input sits at its reference level.

variables.name: effect of Stress and Anxiety on aggression
variables.documentation: High stress makes drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. Centred on 1 at reference stress and floored at zero.

variables.name: stress sensitivity on aggression
variables.documentation: How strongly a deviation of driver stress from its reference level changes the propensity to aggress.

variables.name: reference stress and anxiety
variables.documentation: Normal level of the driver stress and anxiety index, at which the stress effect on aggression equals 1.

variables.name: effect of Frustration on aggression
variables.documentation: Feeling blocked by other drivers converts into anger and aggression. Centred on 1 at reference frustration and floored at zero.

variables.name: frustration sensitivity on aggression
variables.documentation: Strength of the frustration channel into aggressive driving.

variables.name: reference frustration
variables.documentation: Normal level of the frustration index, at which the frustration effect on aggression equals 1.

variables.name: effect of Normalization of Aggressive Driving on aggression
variables.documentation: Learned behaviour channel: the more aggressive driving is seen as normal and acceptable, the more readily drivers engage in it.

variables.name: normalization sensitivity on aggression
variables.documentation: Strength of the learned-behaviour (social normalization) channel. This is the dominant reinforcing gain in the model.

variables.name: reference normalization of aggressive driving
variables.documentation: Normal level of social normalization of aggressive driving, at which its effect on aggression equals 1. Set to the level the learned-behaviour stock would settle at under initial incident density, so the run starts essentially at balance and the reinforcing structure is nudged into motion by initial normalization sitting just above it.

variables.name: effect of Perceived Provocations on aggression
variables.documentation: Being cut off, tailgated or honked at provokes anger and retaliatory behaviour. Centred on 1 at the reference provocation level.

variables.name: provocation sensitivity on aggression
variables.documentation: Strength of the retaliation channel: how strongly extra perceived provocations raise aggressive driving.

variables.name: reference perceived provocations
variables.documentation: Normal level of perceived provocations, at which the provocation effect on aggression equals 1.

variables.name: effect of Personality Traits on aggression
variables.documentation: Impulsive, hostile or competitive personalities raise the population propensity to road rage. Exogenous multiplier centred on 1.

variables.name: personality sensitivity on aggression
variables.documentation: Strength of the personality-trait channel into aggressive driving.

variables.name: reference personality traits
variables.documentation: Normal prevalence of aggressive personality traits, at which the personality effect equals 1.

variables.name: Personality Traits
variables.documentation: Exogenous prevalence of impulsive, hostile or competitive personalities in the driving population (0 to 1 index).

variables.name: Frustration
variables.equation: MIN(1, congestion_weight_on_frustration * congestion_pressure + impatience_weight_on_frustration * Impatience + road_design_weight_on_frustration * Road_Design)
variables.documentation: Index of feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers. It rises with congestion pressure (delays and stop-and-go), with impatience, and with poor road design. Clipped at 1 to stay a bounded index.

variables.name: congestion weight on frustration
variables.documentation: Weight of congestion pressure in forming frustration.

variables.name: impatience weight on frustration
variables.documentation: Weight of impatience in forming frustration.

variables.name: road design weight on frustration
variables.documentation: Weight of poor road design (narrow lanes, confusing intersections) in forming frustration.

variables.name: Impatience
variables.documentation: Index of drivers running late or having a low tolerance for delays. Rises with experienced delay (congestion pressure) and with exogenous schedule pressure.

variables.name: congestion weight on impatience
variables.documentation: Weight of congestion pressure (delay) in forming impatience.

variables.name: schedule pressure weight on impatience
variables.documentation: Weight of running late in forming impatience.

variables.name: schedule pressure
variables.documentation: Exogenous degree to which drivers are running late (0 to 1 index).

variables.name: provocation exposure
variables.documentation: Dimensionless exposure to provoking events: drivers provoked per active incident as a share of the driving population, plus the close-quarters interactions generated by congestion density.

variables.name: share of drivers provoked
variables.documentation: Share of drivers actually provoked, converted from exposure by the saturating form 1 - EXP(-exposure). Approaches 1 asymptotically, so the retaliation channel meets diminishing returns instead of being switched off by a clip.

variables.name: provocation perception time
variables.documentation: Time over which drivers' sense of how often they are cut off, tailgated or honked at adjusts to actual conditions.

variables.name: initial perceived provocations
variables.documentation: Initial perceived provocation level, set to the share of drivers provoked implied by initial incidents and congestion.

variables.name: Perceived Provocations
variables.documentation: Perceived rate at which drivers experience being cut off, tailgated or honked at. A first-order smooth of the actual share of drivers provoked, because provocation is a remembered impression that builds and decays over time rather than tracking conditions instantly.

variables.name: provocations per incident
variables.documentation: Number of drivers provoked (cut off, tailgated, honked at) per active road rage incident. Bridges incidents to a share of the driving population.

variables.name: congestion weight on provocations
variables.documentation: Weight by which congestion density itself raises the perceived rate of provocations.

variables.name: congestion pressure
variables.documentation: Dimensionless measure of how loaded the road network is: queued/delayed vehicles relative to network capacity. Values near or above 1 mean heavy stop-and-go conditions.

variables.name: road network capacity
variables.documentation: Number of vehicles the road network can hold before conditions are perceived as heavily congested.

variables.name: Stress and Anxiety
variables.documentation: A 0 to 1 index of accumulated driver stress and anxiety in the driving population. It builds from stressful driving conditions and decays as drivers recover.

variables.name: initial stress and anxiety
variables.documentation: Initial value of the driver stress index, set near the level indicated by initial driving conditions.

variables.name: stress accumulation
variables.documentation: Build-up of driver stress driven by current conditions. Formulated as indicated stress over an adjustment time so the inflow is always non-negative; the recovery outflow does the draining.

variables.name: stress adjustment time
variables.documentation: Time over which stressful driving conditions translate into accumulated driver stress, and over which drivers unwind from it.

variables.name: stress recovery
variables.documentation: First-order recovery from accumulated stress, using the same adjustment time as the inflow so the pair forms an exact first-order smooth: equilibrium stress always equals indicated stress. Because the flow is proportional to the stock, the stress index can never fall below zero.

variables.name: indicated stress
variables.equation: MIN(1, congestion_weight_on_stress * congestion_pressure + weather_weight_on_stress * Weather_Conditions + sleep_weight_on_stress * Lack_of_Sleep + frustration_weight_on_stress * Frustration + provocation_weight_on_stress * Perceived_Provocations)
variables.documentation: The level of stress that current driving conditions call for: congestion, adverse weather, fatigue, frustration and provocations, each with its own weight, clipped at 1 to keep the index in range.

variables.name: congestion weight on stress
variables.documentation: Weight of congestion pressure in indicated driver stress.

variables.name: weather weight on stress
variables.documentation: Weight of adverse weather in indicated driver stress.

variables.name: sleep weight on stress
variables.documentation: Weight of fatigue (lack of sleep) in indicated driver stress.

variables.name: frustration weight on stress
variables.documentation: Weight of frustration in indicated driver stress.

variables.name: provocation weight on stress
variables.documentation: Weight of perceived provocations in indicated driver stress.

variables.name: Normalization of Aggressive Driving
variables.documentation: The learned-behaviour stock (0 to 1): the degree to which observing aggressive driving from others has made it seem normal and acceptable. It accumulates through social learning and fades with time.

variables.name: initial normalization of aggressive driving
variables.documentation: Initial degree of social normalization of aggressive driving, set just above its equilibrium so the reinforcing learned-behaviour loop is nudged into motion.

variables.name: normalization from observed aggression
variables.documentation: Social learning: witnessing aggressive driving makes it seem normal. The (1 - stock) complement is a structural saturation term so normalization cannot exceed one.

variables.name: learning rate
variables.documentation: Speed at which observed aggressive driving is internalized as normal behaviour.

variables.name: normalization fading
variables.documentation: Gradual erosion of the belief that aggressive driving is normal, as drivers turn over and norms are re-asserted. First-order drain keeps the stock non-negative.

variables.name: normalization fading time
variables.documentation: Average time over which learned acceptance of aggressive driving fades in the absence of new observations.

variables.name: observed aggressive driving
variables.documentation: Share of the driving population that witnesses aggressive driving. Exposure is witnesses per incident times incident density; the share is the standard saturating conversion 1 - EXP(-exposure), which approaches but never reaches 1. Social learning therefore saturates smoothly through diminishing returns rather than hitting an arithmetic ceiling.

variables.name: witnesses per incident
variables.documentation: Number of other drivers who observe each active road rage incident. Bridges incidents to a share of the driving population.

variables.name: Traffic Congestion
variables.documentation: Vehicles queued or delayed in the road network, producing heavy traffic, delays and stop-and-go conditions.

variables.name: initial traffic congestion
variables.documentation: Initial number of queued/delayed vehicles, set near the balance of entering and clearing flows.

variables.name: vehicles entering congestion
variables.documentation: Vehicles joining the congested queue: normal traffic loading, worsened by adverse weather and poor road design, plus extra vehicles delayed by crashes and lane blockages caused by aggressive and distracted driving.

variables.name: baseline traffic inflow
variables.documentation: Normal weekly rate at which vehicles enter congested conditions in the network.

variables.name: effect of Weather Conditions on traffic
variables.documentation: Adverse weather (heavy rain or snow) pushes more vehicles into delayed, congested conditions. Equals 1 in clear weather.

variables.name: weather sensitivity on traffic
variables.documentation: How much severe weather increases the rate of vehicles entering congestion.

variables.name: effect of Road Design on traffic
variables.documentation: Poor road design (narrow lanes, confusing intersections) pushes more vehicles into congested conditions. Equals 1 for ideal design.

variables.name: road design sensitivity on traffic
variables.documentation: How much poor road design increases the rate of vehicles entering congestion.

variables.name: congestion from crashes and blockages
variables.documentation: Aggressive driving combined with distraction raises the risk of accidents and lane blockages, delaying additional vehicles. This closes the congestion reinforcing loop R3.

variables.name: crash and blockage vehicles per incident
variables.documentation: Vehicles delayed per week per active road rage incident at full distraction prevalence, through crashes, near-misses and lane blockages.

variables.name: vehicles clearing congestion
variables.documentation: First-order clearing of queued vehicles. Because it is proportional to the stock, congestion can never go negative (balancing loop B1).

variables.name: congestion clearance time
variables.documentation: Time needed to clear queued vehicles, lengthened by poor road design and adverse weather.

variables.name: normal congestion clearance time
variables.documentation: Clearance time for queued vehicles under good design and clear weather.

variables.name: effect of Road Design on clearance
variables.documentation: Narrow lanes and confusing intersections slow the discharge of queues. Equals 1 for ideal design.

variables.name: road design sensitivity on clearance
variables.documentation: How much poor road design lengthens congestion clearance time.

variables.name: effect of Weather Conditions on clearance
variables.documentation: Heavy rain or snow slows traffic discharge and lengthens clearance time. Equals 1 in clear weather.

variables.name: weather sensitivity on clearance
variables.documentation: How much severe weather lengthens congestion clearance time.

variables.name: Weather Conditions
variables.documentation: Exogenous severity of adverse weather (heavy rain or snow): 0 = clear, 1 = severe.

variables.name: Road Design
variables.documentation: Exogenous index of road design quality where higher means poorer design (narrow lanes, confusing intersections).

variables.name: Lack of Sleep
variables.documentation: Exogenous prevalence of fatigue impairing judgement in the driving population (0 to 1 index).

variables.name: Distracted Driving
variables.documentation: Exogenous prevalence of phone use, texting or eating while driving (0 to 1 index), which raises crash and blockage risk.

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include at least 6 feedback loops and no more than 15 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build a quantitative SFD of the escalation dynamics. Let me first load the model tools.

Model design first. Time horizon 1754 (French and Indian War) to 1780, capturing escalation to hostilities. I'll build 5 stocks, 7 flows, 3 auxiliaries — 15 variables exactly — structured to generate at least six loops.

The prompt got truncated. Retrying more compactly.

Model generated. Now inspecting what was actually built.

Behavior validates well: no stock goes negative, debt declines monotonically toward but never past zero, Taxation rises after 1763 and partially reverses under repeal, the Boston Massacre term becomes significant around 1770, defiance peaks in the early 1770s, and Hostilities depart from zero at 1775.75 — Lexington and Concord. No unit warnings were reported by the engine.

Now the feedback analysis.

Twenty loops identified — fifteen reinforcing, five balancing. Let me get the dominance interpretation.

Model built and validated: exactly 15 variables, no unit warnings from the engine, no stock going negative, and Hostilities departing from zero at 1775.75 — Lexington and Concord — without that date being written into any equation as an event.

The model

Five stocks: French and Indian War Debt (130,000,000 pounds in 1754), Taxation (tax acts), Anti British Sentiment (grievance), Colonial Identity (identity, a ratchet with no outflow), and Hostilities (engagements). Seven flows connect them, and three auxiliaries carry the events you named: Boston Tea Party (defiance), Intolerable Acts (coercion), and Boston Massacre (atrocity).

The feedback analysis returned 20 loops — 15 reinforcing and 5 balancing. Here are the ones that matter.

The escalation, loop by loop

L19 / L18 (balancing) — the fiscal trigger. Britain wanted repayment for defending the colonies in the French and Indian War, so debt drives new taxes imposed, which builds Taxation, which yields revenue that retires debt. This is the loop that was supposed to solve the problem. It runs on a 30-year time constant and retires only 12 percent of the debt in 26 years. Because the debt never clears, the taxes never stop.

L9 / L3 (reinforcing) — the fix that fails. Taxation without representation in Parliament inflames Anti British Sentiment, grievance produces Boston Tea Party defiance, and defiance destroys compliance — smuggling, boycott, tea in the harbour. Collections fall, the debt stays large, and Parliament imposes still more taxes. The harder Britain pulls the revenue lever, the less revenue it gets and the more anger it buys.

L10 (reinforcing) — provocation and reprisal. Defiance provokes the Intolerable Acts, which close the port of Boston until the tea is paid for; collective punishment inflames more grievance, which produces more defiance. This is the classic escalation archetype, and it is what takes over in the early 1770s.

L12 / L14 (reinforcing) — troops among crowds. Coercion puts soldiers where defiant crowds are. The Boston Massacre is the product of the two, and as propaganda it feeds grievance directly. This loop is quadratic in grievance, which is why it grows super-exponentially: by 1780 the massacre term supplies 54 percent of all grievance generation.

L16 (reinforcing) — the identity ratchet. Shared coercion builds Colonial Identity, and identity multiplies defiance. Colonial Identity has no outflow. It goes from 1.0 to 3.42 and never comes back down, so nothing Britain does later can unwind it.

L15 / L13 (reinforcing) — war feeds anger. Once fighting starts, blood already spilt inflames further grievance. In this model it is real but weak, about 6 percent of grievance generation — hostilities are the output of the escalation, not its engine.

L1 / L20 and L2 (balancing) — why restraint failed. Parliament did back down under pressure: Taxation peaks at 2.30 acts in 1772 and then declines as the repeal loop takes hold. But grievance keeps accelerating anyway. Repeal only reduces an inflow to Anti British Sentiment — there is no channel by which concession drains the accumulated stock. Grievance cooling runs on a 10-year memory and is simply outrun. The concession worked on the taxes and failed on the memories.

L17 (balancing) — the trap at the centre. Coercion does suppress visible defiance, dividing it by 1 plus half the coercion. But that same Intolerable Acts link sits inside three reinforcing loops (L10 inflaming, L12 massacre, L16 identity) and only this one balancing loop. Its net effect is escalatory. Repression addressed the symptom and amplified the cause — that is the model's central structural insight.

Why 1775

The outbreak is a nonlinear gate: fighting begins only when grievance amplified by identity exceeds colonial tolerance, and only where coercive force is present to collide with. Around 1775.75 grievance of 6.9 times identity of 1.74 crosses the threshold of 12. The slow fiscal balancing loop had 21 years to solve the debt and could not; the fast defiance-coercion loops needed about a year per turn. That gain mismatch is the whole story.

Honest caveats

Two weaknesses worth flagging. First, a chronology problem: Boston Massacre (1770) is computed from Intolerable Acts (1774). The variable is really "British coercive presence," which existed from 1768 — the label is anachronistic even though the causal logic is right. Second, there is no balancing loop at all on Colonial Identity or Hostilities, and no war-spending inflow to the debt, so the amplifiers run unopposed and the model explains onset but not termination.

Useful next steps: a causal loop diagram of the six or seven loops above, a dominance plot showing the handover from the taxation loops to the coercion-atrocity loops around 1772, or a sensitivity run on the tolerance threshold and massacre coefficient to see how tightly the 1775 date is pinned. Say which you want.

variables.name: French and Indian War Debt
variables.documentation: Debt Britain ran up defending the colonies in the French and Indian War (1754-63) and expected the colonies to help repay. Initial value 130,000,000 pounds. It can only fall, through revenue actually collected in the colonies (debt repayment), so it can never go negative.

variables.name: Taxation
variables.documentation: Cumulative burden of revenue measures laid on the colonies (Stamp Act of 1765 on legal documents, newspapers and playing cards, and its successors). Starts at 0 tax acts because before the war debt matured Parliament levied no internal colonial revenue taxes. Rises with new acts and falls when Parliament backs down and repeals.

variables.name: Anti British Sentiment
variables.documentation: Accumulated colonial grievance against Britain. Starts at 0 in 1754 when the colonists still saw themselves as loyal Britons fighting a common enemy. It accumulates from taxation without representation, the Boston Massacre, the Intolerable Acts and the fighting itself, and drains slowly as memories fade.

variables.name: Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: Sense of being American rather than British, indexed to 1 in 1754 (normal, purely provincial identity). Modeled as a ratchet with no decay: shared grievance and shared coercion forge an identity that never un-forms.

variables.name: Hostilities
variables.documentation: Accumulated armed engagements between colonists and British forces. Zero until grievance amplified by identity exceeds colonial tolerance in the presence of coercion, which in this calibration happens around 1775 (Lexington and Concord).

variables.name: debt repayment
variables.documentation: Revenue actually collected and applied to the debt. It is a first-order drain: the debt divided by a repayment time of 30 years sets the maximum pace (this structure guarantees the stock approaches but never crosses zero), multiplied by the number of tax acts in force times a revenue yield of 0.2 per tax act, and multiplied by a compliance factor 1/(1+0.5*Boston Tea Party) with a defiance sensitivity of 0.5 per unit of defiance: smuggling, boycotts and destroyed cargo mean less and less of the levied revenue ever reaches the Treasury.

variables.name: new taxes imposed
variables.documentation: Parliament legislates new colonial revenue measures in proportion to the debt still outstanding relative to a reference debt of 130,000,000 pounds, at a tax imposition rate of 0.5 tax acts per year at full reference debt. The STEP at 1763 represents the end of the war: Parliament only turned to colonial revenue once the fighting stopped and the bill came due, so Taxation only begins rising after 1763.

variables.name: tax repeal
variables.documentation: Britain occasionally backs down under colonial pressure (repeal of the Stamp Act, partial repeal of the Townshend duties). First-order control on Taxation with a repeal time of 4 years, multiplied by a saturating effect of grievance, Anti British Sentiment/(1 grievance + Anti British Sentiment), which rises toward but never exceeds 1: protest speeds repeal, but no amount of protest gets everything repealed at once. This is the main balancing loop in the model.

variables.name: inflaming of sentiment
variables.documentation: Grievance generation, driven additively by four insults, each with its own weight: taxation without representation in Parliament (0.3 grievance per year per tax act), the Boston Massacre as propaganda (0.5 per year per unit atrocity), the Intolerable Acts as collective punishment (0.4 per year per unit coercion), and blood already spilt in the fighting itself (0.05 per year per engagement, the war-feeds-anger term).

variables.name: cooling of sentiment
variables.documentation: Grievance fades if nothing renews it. First-order control with a grievance memory time of 10 years, which is long: colonial resentment was slow to forget, so this drain is easily outrun by the inflaming loops.

variables.name: strengthening of colonial identity
variables.documentation: Shared grievance and shared coercion (the Boston Port Act punished all thirteen colonies by example, prompting the Continental Congress) forge an American identity at an identity formation rate of 0.03 identity units per year per unit of combined grievance and coercion. Slow but cumulative and irreversible.

variables.name: outbreak of hostilities
variables.documentation: Armed clashes begin only when grievance amplified by American identity exceeds a colonial tolerance threshold of 12 grievance-identity units, and only where coercive force is present to collide with: escalation rate 0.05 engagements per year per unit of excess grievance per unit coercion. The MAX keeps the flow at zero before the threshold is crossed, which in this calibration occurs around 1775.

variables.name: Boston Tea Party
variables.documentation: Organized acts of defiance (non-importation, tarring, and above all the destruction of the tea) showing Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation. It takes both anger and a sense of being a distinct people to act, so it is a defiance propensity of 0.3 times grievance times identity, and it is held down by coercive suppression through 1/(1+0.5*Intolerable Acts), a suppression effectiveness of 0.5 per unit coercion: troops and closed ports raise the price of open defiance without removing its cause.

variables.name: Intolerable Acts
variables.documentation: Harsh punitive laws answering defiance, above all closing the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the ruined tea. A coercion response rate of 0.5 units of coercion per unit of defiance. Parliament takes about a year to legislate its reprisal (the tea was destroyed in December 1773, the Coercive Acts passed in 1774), so the response is smoothed with a one-year response delay starting from zero; the delay also breaks what would otherwise be an instantaneous simultaneous loop between defiance and its suppression.

variables.name: Boston Massacre
variables.documentation: Atrocity produced when troops sent to enforce coercion collide with defiant crowds, as in 1770 when British soldiers fired on a Boston crowd and killed five, an event immediately turned into propaganda. Massacre propensity of 0.3 per unit of coercion per unit of defiance; it requires both an armed enforcing presence and a crowd willing to confront it, which is why it becomes significant only around 1770.

testParams.name: include a min number of feedback loops and a maximum number of variables for Road Rage
testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include at least 6 feedback loops and no more than 15 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build a quantitative SFD of road rage dynamics. First, loading the tools I need.

Model built, run (eval-run-1), data inspected, and feedback structure retrieved. Here is the feedback-based account of how road rage happens and where it is heading.

What the model is composed of (15 variables, exactly at your cap)

Stocks (2): Road Rage Incidents (incidents, init 50), Learned Aggressive Driving Behavior (dmnl, init 0.1) Flows (3): Road Rage Incident Rate, Incident Cooling Off Rate, Change in Learned Aggressive Driving Behavior Auxiliaries (5): Traffic Congestion, Perceived Provocations, Frustration, Driver Stress and Anxiety, Impatience Constants (5): Anger Cooling Off Time (1 week), Aggression Normalization Time (26 weeks), Reference Road Rage Incidents (100), Poor Road Design (0.4), Distracted Driving (0.3)

The incident rate is a saturating function of the average of the three psychological triggers (Frustration, Impatience, Driver Stress and Anxiety), amplified by (1 + Learned Aggressive Driving Behavior). Every physical drain is first-order (Road Rage Incidents / Anger Cooling Off Time), so the incident pool cannot go negative — confirmed in the data (minimum 39.9 incidents). The engine reported no unit warnings.

Simulated behavior (weeks 0–104)

wk 0 wk 4 wk 25 wk 63 wk 104
Road Rage Incidents 50.0 39.9 46.7 52.4 54.3
Learned Aggressive Driving Behavior 0.10 0.15 0.32 0.46 0.51
Perceived Provocations 0.85 0.76 0.92 1.07 1.12
Driver Stress and Anxiety 0.64 0.58 0.66 0.73 0.76

A fast dip, then slow S-shaped growth to a higher endemic level.

The feedback loops the analysis actually found

13 loops: 11 reinforcing, 2 balancing.

Fast escalation loops (all reinforcing, all closing through the incident stock in about a week):

  • L10: Frustration → Road Rage Incident Rate → Road Rage Incidents → Traffic Congestion → Frustration. Incidents block and slow traffic, congestion breeds frustration, frustration breeds more incidents.
  • L11: Frustration → Road Rage Incident Rate → Road Rage Incidents → Perceived Provocations → Frustration. The retaliation loop: aggressive acts are themselves the cut-offs, tailgating and honking that provoke the next driver.
  • L12: Impatience → Road Rage Incident Rate → Road Rage Incidents → Traffic Congestion → Impatience. Incident-induced delay raises impatience, which raises incidents.
  • L5 / L8: Driver Stress and Anxiety (directly, or via Impatience) → Road Rage Incident Rate → Road Rage Incidents → Traffic Congestion → back to stress. The stress-congestion spiral.
  • L4, L6, L7, L9: the same escalation running through longer chains (congestion or provocations → Frustration → Driver Stress and Anxiety → Impatience → rate). These are largely the same physical escalation counted several ways, because frustration, stress and impatience are algebraic cascades of the same two inputs.

Slow norm loops (the ones that actually move the trend):

  • L1 (reinforcing): Change in Learned Aggressive Driving Behavior → Learned Aggressive Driving Behavior → Road Rage Incident Rate → Road Rage Incidents → Perceived Provocations → Change in Learned Aggressive Driving Behavior. Observing aggression normalizes it, normalized aggression produces more aggression.
  • L2 (reinforcing): Learned Aggressive Driving Behavior → Perceived Provocations → Change in Learned Aggressive Driving Behavior → Learned Aggressive Driving Behavior. Once aggression is normal, ordinary driving is read as provocation.

Balancing loops (only two, and both are simple drains):

  • L13: Road Rage Incidents → Incident Cooling Off Rate → Road Rage Incidents. Anger subsides in about a week.
  • L3: goal-seeking adjustment of Learned Aggressive Driving Behavior toward the level implied by provocations, over 26 weeks.

Why the behavior looks the way it does

Weeks 0–4: the only fast loop, L13, dominates. The stock was initialized above the incident rate implied by the initial triggers, so cooling-off exceeds generation and incidents fall to about 39.9 — the quasi-equilibrium consistent with a low normalized-aggression level of 0.1. This first dip is an initialization transient, not a behavior mode of interest.

Weeks 4–104: Road Rage Incidents becomes a fast follower of the slow state. L1 and L2 push Learned Aggressive Driving Behavior from 0.10 to 0.51 over the 26-week normalization time, Perceived Provocations rises past 1.0, and incidents climb 36 percent off the trough. The fast reinforcing loops L4 through L12 contain no slow stock and have loop gain well below 1, so they do not drive the trend — they act as amplifiers that raise the gain and the final level of the slow loops.

Growth decelerates for two structural reasons: L3 closes the gap to a bounded target, and the saturating form of the incident rate reduces marginal sensitivity as trigger pressure grows. That converts what would otherwise be exponential escalation into an S-curve approaching a new, higher endemic equilibrium near 55 incidents.

What this implies for the future

Road rage in this structure is a ratchet, not an explosion. With exogenous drivers held constant, incidents settle at a permanently higher level than they started, because the slow norm stock locks in part of every episode of escalation. A temporary surge in provocations — a bad winter, a construction season, a distraction wave — does not simply wash out: the fast loops amplify it within a week, the norm stock absorbs a share of it, and it then decays only over the 26-week normalization time. Repeated shocks arriving faster than the norm can fade would step the equilibrium upward each time.

Critique and leverage

Structural weaknesses I would flag: the run does not start in equilibrium; Frustration, Driver Stress and Anxiety and Impatience are instantaneous rather than accumulating, which suppresses overshoot; Traffic Congestion has no traffic volume or clearance capacity; and the loop census is lopsided (11 reinforcing versus 2 trivial drains), so bounded growth comes from saturation rather than from any real societal counter-pressure.

Leverage, in order: cut the exogenous seeds Distracted Driving and Poor Road Design, since every loop multiplies them and lowering them shifts the whole equilibrium; weaken the Road Rage Incidents → Perceived Provocations link, which alone closes L1, L6, L9 and L11 and is the only way to starve the norm-learning engine; and speed incident clearance to break the congestion-mediated loops L4, L5, L7, L8, L10, L12 at once. Anger Cooling Off Time is a false lever — it appears in both the rate scale and the drain and cancels at equilibrium, changing settling speed only.

Boundary note: the 15-variable cap forced three background factors outside the model — Weather Conditions, Lack of Sleep and Personality Traits. All three would enter as exogenous multipliers on stress or on the incident rate, so they shift the equilibrium level but add no new loops. Weather in particular is worth adding as a seasonal input if you want the recurring annual pattern.

Next steps I would recommend: re-initialize Road Rage Incidents in equilibrium to clean the transient, make Driver Stress and Anxiety a stock with an adjustment time to test for overshoot, and run a sensitivity analysis on Distracted Driving, Poor Road Design and Aggression Normalization Time. I can also plot the trajectory with dominant-loop bands, or draw the causal loop diagram of the escalation-plus-normalization loopset, if you want to see it.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

Building the escalation model now.

Model built with 82 variables. Now running it to check behavior.

Behavior is credible in shape. Two structural fixes needed: colonial identity erodes toward zero pre-1763 (identity should not decay when there is no grievance yet), and the hostilities outbreak is scaled weakly. Let me check for an edit tool.

No edit_variables tool is registered in this session, so the sanctioned path is the update_model workflow (edit the session file, then push through the tool). Making two minimal, targeted changes.

No errors or unit warnings reported by the engine. Re-running.

All stocks non-negative, identity now holds steady pre-1763, and hostilities show a clean regime change. Now getting the actual feedback loop analysis.

26 loops identified. Now getting the LTM narrative and Seldon's analysis.

Seldon flagged real issues: the 1775 rise is driven by an exogenous pulse hitting a hand-placed threshold rather than endogenously, and several loops implied by the background are missing. Let me close them.

Behavior is now endogenous — escalation pressure keeps climbing after 1773 rather than plateauing. Running Seldon's DT test for integration artifacts.

DT sensitivity is ~20% in magnitude but the qualitative shape is identical. Keeping the finer DT. Now refreshing feedback analysis on the final structure.

I built and validated a simulating stock-flow model of the escalation, 1754 to 1776. Here is what it says.

What the model contains

87 variables. Six stocks carry the story: French and Indian War Debt, Taxation, Anti British Sentiment, Colonial Identity, Acts of Colonial Defiance, and Hostilities. The named events enter as timed shocks whose size and date are separate named constants: Stamp Act Grievance (1765), Boston Massacre Outrage (1770), Boston Tea Party Defiance (1773), Intolerable Acts Severity and Boston Port Closure (1774). Lack of Colonial Representation in Parliament is the multiplier that converts Taxation into anger, so taxation only causes grievance because there is no representation.

The engine reported no errors and no unit warnings. All stocks stay non-negative on first-order outflow control, with no MIN/MAX clamps on stock levels.

The feedback explanation

Feedback analysis on the final run returns 67 loops: 48 reinforcing, 19 balancing. The story is a handful of reinforcing structures slowly outgrowing a set of balancing structures that were, crucially, being dismantled from the inside.

1754 to 1763 — the charge is loaded. Only the debt moves, rising to 90. No sentiment, no defiance, identity flat at its baseline. Nothing endogenous is happening yet; the war is loading the stock that will drive everything.

1763 to 1766 — the balancers hold. Taxation begins, the Stamp Act lands in 1765, and sentiment lifts to about 6. It goes no further because three balancing loops are strong: conciliation (Anti British Sentiment produces British concessions, which repeal taxes and drain the sentiment that prompted them), simple forgetting, and defiance cooling off. The reason conciliation works here is that Loyalty to the Crown stands at 0.90. The Stamp Act crisis does not become a revolution because the grievance stocks are near empty and the accommodation channel is wide open.

1766 to 1772 — the reinforcing loops take over. Sentiment climbs from 6 to 29, Colonial Identity from 5.5 to 18.7, defiance from 0.5 to 9.6. Four reinforcing structures are now turning:

  • The tax-resistance debt trap. Defiance destroys revenue compliance, so the war debt is not retired, so British demand for repayment persists, so more Taxation is imposed on an angrier population. Taxing the colonies destroyed the ability to collect from them.
  • Punitive backlash. Defiance provokes British Coercion, coercion produces harsh law, harsh law produces sentiment, sentiment produces identity, identity produces more defiance. Punishment intended to isolate Boston manufactured a shared political self-image instead.
  • Identity grievance amplification. Anti British Sentiment builds Colonial Identity, and identity amplifies every subsequent grievance. The same measure that read as an administrative nuisance in 1765 read as an assault on rights in 1774.
  • Propaganda circulation. In this model the Boston Massacre is not exogenous — it is a function of British Coercion, because the troops were in Boston as coercion. The massacre feeds propaganda, propaganda feeds sentiment and identity, and identity widens the networks that circulate the propaganda. A single incident becomes a renewable grievance rather than a one-time shock.

The decisive mechanism. Over this same period, Colonial Identity erodes Loyalty to the Crown, from 0.90 down to 0.17. Because concessions are offered to loyal subjects, falling loyalty shuts off British Concessions — which peak around 1772 and then decline even as anger keeps climbing. This registers in the analysis as a reinforcing loop that runs through the conciliation channel: rising identity does not merely lose a race against the escalation loops, it disables the only balancer capable of stopping them. The same growing American identity that made accommodation necessary made it unavailable.

1773 to 1775 — the outbreak. The Boston Tea Party lifts defiance from 9.6 to 25 in a single step and collapses revenue compliance to 0.46, permanently locking in the fiscal grievance. The Intolerable Acts and the closing of the port follow. The port closure came with an escape route — pay for the ruined tea and the port reopens — and the model contains that balancing loop, but willingness to pay falls with Colonial Identity, so the escape route closes itself. Meanwhile Hostilities now feeds back reinforcingly: fighting brings troop reinforcement, which is more coercion, which is more grievance; and shared fighting forges identity faster than grievance alone. Hostilities go from 1.1 in 1773 to 15 in 1774 to 33 in early 1775 and 70 by 1776, while escalation pressure keeps climbing rather than levelling off.

Why 1775 and not 1765

The regime change is a matter of accumulated state, not of any single provocation. In 1765 the grievance stocks were near zero, identity was at baseline, defiance had no organizational base, and high loyalty kept conciliation strong enough to absorb a tax dispute. By 1773 sentiment had accumulated past 29, identity had nearly quadrupled, the propaganda structures were generating grievance without new provocations, and loyalty had fallen far enough that concessions had almost no leverage. The same British policy that could be defused in 1766 was, on the accumulated stocks of 1774, an accelerant.

Leverage

The highest-leverage parameter in the model is the British coercive reflex. Coercion supplies roughly half of escalation pressure by 1775 and feeds six reinforcing loops through the Intolerable Acts and the port closure, while the only balancer it creates — deterrence — is weak. Punishing Boston was self-defeating. But the deeper implication is about timing: the loop that had to be kept alive was conciliation, and its strength was proportional to Loyalty to the Crown. Conciliation, and above all representation, had to arrive before the identity stock accumulated. Once it had, no later concession could work.

Critique and caveats

Honest limits on this model. Lack of Colonial Representation in Parliament is a frozen constant — Britain can never concede the one thing actually at issue, which is the sharpest criticism of the boundary, though it is faithful to the background you gave me. Tax imposition runs as a smooth legislative stream rather than as the discrete series of acts. There is no boycott-to-merchant-losses channel, which is a real repeal mechanism outside your background. Sentiment and identity have no ceilings despite their index labels. And on a DT test at 0.0625 versus 0.25, the magnitude of the 1776 hostilities level shifts by about 20 percent in the steep phase, though the shape — flat through the 1760s, sharp takeoff after 1773 — is unchanged. Treat the levels as an index, not a measurement.

Would you like me to draw the simplified causal loop diagram of this structure, plot Hostilities with the dominant-loop periods shaded, or run a counterfactual — for example, granting representation in 1765, or halving the coercive response — to test the leverage claim?

variables.name: French and Indian War Debt
variables.documentation: Stock of British debt incurred defending the colonies in the French and Indian War (1754-1763). The British want the colonies to repay it, so this debt is the original driver of colonial taxation. Starts at zero in 1754 and accumulates war spending until the war ends.

variables.name: War Spending
variables.documentation: British military spending on the defence of the colonies during the French and Indian War. It runs at a constant annual rate from 1754 and switches off when the war ends in 1763 (the STEP turns spending off).

variables.name: Annual War Spending
variables.documentation: Named constant for the annual rate of British war expenditure charged to colonial defence during the French and Indian War.

variables.name: War End Year
variables.documentation: Year the French and Indian War ends (1763). After this date war spending stops and Parliament begins taxing the colonies to recover the debt.

variables.name: Debt Repayment
variables.documentation: Repayment of the war debt out of revenue actually collected in the colonies. Formulated as first-order control on the debt stock (debt divided by a repayment time) scaled by how much revenue is actually collected, so the debt can never be driven negative.

variables.name: Debt Repayment Time
variables.documentation: Named adjustment time over which the war debt would be retired if revenue collection were at its reference level.

variables.name: Reference Revenue
variables.documentation: Reference (normal) level of colonial revenue used to normalise actual revenue collected in the debt repayment equation.

variables.name: Revenue Collected
variables.documentation: Revenue actually received by the Crown: the level of taxation times its yield, reduced by colonial non-compliance. This is the link that makes defiance starve the Treasury.

variables.name: Revenue Yield per Tax Unit
variables.documentation: Named constant converting a unit of taxation into revenue when compliance is complete.

variables.name: Revenue Compliance
variables.documentation: Fraction of taxes actually paid. Boycotts, smuggling and other acts of colonial defiance reduce compliance toward zero. Bounded below at zero for structural reasons.

variables.name: Non Compliance Strength
variables.documentation: How strongly accumulated acts of colonial defiance destroy tax compliance.

variables.name: Defiance Index Scale
variables.documentation: Full-scale value of the 0-100 defiance index, used to normalise the defiance stock.

variables.name: British Demand for Colonial Repayment
variables.documentation: Normalised British political demand that the colonies repay the cost of their defence. The larger the outstanding war debt relative to a reference debt, the harder Parliament presses for colonial revenue.

variables.name: Reference War Debt
variables.documentation: Reference scale of the war debt used to normalise British demand for repayment.

variables.name: Taxation
variables.documentation: Stock of British taxes in force on the colonies (index of tax burden). Modelled as a stock because taxes once enacted persist until repealed. Zero before 1763 because the colonies were not taxed for imperial revenue.

variables.name: Tax Imposition
variables.documentation: Rate at which Parliament enacts new colonial taxes. Driven by the demand that the colonies repay the war debt (only after the war ends in 1763) plus the discrete enactment of the Stamp Act in 1765.

variables.name: Tax Imposition Sensitivity
variables.documentation: How much new taxation Parliament enacts per year per unit of demand for colonial repayment.

variables.name: Stamp Act Grievance
variables.documentation: The 1765 Stamp Act, which taxed legal documents, newspapers and playing cards. Represented as a one-off pulse that adds a discrete block of taxation (and hence grievance) in 1765.

variables.name: Stamp Act Magnitude
variables.documentation: Size of the tax burden added by the Stamp Act of 1765.

variables.name: Stamp Act Year
variables.documentation: Year the Stamp Act was imposed (1765).

variables.name: Tax Repeal
variables.documentation: Repeal of colonial taxes when loyal petitions produce British concessions (as with the repeal of the Stamp Act). First-order in the tax stock so taxation cannot go negative. This is the conciliation balancing loop.

variables.name: Tax Repeal Time
variables.documentation: Time constant for how quickly Parliament repeals taxes once it decides to concede.

variables.name: British Concessions
variables.documentation: Concessions won by loyal colonial petitioning. Requires both grievance (to motivate petitions) and residual loyalty to the Crown (to make petitions credible), so concessions vanish as colonial identity replaces loyalty.

variables.name: Concession Sensitivity
variables.documentation: Strength of the conciliation response: how readily petitions and loyal protest produce British concessions.

variables.name: Loyalty to the Crown
variables.documentation: Residual attachment to the Crown that makes conciliation possible. It is eroded as a separate American identity accumulates, which is what finally disables the balancing conciliation loop.

variables.name: Loyalty Erosion Strength
variables.documentation: How strongly growing colonial identity erodes loyalty to the Crown.

variables.name: Anti British Sentiment
variables.documentation: Dimensionless 0-100 index stock of colonial anger at Britain. Zero in 1754 (a stable colonial relationship). It accumulates grievance from taxation without representation, from coercion, and from Boston Massacre propaganda, and drains through concessions and the passage of time.

variables.name: Rising Anti British Sentiment
variables.equation: Colonial_Identity_Amplifier * (Tax_Grievance_Sensitivity * Taxation * Lack_of_Colonial_Representation_in_Parliament + Coercion_Grievance_Sensitivity * (Intolerable_Acts_Severity + Boston_Port_Closure) + Propaganda_Grievance_Sensitivity * Boston_Massacre_Propaganda)
variables.documentation: Inflow of anti-British feeling. Taxation only angers colonists because they have no representatives in Parliament, so the two are multiplied. British coercion (the Intolerable Acts and the closure of the port of Boston) and the propaganda use of the Boston Massacre add further grievance, and all of it is amplified by colonial identity.

variables.name: Tax Grievance Sensitivity
variables.documentation: Anger generated per year per unit of taxation when the colonists have no representation at all.

variables.name: Coercion Grievance Sensitivity
variables.documentation: Anger generated per year per unit of severity of the Intolerable Acts and the Boston port closure.

variables.name: Propaganda Grievance Sensitivity
variables.documentation: Anger generated per year per unit of circulating Boston Massacre propaganda.

variables.name: Lack of Colonial Representation in Parliament
variables.documentation: Index of the colonists' complete absence of representatives in Parliament (1 = no representation whatsoever). This is the multiplier that converts taxation into anger: taxation without representation.

variables.name: Colonial Identity Amplifier
variables.documentation: Multiplier by which a stronger sense of American identity increases colonial sensitivity to taxation and to British coercion. Equals 1 when identity is zero.

variables.name: Identity Amplification Strength
variables.documentation: How strongly full colonial identity amplifies grievance at taxation and coercion.

variables.name: Anti British Sentiment Decay
variables.documentation: Cooling of anti-British feeling over time, accelerated by British concessions such as tax repeal. First-order in the sentiment stock so sentiment cannot go negative.

variables.name: Sentiment Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: Time over which colonial anger fades if no new grievance occurs.

variables.name: Sentiment Index Scale
variables.documentation: Full-scale value of the 0-100 anti-British sentiment index.

variables.name: Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: Dimensionless 0-100 index stock of a distinctly American identity. A stock because identity accumulates from shared grievance and propaganda and decays only very slowly. It amplifies grievance, defiance and willingness to fight, and erodes loyalty to the Crown.

variables.name: Initial Colonial Identity
variables.documentation: Weak but non-zero sense of American identity in 1754, before the escalation began.

variables.name: Colonial Identity Formation
variables.documentation: Formation of American identity. A baseline autonomous component from the ordinary growth of colonial society, plus identity forged out of shared anger at Britain and out of the circulation of Boston Massacre propaganda, which taught colonists to see themselves as one people against the Crown.

variables.name: Identity Formation Sensitivity
variables.documentation: Identity formed per year per unit of shared grievance and propaganda.

variables.name: Identity from Hostilities Sensitivity
variables.documentation: Identity formed per year per unit of hostilities, representing how shared fighting against British troops forges a common American nationhood faster than grievance alone.

variables.name: Autonomous Colonial Identity Formation
variables.documentation: Baseline rate at which a distinctly American identity is renewed by the ordinary growth of colonial society (shared newspapers, commerce, generations born in America), independent of any grievance against Britain. Set structurally to exactly offset identity erosion at the initial identity level, so identity holds steady before the escalation begins rather than decaying away.

variables.name: Colonial Identity Erosion
variables.documentation: Very slow fading of identity, given first-order control on the identity stock so it can never go negative.

variables.name: Identity Erosion Time
variables.documentation: Very long decay time for colonial identity, reflecting that identity once formed does not decay quickly.

variables.name: Identity Index Scale
variables.documentation: Full-scale value of the 0-100 colonial identity index.

variables.name: Boston Massacre Outrage
variables.documentation: The 1770 shooting by British soldiers of a crowd of colonists in Boston, in which five people were killed. Its severity is proportional to the coercion that put troops in the streets in the first place, so the massacre is not a bolt from the blue but a product of the coercive response to colonial defiance. A permanent step from 1770 onward, since the event became a fixed grievance.

variables.name: Boston Massacre Magnitude
variables.documentation: Size of the outrage created by the Boston Massacre of 1770.

variables.name: Boston Massacre Year
variables.documentation: Year of the Boston Massacre (1770).

variables.name: Boston Massacre Propaganda
variables.documentation: The massacre used as a propaganda tool by the colonists. Its effect equals the raw outrage times how widely it circulates, and its circulation grows with colonial identity, which closes the reinforcing propaganda loop.

variables.name: Propaganda Circulation
variables.documentation: Effectiveness and reach of colonial propaganda, which rises with a shared American identity (common newspapers, committees and networks). Equals 1 when identity is zero.

variables.name: Propaganda Amplification Strength
variables.documentation: How much a full colonial identity multiplies the circulation and effectiveness of propaganda.

variables.name: Acts of Colonial Defiance
variables.documentation: Dimensionless 0-100 index stock accumulating colonial acts of defiance: boycotts, non-compliance, tarring, and above all the Boston Tea Party. Zero in 1754. Defiance provokes British coercion and starves the Treasury of revenue.

variables.name: New Acts of Defiance
variables.equation: (Defiance_Sensitivity * Anti_British_Sentiment * (1 + Identity_Defiance_Strength * Colonial_Identity / Identity_Index_Scale) + Boston_Tea_Party_Defiance) * Coercive_Deterrence * Restraint_from_War_Costs
variables.documentation: Rate at which colonists commit new acts of defiance. It rises with anti-British sentiment and with colonial identity, receives the single largest act in the Boston Tea Party of 1773, and is held down by British coercive deterrence and by fear of the costs of war.

variables.name: Defiance Sensitivity
variables.documentation: Acts of defiance generated per year per unit of anti-British sentiment.

variables.name: Identity Defiance Strength
variables.documentation: How much a full colonial identity multiplies willingness to act defiantly rather than merely complain.

variables.name: Boston Tea Party Defiance
variables.documentation: The Boston Tea Party of 1773, the major act of defiance against British rule showing that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation. Modelled as a single large pulse into the stock of colonial defiance.

variables.name: Boston Tea Party Magnitude
variables.documentation: Size of the Boston Tea Party as an act of defiance, the largest single act in the model.

variables.name: Boston Tea Party Year
variables.documentation: Year of the Boston Tea Party (1773).

variables.name: Defiance Subsidence
variables.documentation: Fading of active defiance if grievance stops renewing it. First-order in the defiance stock so defiance cannot go negative.

variables.name: Defiance Memory Time
variables.documentation: Time over which acts of defiance remain politically live before subsiding.

variables.name: British Coercion
variables.documentation: British coercive response: troops, customs enforcement and punitive legislation. It is provoked both by accumulated colonial defiance and by actual hostilities, since fighting brings further reinforcement of troops.

variables.name: Coercion Sensitivity
variables.documentation: How much coercion Britain applies per unit of accumulated colonial defiance.

variables.name: Coercion Reinforcement Sensitivity
variables.documentation: Additional coercion Britain applies per unit of actual hostilities, as fighting brings reinforcement of troops and tighter military government.

variables.name: Coercion Reference
variables.documentation: Reference level of coercion used to normalise coercion in the deterrence and Intolerable Acts equations.

variables.name: Coercive Deterrence
variables.documentation: Short-run suppression of open defiance by the presence of British force. Equals 1 with no coercion and falls toward zero as coercion rises. This is the coercive deterrence balancing loop.

variables.name: Deterrence Strength
variables.documentation: How effectively British coercion suppresses open acts of defiance in the short run.

variables.name: Intolerable Acts Severity
variables.documentation: Severity of the harsh British laws the colonists called the Intolerable Acts, passed in 1774 in response to the destruction of the tea. Their severity is proportional to the coercion provoked by colonial defiance, which is what closes the grievance-to-repression spiral.

variables.name: Intolerable Acts Magnitude
variables.documentation: Scale of the punitive legislation known as the Intolerable Acts at reference coercion.

variables.name: Intolerable Acts Year
variables.documentation: Year the Intolerable Acts were passed (1774).

variables.name: Boston Port Closure
variables.documentation: The act that closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined. It bites only to the extent that the colonists refuse to pay: paying would reopen the port. Because a hardening American identity makes payment unthinkable, this escape route closes and the grievance persists.

variables.name: Port Closure Weight
variables.documentation: Share of the Intolerable Acts' severity represented by the closure of the port of Boston.

variables.name: Refusal to Pay for the Ruined Tea
variables.documentation: How strongly a hardening American identity makes the colonists refuse to pay compensation for the tea they had ruined.

variables.name: Payment for the Ruined Tea
variables.documentation: Fraction of the compensation for the ruined tea that the colonists are willing to pay. Paying reopens the port of Boston, which is the escape route the Intolerable Acts themselves offered. A hardening American identity makes payment unthinkable, so this balancing escape route closes itself.

variables.name: Hostilities
variables.documentation: Dimensionless 0-100 index stock of armed hostilities between Britain and the colonies. The reference behaviour: essentially zero through the 1760s and rising sharply from about 1775 as the reinforcing loops overwhelm conciliation and deterrence.

variables.name: Outbreak of Hostilities
variables.documentation: Rate at which confrontation turns into armed hostilities. It is negligible while escalation pressure is below normal and rises steeply once defiance and coercion pass the threshold, and it is amplified by the strength of American identity (a people willing to fight for itself).

variables.name: Hostilities Outbreak Rate
variables.documentation: Reference rate at which hostilities break out when escalation pressure is at its normal (threshold) level.

variables.name: Identity Hostilities Strength
variables.documentation: How much a full American identity multiplies the willingness to take up arms.

variables.name: Escalation Pressure
variables.documentation: Combined pressure toward armed conflict from colonial defiance and British coercion, normalised so that 1 is the level at which open fighting becomes likely.

variables.name: Escalation Reference
variables.documentation: Reference combined level of defiance plus coercion at which escalation pressure equals one.

variables.name: Escalation Effect on Hostilities
variables.documentation: Highly nonlinear effect of escalation pressure on the outbreak of hostilities. Normalised so that pressure of 1 gives an effect of 1; below that, confrontation stays political, above it fighting escalates very steeply.

variables.name: De escalation of Hostilities
variables.documentation: Fading of armed hostilities if the pressures driving them relax. First-order in the hostilities stock so it cannot go negative.

variables.name: Hostilities De escalation Time
variables.documentation: Time over which hostilities subside in the absence of continued escalation pressure.

variables.name: Hostilities Index Scale
variables.documentation: Full-scale value of the 0-100 hostilities index.

variables.name: Fear of War Costs
variables.documentation: Perceived cost of war, rising with actual hostilities. It is the signal that restrains further defiance.

variables.name: Restraint from War Costs
variables.documentation: Damping of new acts of defiance caused by fear of the costs of war. Equals 1 when there are no hostilities and falls as fighting grows. This is the fear-of-war-costs balancing loop.

variables.name: War Cost Fear Strength
variables.documentation: How strongly the prospect of war's costs restrains colonial defiance.

testParams.name: include requested variables for Road Rage
testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how road rage happens and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how road rage incidents might change in the future. Your response must include the variables "Traffic Congestion", "Driver Stress" and "Accidents".

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how road rage happens. I'd like to know what causes road rage in society.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Road rage, defined as aggressive driving behavior caused by anger and frustration, can be triggered by various factors: 
Psychological Factors: 
Stress and Anxiety:
High stress levels can make drivers more irritable and prone to aggressive reactions. 
Personality Traits:
Individuals with impulsive, hostile, or competitive personalities may be more likely to engage in road rage. 
Frustration:
Feeling frustrated or blocked by other drivers can lead to anger and aggression. 
Situational Factors: 
Traffic Congestion:
Heavy traffic, delays, and stop-and-go conditions can increase stress and impatience. 
Perceived Provocations:
Being cut off, tailgated, or honked at can provoke anger and retaliatory behavior. 
Impatience:
Drivers who are running late or have a low tolerance for delays may become aggressive. 
Environmental Factors: 
Road Design:
Poor road design, such as narrow lanes or confusing intersections, can contribute to traffic congestion and frustration. 
Weather Conditions:
Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or snow, can increase stress and make driving more challenging. 
Other Factors: 
Learned Behavior: Observing aggressive driving behavior from others can normalize it and increase the likelihood of engaging in road rage. 
Lack of Sleep: Fatigue can impair judgment and make drivers more susceptible to anger. 
Distracted Driving: Using a phone, texting, or eating while driving can increase the risk of accidents and provoke anger.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build a quantitative SFD of road rage dynamics from the background information provided. Let me start by loading the modeling tools.

Let me check the current model state before building.

Empty model — building from scratch. I'll construct a stock-flow structure around the causal chains in your background material.

Model generated. Now I must inspect what was actually built rather than assume.

Model built with 96 variables, all six stocks initialized in equilibrium (I verified inflow=outflow at t=0 for each). Let me check specs and relationships, then run.

Structure and relationships are complete and coherent. Running the simulation.

Run produced no variables — it failed. Let me diagnose and fix. Loading edit tools.

No edit_variables tool exists in this session — update_model is the designated modification path and it reads the session file. First, let me confirm the failure is real by re-running.

Run genuinely produced no data. I need the engine's error report. Let me check the model file's top-level validation metadata (keys only).

No errors and no unitWarnings fields — the engine reported none. The run failures appear to be environmental (harness names them "eval-run-failed-N"). Let me test whether feedback analysis is available.

Feedback loop data is available. Let me extract the full loop inventory.

27 loops identified (18 reinforcing, 9 balancing), but no LTM dominance scores — those require successful run data. Let me retry the run and independently verify the model won't explode or go negative.

Model verified structurally sound: stocks stay positive, no explosion, bounded oscillating growth. Let me consult Seldon on the feedback structure.

Seldon raised a valid numerical concern: DT=0.125 against 0.5-month time constants under Euler. Let me test DT sensitivity.

DT is well-converged (0.2% variation), but I'll tighten it to 0.0625 as good practice per Seldon's point.

I've built and validated the model. One important caveat up front.

Simulation engine status

The client returned eval-run-failed-1 through -4 with zero variables on every attempt — no run data is available in this environment. So I have no simulated time series to report, and no LTM loop-dominance rankings (those require run data). What I do have is the engine's structural feedback analysis, which ran successfully and returned 27 loops. Everything below about feedback structure comes from that analysis. The engine reported no errors and no unit warnings.

What the model contains

Six stocks, 96 variables, 119 causal links. The stocks are Road Rage Incidents, Driver Stress, Traffic Congestion, Accidents, Learned Aggressive Driving Behavior, and Lack of Sleep. Auxiliaries carry the background's own terms: Impatience, Frustration, Perceived Provocations, Distracted Driving, Road Design inadequacy, Weather Conditions, and Personality Traits susceptibility multiplier.

Every stock is initialized in exact equilibrium (I verified inflow equals outflow at t=0 for all six), and every outflow is first-order — stock divided by a named time constant — so no stock can be driven negative. The exogenous pushes are a traffic demand ramp of 0.5 percent per month and a 12-month Weather Conditions cycle.

The feedback explanation

The analysis returned 18 reinforcing and 9 balancing loops. The reinforcing ones organize into three families.

The congestion hub. Traffic Congestion is the branch point. Loops L1, L4, L5, L8, L10 and L13 all run congestion into Driver Stress through four parallel channels the background names separately — direct congestion pressure, Impatience, Perceived Provocations, and Frustration — and stress then multiplies road rage occurrence. Road rage raises Accidents (L1, L14), accidents block lanes and feed congestion back. L9 does the same thing through Distracted Driving: drivers stuck in stop-and-go traffic reach for phones, which causes crashes, which cause more congestion.

The fatigue detour. L2, L3, L6, L11 and L12 route the same pressure through Lack of Sleep: stress impairs sleep, sleep debt impairs judgment, and impaired judgment raises both road rage and Accidents. This is a slower path, so it lags.

The two spirals that need no congestion at all. These are the ones I'd watch. L18, L20 and L25 are tit-for-tat: incidents raise perceived provocations, provocations both raise Driver Stress and directly trigger retaliation, which produces more incidents. L24 is social learning: incidents create exposure to observed aggressive driving, exposure normalizes it, and a more normalized norm produces more incidents. Because these close without touching Traffic Congestion, they can keep running even if you fix the roads.

What holds it down. L15 is the structurally interesting balancer: heavy congestion lowers travel speeds, which suppresses crash occurrence, partly cancelling the accident-congestion spiral. L23 saturates the aggression norm against a ceiling. The remaining six (L16, L17, L21, L22, L26, L27) are the first-order drains — accident clearance, stress recovery, sleep recovery, norm decay, incident de-escalation, congestion clearing.

Seldon's structural read is that the reinforcing gains here are all below one — the sensitivity exponents are 0.3 to 0.6 and the graphical functions saturate — so this is bounded amplification of an exogenous trend rather than a limits-to-growth overshoot. Since the engine could not run, I checked that independently by reintegrating the equations myself: all six stocks stay positive, nothing explodes, and the result is bounded oscillating growth. I also confirmed DT convergence across four step sizes (0.2 percent variation), and tightened DT to 0.0625 on Seldon's point about Euler resolution. Treat those as structural sanity checks on my part, not as model output.

Structural criticisms worth your judgment

  • Congestion is counted into road rage four times over — via Impatience, via Perceived Provocations, via Frustration, and via direct stress pressure. This follows the background, which lists them as separate triggers, but it does inflate congestion's apparent leverage.
  • No adaptation or enforcement feedback. There is no policing response to visible aggression, no route or mode shift when congestion worsens. Real systems have those balancing responses; without them the model can only escalate.
  • Lack of Sleep is driven only by Driver Stress, making it close to a delayed copy of stress rather than an independent cause.
  • L9 against L15 is a knife edge — distraction pushing accidents up versus low speeds pushing them down nearly cancel. That balance is a parameter accident, not a robust structure, and deserves a sensitivity test.

Where I'd intervene

Traffic Congestion is the highest-leverage target because it feeds five channels at once and sits outside every balancing loop. But the retaliation link and the social learning strength in L24 matter more than they look, because those spirals survive congestion relief — and the norm stock's 12-month decay time means acting there changes the long-run level with a long delay before you see it.

Tell me how you'd like to proceed. I can run a sensitivity analysis on the L9/L15 cancellation, add the missing enforcement and route-shift balancing loops, or dig into any loop family above. If you can get the simulation engine responding on your end, re-running would let me give you actual LTM dominance rankings over time rather than the structural reading I've given here.
