variables.name: Road Rage Incidents
variables.documentation: Stock of aggressive-driving incidents currently active or recent in the metropolitan driving population. It accumulates new occurrences and drains as incidents de-escalate.

variables.name: road rage incident occurrence
variables.documentation: Rate at which new road rage incidents occur. A baseline per-driver propensity is scaled multiplicatively by dimensionless effects of stress, frustration, perceived provocations, learned aggression, fatigue and personality susceptibility.

variables.name: road rage incident de escalation
variables.documentation: First-order de-escalation of active incidents so the stock can never go negative; on average an incident stays 'active' for the average road rage incident duration.

variables.name: initial road rage incidents
variables.documentation: Initial number of active road rage incidents, set at the equilibrium implied by baseline propensity and incident duration.

variables.name: average road rage incident duration
variables.documentation: Average time an incident remains active/recent in the population's experience before it de-escalates.

variables.name: baseline road rage propensity
variables.documentation: Baseline rate at which an average driver initiates a road rage incident under reference conditions.

variables.name: Personality Traits susceptibility multiplier
variables.documentation: Dimensionless constant representing the share of the population with impulsive, hostile or competitive personality traits that scales overall road rage propensity.

variables.name: driving population
variables.documentation: Constant number of drivers in the metropolitan area exposed to congestion, stress and fatigue.

variables.name: Driver Stress
variables.documentation: Accumulated stress and anxiety carried by the driving population. Builds from congestion, weather, impatience and provocations and dissipates through recovery.

variables.name: stress accumulation
variables.documentation: Rate of stress and anxiety build-up, the sum of four dimensionless pressures acting on each driver.

variables.name: stress recovery
variables.documentation: First-order dissipation of accumulated stress through rest and time away from driving.

variables.name: initial Driver Stress
variables.documentation: Initial accumulated stress, set at the reference equilibrium level.

variables.name: stress accumulation per driver
variables.documentation: Stress generated per driver per month per unit of combined driving pressure.

variables.name: stress recovery time
variables.documentation: Average time for accumulated driver stress to dissipate.

variables.name: reference Driver Stress
variables.documentation: Normal level of driver stress used to normalize the stress ratio to one under reference conditions.

variables.name: Driver Stress ratio
variables.documentation: Dimensionless ratio of current stress to its reference level; equals one under normal conditions.

variables.name: Traffic Congestion
variables.documentation: Accumulated congestion on the road network measured in congested vehicle hours, formed by demand, poor road design, weather and accidents, and cleared over time.

variables.name: congestion formation
variables.documentation: Rate at which congestion forms from growing travel demand interacting with inadequate road design and adverse weather, plus blockage caused by accidents.

variables.name: congestion clearing
variables.documentation: First-order dissipation of congestion as traffic flows through the network.

variables.name: congestion from Accidents
variables.documentation: Extra congestion created by accidents blocking lanes; a key reinforcing link from crashes back to congestion.

variables.name: congestion generated per accident
variables.documentation: Congested vehicle hours generated per month by each accident present on the network.

variables.name: initial Traffic Congestion
variables.documentation: Initial congestion stock, set at the reference equilibrium level.

variables.name: congestion clearing time
variables.documentation: Average time for congestion on the network to clear.

variables.name: reference Traffic Congestion
variables.documentation: Normal congestion level used to normalize the congestion ratio to one under reference conditions.

variables.name: congestion ratio
variables.documentation: Dimensionless measure of how congested the network is relative to normal; the main driver of impatience, provocation, distraction and stress.

variables.name: traffic demand
variables.documentation: Exogenous travel demand that grows linearly over the simulation, representing metropolitan growth in driving.

variables.name: initial traffic demand
variables.documentation: Travel demand at the start of the simulation.

variables.name: traffic demand growth rate
variables.documentation: Fractional growth in travel demand per month, driving the long-run escalation of congestion.

variables.name: Road Design inadequacy
variables.documentation: Exogenous constant capturing narrow lanes and confusing intersections that convert travel demand into congestion; one means normal design quality.

variables.name: Accidents
variables.documentation: Accidents that have occurred and are not yet cleared from the network; they add congestion while present.

variables.name: accident occurrence
variables.equation: driving_population * baseline_accident_rate_per_driver * Distracted_Driving_effect_on_accidents * Road_Rage_effect_on_accidents * Lack_of_Sleep_effect_on_accidents * Weather_Conditions_effect_on_accidents * congestion_speed_effect_on_accidents
variables.documentation: Rate of new accidents, raised by distraction, aggression, fatigue and bad weather but lowered by the slower speeds of heavy congestion.

variables.name: accident clearance
variables.documentation: First-order clearance of accidents from the roadway.

variables.name: initial Accidents
variables.documentation: Initial number of accidents present on the network, at the reference equilibrium.

variables.name: baseline accident rate per driver
variables.documentation: Accidents per driver per month under reference conditions.

variables.name: accident clearance time
variables.documentation: Average time an accident remains affecting the network before it is cleared.

variables.name: reference Accidents
variables.documentation: Normal number of accidents used to normalize the accidents ratio to one.

variables.name: Accidents ratio
variables.documentation: Dimensionless indicator of accident load relative to normal, used for monitoring the accident feedback.

variables.name: Learned Aggressive Driving Behavior
variables.documentation: Social normalization of aggressive driving learned by observing other drivers; a slow-moving norm stock that reinforces future road rage.

variables.name: aggression normalization
variables.documentation: Rate at which observed aggression becomes normalized, limited by remaining headroom toward maximum normalization.

variables.name: aggression norm decay
variables.documentation: First-order erosion of the aggressive-driving norm as drivers turn over and memories fade.

variables.name: exposure to observed aggressive driving
variables.documentation: Dimensionless exposure of drivers to visible aggressive driving, proportional to how many incidents are occurring relative to normal.

variables.name: normalization headroom
variables.documentation: Structural saturation limit: the closer the norm is to its maximum, the less additional normalization can occur.

variables.name: maximum normalization
variables.documentation: Upper bound on how normalized aggressive driving can become in this population.

variables.name: social learning strength
variables.documentation: Strength with which exposure to aggressive driving converts into normalized aggressive norms per month.

variables.name: norm decay time
variables.documentation: Average time for learned aggressive driving norms to fade.

variables.name: initial Learned Aggressive Driving Behavior
variables.documentation: Initial normalization of aggressive driving, at the reference equilibrium level.

variables.name: reference Learned Aggressive Driving Behavior
variables.documentation: Normal level of aggressive-driving normalization used for normalization to one.

variables.name: Learned Aggressive Driving Behavior ratio
variables.documentation: Dimensionless ratio of learned aggressive norms to normal.

variables.name: Lack of Sleep
variables.documentation: Accumulated fatigue and sleep debt in the driving population, worsened by stress and anxiety and repaid through rest.

variables.name: sleep deficit accumulation
variables.documentation: Rate at which sleep debt builds, amplified when stress and anxiety impair sleep.

variables.name: sleep deficit recovery
variables.documentation: First-order recovery of sleep debt through rest.

variables.name: sleep deficit per driver
variables.documentation: Sleep debt generated per driver per month under reference stress.

variables.name: sleep recovery time
variables.documentation: Average time for accumulated sleep debt to be repaid.

variables.name: initial Lack of Sleep
variables.documentation: Initial accumulated sleep debt, at the reference equilibrium level.

variables.name: reference Lack of Sleep
variables.documentation: Normal level of sleep debt used to normalize the fatigue ratio to one.

variables.name: Lack of Sleep ratio
variables.documentation: Dimensionless fatigue level relative to normal.

variables.name: reference road rage incidents
variables.documentation: Normal number of active incidents used to normalize the road rage ratio to one.

variables.name: road rage incidents ratio
variables.documentation: Dimensionless level of road rage relative to normal; drives provocations, social learning and accident risk.

variables.name: Impatience
variables.documentation: Impatience of drivers running late with low tolerance for delays, rising with congestion-caused delay and normalized to one at normal congestion.

variables.name: Perceived Provocations
variables.documentation: Being cut off, tailgated or honked at. Rises with the amount of aggressive driving on the road and with congestion-induced proximity.

variables.name: provocation from road rage
variables.documentation: Component of perceived provocation generated by the prevalence of aggressive driving, normalized to one at normal incident levels.

variables.name: provocation from congestion
variables.documentation: Component of perceived provocation from close-quarters driving in congestion, normalized to one at normal congestion.

variables.name: reference Perceived Provocations
variables.documentation: Normal level of perceived provocation used for normalization.

variables.name: Perceived Provocations ratio
variables.documentation: Dimensionless perceived provocation relative to normal.

variables.name: Frustration
variables.documentation: Feeling blocked by other drivers. A saturating function of the combined pressure of congestion and perceived provocations, normalized to one under normal conditions.

variables.name: Distracted Driving
variables.documentation: Phone use, texting and eating while driving, which rises when drivers are stuck in slow stop-and-go traffic; normalized to one at normal congestion.

variables.name: Weather Conditions
variables.documentation: Exogenous seasonal severity of adverse weather such as heavy rain or snow, oscillating around one.

variables.name: weather amplitude
variables.documentation: Amplitude of the seasonal swing in weather severity.

variables.name: weather period
variables.documentation: Length of the seasonal weather cycle.

variables.name: Weather Conditions severity multiplier
variables.documentation: Dimensionless multiplier by which adverse weather increases congestion formation; equals one at normal weather.

variables.name: weather congestion sensitivity
variables.documentation: Elasticity of congestion formation to weather severity.

variables.name: Weather Conditions pressure on stress
variables.documentation: Dimensionless stress pressure from driving in adverse weather; equals one at normal weather.

variables.name: weather stress sensitivity
variables.documentation: Elasticity of driver stress pressure to weather severity.

variables.name: Weather Conditions effect on accidents
variables.documentation: Dimensionless multiplier by which adverse weather raises accident occurrence; equals one at normal weather.

variables.name: weather accident sensitivity
variables.documentation: Elasticity of accident occurrence to weather severity.

variables.name: Traffic Congestion pressure on stress
variables.documentation: Dimensionless stress pressure created by heavy traffic, delays and stop-and-go conditions; equals one at normal congestion.

variables.name: Impatience pressure on stress
variables.documentation: Dimensionless stress pressure from impatience; equals one when impatience is at its normal index value of one.

variables.name: impatience stress sensitivity
variables.documentation: Elasticity of stress pressure to impatience.

variables.name: Perceived Provocations pressure on stress
variables.documentation: Dimensionless stress pressure from being cut off, tailgated or honked at; equals one at normal provocation.

variables.name: provocation stress sensitivity
variables.documentation: Elasticity of stress pressure to perceived provocations.

variables.name: Driver Stress effect on road rage
variables.documentation: Dimensionless amplification of road rage occurrence by accumulated stress and anxiety; equals one at normal stress.

variables.name: Frustration effect on road rage
variables.documentation: Dimensionless amplification of road rage by frustration at being blocked; equals one at normal frustration.

variables.name: frustration road rage sensitivity
variables.documentation: Elasticity of road rage occurrence to frustration.

variables.name: Perceived Provocations effect on road rage
variables.documentation: Dimensionless amplification of road rage by retaliatory reactions to perceived provocations; equals one at normal provocation.

variables.name: provocation road rage sensitivity
variables.documentation: Elasticity of road rage occurrence to perceived provocations.

variables.name: Learned Aggressive Driving Behavior effect on road rage
variables.documentation: Dimensionless amplification of road rage where aggressive driving has been socially normalized; equals one at normal norms.

variables.name: social learning road rage sensitivity
variables.documentation: Elasticity of road rage occurrence to learned aggressive driving norms.

variables.name: Lack of Sleep effect on road rage
variables.documentation: Dimensionless amplification of road rage by fatigue impairing judgment and making drivers more susceptible to anger; equals one at normal fatigue.

variables.name: sleep road rage sensitivity
variables.documentation: Elasticity of road rage occurrence to accumulated sleep deficit.

variables.name: Distracted Driving effect on accidents
variables.documentation: Dimensionless multiplier by which phone use, texting and eating while driving raise accident risk; equals one at normal distraction.

variables.name: distraction accident sensitivity
variables.documentation: Elasticity of accident occurrence to distracted driving.

variables.name: Road Rage effect on accidents
variables.documentation: Dimensionless multiplier by which aggressive driving raises accident occurrence; equals one at normal incident levels.

variables.name: Lack of Sleep effect on accidents
variables.documentation: Dimensionless multiplier by which fatigue raises accident occurrence; equals one at normal fatigue.

variables.name: sleep accident sensitivity
variables.documentation: Elasticity of accident occurrence to accumulated sleep deficit.

variables.name: congestion speed effect on accidents
variables.documentation: Balancing mechanism: heavy stop-and-go traffic lowers travel speeds and therefore reduces crash occurrence; equals one at normal congestion.

variables.name: Driver Stress effect on sleep loss
variables.documentation: Dimensionless amplification of sleep debt accumulation when stress and anxiety impair sleep; equals one at normal stress.

errorExplanations.name: total_incubation
errorExplanations.problem: Should use DELAY3 with the 'Infection' flow as input, not the 'Exposed population' stock divided by a time constant.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll start by retrieving the current model to inspect its structure and formulations.

Now let me examine the model structure. I'll analyze the formulation idiom used throughout before editing.

The model's delay idiom is now unambiguous. Every stock in this model drains via DELAY3(<sum of that stock's inflows>, <residence time>) — a third-order Erlang material delay:

Stock Inflow(s) fed into DELAY3 Delay time
Presymptomatic infectious Incubation + Influx... Presymptomatic_period/Days_per_week
Asymptomatic infectious Asymptomatic_incubation Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections/Days_per_week
Symptomatic infectious Developing_symptoms Average_length_of_symptomatic_period
Recovered population Recovery + Recovery_without_symptoms Average_immunity_period
Exposed population Exposed_population/Avg_period_asymp/Days_per_week ← deviant Average_COVID_incubation_time/Days_per_week

Total_incubation is the sole break in the pattern, and it is also the sole variable the engine's unit checker flags. Let me fix it.

The warning may be stale from the pre-edit state. Let me re-fetch to confirm.

Equation is fixed. The warning text is identical to the pre-edit one (People*Weeks/Days^2 is exactly what the old equation implied), suggesting it's cached. Let me tag the other DELAY variable for consistency, then run the model to force a fresh unit check.

Simulation ran. Now let me verify behavior — check for impossible negatives and conservation.

No negatives, and behavior is epidemiologically plausible. But the conservation check shows a discrepancy worth chasing — total population grows only ~1,800 while the imported-case inflow should add far more. Let me verify.

Two anomalies surfaced. Let me test them rigorously before drawing conclusions.

Both confirmed to machine precision. I found two additional, serious defects. Let me probe the imported-cases flow before deciding the fix.

Confirmed: this engine does not evaluate graphical functions attached to flow variables — it silently uses the raw equation TIME. Let me now repair the social distancing lookup, whose x-coordinates are being ignored.

This evenly-spaced grid reproduces the author's intended policy timeline and is correct under both interpolation semantics. Applying it:

Social distancing now tracks the intended policy timeline (residual is confined to the 1-week smoothing of the original sub-week steps). Let me confirm the final model state.

Analysis complete. I found and fixed the formulation errors, and diagnosed two further defects empirically.

Error 1 — Total_incubation (the main formulation error)

Was:

DELAY3(Exposed_population/Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections/Days_per_week,
       Average_COVID_incubation_time/Days_per_week)

Now:

DELAY3(Infection, Average_COVID_incubation_time/Days_per_week)

This single equation contained three compounded errors:

1a. Wrong delay style — a first-order drain jammed inside a third-order delay. Every other stock in this model drains with one consistent idiom: outflow = DELAY3(sum of that stock's inflows, residence time).

Stock Outflow formulation
Presymptomatic DELAY3(Incubation + Influx…, Presymptomatic_period/Days_per_week)
Asymptomatic DELAY3(Asymptomatic_incubation, Avg_period_asymp/Days_per_week)
Symptomatic DELAY3(Developing_symptoms, Average_length_of_symptomatic_period)
Recovered DELAY3(Recovery + Recovery_without_symptoms, Average_immunity_period)

The Exposed stock was the sole deviation: it passed Exposed_population/τ — a first-order exponential drain — as the input to a DELAY3, stacking an exponential outflow on top of a third-order delay and delaying the cohort twice. Under the model's idiom the input must be the inflow to the Exposed stock, which is Infection.

1b. Wrong parameter. The drain used Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections (6 days — how long an asymptomatic infectious person stays infectious). Nothing about the exposed/incubating pool is governed by that constant; it is a copy-paste from Recovery_without_symptoms. The correct time constant, Average_COVID_incubation_time, was already correctly present in the second argument.

1c. Dimensional error. Exposed_population/Avg_period/Days_per_week = Person/Day ÷ (Day/Week) = Person·Week/Day², against a declared Person/Week. The second division should have been a multiplication had that form been kept at all. This is exactly the engine's reported warning (People*Weeks/Days^2). The corrected equation is clean: Person/Week delayed by Day÷(Day/Week) = Week, yielding Person/Week.

Error 2 — Social_distancing_measures lookup timing (fixed)

The engine distributes graphical-function y-values evenly across the x-domain and ignores the intermediate x-coordinates. I verified this to machine precision (max error 1.7e-10 against an evenly-spaced model; the declared x,y pairs were rejected at error 0.61).

The original table encoded step changes via near-duplicate x pairs (8.9/9, 9.9/10, 10.9/11, 18.9/19 …). Spread evenly over the 0–104 domain, the intended timeline was stretched by ~3x: full lockdown landed at week 34.7 instead of week 11, and first measures at week ~11.5 instead of week 9.

I resampled the author's intended piecewise-linear curve onto an evenly spaced 1-week grid over the same 0–104 domain. This is robust: dense evenly-spaced points on the same curve reproduce it correctly under either interpolation convention. Policy timing now lands correctly (measures week 9, tightening week 10, lockdown week 11, easing weeks 19/22, retightening 41/50/56). Residual: the original 0.1-week steps are now 1-week ramps. Say the word if you want exact 0.1-week resolution (1041 points).

Error 3 — Influx_of_presymptomatic_infectious_people_from_abroad (diagnosed, not fixed — blocked by your constraints)

This flow evaluates to raw TIME; its graphical function is never applied. Verified: max|influx − TIME| = 0.000e+00 across the run, and re-supplying the lookup explicitly did not change it. This engine evaluates graphical functions on variable type but not on flow type.

Consequence: instead of the intended importation pulse (peak 2000 people/week at week 8, second wave ~weeks 26–34), the model imports a linear ramp reaching 60 people/week — 1,800 people total versus roughly 10,800 intended. The epidemic is being seeded by the wrong driver entirely.

The fix requires moving the lookup onto a converter that feeds the flow — which means adding one variable and one relationship, both of which you explicitly prohibited. So I left the structure untouched and the lookup attached (it documents intent and other engines may honor it). This needs your decision.

Validation after fixes

No stock goes negative; the Susceptible→Infection formulation is self-limiting as S→0, so no clamps were needed. Stock conservation holds exactly (all seven stocks sum to 17,000,000 plus cumulative importation). Peak symptomatic 60,393 at week 50; 9,834 cumulative deaths at week 60.

Two notes. First, the engine still emits the Total_incubation unit warning, but its text (People*Weeks/Days^2) is precisely the dimension of the removed equation and cannot be produced by the current one — it is a cached value; reload the model in your client to clear it. Second, per your constraint I did not touch the relationships section, so Exposed population → Total incubation and Average period of asymptomatic infections → Total incubation are now stale connectors and Infection → Total incubation is missing. Tell me if you want those three realigned.

I have not run feedback analysis, so I have made no claims here about loop structure or dominance. If you want to confirm the corrected model produces the right behavior for the right reasons, I can run Loops That Matter next.

errorExplanations.problem: Should use the flows 'Incubation + Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad' as input to DELAY3, not the stock 'Presymptomatic infectious' divided by a time constant.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll start by retrieving the current model to inspect its structure and formulations.

Model retrieved. Let me examine the structure carefully before making changes.

Model architecture (SEIR variant):

  • Susceptible → Exposed → {Presymptomatic → Symptomatic, Asymptomatic} → Recovered → Susceptible
  • Plus Cumulative COVID deaths as a sink accumulator.

Delay style used throughout: every stock's outflow is formulated as a third-order material delay of that stock's inflow:

Stock Inflow Outflow formulation
Exposed Infection Total_incubation = DELAY3(Infection, τ)
Asymptomatic Asymptomatic_incubation Recovery_without_symptoms = DELAY3(Asymptomatic_incubation, τ)
Symptomatic Developing_symptoms Total_exiting = DELAY3(Developing_symptoms, τ)
Recovered Recovery + Recovery_without_symptoms Losing_immunity = DELAY3(..., τ)
Presymptomatic Incubation + Influx Developing_symptoms — the odd one out

Developing_symptoms is the only outflow that breaks this pattern, and it is also the only variable the engine's unit checker flags.

Let me verify the declared causal arrows into that flow:

The declared arrows confirm the author's intent: this flow is drawn as a drain of the Presymptomatic infectious stock (arrows from Presymptomatic infectious, Presymptomatic period, Days per week), not as a delayed inflow. The arrow from Average period of asymptomatic infections is the vestige of the error.

Applying the fix:

The warning text returned may be stale from the pre-edit state. Let me re-fetch the model to confirm the authoritative current state:

Equation is corrected. Note the warning message still describes People*Weeks/Days^2 — which is exactly what the old equation implied (Person/Day/(Day/Week)), so this is a stale cached warning. Let me clean up the now-orphaned causal arrow and re-run to force unit re-evaluation.

The warning string is byte-identical to the pre-edit one and exactly matches the old equation's dimensions (Person / Day / (Day/Week) = Person·Week/Day²), which the current equation cannot produce. Let me confirm by checking the simulated behavior, and also rewrite the expression in the equivalent multiplication form to force a recompute:

No stock goes negative, and conservation holds exactly: living population + cumulative deaths = 17,000,000 + the exogenous influx from abroad (~1,800 people integrated over the run). The epidemic peaks at week 18–19, and deaths (68,895) = 1% CFR × 6.89M symptomatic cases, which reconciles correctly with the 50% asymptomatic share.

Now let me settle whether that unit warning is stale or real by rewriting the expression in an algebraically identical form:

Definitive: the warning text is byte-identical across three structurally different equations, including Presymptomatic_infectious*Days_per_week/Presymptomatic_period, which cannot possibly yield Person·Week/Day². A live checker would report different implied units for each. This is a stale cached warning from the original equation, not a live finding.

Reverting to the form that matches the model's house style (days converted to weeks via /Days_per_week, as Total_incubation and Recovery_without_symptoms both do):

Model validated. The engine evaluates Developing_symptoms as exactly Presymptomatic_infectious × 7/3 (deviation ~1e-10), confirming the residence time resolves to 3/7 week as intended. Results are identical to the previous run, as the two algebraic forms are equivalent.

Analysis

I found one variable containing formulation errors — Developing symptoms, which is also the only element the engine's unit checker flagged. It contained three compounded errors.

Original:

DELAY3(Presymptomatic_infectious/Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections/Days_per_week,
       Presymptomatic_period/Days_per_week)

Corrected:

Presymptomatic_infectious/(Presymptomatic_period/Days_per_week)

Error 1 — Wrong time constant

The drain used Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections (6 days, the residence time in the Asymptomatic infectious stock) to empty the Presymptomatic infectious stock. This is the wrong branch of the model entirely: it borrowed a parameter belonging to the asymptomatic pathway to control a flow on the presymptomatic pathway. The correct parameter, Presymptomatic_period (3 days), was already defined and already had a causal arrow drawn into this flow, but appeared only in the delay-time argument. Fix: the drain now divides by Presymptomatic_period, and the stale arrow from Average period of asymptomatic infections was removed so the diagram matches the equation.

Error 2 — Inverted unit conversion (the dimensional failure)

X/Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections/Days_per_week is left-associative, so it evaluates as (Person/Day)/(Day/Week) = Person·Week/Day² — precisely the People*Weeks/Days^2 the engine reported against a declared Person/Week. Converting a per-day rate to a per-week rate requires multiplying by Days_per_week, or equivalently dividing the period by it first. Fix: parenthesized as Presymptomatic_period/Days_per_week, which yields a residence time in weeks (Day ÷ Day/Week = Week), giving Person/Week. This matches how Total_incubation and Recovery_without_symptoms already perform the same day-to-week conversion.

Error 3 — Redundant DELAY3 double-counting the presymptomatic period

The inner expression was already a complete drain of the presymptomatic stock over a presymptomatic-length period. Wrapping it in DELAY3(..., Presymptomatic_period/Days_per_week) applied that same delay a second time, roughly doubling the effective presymptomatic residence time. It also broke the stock–outflow correspondence: the stock drained on one time constant while its outflow was reported on another, so the outflow no longer reconciled with the contents of the stock it came from. Fix: removed the wrapper.

A note on delay style, and one constraint that forced a judgment call

You asked me to respect the existing pipeline-vs-exponential style, so this deserves explicit flagging. Every other outflow in this model is a third-order material delay of its stock's inflow:

Stock Outflow formulation
Exposed DELAY3(Infection, τ)
Asymptomatic DELAY3(Asymptomatic_incubation, τ)
Symptomatic DELAY3(Developing_symptoms, τ)
Recovered DELAY3(Recovery + Recovery_without_symptoms, τ)

Strict stylistic consistency would therefore make this DELAY3(Incubation + Influx_of_presymptomatic_infectious_people_from_abroad, Presymptomatic_period/Days_per_week). I did not do this, because it would require two new causal arrows (Incubation → Developing symptoms and Influx… → Developing symptoms), which your instructions prohibit without exception.

I resolved the conflict in favour of the hard constraint, and the model's own diagram supports that choice: the arrows drawn into this flow are Presymptomatic infectious, Presymptomatic period, and Days per week — exactly the inputs a first-order stock drain needs, and notably unlike every other delay in the model, which does carry an inflow→outflow arrow. So the author appears to have drawn this one deliberately as a stock drain. The consequence is that the presymptomatic stage is now a first-order (exponential) delay while the other stages remain third-order; if you would rather have uniformity, tell me and I'll switch it to the DELAY3 form and add the two arrows.

Verification

  • No stock goes negative anywhere in the run.
  • Conservation holds: living population + cumulative deaths = 17,000,000 + the ~1,800 people integrated from the exogenous influx.
  • Deaths (68,895) reconcile as 1% CFR × 6.89M symptomatic cases, consistent with the 50% asymptomatic share against a 13.66M drop in susceptibles.
  • Epidemic peaks at week 18–19, after the social-distancing ramp at weeks 9–11.

Two disclosures. First, I set uniflow = true on this flow; it is strictly one-directional and cannot go negative given the corrected formulation, so this is a safety annotation with no effect on results. Second, the engine kept returning the same unit warning after every edit — including for a form that cannot possibly produce those dimensions. Identical text across three structurally different equations indicates a stale cached warning rather than a live finding; the numerical check above confirms the equation now evaluates correctly. Worth re-opening the model fresh to confirm the warning clears on your side.

One thing I left alone: Total_incubation and Total_exiting_symptomatic_infectious are plain variables whose equations use DELAY3 but which don't carry the delayVariable sub-type. That's a rendering annotation with no effect on simulation, so I didn't touch it — say the word if you want it set.

Want me to run the feedback-loop analysis to confirm the corrected presymptomatic timing produces the behaviour for the right structural reasons?

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll start by retrieving the current model to inspect its structure and formulations.

Model retrieved. Let me establish a baseline by running the current model before changing anything.

The baseline confirms a behavioral pathology: Asymptomatic_infectious balloons to 7.8M and is still holding 4.6M at week 60 — it never drains, while Symptomatic_infectious correctly peaks and clears. Let me apply the fix.

The equation is updated; the reported warning text still describes the old equation (People*Weeks/Days^2 is exactly what Asymptomatic_infectious/Day/(Day/Week) produced), so it looks stale. Let me re-run to force a fresh unit check.

Behavior is now correct and conservation holds (1.7e7 − 69,451 deaths + ~1,450 arrivals ≈ 1.6932e7). The engine clearly ran the new equation, but the unit warning text is byte-identical to before and describes the old expression exactly. Let me force a revalidation to confirm it's stale.

Definitive: with the equation reduced to bare Asymptomatic_incubation (declared units Person/Week, identical to the variable's own units), the checker still emits the byte-identical People*Weeks/Days^2 message. That is dimensionally impossible for that equation — the warning is a cached artifact of the original equation, not a live check. Reverting to the correct fix.

Fix is in place with documentation intact. Final verification run:

I analyzed all 34 variables against the model's own formulation conventions, ran a before/after comparison, and verified non-negativity and conservation. Here is what I found.

Errors found and fixed

Error 1 — Recovery without symptoms: broken cohort-outflow formulation (the only formulation error in the model)

Before:

DELAY3(Asymptomatic_infectious/Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections/Days_per_week,
       Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections/Days_per_week)

After:

DELAY3(Asymptomatic_incubation,
       Average_period_of_asymptomatic_infections/Days_per_week)

This single equation contained three compounding defects:

1a. Wrong DELAY3 input — inconsistent with the model's delay style. Every other cohort transition in this model uses one consistent convention: the outflow of a stock is a third-order material delay of that stock's inflow, with the delay time equal to the residence time in the cohort. Total incubation = DELAY3(Infection, …); Developing symptoms = DELAY3(Incubation+Influx…, …); Total exiting symptomatic infectious = DELAY3(Developing symptoms, …); Losing immunity = DELAY3(Recovery+Recovery without symptoms, …). Recovery without symptoms was the sole exception — it fed the stock into the delay instead of the stock's inflow, Asymptomatic incubation. That is a hybrid of two incompatible idioms: it takes a first-order exponential-drain expression (stock / residence time) and then pushes it through a further third-order delay, so the asymptomatic residence time was applied twice. The fix restores the DELAY3-of-inflow pipeline convention used everywhere else.

1b. Inverted unit conversion, making the drain ~49x too slow. The input divided by Days_per_week (7 Day/Week) when it needed to multiply to convert a per-day rate to a per-week rate. The intended weekly drain is A/(6/7 Week) = 1.167·A per week; the equation computed A/6/7 = 0.0238·A per week — 49 times too slow.

1c. Dimensional inconsistency. Person / Day / (Day/Week) yields Person·Week/Day², not Person/Week. This is exactly the discrepancy the engine's unit checker reported ("Recovery without symptoms" has units "Person/Week" but the equation suggests units "People*Weeks/Days^2"). Correcting the input resolves it: Asymptomatic incubation is already Person/Week, and the delay time Day/(Day/Week) is Week, so DELAY3 returns Person/Week as declared.

Behavioral evidence. In the original model the asymptomatic cohort could not drain: Asymptomatic infectious ballooned to 7.84M and was still holding 4.58M people at week 60, permanently "infectious," which drove Susceptible population down to 27k — a runaway epidemic that was purely an artifact of the bad drain rate. After the fix the model produces a credible single wave peaking near week 18 (asymptomatic peak 1.22M), clearing to ~41 people by week 60, with susceptibles bottoming at 3.22M and then replenishing as immunity wanes. Cumulative deaths fall from 106k to a plausible 69.5k.

Validation after the fix: all seven stocks stay non-negative across the full run, and conservation holds exactly — living population + cumulative deaths − initial 1.7e7 equals the running integral of arrivals from abroad (0 → 1,727), monotonically increasing as expected.

Formulations I checked and found correct

The unit conversions in Total incubation, Developing symptoms (both Day → Week via Days_per_week) and in Total exiting symptomatic infectious and Losing immunity (already in Weeks, correctly not converted) are all right. The Incubation/Asymptomatic incubation split by Share of asymptomatic infections and the Recovery/Dying of COVID split by Case fatality rate are complementary and sum exactly to their sources, with no double-counting. Infection is dimensionally clean, and Total population correctly excludes Cumulative COVID deaths while including all six living stocks.

Two things to flag, neither of which I changed

  1. The engine's unit warning is stale and can be ignored. It still reports the identical People*Weeks/Days^2 message after the fix. I verified this is a cached artifact: I temporarily reduced the equation to bare Asymptomatic_incubation — whose units are Person/Week, identical to the variable's own declared units — and the checker still emitted the byte-identical message, which is dimensionally impossible. The message text describes the original expression exactly. It should clear when the model is reloaded in your client.

  2. One pre-existing arrow is now stale. The relationships list still contains Asymptomatic infectious → Recovery without symptoms and lacks Asymptomatic incubation → Recovery without symptoms. Notably, the arrow list already follows the correct convention everywhere else — there is no Symptomatic infectious → Total exiting symptomatic infectious or Exposed population → Total incubation arrow — which independently confirms the DELAY3-of-inflow reading. I left the relationships section completely untouched per your instruction not to add relationships; you may want to re-sync that one arrow in your client.

I added no variables, renamed nothing, and added no relationships. Would you like me to run the feedback analysis to confirm the corrected model produces its behavior through the intended mechanisms?

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll start by retrieving the current model to inspect its structure and formulations.

The model ran but produced no data — indicating a fatal formulation problem. Let me apply the fixes I've identified.

The run now succeeds. Let me verify the behavior.

Let me verify whether the graphical function on the influx flow is actually being evaluated by the engine.

Confirmed: the engine does not evaluate graphical functions attached to flow-type variables. Let me restore the minimal-diff state and do a final validation run.

The model now simulates. Here is the full audit.

Errors found and fixed

1. Influx_of_presymptomatic_infectious_people_from_abroad — lookup driven by DT instead of TIME

Was: equation: "DT" (with a graphical function whose x-axis runs 0 → 104)

Why it was an error: This flow carries a graphical function that is a time series of imported presymptomatic cases — the x-axis is weeks of simulation time (peak of 2000 person/week around week 8, a second bump around week 34, tapering to 5 by week 52). DT is the integration-timestep builtin, a constant 0.0078125 Week. Feeding DT into the lookup pins the lookup input at a fixed near-zero value for the entire 60-week run, which destroys the imported-case profile entirely. The model's other time-indexed lookup, Social_distancing_measures, correctly uses TIME — so this also broke the model's own stylistic convention. This matters more than usual here because every infectious stock initialises at zero: this influx is the only seed of the epidemic, so a broken lookup means a broken epidemic.

Fix: equation: "TIME".

2. Total_incubation and Total_exiting_symptomatic_infectious — DELAY3 converters not declared as delay variables

Was: both are plain variables of type variable holding DELAY3(...) with no subType.

Why it was an error: A DELAY3 is a third-order material delay — it carries hidden internal state (three cascaded stages) that the engine must allocate and integrate alongside the explicit stocks. A converter whose equation contains a DELAY/SMTH builtin must be declared subType: "delayVariable" so that state is created. Without it the model would not simulate at all: the original run returned zero variables. The three DELAY3s that sit on flow variables (Developing_symptoms, Recovery_without_symptoms, Losing_immunity) do not need the flag, which is why only these two converters were affected.

Fix: subType: "delayVariable" on both.

Verification

Post-fix simulation (eval-run-4) is well behaved:

  • No stock goes negative. Susceptible bottoms at 3.22M and recovers to 8.87M as immunity wanes; all other stocks have min = 0.
  • Conservation holds. Living population + cumulative deaths = 17,000,000 + the integral of the influx from abroad (17,001,800 at t=60 vs. an initial 17,000,000 plus ~1,800 arrivals). Nothing is created or destroyed by the delay chain.
  • Reference mode is epidemic-shaped: a wave peaking at ~1.43M symptomatic infectious, 69,451 cumulative deaths, with waning immunity returning people to Susceptible from roughly week 40 onward.

Formulations I checked and found correct

The delay style is internally consistent and I changed none of it. Every stock's outflow is a DELAY3 of exactly that stock's inflow(s) over the residence time, which is what makes the chain conserve people:

Stock Inflow(s) Outflow formulation
Exposed Infection DELAY3(Infection, incubation/Days_per_week)
Presymptomatic Incubation + Influx DELAY3(Incubation + Influx, Presymptomatic_period/Days_per_week)
Symptomatic Developing symptoms DELAY3(Developing_symptoms, Average_length_of_symptomatic_period)
Asymptomatic Asymptomatic incubation DELAY3(Asymptomatic_incubation, asympt_period/Days_per_week)
Recovered Recovery + Recovery w/o symptoms DELAY3(Recovery + Recovery_without_symptoms, Average_immunity_period)

Also verified correct: the Day / (Day/Week) = Week conversions via Days_per_week on the three parameters expressed in days (and correctly absent on Average_length_of_symptomatic_period and Average_immunity_period, which are already in weeks); the complementary splits (1-Share_of_asymptomatic) / Share_of_asymptomatic and (1-CFR) / CFR, which each sum to the parent rate; Total_population correctly summing the six living stocks and excluding Cumulative_COVID_deaths; the infection formulation Infectious × Contacts × Infectivity × Susceptible_share, dimensionally Person/Week; and every inflow/outflow assignment against the relationship list.

One issue I could not fix within your constraints

The engine does not evaluate graphical functions attached to flow-type variables. I confirmed this experimentally: Influx_of_presymptomatic_infectious_people_from_abroad returns raw TIME (0 → 60 linearly) rather than its lookup, whereas the identically-formulated Social_distancing_measures — same TIME equation, but type variable — does evaluate its table. The formulation is now correct, but the intended imported-case profile is not being applied. The standard remedy is to move the lookup onto a converter and have the flow reference it, which requires a new variable — outside the bounds you set, so I left the correct formulation in place and am flagging it instead.

Separately, worth knowing: the engine spaces graphical-function points evenly across the x-range rather than honouring the authored x-values. For Social_distancing_measures (19 points over 0–104) this stretches the policy timeline — the 0.7 lockdown level you drew at week 11 actually bites around week 34.7 in simulation. I did not alter the table data, since this is a representation issue rather than an error in your formulation, but if you want the drawn timeline to be what runs, the points would need re-specifying on an even grid.

Want me to run feedback loop analysis to confirm the behaviour is arising from the right structure, or plot the epidemic wave?

Let me run the model to see the engine's diagnostics and baseline behavior.

The model run produced no data — it failed. Let me examine the formulations closely and apply fixes. First, a clear structural error: the graphical-function driver.

That fixed the run failure. Now let me inspect behavior.

Behavior reveals a second defect: the influx flow is outputting raw TIME (0.906 at t=0.906, 59.7 at t=59.7) rather than its graphical function. Let me check sub-types and test.

Confirmed: the graphical function attached to the flow is not being evaluated — the flow emits raw TIME. Let me test whether flow attributes affect this.

The engine evaluates graphical functions on an evenly-spaced x-grid (exact match, error 0.00000), ignoring supplied x-values. Let me run one clean diagnostic on the flow's lookup.

Confirmed — the engine never evaluates a graphical function on a flow. Restoring the authored form:

The feedback structure is coherent. Let me get an expert critique of the formulations.

Audit complete

I found and fixed the errors below. Everything else in the formulation checked out — I verified each cohort pipeline, the contagion equation, the fractional splits, the time-unit conversions, conservation of persons, and non-negativity of every stock.

Errors found and fixed

1. Social_distancing_measures was driven by DT instead of TIME — CRITICAL

Was: DT Now: TIME

Why it was an error. This variable is a graphical function whose x-axis spans 0 to 104 weeks — it is a policy timeline (lockdown, relaxation, re-tightening) and must be indexed by simulation time. DT is the integration step, a constant 0.0078125 Week. The lookup was therefore being evaluated at the same point forever, pinning social distancing at 0 and eliminating the entire policy intervention from the model. It also broke dimensionally: DT is the step size, not elapsed time.

Evidence. With DT in place the model would not simulate at all — run_model returned a failed run with zero variables. Replacing it with TIME made the model run immediately. This was the one error with a hard, blocking consequence.

2. Missing delayVariable sub-type on two DELAY3 auxiliaries

Affected: Total_incubation, Total_exiting_symptomatic_infectious

Both are plain auxiliaries whose equations contain DELAY3, but neither was tagged as a delay variable. Every other delay in the model sits on a flow, so these two were the only untagged cases. The declaration is required so the tooling constructs the delay's internal state rather than treating the expression as a simultaneous algebraic equation. Behaviour is unchanged; the declaration is now correct.

3. Minor: import flow could go negative

Set uniflow = true on Influx_of_presymptomatic_infectious_people_from_abroad. Arrivals from abroad are a one-directional physical process and must never subtract from the presymptomatic stock.

What I verified as correct (no changes made)

Your delay style is consistent and right throughout. Every cohort stock's outflow is a third-order pipeline delay of that same stock's inflow, with the delay time matched to the cohort it governs:

Stock Inflow Outflow Delay time
Exposed Infection Incubation + Asymptomatic incubation = DELAY3(Infection, ...) incubation time
Presymptomatic Incubation + Influx DELAY3(Incubation+Influx, ...) presymptomatic period
Asymptomatic Asymptomatic incubation DELAY3(Asymptomatic_incubation, ...) asymptomatic period
Symptomatic Developing symptoms Recovery + Dying = DELAY3(Developing_symptoms, ...) symptomatic period
Recovered Recovery + Recovery w/o symptoms DELAY3(Recovery+Recovery_without_symptoms, ...) immunity period

Three details that are easy to get wrong and that you got right: the foreign influx is included inside the Developing_symptoms delay input, so imported cases actually drain out of the presymptomatic stock; the asymptomatic share and the case fatality rate both split an exit flow rather than a stock, so neither distorts residence time and the branches sum exactly to the pipeline output; and the day-denominated parameters are divided by Days_per_week while the already-weekly ones correctly are not.

Contagion form and units are also correct — Person times 1/Week times two dimensionless terms gives Person/Week. The engine reported no unit warnings.

Validation results after the fixes: no stock goes negative (susceptible bottoms out at 3.22 million), and person-conservation holds to a relative error of 1.4e-08 against 17,000,000 plus 1,800 cumulative imports. Loop analysis returns 27 loops with the expected epidemic architecture — contagion reinforcing loops through the three infectious stocks, susceptible-depletion balancing loops through the contact-chance term, recovery balancing loops, and reinforcing loops through immunity loss back to susceptible.

Two platform-level problems you need to know about

These are not mistakes in your equations, and neither can be repaired without adding a variable, which you asked me not to do. Both materially distort the simulation.

The graphical function on Influx_of_presymptomatic_infectious_people_from_abroad is never evaluated. The variable is typed as a flow, and this engine only wires graphical functions to variable-typed items. The flow is emitting its raw equation instead — I confirmed this by setting the equation to the constant 8 and getting a flat 8 back rather than the lookup value. So instead of your importation curve (peaking at 2000 per week around week 8, with a second travel bump near week 34), the model is seeding the epidemic with TIME itself: 1 person/week at week 1 rising linearly to 60 by week 60. The authoring is correct per the tool's own convention; the engine simply does not honour it on a flow. The fix requires moving the lookup into a variable that the flow then references.

Graphical function x-values are ignored; y-points are spread evenly across the x-range. I confirmed this exactly — simulated Social_distancing_measures matches an even-grid interpolation over 0 to 104 to zero error across all 200 output points, while diverging from your authored breakpoints by up to 0.61. The consequence is severe: your table specifies distancing reaching 0.7 at week 11, but the model applies it at week 34.7. That is why you are seeing an 80 percent attack rate. At the authored timing, contacts drop to 2.25 per week and the effective reproduction number falls to roughly 0.91, which would have suppressed the wave. I did not silently rewrite your table data to compensate, because that would bake an engine workaround into the model and leave it wrong if the engine is later corrected — but you should treat the current wave size as an artifact, not a result.

Want me to plot the current trajectories, or re-specify the two lookups on an even grid so the intended policy timing takes effect?

errorExplanations.name: total_population
errorExplanations.problem: Total population should be an auxiliary/converter variable that sums the population stocks, not a stock.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll start by retrieving the current model to inspect its structure and formulations.

The run failed — the model does not simulate. Now applying fixes.

Conservation verified exactly. Let me confirm the unit checker is now clean.

The model now runs and is behaviorally sound. Here is the full analysis.

Errors found and fixed

Error 1 — Total population was formulated as a stock accumulating a level, not a rate (fatal)

What was wrong. Total population was a stock initialized at 0, fed by an inflow Total population net flow whose equation was:

Susceptible_population + Exposed_population + Asymptomatic_infectious
+ Presymptomatic_infectious + Symptomatic_infectious + Recovered_population

That expression is a level (Person), not a rate (Person/Week). This is the error the engine's unit checker flagged: "Total population net flow has units Person/Week but the equation suggests units Person."

Why it is an error. Three compounding problems:

  1. Double accounting. Every person counted by the expression is already accumulated inside one of the six compartment stocks. Integrating that sum again makes Total population grow without bound at roughly 17,000,000 people per week. Total population is an accounting identity, not an accumulation — it must be an auxiliary. A stock is only appropriate for a quantity whose value is the history of its own flows; here the value is fully determined at every instant by the six compartments.
  2. Dimensional inconsistency, as reported by the engine.
  3. Division by zero at t = 0. Total population started at 0, and Chance of contact with an susceptible person divides by it. The model failed to simulate at all — the baseline run returned no data.

How I fixed it. I converted Total population from a stock to an auxiliary variable holding exactly the expression that had been misplaced on the flow:

Total_population = Susceptible_population + Exposed_population + Asymptomatic_infectious
                 + Presymptomatic_infectious + Symptomatic_infectious + Recovered_population

units Person. The now-vestigial flow Total population net flow was removed — a flow cannot exist without a stock, and its content had moved to the auxiliary.

Note on your constraints. This fix adds no variables, no relationships and no feedback loops, and renames nothing. That drove the choice of fix. The alternative repair — keeping Total population as a stock and rewriting its net flow as Influx of presymptomatic infectious people from abroad − Dying of COVID — is also mathematically valid, but it would have required deleting the six declared relationships into the net flow and inventing two new ones. Your existing relationship set (all six compartment stocks pointing into the net flow) makes the intent explicit: total population is the sum of the compartments. Collapsing the degenerate stock-flow pass-through into the auxiliary preserves that exact dependency set with zero additions.

Error 2 — unguarded division in Chance of contact with an susceptible person

What was wrong. Susceptible_population / Total_population.

Why it is an error. An unguarded division by a population aggregate that can in principle reach zero. This is what actually crashed the original model, and it remains a latent robustness defect under extreme-condition testing (for example, driving initial susceptibles to zero).

How I fixed it. Switched to the safe-division operator, which returns 0 rather than failing when the denominator is 0:

Chance_of_contact_with_an_susceptible_person = Susceptible_population // Total_population

Formulations I checked and found correct

I want to be explicit about what I did not change, since your delay style is deliberate and consistent:

  • All five DELAY3 chains are correct. In each case the delayed argument is exactly the set of inflows to the corresponding stock, so material is conserved through the pipeline: Total incubation delays Infection; Developing symptoms delays Incubation + Influx from abroad (both Presymptomatic inflows — correctly including the import); Recovery without symptoms delays Asymptomatic incubation; Total exiting symptomatic infectious delays Developing symptoms; Losing immunity delays Recovery + Recovery without symptoms.
  • Delay-time unit handling is correct throughout. Durations stored in Day are consistently divided by Days per week (incubation, presymptomatic, asymptomatic periods); durations already stored in Week are correctly not divided (Average length of symptomatic period, Average immunity period). This is a common place to find an error and yours is clean.
  • Both fraction splits are complementary and conserve material: Incubation + Asymptomatic incubation sum exactly to Total incubation, and Recovery + Dying of COVID sum exactly to Total exiting symptomatic infectious.
  • The infection formulation is the standard, dimensionally correct one: Person × 1/Week × Dmnl × Dmnl = Person/Week.
  • No hard-coded empirical constants appear inline. Every parameter is a named variable; the only inline numbers are structural complements of the form 1 − x.

Verification

Simulation eval-run-2 completes over the full 0–60 week horizon.

  • No stock goes negative. Minimum value across all six compartments and cumulative deaths is 0.
  • Conservation law holds exactly. Testing Total population(60) = Total population(0) + ∫Influx − Cumulative deaths: expected 16,932,349.2, actual 16,932,349.0 — a residual of 0.2 person out of 17 million, which is trapezoidal integration error in the check itself, not model leakage.
  • Behavior is epidemiologically credible. A single wave peaks around week 17–18 (infection rate ~2.87 million/week), susceptibles fall from 17.0M to a trough of 3.22M, recovered peaks at 13.65M, cumulative deaths settle at 69,451 (0.41% of population, consistent with a 1% case fatality rate applied to the symptomatic half of infections). After week 27 the susceptible pool slowly refills as the 52-week immunity delay matures.

One caveat

The engine is still echoing the original unit warning for Total population net flow. I verified that variable no longer exists anywhere in the model — it is absent from the variables section, no equation references it, and no relationship targets it. The message is a stale cached result from the pre-fix unit-check pass, not a live warning. It should clear on model reload.

Suggested next steps: I have not run feedback analysis, so I have deliberately said nothing about the model's loop structure or what drives the wave shape. If you want that, I can run the Loops That Matter analysis to identify which structures dominate at each phase of the epidemic — that would be the natural way to confirm the model produces the right behavior for the right reasons before you move to policy testing on the social distancing schedule.

errorExplanations.name: infectious_population
errorExplanations.problem: Infectious population should be an auxiliary/converter variable that sums the three infectious stocks, not a stock.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll start by retrieving the current model to inspect its structure and formulations.

Now let me check the run history and then apply fixes.

Confirmed the pathology. Now applying fixes.

The removed variable is gone; the reported warning appears stale. Re-running to refresh the engine's unit check.

Analysis complete — one formulation error found and fixed

Error 1: Infectious population was formulated as a stock instead of an auxiliary identity

What it was:

Infectious population          [STOCK]   initial = 0
  inflow: Infectious population net flow
Infectious population net flow [FLOW]    = Symptomatic_infectious
                                         + Presymptomatic_infectious
                                         + Asymptomatic_infectious
                                         units: Person/Week

Why it is an error — three distinct defects, all from the same root:

  1. Dimensional inconsistency. The engine's unit checker flagged this directly: "Infectious population net flow has units Person/Week but the equation suggests units Person." The right-hand side is a sum of three levels (Person). Assigning it to a rate makes the model integrate person-weeks, not people.

  2. Double counting. Every individual in this quantity is already accumulated in one of the three infectious stocks. A quantity that is definitionally the sum of existing stocks is an identity, not an accumulation. Integrating it counts each person once per unit of time they remain infectious.

  3. No outflow, so it could never decline. The stock had an inflow and no outflow. Since the three infectious stocks are non-negative, the inflow was always ≥ 0, making Infectious population monotonically non-decreasing by construction — it can only ratchet upward, forever. It reached 27.5 million by week 60 in a population of 17 million, and this bogus level is the multiplier in the Infection equation.

How I fixed it:

Infectious population [VARIABLE] = Presymptomatic_infectious
                                 + Symptomatic_infectious
                                 + Asymptomatic_infectious
                                 units: Person

Converted to an auxiliary and removed the now-redundant Infectious population net flow, which existed only to service the erroneous stock. The three causal arrows (Presymptomatic / Symptomatic / Asymptomatic → Infectious population) were re-anchored directly onto the auxiliary — these are the same causal paths that previously ran through the deleted pass-through node, so no new relationship or loop was introduced. No variables were added and nothing was renamed.

Behavioral evidence

Before After
Infectious population rises monotonically to 27.5M (> total population), never turns over single wave, peaks 3.26M at week 19
Susceptible trough 15,200 (0.09% remaining) 3.22M (18.9% remaining) at week 24
Cumulative deaths 119,100 69,451
Population conservation — living + dead = 17,001,800 vs. 17,000,000 initial + 1,800 imported; residual 0.23 persons (material still in the DELAY3 pipelines)

No stock goes negative at any point; all six stocks bottom out at exactly 0 or above. Conservation is exact.

Formulations I verified as correct (no change made)

You asked me to respect the existing delay style — it is clean and consistent, and I found no defect in it:

  • All six material delays use DELAY3 consistently (Total incubation, Developing symptoms, Recovery without symptoms, Total exiting symptomatic infectious, Losing immunity). No mixing of SMTH information delays with material delays.
  • Day→Week conversion is applied exactly where needed and correctly omitted elsewhere. The three delay times denominated in Days (Average COVID incubation time, Presymptomatic period, Average period of asymptomatic infections) are each divided by Days per week; the two already in Weeks (Average length of symptomatic period, Average immunity period) are correctly not divided. This was the most likely place for a hidden error and it is clean.
  • Every stock's outflow is the DELAY3 of its own inflow, so each cohort conserves material through the chain: Exposed, Presymptomatic (including the imported influx), Symptomatic, Asymptomatic, and Recovered all balance.
  • Splits sum to unity: Incubation + Asymptomatic incubation = Total incubation, and Recovery + Dying of COVID = Total exiting symptomatic infectious.
  • Infection is dimensionally sound: Person × (1/Week) × Dmnl × Dmnl = Person/Week.
  • Total population correctly excludes Cumulative COVID deaths (living denominator for the contact fraction).
  • Contacts per person per week has the correct sign: more distancing → fewer contacts.
  • DT = 1/128 week is comfortably below the shortest delay stage (0.143 week for the third-order 3-day delays).

Two notes, no action taken

  1. Stale warning. The engine still echoes the Infectious population net flow unit warning even after the variable was removed (confirmed absent — the model now has 34 variables and no element by that name). Re-running and re-validating did not clear it; it appears to be a cached artifact on the client side rather than a live finding.
  2. uniflow is not set on any flow. Not an error here — every flow is either a DELAY3 of a non-negative input or a product of non-negative terms, and none went negative in simulation. Setting uniflow = true on the one-directional flows would be defensive hardening, not a correction, so I left it alone.

Would you like me to run the feedback loop analysis to confirm the corrected model produces its wave for the right structural reasons, or test it under extreme conditions (zero distancing, 100% distancing, zero influx)?

testParams.name: Exponential Growth Pattern
testParams.prompt: Please create a model that demonstrates exponential growth behavior. The model must include a variable named 'output' that shows this behavior over time.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a model that exhibits exponential growth behavior in the 'output' variable.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Exponential growth occurs when the rate of increase is proportional to the current value. This creates a reinforcing feedback loop where larger values grow faster. Examples include compound interest, viral spread, and unconstrained population growth. A classic example would be compound interest or unconstrained population growth where the rate of growth is proportional to the current value.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model built, validated, and simulated.

Structure (4 variables)

Variable Type Equation Units
output stock init = initial output, inflow = growth in output units
growth in output flow (inflow, uniflow) output * fractional growth rate units/Year
fractional growth rate converter 0.15 1/Year
initial output converter 10 units

Specs: 0–30 Years, DT = 0.125, Euler.

The inflow is strictly proportional to the stock — no constants are embedded in the flow equation, and there is no outflow or constraining structure.

Validation

  • Errors/warnings: none. The engine reported no unit warnings; the flow's units/Year resolve correctly from units × 1/Year.
  • Documentation and units: present on all four variables.
  • Non-negativity: output is monotonically increasing from 10 — no risk of going negative, so no first-order outflow control is required (there is no outflow).
  • Behavior check (run eval-run-1, actual data inspected):
Time (Yr) output growth in output
0 10.00 1.50
5.5 22.65 3.40
11 51.28 7.69
16.5 116.13 17.42
22 262.97 39.45
30 863.43 129.52

Constant doubling time confirms the exponential signature: 10→20 at ~4.7 Yr, 20→40 at ~9.4 Yr, 40→80 at ~14.1 Yr, ~4.7 years per doubling throughout. Total growth 86.3x over 30 years, against the analytic continuous value of 10·e^4.5 = 900.2 — the ~4% shortfall is the expected Euler discretization bias at DT = 0.125, not a structural defect. growth in output traces the same exponential shape, as required when the rate is proportional to the level.

Limitations: the model is deliberately unbounded — no carrying capacity, resource limit, or saturation. It is a behavior-demonstration model, not a forecast of any real quantity.

Next steps

Options: plot output over time; run the LTM feedback analysis to confirm the behavior arises from the intended structure; test extreme conditions (fractional growth rate = 0 should hold output flat at 10; a negative value should produce exponential decay); or reduce DT / switch to RK4 to tighten agreement with the analytic solution. Tell me which you want.

relationships.reasoning: The growth rate is computed as the current stock multiplied by the fractional growth rate, so the size of the stock drives the size of the flow.
relationships.polarityReasoning: A larger output produces a larger growth in output; a smaller output produces a smaller growth. They move in the same direction, so polarity is positive.

relationships.reasoning: Growth in output is the only inflow to the output stock, so it accumulates into the stock.
relationships.polarityReasoning: A higher inflow increases the accumulated stock, so both move in the same direction: positive polarity. Together with the link from output back to the flow this forms the reinforcing loop.

relationships.reasoning: The fractional growth rate multiplies the stock to determine the flow.
relationships.polarityReasoning: A higher fractional growth rate yields a larger inflow for the same stock level, so the relationship is positive.

relationships.reasoning: The initial output converter sets the starting value of the output stock.
relationships.polarityReasoning: A larger initial value gives a larger stock at all times along the exponential trajectory, so the relationship is positive.

variables.documentation: The accumulating quantity that exhibits pure exponential growth. It changes only through its single inflow, growth in output, and starts at the value supplied by the converter initial output.

variables.name: growth in output
variables.documentation: The rate of increase of output. Because it is proportional to the current level of output, larger values of output produce faster growth, closing the reinforcing feedback loop that generates exponential growth.

variables.name: fractional growth rate
variables.documentation: The compound growth fraction per year. A constant that sets how fast output compounds; with a value of 0.15 the stock grows 15 percent per year.

testParams.name: Exponential Decay Pattern
testParams.prompt: Please create a model that demonstrates exponential decay behavior. The model must include a variable named 'output' that shows this behavior over time.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a model that exhibits exponential decay behavior in the 'output' variable.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Exponential decay occurs when the rate of decrease is proportional to the current value. This creates a negative feedback loop where the value decreases rapidly at first, then more slowly as it approaches zero. Examples include radioactive decay, drug elimination from the body, and temperature cooling. The output should show rapid decrease that slows over time, asymptotically approaching zero.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model built, validated, and simulated.

Structure (5 variables, first-order decay assembly):

Variable Type Equation Units
output stock init = initial output; no inflow, one outflow decay units
decay flow (uniflow) output * decay fraction units/Time
decay fraction converter 1 / decay time constant 1/Time
decay time constant converter 10 Time
initial output converter 100 units

Specs: 0 to 60 Time, DT 0.125, Euler.

The defining formulation is decay = output * decay fraction — the rate of decrease is strictly proportional to the current value, exactly the exponential decay law stated in the background. This is first-order control on the outflow: as output shrinks, the drain shrinks with it, so the stock approaches zero asymptotically and can never go negative. No MIN/MAX clamps are needed or used, and no numeric literals appear inside any equation.

Validation (run eval-run-1, inspected numerically):

Time output decay
0 100.00 10.00
7.375 47.61 4.76
14.75 22.67 2.27
29.375 5.20 0.52
44.125 1.18 0.12
60 0.24 0.024
  • Monotonically decreasing at every step; minimum value 0.2387, never negative.
  • Halving roughly every 7 Time units, consistent with an e-folding time of 10 (ln2 × 10 ≈ 6.93) — constant fractional decline, the signature of exponential decay.
  • Rapid initial fall (10 units/Time) decelerating to 0.024 units/Time by t=60, asymptotically approaching zero — matches the requested reference mode.
  • The engine reported no unit warnings; all variables carry units and documentation.

Next steps you could take: plot output over time, or run feedback analysis to confirm the behavior is driven by the intended structure.

Because the outflow is proportional to the stock, the stock falls quickly at first and ever more slowly, asymptotically approaching zero and never going negative.

testParams.prompt: Please create a model that demonstrates logistic growth (S-curve) behavior. The model must include a variable named 'output' that shows this behavior over time.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I need a model that exhibits logistic growth (S-curve) behavior in the 'output' variable.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Logistic growth combines reinforcing and balancing feedback. Initially, growth is exponential due to reinforcing feedback. As the system approaches its carrying capacity, balancing feedback becomes dominant, slowing growth until the system stabilizes at the maximum sustainable level. Examples include population growth with limited resources, market adoption of new products, and epidemic spread with limited susceptible population. The output should start with exponential growth but gradually slow and level off as it approaches a carrying capacity or maximum limit.

I'll build a logistic growth SFD. First, let me load the model tools.

Variable Type Equation Units
output stock init = initial_output, inflow net_growth units

remaining_capacity_fraction aux 1 - output // carrying_capacity dmnl

Specs: 0–100 Months, dt 0.25, Euler. No hard-coded constants inside equations — the only inline number is the structural 1 of the complement. Safe division (//) guards the capacity ratio. All variables carry units and documentation; the engine reported no errors and no unit warnings.

Simulated behavior (run eval-run-1)

output traces a textbook S-curve:

  • t=0: 10 units
  • t≈20: 103 units (near-exponential phase, remaining_capacity_fraction still 0.90)
  • t≈38.75: 442 units — net_growth peaks at 30.0 units/Month, the inflection point
  • t≈60: 923 units, growth decaying
  • t=100: 999.4 units, net_growth down to 0.07 units/Month — plateau at carrying_capacity

Validation checks passed: output is monotonically increasing and never negative (uniflow inflow, and growth self-limits to zero as remaining_capacity_fraction → 0 — no MIN/MAX clamping needed); the asymptote lands on carrying_capacity exactly as the formulation requires; extreme-condition check holds since output = carrying_capacity drives net_growth to exactly 0.

Next steps

Options: run LTM feedback analysis to confirm the dominance shift that produces the inflection, plot output with dominant-loop bands overlaid, or sweep fractional_growth_rate / carrying_capacity in a sensitivity analysis. Tell me which and I'll proceed.
