variables.name: Susceptible People
variables.documentation: The number of people in the population who have not yet been infected and are therefore at risk of catching the disease. It is depleted only by the infection rate as susceptible people come into contact with infected people and become infected. It starts at the whole population minus the small seed of initially infected people.

variables.name: Infected People
variables.documentation: The number of people who are currently infectious and able to transmit the disease to susceptible people through contact. It is increased by new infections and drained as people recover after the average duration of illness. It begins with the small seed of initially infected people that starts the outbreak.

variables.name: Recovered People
variables.documentation: The number of people who have passed through the illness and are now immune, no longer able to be infected or to infect others. It accumulates the recovery rate. At the start of the outbreak nobody has yet recovered, so it begins at zero.

variables.name: Infection Rate
variables.documentation: The number of people becoming infected each day. This is the standard mass-action formulation: each susceptible person makes Contact Rate contacts per day, a fraction of those contacts (Infected People divided by Total Population) are with infectious people, and each such contact transmits with probability Infectivity. The safe-division operator prevents a divide-by-zero if the population were ever zero. This flow moves people from the susceptible stock into the infected stock.

variables.name: Recovery Rate
variables.documentation: The number of infected people recovering each day. It is a first-order outflow: on average each infected person remains infectious for the average duration of illness, so a constant fraction of the infected stock recovers each day. Because the flow is proportional to the stock, it slows as the stock empties and infected people can never go negative. This flow moves people from the infected stock into the recovered stock.

variables.name: Contact Rate
variables.documentation: The average number of other people each person comes into physical contact with per day. Together with infectivity it determines how quickly the disease spreads. It is held constant here, representing an unchanged pattern of social mixing during the outbreak.

variables.name: Infectivity
variables.documentation: The probability that a single contact between a susceptible person and an infected person actually transmits the disease. It captures the intrinsic transmissibility of the pathogen, as distinct from how often people meet.

variables.name: Average Duration of Illness
variables.documentation: The average number of days a person remains infectious before recovering. It sets the residence time of people in the infected stock and therefore how long each infected person has to pass the disease on.

variables.name: Total Population
variables.documentation: The total size of the population in the outbreak, computed as the simple sum of the three groups. It is an algebraic aggregation rather than an accumulation, so it is an auxiliary and not a stock. Because every flow moves people from one group to another without adding or removing anyone, this total stays constant, which is the conservation check for the model. It is used to compute the fraction of contacts that are with infected people.

variables.name: Initial Infected People
variables.documentation: The small seed of infected people present at time zero that starts the outbreak. It sets the initial value of the infected stock and is subtracted from the initial population to give the initial susceptible stock.

variables.name: Initial Population
variables.documentation: The size of the population at the start of the outbreak. It determines the initial value of the susceptible stock, together with the initially infected seed.

testParams.name: Software Project Rework variable documentation
testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete stock-and-flow model of software project rework. Make sure that every variable in the model is clearly documented, describing what it represents and its role within the system.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand why software projects run late even when the team works hard, and how undiscovered errors and schedule pressure feed on each other over the life of a project.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A software project has a fixed scope of work. Tasks begin in a backlog of work still to be done and move to a pool of completed work as the team finishes them at a work rate. The work rate depends on the number of developers and their productivity. Not all completed work is actually correct: a fraction contains defects and becomes undiscovered rework instead of being truly finished. Undiscovered rework is not visible to the team until it is found during testing, after a discovery delay, at which point it flows back into the backlog of work to be done. As the deadline approaches with work remaining, schedule pressure rises. Higher schedule pressure pushes developers to work faster, raising the work rate, but it also raises the fraction of work done incorrectly (haste makes waste), which generates still more undiscovered rework and further delays the project. Sustained overtime also erodes productivity as developers fatigue.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand why software projects run late even when the team works hard, and how undiscovered errors and schedule pressure feed on each other over the life of a project.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build this model. Let me load the necessary tools first.

No assembly tools are registered in this session, so I'll formulate from the canonical rework-cycle generic structure directly.

The prompt was truncated. Retrying with a more compact structure spec.

Model generated. Now inspecting what was actually built.

Structure looks right, with first-order control on both the backlog and fatigue. Running it.

Run returned no data with a failure-flagged run id. Let me diagnose.

No edit_variables tools in this session — update_model's contract makes the session file the editing surface here. Let me diagnose the failure.

Found the failure cause: the variable names on disk use spaces (Work to Be Done), but every equation references underscored names (Work_to_Be_Done). read_model_section normalizes names for display, which hid the mismatch — so all 31 equations had unresolved references and the run died. Let me canonicalize to underscores.

All references now resolve. Pushing and re-running.

Still failing, so the name mismatch wasn't the root cause. Let me simulate the equations numerically myself to find the blowup.

Numerically the model is clean — conservation holds exactly (total = 800.00 tasks), nothing goes negative, and it reproduces the reference mode. But this exposed a real structural flaw: after the deadline, Time_Remaining hits 0, safe division drives Required_Work_Rate to 0, so Schedule_Pressure collapses to zero exactly when the project is most late. Let me fix that and remove the empty artifacts.

Run succeeded (eval-run-3 — no failure flag). The // operator and/or empty graphicalFunction artifacts were what the engine rejected. Let me verify the behavior.

The model is built, running, and validated. 32 variables, all with units and documentation.

What was built

Stocks (4) — the first three conserve the fixed scope in tasks:

  • Work_to_Be_Done — the backlog, initialized to Total_Scope_of_Work (800 tasks)
  • Work_Done — the pool of work truly finished and correct
  • Undiscovered_Rework — completed work that actually contains defects, invisible until testing
  • Fatigue — accumulated toll of sustained overtime

Flows (6)

  • Work_Rate = MIN(Developers * Productivity, Work_to_Be_Done / Minimum_Task_Completion_Time) — the MIN is first-order control so the backlog cannot be driven negative
  • Rework_Generation_Rate = Work_Rate * Fraction_of_Work_Done_Incorrectly
  • Correct_Work_Completion_Rate = Work_Rate * (1 - Fraction_of_Work_Done_Incorrectly)
  • Rework_Discovery_Rate = Undiscovered_Rework / Rework_Discovery_Delay — first-order discovery returning defects to the backlog
  • Fatigue_Buildup_Rate / Fatigue_Recovery_Rate — buildup only from hours above a normal week; first-order recovery

Three normalized graphical functions carry the nonlinearities: Overtime_Multiplier and Effect_of_Schedule_Pressure_on_Error_Fraction (both on Schedule_Pressure, passing through 1 at normal pressure), and Fatigue_Effect_on_Productivity (1 at zero fatigue, declining to a floor). No hard-coded constants appear in any equation — every parameter is a named variable.

Two defects I found and fixed

  1. The generated model would not simulate at all. The first two runs came back failure-flagged with empty data. Two causes: variable names on disk used spaces while every equation referenced underscored names (read_model_section normalizes names for display, which hid this), and the // safe-division operator plus empty graphicalFunction: {points: []} artifacts were rejected by this engine. Canonicalized names and replaced safe division with a structural fix.

  2. Schedule pressure collapsed to zero at the deadline — a genuine structural flaw, not just a syntax issue. With Time_Remaining reaching 0, Required_Work_Rate went to 0 and pressure vanished exactly when the project was most late. I added Minimum_Time_Remaining as a floor, so pressure stays high past the deadline (it now peaks near 25 and saturates the lookups rather than disappearing).

Validation

  • Conservation holds exactly: Work_to_Be_Done + Work_Done + Undiscovered_Rework = 800.0000 at every timestep
  • No variable goes negative anywhere in the run
  • Extreme conditions: at zero pressure the error fraction is 0.113, not zero — baseline defects persist without pressure, as they should
  • Reference mode reproduced: the 60-week project reaches 99% truly complete at week 113

The telling number: at the deadline the team perceives 66% complete while only 62% is genuinely done, with 270 tasks of visible backlog and 32.5 tasks of hidden rework. Work_Remaining deliberately excludes Undiscovered_Rework, so the gap between Perceived_Fraction_Complete and Fraction_of_Scope_Truly_Complete is the project's hidden debt. Fraction_of_Work_Done_Incorrectly climbs from 0.132 to 0.525 as pressure builds, and productivity's overtime gain is partly given back as Fatigue peaks at 0.689.

I have not run loop dominance analysis, so I'm not characterizing the feedback structure yet. Worth doing next:

  • Loops That Matter analysis to establish which loops actually drive the overrun and how dominance shifts across the project — this is what would answer your "feed on each other" question rigorously
  • Plot the perceived-vs-true completion divergence, or the rework/pressure/error trio
  • Policy tests: shorten Rework_Discovery_Delay (test earlier), or relax Deadline, to see which yields earlier true completion
  • Sensitivity on Rework_Discovery_Delay and Normal_Fraction_of_Work_Done_Incorrectly

One caveat to flag: peak Schedule_Pressure near 25 sits at the far end of the lookup domain where both pressure functions saturate. That's deliberate death-march behavior, but the results in that regime depend on the saturation values I chose rather than on curve shape, and Minimum_Time_Remaining = 1 week is the parameter setting it.

variables.name: Work_to_Be_Done
variables.documentation: The backlog of project work still to be done. It starts at the full project scope, is drained as the team completes tasks, and is refilled when defective work is discovered in testing and must be redone. This is the stock the team looks at when judging how much is left.

variables.name: Work_Done
variables.documentation: The pool of work that is truly finished and correct. Only correctly completed work enters here, so this stock measures real progress toward the fixed scope.

variables.name: Undiscovered_Rework
variables.documentation: Work that has been completed but actually contains defects. It is invisible to the team until testing reveals it, which is why projects can appear on schedule until very late.

variables.name: Fatigue
variables.documentation: A dimensionless accumulation of the toll of sustained overtime on the development team. It builds only while people work more than a normal workweek and decays when overtime stops.

variables.name: Work_Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which the team completes tasks. It is the smaller of the team's effective capacity (developers times productivity) and the rate at which the remaining backlog could physically be finished, so the backlog can never go negative.

variables.name: Rework_Generation_Rate
variables.documentation: The portion of completed work that contains defects and therefore flows into undiscovered rework rather than into truly finished work.

variables.name: Correct_Work_Completion_Rate
variables.documentation: The portion of completed work that is done correctly the first time and therefore represents genuine progress.

variables.name: Rework_Discovery_Rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which testing uncovers defective work. First-order discovery: a constant fraction of the undiscovered rework pool surfaces each week and returns to the work to be done backlog.

variables.name: Rework_Discovery_Delay
variables.documentation: Average time between creating a defect and discovering it in testing. A long delay is what hides the true state of the project from the team.

variables.name: Minimum_Task_Completion_Time
variables.documentation: The shortest average time it takes to work through the remaining backlog. It provides the first-order control in the work rate so the backlog cannot be driven below zero.

variables.name: Developers
variables.documentation: The constant number of developers assigned to the project. Staffing is deliberately held fixed so the model isolates the pressure, error and fatigue loops.

variables.name: Normal_Productivity
variables.documentation: Tasks completed per developer per week under normal conditions, that is with no overtime and no fatigue. It is the reference point for productivity and for normal team capacity.

variables.name: Productivity
variables.documentation: Effective tasks completed per developer per week. Normal productivity is raised by overtime worked under schedule pressure and eroded by accumulated fatigue.

variables.name: Overtime_Multiplier
variables.documentation: Effect of schedule pressure on hours worked, expressed as a ratio to the normal workweek. It equals one when there is no pressure, rises as pressure builds, and saturates at the maximum sustainable workweek ratio. This is the mechanism by which pressure raises the work rate.

variables.name: Deadline
variables.documentation: The scheduled project completion date, measured in weeks from project start. It is fixed, so as time passes the time remaining shrinks and pressure grows.

variables.name: Minimum_Time_Remaining
variables.documentation: The shortest planning horizon the team will work against, used as a floor on time remaining. It keeps schedule pressure finite and, critically, keeps pressure high rather than letting it vanish once the deadline has passed.

variables.name: Time_Remaining
variables.documentation: Weeks left until the deadline, floored at a minimum planning horizon. The floor matters: without it, time remaining reaches zero at the deadline and the required work rate would collapse to zero, perversely relieving all schedule pressure exactly when the project is most late.

variables.name: Work_Remaining
variables.documentation: The work the team believes is still left. It equals the visible backlog only; undiscovered rework is deliberately excluded because the team cannot see it. This is the key reason projects look on schedule until late.

variables.name: Required_Work_Rate
variables.documentation: The completion rate the team would need to sustain in order to finish the visible remaining work by the deadline. Safe division returns zero when no time remains.

variables.name: Indicated_Work_Rate
variables.documentation: The rate the team could achieve under normal conditions with no overtime and no fatigue. It is the reference against which the required rate is compared.

variables.name: Schedule_Pressure
variables.documentation: Ratio of the work rate required to hit the deadline to the rate achievable under normal conditions. Values above one mean the team is behind and must work harder or faster.

variables.name: Normal_Fraction_of_Work_Done_Incorrectly
variables.documentation: Baseline share of completed work containing defects when the team is under normal schedule pressure.

variables.name: Effect_of_Schedule_Pressure_on_Error_Fraction
variables.documentation: Normalized multiplier capturing haste makes waste: it equals one at normal pressure and rises as pressure grows, because rushed and tired work skips reviews and checks.

variables.name: Fraction_of_Work_Done_Incorrectly
variables.documentation: Share of completed work that actually contains defects. Pressure raises this fraction, which generates more undiscovered rework and further delays the project. Capped at one because no more than all the work can be wrong.

variables.name: Fatigue_Buildup_Rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which fatigue accumulates. Only hours worked above the normal workweek contribute, so working a normal week builds no fatigue.

variables.name: Fatigue_Recovery_Rate
variables.documentation: First-order recovery from fatigue, so accumulated fatigue decays toward zero and can never go negative.

variables.name: Fatigue_Buildup_Time
variables.documentation: Time constant governing how quickly sustained overtime translates into fatigue.

variables.name: Fatigue_Recovery_Time
variables.documentation: Average time required for the team to recover from accumulated fatigue once overtime is reduced.

variables.name: Fatigue_Effect_on_Productivity
variables.documentation: Normalized multiplier on productivity from fatigue. It equals one with no fatigue and declines toward a floor as fatigue accumulates, so the short-term gain from overtime is progressively given back.

variables.name: Total_Scope_of_Work
variables.documentation: The fixed total scope of the project in tasks. It sets the initial backlog and serves as the denominator for the completion indicators.

variables.name: Fraction_of_Scope_Truly_Complete
variables.documentation: Share of the total scope that is genuinely finished and correct. This is the honest measure of progress.

variables.name: Perceived_Fraction_Complete
variables.documentation: Share of scope the team believes is finished, since defective work looks complete until it is tested. Comparing this with the truly complete fraction exposes the illusion of progress.

testParams.name: Fishery Boom and Bust variable documentation
testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete stock-and-flow model of fishery boom and bust. Make sure that every variable in the model is clearly documented, describing what it represents and its role within the system.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how a commercial fishery can collapse from overharvesting, and why fishing fleet investment tends to drive boom-and-bust cycles in the fish population.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A fish population grows through births and shrinks through natural deaths and through harvesting by a fishing fleet. The population regenerates fastest at intermediate levels and its net regeneration falls toward zero as it approaches the carrying capacity of the habitat or is driven near depletion. The harvest rate rises with both the number of fishing ships and the density of fish, since the catch per ship is higher when fish are abundant. Revenue from the harvest, less the operating cost of running the ships, determines the profit per ship. Profit drives investment in new ships, though new capacity is added only after a construction and financing delay; when profit turns negative, ships are scrapped or leave the fishery. More ships raise the harvest, which depletes the fish population, which lowers the catch per ship and eventually profit — a balancing process — but the investment delays cause the fleet to overshoot the sustainable level, producing cycles of boom and collapse.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how a commercial fishery can collapse from overharvesting, and why fishing fleet investment tends to drive boom-and-bust cycles in the fish population.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll start by loading the model generation tools and building the fishery model.

Loading complete. Now generating the stock-and-flow model.

Found a real problem: the graphical functions are being evaluated with uniformly-spaced x points, so my non-uniform lookups are misread by the engine. The fleet shrinks despite large profits. I'll rewrite all four lookups on uniform grids and retune.

Sustained boom-and-bust cycles now emerge. Verifying model validity.

Model built, validated, and simulated. Here is what is actually in it.

Structure (2 stocks, 5 flows, 20 auxiliaries/constants — all documented, all with units)

Fish Population (fish, initial 8000)

  • inflow births = Fish Population * fractional birth rate * crowding effect on births
  • outflow natural deaths = Fish Population // average fish lifetime
  • outflow harvest rate = Fishing Ships * catch per ship

Fishing Ships (ships, initial 10)

  • inflow new ship construction = DELAY3(desired ship additions, construction and financing delay)
  • outflow ship scrapping = Fishing Ships * fractional scrapping rate

Resource side: carrying capacity of the habitat (10000 fish), fish density relative to carrying capacity, fractional birth rate (0.8/Year), average fish lifetime (5 Years), and the lookup crowding effect on births, which falls from 1.0 in an empty habitat to exactly 0.25 at the carrying capacity — the value at which births precisely offset natural deaths, so net regeneration hits zero at capacity. Since births are also proportional to spawner numbers, absolute net regeneration peaks at intermediate population (about 2400 fish/Year near half of capacity) and vanishes at both depletion and capacity.

Harvesting: catch per ship = maximum catch per ship (200 fish/(ship·Year)) × effect of fish density on catch per ship, a lookup through the origin that saturates at full density. Passing through (0,0) means harvest shuts itself down as the stock is driven near depletion.

Economics: revenue per ship = catch per ship × price per fish (20 Dollars/fish); profit per ship = revenue per ship − operating cost per ship (2000 Dollars/(ship·Year)); return on investment per ship = profit per ship // operating cost per ship — a dimensionless signal feeding both decision points.

Fleet decisions: desired ship additions = Fishing Ships × maximum fractional fleet growth rate (0.3/Year) × effect of profit on investment (zero while loss-making, rising to 1.15 at maximum returns), delayed 3 Years through construction and financing delay. fractional scrapping rate = normal fractional scrapping rate (0.1/Year) × effect of losses on scrapping, which reaches 5× normal under severe losses and drops to 0.5× when profitable.

Correction made during validation

The generator wrote all four lookups on non-uniform x grids. The engine evaluates graphical functions on evenly-spaced points, so it read them at the wrong abscissas — the first run had the fleet shrinking while profit per ship was 1280 Dollars/(ship·Year). I rewrote all four on uniform grids (density 0→1.5 step 0.1; ROI −1→+1 step 0.25) and retuned. This is why inspecting simulated numbers rather than trusting generated structure matters.

Behavior (run eval-run-2, 0–100 Years, DT 0.125, Euler)

Sustained oscillation, period roughly 22 Years:

trough peak
Fish Population 1391 fish ~7200 fish
Fishing Ships 4.7 ships 21.3 ships
profit per ship −933 +1404 Dollars/(ship·Year)

First cycle: fleet doubles from 10 to 21 ships by Year 6 while the fish fall from 8000 to 2579; profit per ship goes negative at about Year 5, but ships keep arriving until Year 6.5 because of the 3-Year construction pipeline. Fish bottom out at 1392 in Year 10, fleet bottoms at 4.7 in Year 17, fish recover to 7219 by Year 22 — and the next boom begins.

Validation checks passed: no unit warnings reported by the engine; every variable has units and documentation; both stocks remain strictly positive at all times (all four outflows are first-order or shut off at zero stock — no MIN/MAX clamps anywhere); no hard-coded constants inside equations; safe division used on all three ratios.

Worth noting: the fleet's break-even catch is 100 fish/(ship·Year), reached at only 30% of carrying capacity — well below the 50% density that gives maximum sustainable yield. Economically, expansion remains attractive until the stock is already deep into depletion.

Useful next steps: run feedback-loop analysis (LTM) to identify which structure dominates during the boom versus the collapse phase, plot Fish Population and Fishing Ships with dominant-loop shading, test policies (a cap on maximum fractional fleet growth rate, a shorter construction and financing delay, or a harvest quota), or run sensitivity on the delay to confirm it is the oscillation driver.

variables.name: Fish Population
variables.documentation: The biological resource stock: the number of fish alive in the fishery. It accumulates births and is drained by natural deaths and by harvesting from the fleet. It starts at 8000 fish, well below the carrying capacity of 10000 but a healthy, productive population. This stock is the heart of the resource side of the system: its level determines fish density, which controls both the regeneration of the resource and the productivity (catch per ship) of the fishing fleet.

variables.name: births
variables.documentation: Fish born per year. Proportional to the existing population times the maximum fractional birth rate, scaled down by crowding as the population approaches the carrying capacity of the habitat. This formulation makes regeneration fastest at intermediate population levels: at very low populations there are few spawners, and at high populations crowding suppresses reproduction.

variables.name: natural deaths
variables.documentation: Fish dying of natural causes per year. Formulated as a first-order outflow (population divided by average fish lifetime) so that deaths shrink proportionally as the stock shrinks and the stock can never be driven negative.

variables.name: harvest rate
variables.documentation: Fish caught per year by the fleet. It equals the number of ships times the catch each ship achieves. Because catch per ship itself rises with fish density, the harvest rises with both fleet size and fish abundance. This is the link through which economic decisions deplete the biological resource.

variables.name: Fishing Ships
variables.documentation: The capital stock of the fishery: the number of active fishing ships. It accumulates newly constructed ships and is reduced by scrapping or exit from the fishery. It starts small (10 ships) so the fishery begins profitable and under-exploited. Because ships are ordered on the basis of current profit but only arrive after a construction and financing delay, this stock is the source of overshoot in the system.

variables.name: new ship construction
variables.documentation: Ships entering service per year. Orders placed today (desired ship additions) only become operating capacity after a construction and financing delay, represented with a third-order material delay. This pipeline delay means capacity keeps arriving after the fishery has already ceased to be profitable, which is the key mechanism behind fleet overshoot and resource collapse.

variables.name: ship scrapping
variables.documentation: Ships leaving the fishery per year through scrapping, sale, or redeployment. Formulated as a first-order outflow: fleet size times the fractional scrapping rate, so the fleet can shrink but never go negative. Scrapping accelerates sharply when the fishery is losing money.

variables.name: carrying capacity of the habitat
variables.documentation: The maximum number of fish the habitat can support. It is the reference level against which the fish population is compared to compute density, and it is the point at which crowding drives reproduction to zero.

variables.name: fractional birth rate
variables.documentation: The maximum fraction of the fish population born per year, achieved when the habitat is empty enough that crowding has no effect. Together with the average fish lifetime it sets the maximum intrinsic regeneration rate of the resource.

variables.name: average fish lifetime
variables.documentation: Average lifespan of a fish in the absence of fishing. Its inverse is the fractional natural mortality rate. With a maximum fractional birth rate of 0.8 per year, this gives a maximum net intrinsic growth of about 0.6 per year at low density.

variables.name: crowding effect on births
variables.documentation: Dimensionless multiplier on the fractional birth rate representing competition for food, spawning grounds and space. It is 1 in an empty habitat and declines steadily with crowding, reaching 0.25 exactly at the carrying capacity of the habitat - the value at which births just offset natural deaths, so NET regeneration falls to zero there. Above capacity it falls further, pushing the population back down. Because births are also proportional to the number of spawners, this shape makes absolute net regeneration greatest at intermediate population levels (peaking near half of capacity) and small near both depletion and capacity. Points are evenly spaced over a relative density of 0 to 1.5.

variables.name: fish density relative to carrying capacity
variables.documentation: The fish population expressed as a fraction of the habitat's carrying capacity. This normalized measure of abundance drives both the crowding of reproduction and the ease with which ships find fish, so it is the single state signal linking biology to economics. Safe division is used so the model is robust if capacity were ever set to zero.

variables.name: catch per ship
variables.documentation: Fish landed per ship per year. Equal to the maximum catch a ship could take when fish are fully abundant, degraded by the effect of fish density on catch. Catch per ship is the productivity of capital in this system: it is high when fish are abundant and falls toward zero as the resource is driven near depletion, which is what eventually kills profitability.

variables.name: maximum catch per ship
variables.documentation: The annual catch one ship can achieve when the fish population is at full density, set by the ship's gear, crew and days at sea. It scales the technical harvesting capability of the fleet.

variables.name: effect of fish density on catch per ship
variables.documentation: Dimensionless search-and-encounter multiplier: how easily a ship fills its hold given how thick the fish are. It is 0 at zero density (no fish, no catch), rises steeply at low density because scarce fish are still findable in the remaining shoals, and saturates at 1 once the population is at full density, where the ship's own hold, gear and days at sea become the binding constraint. Passing through the origin is essential: it makes harvesting shut itself down as the stock collapses, so the Fish Population can never be driven negative. Points are evenly spaced over a relative density of 0 to 1.5.

variables.name: revenue per ship
variables.documentation: Annual gross income earned by one ship: its catch valued at the market price of fish. This is the economic reward signal transmitted from the state of the resource to the investors.

variables.name: price per fish
variables.documentation: Exogenous market price received for each fish landed. Held constant here so that the boom-and-bust dynamics come from the fleet-resource interaction rather than from price feedback.

variables.name: operating cost per ship
variables.documentation: Annual cost of running one ship: fuel, crew, maintenance and debt service. It is incurred whether or not the ship catches much, so it sets the break-even catch below which the fishery loses money (here 100 fish per ship per year, reached at roughly 20 percent of carrying capacity).

variables.name: profit per ship
variables.documentation: Annual net earnings of one ship: revenue from the harvest less the operating cost of running the ship. It can be negative when fish are scarce, which is what triggers exit from the fishery.

variables.name: return on investment per ship
variables.documentation: Profit expressed as a dimensionless fraction of operating cost. Normalizing profitability this way lets the same signal drive both the investment and the scrapping decisions through unit-free lookup functions. It equals -1 when a ship catches nothing and is positive whenever revenue exceeds cost. Safe division guards against a zero cost.

variables.name: effect of profit on investment
variables.documentation: Dimensionless willingness of owners and lenders to finance new ships, as a function of the return on investment per ship. It is zero whenever the fishery is losing money, small at break-even, and rises steeply through the profitable range to slightly above 1 when returns are at their technical maximum. This is the multiplier through which profit drives investment in new ships. Points are evenly spaced over a return on investment of -1 (a ship catching nothing) to +1 (a ship catching its maximum).

variables.name: desired ship additions
variables.documentation: Ships ordered per year. Investment is proportional to the existing fleet (bigger fleets attract and finance more expansion) times the maximum fractional growth rate, modulated by current profitability. Because it responds to today's profits, which reflect today's still-abundant fish, orders keep flowing right up to the moment of collapse.

variables.name: maximum fractional fleet growth rate
variables.documentation: The fastest fraction of the existing fleet that can be ordered per year under normal strong profitability, limited by shipyard capacity and access to finance. It sets the aggressiveness of the boom.

variables.name: construction and financing delay
variables.documentation: Average time between deciding to add a ship and that ship fishing: arranging finance, building and outfitting. This delay is the key source of overshoot, because the fleet keeps growing for years after the fish population has already begun to fall.

variables.name: fractional scrapping rate
variables.documentation: The fraction of the fleet retired per year. It equals the normal wear-out rate amplified when the fishery is losing money, since owners lay up, sell or scrap ships far faster than physical wear alone would dictate once profits turn negative.

variables.name: normal fractional scrapping rate
variables.documentation: Baseline retirement rate of ships from physical wear-out, corresponding to an average ship life of about ten years when the fishery is neither strongly profitable nor loss-making.

variables.name: effect of losses on scrapping
variables.documentation: Dimensionless multiplier on the normal fractional scrapping rate, driven by the return on investment per ship. When losses are severe, owners lay up, sell or scrap ships up to five times faster than physical wear-out alone would dictate; when the fishery is profitable, ships are kept in service longer and the multiplier falls below 1. This asymmetric exit response lets the fleet contract quickly once the fishery turns unprofitable, which allows the fish to recover and sets up the next boom.

failures.details: Documentation for variable "carrying capacity of the habitat" was judged low quality: The documentation inaccurately states that carrying capacity is the point where crowding drives reproduction to zero. In this model, crowding reduces births to balance natural mortality at carrying capacity (so net population growth is zero), while gross reproduction only falls to zero at 1.5 times carrying capacity.

testParams.name: Market Growth and Capacity variable documentation
testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete stock-and-flow model of market growth and capacity. Make sure that every variable in the model is clearly documented, describing what it represents and its role within the system.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand why a fast-growing company's sales can stall or oscillate as it struggles to expand production capacity quickly enough to meet demand.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A company's installed base of customers grows as the sales force wins new customers and shrinks as existing customers are lost. Customers place orders, and orders that cannot be filled immediately accumulate in a backlog. Production capacity limits how quickly the backlog can be filled, so the delivery delay experienced by customers is the backlog divided by the available capacity. A longer delivery delay reduces the company's attractiveness, which lowers the order rate and slows customer acquisition — a balancing loop that constrains growth. Revenue from filled orders funds investment in both the sales force and additional production capacity, but new capacity comes online only after a construction delay. A larger sales force wins customers faster, creating a reinforcing growth loop, while the capacity and delivery-delay dynamics push back against that growth and can cause sales to overshoot and oscillate.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand why a fast-growing company's sales can stall or oscillate as it struggles to expand production capacity quickly enough to meet demand.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll load the model generation tools and build this market growth and capacity model.

Model built and runs clean with no negative stocks, but behavior is smooth balanced exponential growth — no overshoot or oscillation. Let me explore the parameter space offline to find a regime that reproduces the reference mode.

The instantaneous attractiveness response acts as a fast first-order damper, which is why no oscillation is possible. Customers judge service on recent experience, not instantaneously — let me test adding a reputation/perception lag.

Perception lag on delivery delay produces the overshoot-and-oscillation reference mode. Let me examine the best candidates in detail.

Behavior now matches the reference mode and passes extreme-condition tests. Let me find the proper editing tools.

The only editing path registered in this session is update_model, which per its contract reads the session file after edits. Let me inspect the file structure.

Now applying the structural change and recalibrated parameters to the session model file, then pushing via update_model.

Engine output matches my offline analysis exactly. Verifying documentation and units coverage:

Model built, validated, and simulating the reference mode. No unit warnings or errors reported by the engine.

What is actually in the model

6 stocks

Stock Units Init Inflow Outflow
Installed Base of Customers customers 100 New Customers Won Customers Lost
Backlog orders 60 Order Rate Order Fill Rate
Sales Force people 3 Sales Force Hiring Rate Sales Force Attrition Rate
Production Capacity orders/Month 80 Capacity Coming Online Capacity Depreciation
Capacity Under Construction orders/Month 18 Capacity Construction Starts Capacity Coming Online
Perceived Delivery Delay Month Backlog // Production Capacity Change in Perceived Delivery Delay (biflow) —

Key equations as built

  • Delivery Delay = Backlog // Production Capacity
  • Attractiveness = Reference Delivery Delay // (Reference Delivery Delay + Perceived Delivery Delay)
  • Order Rate = Installed Base of Customers * Normal Order Rate per Customer * Attractiveness
  • New Customers Won = Sales Force * Customers Won per Salesperson * Attractiveness
  • Order Fill Rate = MIN(Production Capacity, Backlog // Minimum Order Processing Time)
  • Revenue = Order Fill Rate * Price per Order, split by Fraction of Revenue Invested and Fraction of Investment to Sales Force into Investment in Sales Force and Investment in Production Capacity
  • Capacity Construction Starts = Investment in Production Capacity // Cost per Unit of Capacity; Capacity Coming Online = Capacity Under Construction // Construction Delay

All 37 variables have units and documentation. Every outflow is fractional or first-order controlled; the only inline numbers are stock initial values and the structural complement 1 - Fraction of Investment to Sales Force.

One structural addition beyond your background text

The generated model had Attractiveness respond instantaneously to Delivery Delay. Simulated, that produced pure smooth exponential growth — no stall, no oscillation, ever. I confirmed this was structural, not parametric: a 6,480-point sweep over the investment split, capacity cost, construction delay, reference delay and salesperson productivity produced zero oscillatory cases. An instantaneous service-quality response is a fast first-order damper that pins delivery delay and rules out overshoot by construction.

So I added Perceived Delivery Delay (an information stock: the service reputation the market currently believes) and Delivery Delay Perception Time (15 Months). Attractiveness now responds to the perceived, not the instantaneous, delay. This is the only element not stated in your background, and it is what makes the reference mode reachable.

Behavior (run: eval-run-2)

Order Rate turning points: peak 119.9 at month 13.9 → trough 74.5 at month 30.1 → peak 117.3 at month 53.1 → trough 105.2 at month 68.8 → peak 139.6 at month 100.1. Growth of 3x, a 38% collapse, then oscillation of decaying amplitude on a rising trend. Delivery Delay runs 0.28 → 4.00 → 2.40 Months; Attractiveness falls 0.46 → 0.16; Production Capacity only reaches 150 from 80.

Validation performed

  • No stock goes negative: minima are base 100, Backlog 22.5, Sales Force 3.0, Capacity 80.0, Under Construction 17.8, Perceived Delay 0.59.
  • Conservation holds: Backlog and customer integrals reconcile to within trapezoid error on the downsampled output (0.8% and 0.01%).
  • Identities exact: Revenue = Fill Rate × Price and Delivery Delay = Backlog ÷ Capacity to machine precision.
  • Not a numerical artifact: turning points are stable across dt = 0.25, 0.125, 0.0625, 0.03125.
  • Extreme conditions: zero initial sales force still grows off the existing base; diverting all investment away from capacity makes capacity depreciate and order rate decline (40 → 30); a 1-month construction delay raises month-120 orders to 220; a 2,000-unit initial capacity gives unconstrained exponential growth to 2,720 — confirming the constraint originates in the capacity structure.

I have not run loop-dominance analysis, so I am deliberately not attributing this behavior to any particular feedback structure yet.

Suggested next step: run Loops That Matter feedback analysis to establish which loops actually dominate each phase — the growth run-up, the stall, and each oscillation — and verify the model produces the right behavior for the right reasons. Informative plots would be Order Rate against Production Capacity, and Delivery Delay against Perceived Delivery Delay. Also worth testing: Fraction of Investment to Sales Force (currently 0.65) as a policy lever, and sensitivity to Construction Delay and Delivery Delay Perception Time.

variables.name: Installed Base of Customers
variables.documentation: The accumulated number of active customers the company serves. It rises as the sales force wins new customers and falls as customers are lost. It is the primary driver of the order rate.

variables.name: New Customers Won
variables.documentation: Rate at which the sales force acquires new customers. Each salesperson wins a normal number of customers per month, scaled by how attractive the company currently is (which falls when delivery delay is long).

variables.name: Customers Lost
variables.documentation: Rate at which existing customers leave, formulated as a constant fractional loss of the installed base so that churn scales with the size of the customer base.

variables.name: Customer Loss Fraction
variables.documentation: Fraction of the installed base lost each month (average customer lifetime is the inverse of this fraction).

variables.name: Customers Won per Salesperson
variables.documentation: Normal productivity of a salesperson: customers acquired per salesperson per month when the company is fully attractive.

variables.name: Backlog
variables.documentation: Unfilled orders waiting to be produced and shipped. Orders accumulate here when the order rate exceeds the rate at which capacity can fill them; the size of this stock relative to capacity defines the delivery delay customers experience.

variables.name: Order Rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which customers place orders. Proportional to the installed base and to normal ordering per customer, reduced by poor attractiveness when delivery delays lengthen.

variables.name: Normal Order Rate per Customer
variables.documentation: Orders placed per customer per month under normal (fully attractive) service conditions.

variables.name: Order Fill Rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which orders are produced and shipped. It is limited either by available production capacity or by the minimum time it physically takes to process the current backlog, whichever is smaller. This first-order formulation prevents the backlog from going negative.

variables.name: Minimum Order Processing Time
variables.documentation: Shortest possible time to process an order even when capacity is abundant; it sets the floor on delivery delay and keeps the backlog non-negative.

variables.name: Delivery Delay
variables.documentation: Average time customers wait for their orders, computed as the backlog divided by the capacity available to work it off. Safe division avoids a divide-by-zero if capacity is ever zero.

variables.name: Perceived Delivery Delay
variables.documentation: The delivery delay that customers and prospects currently believe the company has, built up from the service they and their peers have actually experienced. It is an information stock representing the company reputation for service, and it lags the true delivery delay. Its role is to put a delay inside the balancing loop: the market keeps ordering enthusiastically for a while after service has actually deteriorated, and keeps holding back for a while after service has recovered. It is initialized at the true initial delivery delay so the model starts in informational equilibrium.

variables.name: Change in Perceived Delivery Delay
variables.documentation: Rate at which the market revises its belief about delivery delay toward the delay actually being experienced, a first-order information adjustment. It is positive when service is worse than the market yet realizes and negative when service has improved but the reputation has not yet caught up, so it is a biflow.

variables.name: Delivery Delay Perception Time
variables.documentation: Average time the market takes to recognize a change in the delivery delay it experiences. This reputation lag sets how long the balancing effect of poor service is postponed, and is a principal determinant of how far sales overshoot and how strongly they oscillate.

variables.name: Reference Delivery Delay
variables.documentation: The delivery delay customers consider normal or acceptable; it is the benchmark against which actual delivery delay is judged when forming attractiveness.

variables.name: Attractiveness
variables.documentation: Dimensionless measure of how appealing the company is to customers and prospects. It equals one when the perceived delivery delay is zero and declines toward zero as the perceived delay grows relative to the reference delivery delay. It feeds both the order rate of existing customers and the sales force ability to win new customers, forming the balancing loops that limit growth. Because it responds to the perceived rather than the instantaneous delay, the constraint on growth arrives late, which is what allows sales to overshoot before being pulled back.

variables.name: Sales Force
variables.documentation: Number of salespeople employed. A larger sales force wins customers faster, which raises revenue and funds still more salespeople - the reinforcing growth engine of the company.

variables.name: Sales Force Hiring Rate
variables.documentation: Rate of hiring salespeople. The firm closes the gap between the sales force it can afford (desired) and the one it has over an adjustment time, and also replaces those who leave. Hiring cannot be negative.

variables.name: Desired Sales Force
variables.documentation: The size of sales force the company can afford, equal to the money budgeted for selling divided by the monthly cost of one salesperson. This is how revenue funds sales growth.

variables.name: Sales Force Adjustment Time
variables.documentation: Average time it takes to recruit and bring the sales force to its desired size.

variables.name: Cost per Salesperson
variables.documentation: Fully loaded monthly cost of employing one salesperson; converts sales budget dollars into headcount.

variables.name: Sales Force Attrition Rate
variables.documentation: Rate at which salespeople quit, a constant fraction of the current sales force.

variables.name: Sales Force Attrition Fraction
variables.documentation: Fraction of salespeople who leave the company each month.

variables.name: Production Capacity
variables.documentation: Maximum rate at which the company can fill orders. It grows only as construction projects are completed and shrinks through depreciation, so it cannot respond instantly to demand.

variables.name: Capacity Coming Online
variables.documentation: Rate at which capacity under construction is completed and becomes usable. Formulated as a simple first-order delay on the construction pipeline, representing the construction delay.

variables.name: Capacity Depreciation
variables.documentation: Rate at which existing capacity wears out or is retired, a constant fraction of installed capacity.

variables.name: Capacity Depreciation Fraction
variables.documentation: Fraction of production capacity lost to wear and retirement each month.

variables.name: Capacity Under Construction

testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete, simulatable quantitative stock-and-flow model of population growth. Every stock must have a numeric initial value, every flow and auxiliary must have a well-defined equation, and the model must include simulation specifications (start time, stop time, time step, and time units) covering the full horizon described. The model must be able to run to completion in a system dynamics simulator without errors.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to project how a population changes over time given its birth and death processes.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A single population is a stock of individuals. It increases through births and decreases through deaths. Births each year equal the current population multiplied by a fractional birth rate, and deaths each year equal the current population multiplied by a fractional death rate. Use an initial population of 1000 individuals, a fractional birth rate of 0.03 per year, and a fractional death rate of 0.015 per year. Simulate from year 0 to year 100 with a time step of 0.25 years, using years as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to project how a population changes over time given its birth and death processes.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build this model. Loading the required tools first.

Structure and specs match the background exactly. Running the simulation.

Model built, validated, and simulated successfully.

Structure (6 variables)

Variable Type Equation Units
Population stock init = initial_population; inflow Births, outflow Deaths individuals
initial_population constant 1000 individuals
Births flow (uniflow) Population * fractional_birth_rate individuals/year
Deaths flow (uniflow) Population * fractional_death_rate individuals/year
fractional_birth_rate constant 0.03 1/year
fractional_death_rate constant 0.015 1/year

Specs: start 0, stop 100, dt 0.25, time units years, Euler integration.

Note the generator abstracted the initial value into a named constant initial_population rather than embedding 1000 in the stock equation — consistent with the no-hard-coded-constants rule. The stock still resolves to a numeric 1000 at t=0.

Validation

Dimensional consistency: individuals × 1/year = individuals/year for both flows. The engine reported no unit warnings, and no errors or warnings of any kind.

Structural critique:

  • Conservation holds — Population changes only via the two flows; no flow appears as both inflow and outflow.
  • Both flows are marked uniflow, correctly preventing births or deaths from running negative.
  • No first-order-control problem exists here: both flows are proportional to the stock itself, so as Population approaches zero both flows approach zero. The stock is structurally incapable of going negative without any MIN/MAX clamping.
  • Boundary limitation worth flagging: with constant fractional rates there is no density dependence (no carrying capacity, no resource or crowding feedback), so growth is unbounded by construction. That is exactly what the background specifies, but it means the model is only credible over horizons where the rates can plausibly be treated as fixed.

Behavioral verification (inspected numerically from eval-run-1):

  • Population: 1000 at t=0 → 4469.13 at t=100, monotonically increasing, minimum 1000. Never negative.
  • Births: 30 → 134.07/year. Deaths: 15 → 67.04/year. Both remain positive, and Births stays exactly 2× Deaths throughout, as the 0.03/0.015 rate ratio requires.
  • Net flow at t=0 = 15 individuals/year, matching 1000 × (0.03 − 0.015).
  • Reference mode: net fractional growth of 1.5%/year predicts an analytic value of 4481.69 at t=100. The simulated 4469.13 is 0.28% low — the expected Euler discretization error at dt=0.25. Reducing dt or switching to RK4 would close that gap, but the 0.25-year step was specified and the error is negligible for this purpose.

The model has passed both structural and behavioral critique and runs cleanly to completion.

Next steps

Options, in rough order of value:

  1. Feedback analysis — run LTM to confirm the growth arises from the right structure rather than merely producing the right numbers.
  2. Extreme-conditions tests — set initial_population to 0 (population should stay at 0 forever), or set fractional_death_rate above fractional_birth_rate (should decay asymptotically toward 0 without crossing it).
  3. Sensitivity analysis on the two fractional rates to quantify how the 100-year outcome responds to rate uncertainty.
  4. Visualization — a time series of Population with Births and Deaths would show the diverging flows driving the gap. I have not created any charts; tell me if you want one.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how the balance of a savings account evolves as it earns interest and money is added and withdrawn.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A savings account has a single stock: its balance, in dollars. The balance grows through an inflow made up of interest earned plus regular deposits, and shrinks through an outflow of regular withdrawals. Interest earned each year equals the current balance multiplied by an annual interest rate. Use an initial balance of 5000 dollars, an annual interest rate of 0.03 per year, deposits of 2400 dollars per year, and withdrawals of 1200 dollars per year. Simulate from year 0 to year 30 with a time step of 0.25 years, using years as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how the balance of a savings account evolves as it earns interest and money is added and withdrawn.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll load the model generation tools and build this.

Model built, validated, and simulated successfully.

Structure (8 variables)

Stock

  • Savings_Account_Balance (dollars) = initial_balance, inflow deposits_and_interest, outflow regular_withdrawals

Flows

  • deposits_and_interest (dollars/year) = interest_earned + regular_deposits — uniflow
  • regular_withdrawals (dollars/year) = withdrawal_rate — uniflow

Auxiliaries / constants

  • interest_earned (dollars/year) = Savings_Account_Balance * annual_interest_rate
  • annual_interest_rate (1/year) = 0.03
  • regular_deposits (dollars/year) = 2400
  • withdrawal_rate (dollars/year) = 1200
  • initial_balance (dollars) = 5000

Specs: 0 to 30 years, dt = 0.25, Euler, time units years.

Validation

  • No errors or unit warnings reported by the engine. Every variable has units and documentation.
  • No hard-coded constants inside equations — all four numeric values are abstracted into named constants (initial_balance, annual_interest_rate, regular_deposits, withdrawal_rate).
  • Dimensional check: balance (dollars) × rate (1/year) → dollars/year, matching both flows.
  • Negativity: not a concern here. Net non-interest cash flow is +1200 dollars/year and interest is non-negative, so the balance never approaches zero. No clamping needed.

Run result (eval-run-1)

Year Balance Interest earned
0 5,000 150
10.5 21,589 648
20.25 42,426 1,273
30 70,311 2,109

Accelerating growth, as expected. Sanity check against the closed-form solution B(t) = (B0 + net/r)·e^(rt) − net/r gives 70,682 at year 30; the Euler run's 70,311 is within 0.5 percent, consistent with a 0.25-year discrete step. Behavior is credible.

Note that interest_earned overtakes withdrawal_rate around year 26 — the point at which the account becomes self-sustaining against withdrawals from interest alone.

Next steps you might want: a time-series plot of the balance, a feedback-loop dominance analysis to see how the drivers of growth shift over the horizon, or a sensitivity run on annual_interest_rate and withdrawal_rate.

testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete, simulatable quantitative stock-and-flow model of infectious disease spread. additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how an infectious disease moves through a fixed population during an outbreak.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Use the classic SIR structure with three stocks: susceptible people, infected people, and recovered people. Susceptible people become infected and flow into the infected stock; infected people recover and flow into the recovered stock. The infection rate equals the contact rate times the infectivity times the number of infected people times the fraction of the total population that is still susceptible (susceptible divided by total population). The recovery rate equals the infected population divided by the average duration of illness. Use a total population of 10000, with 9990 initially susceptible, 10 initially infected, and 0 recovered. Use a contact rate of 6 contacts per person per day, an infectivity of 0.05, and an average duration of illness of 5 days. Simulate from day 0 to day 100 with a time step of 0.5 days, using days as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how an infectious disease moves through a fixed population during an outbreak.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build the classic SIR model per your specification.

Model built, validated, and simulated successfully.

Structure (9 variables, exactly as specified)

Stocks

Stock Initial Units
susceptible_people 9990 people
infected_people 10 people
recovered_people 0 people

Flows

  • infection_rate = contact_rate * infectivity * infected_people * (susceptible_people / total_population) — outflow of susceptible_people, inflow to infected_people, uniflow, people/day
  • recovery_rate = infected_people / average_duration_of_illness — outflow of infected_people, inflow to recovered_people, uniflow, people/day

Constants

  • total_population = 10000 people
  • contact_rate = 6 contacts/person/day
  • infectivity = 0.05 dimensionless
  • average_duration_of_illness = 5 days

Specs: 0 to 100 days, dt = 0.5, Euler, time units days.

No numeric constants are embedded in any equation — all four parameters are named auxiliaries. Every variable has units and documentation. The engine reported no errors and no unit warnings.

Validation of run eval-run-1

  • Conservation holds exactly: S + I + R = 10000.0000 at every reported time point. The population is closed, as required.
  • No impossible negatives: minimum susceptible = 4262.8, minimum infected = 10, minimum recovered = 0. The infected stock is drained by a first-order outflow (infected_people / average_duration_of_illness), which self-limits as the stock empties — no clamping needed.
  • Reference mode fit: the epidemic shows the expected shape. Infected grows from 10, peaks at ~644.6 around day 57, then declines to ~78.5 by day 100. Susceptible falls monotonically from 9990 to ~4263; recovered rises monotonically to ~5659. Roughly 57 percent of the population is infected over the horizon, and the outbreak burns out with susceptibles left over rather than infecting everyone.
  • Structural check: each flow appears as an outflow of one stock and an inflow of the next, never both on the same stock, so the SIR chain is conservative by construction. Both flows are marked uniflow, so neither can run backward.

Suggested next steps

Informative things to look at, if you want them: a time-series plot of the three stocks together to see the epidemic curve, or a dominance analysis to explain why the peak occurs when it does and why the outbreak dies out with susceptibles remaining. Also worth testing: extreme conditions (infectivity = 0 should hold infected flat at the recovery decay; contact rate very high should compress and heighten the peak), and sensitivity of peak infected to contact_rate and infectivity.

What would you like to do next?

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how a store's inventory responds when it continuously reorders stock toward a target level.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: A store holds a single stock of inventory, in units. Inventory rises through a production/delivery inflow and falls through a shipment outflow. Shipments equal customer demand, which is a constant 100 units per week. The store wants to keep inventory at a desired level equal to a target coverage of expected sales: desired inventory equals demand multiplied by a desired coverage of 4 weeks. The production rate equals demand plus a correction that closes the gap between desired inventory and current inventory over an inventory adjustment time of 8 weeks (that is, production equals demand plus (desired inventory minus inventory) divided by the adjustment time). Start with an initial inventory of 200 units, which is below the desired level, so the correction loop is active. Simulate from week 0 to week 52 with a time step of 0.25 weeks, using weeks as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how a store's inventory responds when it continuously reorders stock toward a target level.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll load the model generation tools and build this.

Model built, validated, and simulated successfully.

Structure (8 variables)

Stock

  • Inventory — units, initial value initial_inventory = 200 units. Inflow: production. Outflow: shipments.

Flows

  • production = customer_demand + (desired_inventory - Inventory) // inventory_adjustment_time — units/week, uniflow
  • shipments = customer_demand — units/week, uniflow

Auxiliaries / parameters

  • customer_demand = 100 units/week
  • desired_coverage = 4 weeks
  • desired_inventory = customer_demand * desired_coverage = 400 units
  • inventory_adjustment_time = 8 weeks
  • initial_inventory = 200 units

No numeric constants appear inside any behavioral equation — every parameter is a named variable, including the stock's initial value. Safe division (//) guards the adjustment-time divisor. All variables carry units and documentation.

Specs: start 0, stop 52, dt 0.25, time units weeks, Euler.

Validation

  • get_current_model returned no errors and no unit warnings.
  • Run eval-run-1 completed to week 52 without errors.
  • Inspected numerical output:
Variable t=0 t=52
Inventory 200 399.73
production 125 100.03
shipments 100 100
desired_inventory 400 400

Inventory is monotonically non-decreasing (min = 200 at t=0, max = 399.73 at t=52), never goes negative, and closes on the 400-unit target smoothly rather than overshooting or oscillating. production begins at exactly 100 + (400−200)/8 = 125 units/week and decays to demand as the gap closes. Conservation checks out: the net accumulation of 199.73 units matches the integral of production − shipments, and with shipments held at demand the stock's trajectory is driven entirely by the correction term. No first-order-control problem exists here — production is inherently self-limiting and shipments is exogenous at a level inventory always covers, so no MIN/MAX clamps were needed anywhere.

One documented boundary assumption: shipments = customer_demand unconditionally, so the model does not represent stockouts. That is faithful to the specification given, but it means the model would ship goods even at zero inventory — worth noting if you later want to stress-test with demand shocks.

Suggested next steps

  • Ask me to explain why the trajectory has this shape — I'd run feedback analysis and Seldon to ground that in the model's actual causal structure rather than asserting it.
  • Plot Inventory against desired_inventory, plus production vs shipments, to see the approach and the closing gap.
  • Sensitivity on inventory_adjustment_time and desired_coverage — the two policy levers.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand how the populations of a predator and its prey rise and fall together over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Use the classic Lotka-Volterra structure with two stocks: a prey population and a predator population. The prey population grows through prey births and shrinks through prey deaths caused by predation. Prey births equal a prey birth rate coefficient times the prey population. Prey deaths equal a predation coefficient times the prey population times the predator population. The predator population grows through predator births and shrinks through predator deaths. Predator births equal a predator efficiency coefficient times the prey population times the predator population. Predator deaths equal a predator death rate coefficient times the predator population. Use an initial prey population of 100 and an initial predator population of 20. Use a prey birth rate coefficient of 0.5, a predation coefficient of 0.02, a predator efficiency coefficient of 0.01, and a predator death rate coefficient of 0.4 (all per appropriate time unit). Because this system oscillates, use a small time step for numerical stability: simulate from time 0 to time 50 with a time step of 0.03125, using months as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand how the populations of a predator and its prey rise and fall together over time.

  • Predator_Births = Predator_Efficiency_Coefficient * Prey_Population * Predator_Population — predators/months
  • Predator_Deaths = Predator_Death_Rate_Coefficient * Predator_Population — predators/months

Constants

  • Prey_Birth_Rate_Coefficient = 0.5 (1/months)
  • Predation_Coefficient = 0.02 (1/(predators*months))
  • Predator_Efficiency_Coefficient = 0.01 (1/(prey*months))
  • Predator_Death_Rate_Coefficient = 0.4 (1/months)

Specs: 0 to 50 months, dt = 0.03125, RK4. No hard-coded constants inside equations; every value is a named auxiliary. All variables carry units and documentation.

Validation

The engine reported no errors and no unit warnings. Run eval-run-1 completed over the full horizon.

Behavioral checks on the actual data:

  • Both stocks remain strictly positive throughout — Prey_Population ranges 8.35 to 112.77, Predator_Population ranges 6.31 to 63.48. No clamping was needed; the mass-action outflows are inherently proportional to the stock they drain, which is the first-order control that keeps them positive.
  • Sustained oscillation with roughly a 16-month period, roughly three cycles over the horizon. Predator peaks trail prey peaks by about 2 months (e.g. prey peaks near t=15.3 and t=16.3, predators peak near t=18.4), the expected phase lag.
  • Conserved-quantity test: the Lotka-Volterra invariant 0.01*prey - 0.4*ln(prey) + 0.02*pred - 0.5*ln(pred) drifts by 0.091 over 50 months, a slow outward spiral visible as prey peaks creeping from about 102 to 113. This is ordinary numerical integration drift for a neutrally-stable center, not a structural defect. The specified dt of 0.03125 keeps it modest. A smaller dt would shrink it further if you want closer amplitude conservation.

Limitations worth stating

The pure Lotka-Volterra form has no prey carrying capacity and no predator satiation, so prey grow exponentially without predators and the cycle amplitude is set entirely by initial conditions rather than by any restoring structure. That is faithful to the specification, but it is why the system is neutrally stable rather than converging to a limit cycle.

Next steps

Options: plot the two populations over time or as a phase portrait; run feedback analysis to see which loops dominate at each stage of the cycle; or test extreme conditions such as zero initial predators. Let me know which you want.

testParams.name: Software Project Rework simulates to completion
testParams.prompt: Using the information I have given you, please build a complete, simulatable quantitative stock-and-flow model of software project rework. Every stock must have a numeric initial value, every flow and auxiliary must have a well-defined equation, and the model must include simulation specifications (start time, stop time, time step, and time units) covering the full horizon described. The model must be able to run to completion in a system dynamics simulator without errors.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I want to understand why a software project takes longer than planned once undiscovered rework is taken into account.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Model a fixed-scope software project with three stocks, all measured in tasks: work to be done, undiscovered rework, and work truly done. The team completes tasks at a work rate that flows out of work to be done. The work rate equals the number of developers times their productivity. A fraction of completed work is done correctly and flows into work truly done; the remaining fraction contains defects and flows into undiscovered rework instead. Undiscovered rework is not visible immediately: it is detected and flows back into work to be done at a rework discovery rate equal to the undiscovered rework stock divided by an average discovery delay. Use an initial work to be done of 500 tasks, an initial undiscovered rework of 0 tasks, and an initial work truly done of 0 tasks. Use 10 developers, a productivity of 0.4 tasks per developer per week, a fraction correct of 0.85 (so 0.15 of completed work becomes undiscovered rework), and an average discovery delay of 4 weeks. To avoid completed work continuing to be generated once the backlog is empty, the work rate should not exceed the amount of work remaining to be done. Simulate from week 0 to week 200 with a time step of 0.25 weeks, using weeks as the time unit.

expectations.problemStatement: I want to understand why a software project takes longer than planned once undiscovered rework is taken into account.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll start by loading the model generation tools.

Diagnosing the run failure. Testing whether the DT reference in work_rate is the culprit.

DT confirmed as the failure cause. Now testing an engine-supported time-step reference.

TIME_STEP works. Verifying behavior and conservation.

Model built, validated, and running cleanly.

Structure (11 variables, all units defined)

Stocks (tasks)

Stock Initial Inflows Outflows
work to be done 500 rework discovery rate work rate
undiscovered rework 0 generation of undiscovered rework rework discovery rate
work truly done 0 work done correctly —

Flows (tasks/week)

  • work rate = MIN(developers*productivity, work_to_be_done/TIME_STEP) — the MIN is a structural clipping limit so the team cannot complete more than the backlog holds
  • work done correctly = work_rate*fraction_correct
  • generation of undiscovered rework = work_rate*(1 - fraction_correct)
  • rework discovery rate = undiscovered_rework/average_discovery_delay (first-order drain)

Constants: developers = 10 (developers), productivity = 0.4 (tasks/developer/week), fraction correct = 0.85 (dimensionless), average discovery delay = 4 (weeks)

Specs: 0 to 200 weeks, DT = 0.25, time units weeks, Euler.

Build issue found and fixed

The generator wrote work_to_be_done/DT. That reference aborted the simulation (two failed runs). I isolated it by substituting a plain developers*productivity equation — which ran — then restored the backlog constraint using TIME_STEP, which this engine accepts. No arbitrary constant was introduced.

Validation (run eval-run-4)

  • No unit warnings and no errors reported by the engine.
  • Conservation holds exactly: work to be done + undiscovered rework + work truly done = 500.000 tasks at every sampled point from t=0 to t=200.
  • No stock goes negative: minima are 0.0000 for all three stocks and for work rate.
  • Terminal state correct: work truly done = 499.99998 tasks, work to be done ≈ 1.4e-06, undiscovered rework ≈ 2.2e-05.
  • Behavior: work rate holds flat at 4.000 tasks/week while the backlog is non-empty (t=0 to ~146), with rework discovery rate settling at 0.600 tasks/week and undiscovered rework holding a steady 2.400 tasks. Past t≈146 the backlog empties and the work rate tapers as the hidden stock drains — 0.576 at t=146.75, 0.301 at t=149.75, 0.035 at t=159.75.
  • Schedule outcome: work truly done crosses 499.5 tasks at week 154.75, against the naive plan of 500 / (10 x 0.4) = 125 weeks — roughly 24 percent over plan. Note the long thin tail: the model spends its last ~8 weeks draining a stock of well under one task, so the strict 100-percent-complete date is asymptotic rather than sharp.

One structural caveat worth flagging: because average discovery delay is a fixed 4 weeks and the discovery rate is proportional to the hidden stock, defects created in the final days are still being discovered long after the team has effectively stopped. That is the intended first-order formulation from your background information, but it means the completion date should be read off a tolerance threshold, not off exact equality with 500.

Next steps

I have not run feedback analysis yet, so I have deliberately said nothing about loop structure or dominance. Worthwhile options:

  1. Run feedback analysis to identify which loops drive the schedule extension and how dominance shifts across the flat phase and the tail.
  2. Plot the three stocks together, optionally with dominant-loop bands overlaid.
  3. Sensitivity analysis on fraction correct and average discovery delay to see which drives completion-date variance.

variables.name: work to be done
variables.documentation: The backlog of tasks that the team still believes must be executed. It starts at the full fixed scope of 500 tasks, is drained as developers complete work, and is refilled whenever previously hidden defects are discovered and must be redone. This refilling is the core reason the project takes longer than the naive plan.

variables.name: undiscovered rework
variables.documentation: Tasks that were completed with defects but whose defects are not yet known to the team. This stock is the hidden 'debt' of the project: it looks like progress but will later reappear as work to be done. It starts empty.

variables.name: work truly done
variables.documentation: Tasks completed correctly, which never need to be revisited. The project is genuinely finished when this stock reaches the full scope of 500 tasks. It starts empty.

variables.name: work rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which the team completes tasks, drawn out of the backlog. Normally it is simply the number of developers times their productivity. The MIN with the remaining backlog divided by the time step prevents the team from completing more work than actually remains, so no completed work (and no new rework) is generated once the backlog is empty.

variables.name: work done correctly
variables.documentation: The portion of the completed work that is free of defects and therefore accumulates permanently in work truly done. It is the work rate multiplied by the fraction of work that is done correctly.

variables.name: generation of undiscovered rework
variables.documentation: The portion of completed work that contains defects. It flows into the undiscovered rework stock rather than into work truly done. It is the work rate times the complement of the fraction correct.

variables.name: rework discovery rate
variables.documentation: The rate at which hidden defects are found, e.g. through testing or integration. Formulated as a first-order drain of the undiscovered rework stock over an average discovery delay. Discovered rework leaves the hidden stock and reappears in work to be done, extending the schedule.

variables.name: developers
variables.documentation: The fixed size of the development team.

variables.name: productivity
variables.documentation: Average number of tasks each developer completes per week, regardless of whether the task is done correctly.

variables.name: fraction correct
variables.documentation: Share of completed work that is defect free. The remaining share (1 minus this value, here 0.15) becomes undiscovered rework.

variables.name: average discovery delay
variables.documentation: Average time between creating a defect and discovering it. The longer this delay, the more hidden rework the project carries and the later the schedule slips become visible.

Cross-module coupling is carried entirely by the two ghosts: predation into the hare module via hare.lynx, and prey-availability into the lynx module via lynx.hare density.
