additionalParameters.problemStatement:
I've created this modular model simulating the urban dynamics in a city.
            Please recreate the system with no modules, while preserving key causal relationships.

            Component naming instructions:
            - Name components by removing the module name, and changing nothing else.
              For instance, 'Population.target housing per person' should be renamed to 'target housing per person'.
            Any other naming convention is unacceptable and will cause issues in my simulation.

            Try to preserve the key causal relationships and processes exactly.
            You are allowed to remove variables and modify relationships that are no longer appropriate in a non-modular context.
            Do not add any components that do not have a modular equivalent in my source model.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll start by inspecting the current model structure.

Model retrieved: three modules (Population, Housing, Commerce) with cross-level ghosts. I'll flatten by removing the ghosts and stripping module prefixes.

Now renaming all variables to strip module prefixes.

Relationships still carry module-qualified names. I'll rebuild them flat, restoring the cross-module links that previously ran through the ghosts.

Now validating the full model and running it.

The model is now fully flat. Summary of what was done:

Structure removed (module scaffolding only):

  • 4 cross-level ghost variables that existed solely to pass values between modules: Population.Housing_Stock, Population.total_jobs, Housing.Population, Commerce.Population. In a flat model these are redundant — the real Housing_Stock, total_jobs, and Population are directly visible to every equation.
  • The self-referential ghost link artifacts in the relationships section.

Renaming: every remaining variable had its module prefix stripped and nothing else changed (Population.target_housing_per_person → target_housing_per_person, etc.). All 31 variables retain their original equations, units, documentation, and graphical functions verbatim.

Causal links preserved: the four inter-module connections that previously routed through ghosts now connect the real variables directly:

  • Housing_Stock → relative_housing_availability (+)
  • total_jobs → relative_job_availability (+)
  • Population → relative_housing_demand (+)
  • Population → relative_labor_availability (+)

All 43 relationships are flat-named with original polarities and reasoning intact.

Final model: 3 stocks (Population 10,000 people; Housing_Stock 4,000 units; Business_Structures 500 structures), 6 flows (births, deaths, migration, construction, demolition, business starts, closures), and 21 auxiliaries including the three original graphical functions. Specs unchanged: 0–50 years, dt 0.25, Euler.

Validation: the model runs cleanly (run eval-run-1). No stock goes negative — Population 10,000 → 22,537; Housing Stock 4,000 → 11,802; Business Structures 500 → 1,202. Relative housing availability rises from 1.00 to 1.31 and relative job availability from 1.00 to 1.07, so the ratio-based multipliers stay in the interpolated range of their graphical functions rather than pinning at an endpoint. Growth is smooth and monotonic, matching the modular original's construction.

Next steps you might want: feedback loop analysis (LTM) to confirm the flattened model reproduces the same loop structure and dominance pattern as the modular version, or a time-series plot of the three stocks.

additionalParameters.problemStatement:
I've created this modular model simulating a predator-prey ecosystem.
            Please add a third module called 'cougars', representing cougars.
            
            As an apex predator, cougars are not hunted by any animal, and hunt lynxes to survive. 
            Cougars do not have any direct interactions with hares.

            Use the following component names in each module where appropriate:
            [animals], 
            [animal] births, [animal] deaths, 
            [animals] killed per [animal], [animal] density,
            [animal] birth fraction, [animal] death fraction
            - Note: [animal] is either "hare", "lynx", or "cougar"
            - Note: [animals] is either "hares", "lynx", or "cougars" (note the plural of "lynx" is "lynx")
            
            When ghosting, preserve the same variable name as in the source module. For instance, a ghost of "Hares.Hares"
            should be named "Lynx.Hares" in the "Lynx" module.

            You may add any necessary components, using appropriate names (as listed above) whenever possible.
            Do not modify or remove any existing causal relationships between lynxes and hares.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll start by inspecting the current model structure.

Model inspected: two modules (Hares, Lynx), classic Lotka-Volterra-style predator-prey with graphical functions for kills-per-predator and predator mortality. I'll add a Cougars module mirroring this generic structure one trophic level up.

Now I'll wire the new predation outflow into the Lynx stock.

Structure is in place with no errors or warnings. Running the simulation to verify behavior.

The Cougars module is built and integrated. Simulation could not produce data in this environment — run_model returned run eval-run-failed-1 with no variables, so no behavioral verification was possible. The structural validation passed: get_current_model reported no errors and no unit warnings after every edit.

What was added:

New module: Cougars

  • Cougars.Cougars — stock, initial 30 cougars; inflow cougar births, outflow cougar deaths only (no predation outflow, since cougars are apex predators and nothing hunts them)
  • Cougars.cougar births = Cougars * cougar_birth_fraction (cougars/year, uniflow)
  • Cougars.cougar deaths = Cougars * cougar_death_fraction (cougars/year, uniflow)
  • Cougars.cougar birth fraction = 0.2 per year
  • Cougars.cougar death fraction — graphical function of lynx density, falling from 0.90/year at zero lynx density to 0.06/year at 3 lynx/arce (starvation mortality, mirroring the existing lynx-mortality-vs-hare-density formulation)
  • Cougars.lynx density — ghost of Lynx.lynx density

Additions to the Lynx module (nothing existing was changed except the stock's outflow list)

  • Lynx.area — ghost of Hares.area
  • Lynx.lynx density = Lynx / area (lynx/arce)
  • Lynx.lynx killed per cougar — graphical function of lynx density, 0 at zero density and saturating near 5.2 lynx/cougar/year
  • Lynx.Cougars — ghost of Cougars.Cougars
  • Lynx.lynx predation deaths = Cougars * lynx_killed_per_cougar (lynx/year, uniflow), added as a second outflow of Lynx.Lynx

Predation mortality was added as a separate outflow rather than folded into lynx deaths, so the existing hare density → lynx death fraction → lynx deaths chain and every other hare-lynx relationship remain untouched. Cougars have no link of any kind to hares. Both new outflows carry first-order control: predation goes to zero as lynx density goes to zero (the kills-per-cougar table is anchored at the origin), and cougar deaths are proportional to the cougar stock.

Thirteen causal relationships were added with polarities and reasoning to match the new equations.

Next steps once a working simulation engine is available: run the model, inspect Hares, Lynx, and Cougars for negative values and for reasonable three-level trophic behavior, then call get_feedback_information to analyze which structures drive the resulting dynamics. The cougar birth fraction and the two new graphical functions are the parameters most worth testing for sensitivity, since they jointly set whether the cougar population is viable.

variables.name: Cougars.Cougars
variables.documentation: Initially, there are 30 cougars in the ecosystem. Cougars are the apex predator: nothing hunts them, so the stock only drains through natural/starvation mortality.

variables.name: Cougars.cougar births
variables.documentation: A compounding process is used to depict cougar births. The births flow is the product of Cougars and their natality, exactly as in the hare and lynx modules.

variables.name: Cougars.cougar deaths
variables.documentation: A draining process. Some fraction of the cougar population dies each year. Because no animal hunts cougars, all cougar mortality is natural mortality and starvation, which depends on the availability of their prey (lynx).

variables.name: Cougars.cougar birth fraction
variables.documentation: On average, each cougar will generate 0.2 offspring per year. Cougars are large, slow-reproducing apex predators, so their natality is lower than that of lynx.

variables.name: Cougars.cougar death fraction
variables.documentation: Cougar mortality -- the fraction of the cougar population that dies each year -- depends on lynx density. With fewer lynx to hunt, a greater fraction of the cougar population starves. This is the same formulation used for lynx mortality as a function of hare density.

variables.name: Cougars.lynx density
variables.documentation: Ghost of lynx density from the Lynx module. It is the food-availability signal that sets cougar mortality.

variables.name: Lynx.area
variables.documentation: Ghost of the ecosystem area defined in the Hares module, used here to compute lynx density.

variables.name: Lynx.lynx density
variables.documentation: The average density of lynx in the ecosystem. It drives both how many lynx each cougar can kill and how many cougars can be sustained.

variables.name: Lynx.lynx killed per cougar
variables.documentation: The number of lynx killed per cougar per year increases with the density of lynx in the ecosystem, saturating as cougars become handling-time limited. When lynx density is 0 there are no lynx to find, so kills per cougar must be 0.

variables.name: Lynx.Cougars
variables.documentation: Ghost of the cougar population from the Cougars module. Cougars are the external resource consuming lynx.

variables.name: Lynx.lynx predation deaths
variables.documentation: In this external resource process, cougars are the resource underwriting the consumption of lynx. Each cougar has a productivity given by lynx killed per cougar. This is kept as a separate outflow so the pre-existing starvation mortality of lynx (driven by hare density) is unchanged.

additionalParameters.problemStatement:
I've created this modular model simulating the urban dynamics in a city.
            However, I no longer need to simulate commerce dynamics. Please remove the 'Commerce' module from my model.

            Please do not add any variables or modify any processes or relationships unrelated to commerce.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll start by loading the model inspection tools and retrieving the current model structure.

Model retrieved. Commerce module contains 11 variables, and it exports total_jobs into the Population module via a cross-level ghost, which feeds the job-attractiveness branch of migration. Removing Commerce requires removing that dangling job chain as well.

Now I need to repair the migration equation, which still references the removed jobs branch.

Clean — no Commerce references or dangling equations remain. Running the model to verify it still simulates.

The Commerce module has been removed. Summary of what changed:

Removed — Commerce module (11 variables):

  • Stock: Business_Structures
  • Flows: business_starts, business_closures
  • Auxiliaries: base_start_fraction, closure_fraction, target_labor_per_business, relative_labor_availability, start_multiplier, jobs_per_structure, total_jobs
  • Cross-level ghost: Commerce.Population

Removed — orphaned Commerce consumers inside Population (4 variables): Commerce exported total_jobs into the Population module through a cross-level ghost. That ghost fed a chain that existed only to convert commerce output into migration pressure, so it had to go with the module or it would have left a dangling reference:

  • Population.total_jobs (ghost of Commerce.total_jobs)
  • Population.relative_job_availability
  • Population.attractiveness_from_jobs
  • Population.target_jobs_per_person

Repaired — one equation: Population.migration referenced the deleted jobs branch. It was the average of two attractiveness multipliers; with the jobs term gone it now uses the surviving housing term alone:

  • Before: Population*base_migration_fraction*((attractiveness_from_housing+attractiveness_from_jobs)/2)
  • After: Population*base_migration_fraction*attractiveness_from_housing

All causal arrows touching the deleted variables were removed automatically. Nothing was added, and Housing and the demographic aging chain (births, deaths, birth_fraction, death_fraction) are untouched.

Result: 20 variables, 28 relationships, two modules (Population, Housing). get_current_model returned no errors and no unit warnings, and no equation references a deleted variable.

One caveat you should know about: I could not verify the model's behavior. run_model reports success but returns runs named eval-run-failed-1 / eval-run-failed-2 with empty variable lists, and get_variable_data returns {} — the simulation engine is not producing output in this environment. So the structural edit is validated, but the behavioral checks I would normally do (Population and Housing_Stock staying non-negative, conservation, reference-mode fit) have not run. Worth a simulation on your end to confirm.

Structurally, the edit does change the model's dynamics in a way you should expect: migration is now driven by housing availability alone rather than a blend of housing and jobs, so net migration will respond about twice as strongly to a given housing imbalance as it did before. If you want migration to keep its previous sensitivity, lowering base_migration_fraction would compensate — say the word and I'll adjust it.

testParams.prompt:
Please give me a quantitative model that captures the key causal processes described in the background information.
Make sure to create a model with exactly the specified modules; do not add any additional modules beyond what is specified.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.


            At a certain business, employees are sorted in a three-role hierarchy.
            New hirees start with the "rookie" status.
            Rookies that perform well are promoted to associates.
            Associates that perform well are promoted to partners.
            To keep the hierarchy stable, the business promotes a strict percentage of each role every year.
            Some employees may also leave the company, whether due to personal reasons or exceptionally poor performance.
            A stable percentage of employees at each level of the company leave the company each year.
            The business also onboards a constant number of new hirees every year.

            Use the following component names as appropriate:
            rookies, associates, partners, promotion_rate, departure_rate, hire_rate,
            rookie_promotions, associate_promotions, rookie_hires,
            rookie_departures, associate_departures, partner_departures

            Do not create any modules in this model.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll start by loading the model generation tools.

Model built, validated, and simulated. No modules were created, as specified.

Structure (12 variables, no modules)

Stocks (people) — a three-stage aging chain through the role hierarchy:

Stock Initial Inflows Outflows
rookies 100 rookie_hires rookie_promotions, rookie_departures
associates 50 rookie_promotions associate_promotions, associate_departures
partners 20 associate_promotions partner_departures

Flows (people/Year) — every promotion flow is shared, serving as the outflow of one role and the inflow of the next, so people are conserved as they move up the hierarchy:

  • rookie_hires = hire_rate — constant onboarding, independent of firm size
  • rookie_promotions = rookies * promotion_rate
  • rookie_departures = rookies * departure_rate
  • associate_promotions = associates * promotion_rate
  • associate_departures = associates * departure_rate
  • partner_departures = partners * departure_rate

Constants: promotion_rate = 0.2 1/Year, departure_rate = 0.1 1/Year, hire_rate = 50 people/Year.

Every outflow is first-order fractional on its own stock, so no stock can be driven negative — no MIN/MAX clamps were needed. All flows are uniflow (people cannot move backwards into a lower role). Specs: 0–50 Years, DT 0.25, Euler.

Validation

  • No errors and no unit warnings reported by the engine.
  • Simulation eval-run-1 completed. All three stocks rise monotonically from their initial values and show goal-seeking approach; minimums equal the initial values, so nothing goes negative.
  • Analytic equilibria confirmed numerically: rookies → hire_rate/(promotion_rate+departure_rate) = 166.67 (reached); associates → 111.11 (reached); partners → 222.2 (at 220.1 by year 50 — the slowest level, since partners drain only through departures and therefore have the longest residence time).
  • Conservation check holds: at equilibrium total departures = 16.67 + 11.11 + 22.22 = 50 people/Year, exactly matching hire_rate.

One structural note worth flagging: because hire_rate is a fixed number rather than a function of headcount, the firm's total size is pinned at hire_rate / departure_rate = 500 people regardless of the promotion rate. Promotion rate only redistributes people among the three roles.

Next steps I'd suggest: run feedback analysis to identify which mechanisms dominate each phase of the transient, or test parameter sensitivity on promotion_rate to see how the role mix shifts. Let me know which you want.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.


            In a certain ecosystem, there are two animal populations: foxes and chickens.
            Initially, chickens significantly outnumber foxes.
            The chickens reproduce at a steady percentage rate per day.
            The foxes depend on the chickens for food. Each fox eats one chicken per day.
            Foxes also reproduce at a steady percentage rate per day, but slower than the chickens.
            
            Use the following component names as appropriate:
            fox_reproductionRate, fox_count, fox_reproduction,
            chicken_reproductionRate, chicken_count, chicken_reproduction, chicken_predation
            
            Do not create any modules in this model.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build this predator-prey model. Let me load the required tools first.

No edit_variables tool in this session, so I'll adjust the parameters in the session file and push via update_model.

Rationale: at 0.1/day chicken growth, predation (1 chicken/fox/day) is dynamically irrelevant — both stocks just grow exponentially and the predation mechanism the background describes never bites. Reparameterizing to chicken 0.02/day and fox 0.01/day keeps every stated constraint (steady percentage rates, foxes slower than chickens, chickens initially far outnumbering foxes) while making the predation coupling actually operative.

Model built, validated, and simulated. No modules (as required), no errors or unit warnings reported by the engine.

Structure as actually built

Stocks

  • chicken_count — 500 chickens; inflow chicken_reproduction, outflow chicken_predation
  • fox_count — 10 foxes; inflow fox_reproduction only (no mortality flow, per the background)

Flows

  • chicken_reproduction = chicken_count * chicken_reproductionRate (chickens/day)
  • fox_reproduction = fox_count * fox_reproductionRate (foxes/day)
  • chicken_predation = fox_count * fox_consumptionRate * prey_availabilityEffect (chickens/day)

Converters

  • chicken_reproductionRate = 0.02 /day
  • fox_reproductionRate = 0.01 /day — steady percentage rate, slower than chickens
  • fox_consumptionRate = 1 chicken/fox/day — the "each fox eats one chicken per day" figure, abstracted into a named variable rather than hard-coded
  • predation_halfSaturationChickens = 10 chickens — reference prey density
  • prey_availabilityEffect = chicken_count // (chicken_count + predation_halfSaturationChickens) — dimensionless, 0 to 1

The availability effect is the first-order control on the predation outflow: hunting success falls smoothly as chickens become scarce, so the outflow tapers before the stock can cross zero. No MIN/MAX clamps.

Parameter choice worth flagging

The generator's first pass used 0.1/day for chickens. At that rate, births (50/day at t=0) swamp predation (10/day) by 5x and the gap widens forever — both stocks just grow exponentially and the predation mechanism described in the background never influences behavior. I reset the rates to 0.02/day (chickens) and 0.01/day (foxes). Every stated constraint still holds: both are steady percentage rates, foxes are slower, chickens initially outnumber foxes 50:1. But now predation (9.8/day) is comparable to births (10/day) at the initial state, so the described coupling is dynamically live.

Simulated behavior (run eval-run-2, 0–200 days, dt 0.125, RK4)

  • chicken_count holds near 500 for roughly 20 days, then declines at an accelerating rate: 466 at day 25, 311 at day 50, 122 at day 65, 43 at day 70, effectively extinct by day 75
  • fox_count grows steadily and monotonically throughout — 10 to 20 by day 70, reaching 74 by day 200
  • prey_availabilityEffect stays above 0.95 until day 60, then drops sharply (0.81 at day 70, 0.007 at day 75) as the taper engages
  • chicken_count never goes meaningfully negative; the terminal value of -1e-323 is denormal floating-point underflow after the stock decays through 300+ orders of magnitude, not a structural violation

Structural critique

The main limitation is inherent to the specification: fox_reproduction depends only on fox_count, not on food intake. Foxes therefore keep multiplying after their food source is gone. There is also no fox mortality and no chicken carrying capacity, so neither population has an upper bound from its own side. Adding a food-per-fox driven fox mortality flow would close the predator side and produce the classic oscillation, but the background explicitly states foxes reproduce at a steady percentage rate, so I left it out.

Would you like me to run feedback loop analysis to explain why the collapse happens when it does, plot the two populations, or test the fox-mortality variant as a comparison run?

variables.documentation: The accumulated number of foxes (predators) in the ecosystem. It starts small relative to the chicken population and changes only through fox reproduction, since no fox mortality flow is included in this model.

variables.name: chicken_count

variables.name: fox_reproductionRate
variables.documentation: The fractional rate at which the fox population reproduces each day. Set to 1 percent per day, deliberately slower than the chicken reproduction rate, reflecting the slower breeding cycle of the predator.

variables.name: chicken_reproductionRate
variables.documentation: The fractional rate at which the chicken population reproduces each day. Chickens reproduce at a steady percentage rate, faster than foxes. variables.name: fox_reproduction
variables.documentation: New foxes born per day. It is proportional to the existing number of foxes times the fractional fox reproduction rate, the standard formulation for percentage growth of a population. Marked one-directional because births can never be negative.

variables.name: chicken_reproduction
variables.documentation: New chickens born per day. It is proportional to the existing number of chickens times the fractional chicken reproduction rate. Marked one-directional because births can never be negative.

variables.name: fox_consumptionRate
variables.documentation: The number of chickens a single fox eats per day when chickens are abundant. The problem states each fox eats one chicken per day, so this per-fox consumption rate is abstracted into this named converter rather than being hard-coded inside the predation equation.

variables.name: predation_halfSaturationChickens
variables.documentation: Reference chicken density used to normalize prey availability. When the chicken count equals this reference value, foxes can only realize half of their potential consumption because prey are hard to find. It provides the first-order control that prevents the chicken stock from going negative without using clamping functions.

variables.name: prey_availabilityEffect
variables.documentation: A dimensionless multiplier between 0 and 1 describing how easily foxes can actually find chickens. It approaches 1 when chickens are abundant relative to the reference density (foxes eat their full ration) and smoothly approaches 0 as the chicken count approaches zero (hunting fails). This smooth saturation is the first-order control that keeps the chicken population non-negative.

variables.name: chicken_predation
variables.documentation: Chickens eaten per day. Potential predation is the number of foxes times the per-fox consumption rate; this potential is scaled by the prey availability effect so that realized predation tapers smoothly as chickens become scarce. Marked one-directional because chickens eaten can never be negative.

Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.


            In a certain city, a population depends on a nonrenewable resource.
            The population reproduces and dies off at steady rates proportional to the total population.
            The resource starts with a large initial quantity, but cannot be refilled.
            Over time, the resource diminishes at a rate proportional to the population.
            Define the "resource density" as the ratio of resource quantity to the population.
            If the resource density drops below a fixed threshold, then members of the population migrate away at
            a rate proportional to the total population and the difference between the resource density 
            and the minimum threshold.

            Please create a model with two modules, 'population' and 'resource'.

            Use the following component names within each module as appropriate:
            count, birth rate, births, death rate, deaths, usage rate, usage, density, density threshold, migrations

            All "rate" variables should be constant percentages.
            Please compute the resource density inside the 'resource' module, not the 'population' module.
            (The resource density threshold should be in the 'population' module, however.)
            Do not create any intermediate variables when calculating population migrations.

            When creating a ghost component, preserve the name of the original component, including the module prefix (separated by a space rather than a period).
            So, a ghost of "module1.component" in module2 should be named "module2.module1 component".

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll start by loading the model generation tools.

Now generating the model.

Model built and validated structurally. Two modules, exactly as specified.

Model contents (14 variables, no errors or unit warnings reported by the engine):

population module

  • count — stock, people, initial 10,000; inflow births, outflows deaths and migrations
  • birth rate — 0.03 1/Year; births = birth rate * count
  • death rate — 0.02 1/Year; deaths = death rate * count
  • density threshold — 5 units/people (the minimum resource density)
  • migration rate — 0.02 people/(units*Year), the proportionality constant
  • migrations = MAX(0, migration rate * count * (density threshold - resource density)) — no intermediate variables; the MAX gate keeps the flow at zero while density is at or above threshold
  • population.resource density — ghost of resource.density

resource module

  • count — stock, units, initial 1,000,000; no inflow (nonrenewable), single outflow usage
  • usage rate — 0.1 units/(people*Year); usage = usage rate * resource.population count
  • density = count // resource.population count — computed here in the resource module, protected division
  • resource.population count — ghost of population.count

Ghost naming follows your convention (module prefix preserved, dot replaced by a space).

Specs: 0–200 years, dt 0.25, Euler, time units Year. All variables carry units and documentation.

Note on simulation: run_model returned run IDs eval-run-failed-1 and eval-run-failed-2 with no variable data attached, so the client-side engine did not produce time series in this environment. I therefore cannot report simulated behavior or loop dominance.

An analytic check on the structure, however, confirms the formulation is well-posed: writing D = R/P, the density obeys dD/dt = -(usage rate) - D[(birth rate - death rate - migration rate * threshold) + migration rate * D]. With the chosen parameters this has a stable root at D = 2.5 units/person, so density settles above zero and the resource stock asymptotes downward without crossing zero — the migration outflow provides the needed first-order control on the population as scarcity bites, rather than a clamp.

Next steps I would recommend: retry the run once the engine is available, then check population.count for the overshoot peak and confirm resource.count stays non-negative, followed by feedback analysis to identify which mechanism dominates each phase.

Specs: 0–50 years, DT 0.125, Euler, time units years.

Structural critique

  • Conservation holds: every promotion flow is consumed exactly once as the next level's inflow via a ghost, so no employees are created or destroyed in transit; the only boundary crossings are hires in and the three departures out.
  • Every outflow is first-order (proportional to its own stock), so no count can be driven negative — no MIN/MAX clamping needed.
  • No hard-coded constants in any equation; all rates, hiring level, and initial conditions are named variables.
  • All 20 variables have units and documentation. get_current_model reported no errors and no unitWarnings.

One caveat: run_model returned success: true but the resulting runs (eval-run-failed-1, eval-run-failed-2) contain zero variables, and get_variable_data came back empty for all three count stocks. So I could not verify simulated behavior numerically in this environment — I am reporting structure only, and deliberately not characterizing dynamics or feedback structure I have not measured.

Suggested next steps: re-attempt run_model if a simulation engine becomes available, then check the three count trajectories against expected equilibria; after that, feedback analysis would show which mechanisms govern the transient.

testParams.prompt:
Please give me a quantitative model that captures the key causal processes described in the background information.
Make sure to create a model with exactly the specified modules; do not add any additional modules beyond what is specified.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.


            In a certain ecosystem, there are three animal populations: lions, foxes, and chickens.
            
            All species reproduce and naturally die out at specific, stable percentage rates.
            Furthermore, the chicken population is predated at a rate proportional to the fox population,
            and the fox population is predated at a rate proportional to the lion population.
            
            Create a model with three modules named 'lions', 'foxes', and 'chickens'.
            
            Use the following component names within each module as appropriate:
            count, birth rate, death rate, births, deaths, predation rate

            In particular, "[animal].predation rate" should refer to the number of [animal]s that die off due to that animal's predator.

            When creating a ghost component, preserve the name of the original component, including the module prefix (separated by a space rather than a period).
            So, a ghost of "module1.component" in module2 should be named "module2.module1 component".

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build this three-module predator-prey model. Let me load the required tools first.

Simulation is unavailable in this environment (the run returned no data). Let me improve the parameterization so the predation mechanisms are actually dynamically active, then re-verify structure.

The model is built and verified structurally. Simulation could not execute in this environment — both run attempts returned empty datasets (eval-run-failed-1, eval-run-failed-2), so I have no numerical output to interpret and will not characterize behavior without it.

What is in the model

Exactly three modules: lions, foxes, chickens. No others.

lions (apex level — no predation rate, per the background, since nothing preys on lions)

  • lions.count — stock, 10 lions; inflow lions.births, outflow lions.deaths
  • lions.birth rate 0.15 1/Year, lions.death rate 0.1 1/Year
  • lions.births = lions.count * lions.birth rate (lions/Year, uniflow)
  • lions.deaths = lions.count * lions.death rate (lions/Year, uniflow)

foxes

  • foxes.count — stock, 100 foxes; inflow foxes.births, outflows foxes.deaths and foxes.predation rate
  • foxes.birth rate 0.5 1/Year, foxes.death rate 0.2 1/Year
  • foxes.births, foxes.deaths — first-order on the stock
  • foxes.lions count — ghost of lions.count (units: lions), named per the required convention
  • foxes.predation fraction per lion 0.03 1/(lions·Year)
  • foxes.predation rate = foxes.count * foxes.predation fraction per lion * foxes.lions count (foxes/Year) — foxes dying off because of lions

chickens

  • chickens.count — stock, 1000 chickens; inflow chickens.births, outflows chickens.deaths and chickens.predation rate
  • chickens.birth rate 0.6 1/Year, chickens.death rate 0.3 1/Year
  • chickens.births, chickens.deaths — first-order on the stock
  • chickens.foxes count — ghost of foxes.count (units: foxes)
  • chickens.predation fraction per fox 0.003 1/(foxes·Year)
  • chickens.predation rate = chickens.count * chickens.predation fraction per fox * chickens.foxes count (chickens/Year) — chickens dying off because of foxes

Formulation notes

  • Predation is proportional to the predator population as the background specifies, and also to the prey stock itself. That second factor is deliberate: it gives each prey stock first-order control on its outflow, so predation shuts down as prey become scarce and neither foxes.count nor chickens.count can be driven negative. No MIN/MAX clamps were used.
  • Ghost naming follows the stated rule exactly: foxes.lions count and chickens.foxes count preserve the source module prefix with the dot replaced by a space, and both carry crossLevelGhostOf pointers to their originals.
  • No hard-coded constants in equations. Every rate and coefficient is a named variable with units.
  • Parameters are set so predation is dynamically active at t=0 rather than negligible: 0.03 × 10 lions = 0.3/Year offsets fox net natural growth (0.5 − 0.2), and 0.003 × 100 foxes = 0.3/Year offsets chicken net natural growth (0.6 − 0.3). Only the lions' net rate (+0.05/Year) is unbalanced initially, so the lion level is what perturbs the system.
  • Specs: 0 to 40 Year, dt 0.0625, RK4. The 40-year horizon keeps populations in a legible numeric range — with no density dependence anywhere in the background information, none of the three stocks has a carrying capacity, so any species released from predation grows without bound over long horizons.
  • get_current_model reported no errors and no unit warnings.

Caveats worth flagging

The background specifies stable percentage birth and death rates for all species, which means predator reproduction does not depend on prey availability — there is no numerical response. This is a one-directional cascade, not classic Lotka-Volterra coupling. I modeled exactly what was described rather than adding prey-dependent predator births.

Since the engine produced no run data, the model has not yet earned behavioral credibility. Once simulation is available, I would want to check the reference-mode fit, confirm no stock goes negative, and run get_feedback_information to establish which structures actually drive the trajectories before saying anything about causal dominance.

  • Both rate constants are abstracted into named auxiliaries rather than hard-coded inside the flow equations, per formulation standards.

  • Depletion is deliberately a pure constant with no first-order control, because the background specifies a fixed five frimbulators per week. Note this means the stock could in principle go negative if it ever fell below the break-even level; at the stated initial value of 100 it does not, but that is a property of the parameters rather than of the structure.

Simultaneously, each day the stock has outgoing 20% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we start the period with ninety auspongs. Every day, this inventory is enhanced by 20% of the current povals count. Simultaneously, each day the stock loses a constant twelve auspongs.  Meanwhile, we begin with forty-five dominitoxings. Every day, this inventory is enhanced by exactly twelve new dominitoxings. Simultaneously, each day the stock loses 30% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build this three-stock model with modules. Let me load the required tools first.

Model built and validated. The simulation engine returned an empty run in this environment (eval-run-failed-1 with no variables), so I verified behavior analytically instead of from run output.

Structure — 3 modules, 17 variables

dominitoxings (source of the cascade)

  • dominitoxings.count — stock, 45 dominitoxings
  • + dominitoxings.new dominitoxings = dominitoxings arrival rate (12 dominitoxings/Day)
  • − dominitoxings.dominitoxings departures = count * dominitoxings departure fraction (0.30 1/Day)

povals

  • povals.count — stock, 35 povals
  • + povals.poval replenishment = povals.dominitoxings count * poval replenishment fraction (0.30 povals/dominitoxings/Day)
  • − povals.poval outflow = count * poval outflow fraction (0.20 1/Day)
  • povals.dominitoxings count — ghost of dominitoxings.count

auspongs

  • auspongs.count — stock, 90 auspongs
  • + auspongs.auspong enhancement = auspongs.povals count * auspong enhancement fraction (0.20 auspongs/povals/Day)
  • − auspongs.auspong losses = auspong loss rate (12 auspongs/Day)
  • auspongs.povals count — ghost of povals.count

Causal relationships captured (16)

The cross-module chain is dominitoxings → povals → auspongs, one-directional. Each stock also has the internal links between its level, its rate constants, and its flows.

Validation

  • No errors and no unit warnings reported by the engine.
  • Every rate/fraction is a named constant; no numeric literals inside flow equations.
  • Conversion constants carry explicit cross-unit dimensions (povals/dominitoxings/Day, auspongs/povals/Day).
  • Ghosts used instead of duplicated stocks, so no double accumulation.
  • Negativity check: dominitoxings and povals both have first-order proportional outflows, so neither can go negative. Auspongs has a constant outflow (as the background explicitly specifies), which is the one structure without first-order control. Analytically, povals(t) = 60 − 15e^(−0.3t) − 10e^(−0.2t) ≥ 35 for all t, so enhancement is at worst ~7 auspongs/Day at t=0, and the cumulative deficit converges to 20 — auspongs falls from 90 toward 70 and never approaches zero. Faithful to the source text and safe over any horizon.

Equilibria implied by the structure: dominitoxings → 40, povals → 60, auspongs → 70.

What would you like next — retry the simulation, run feedback loop analysis, or plot the three stocks?

Simultaneously, each quarter the stock experiences losses of a constant eighteen pablanksills.  Meanwhile, there are initially seventy posistorathers. Every quarter, this inventory increases due to exactly twenty-five new posistorathers. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock loses 35% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we begin with ninety-five crypterals. Every quarter, this inventory is enhanced by exactly eighteen new crypterals. Every quarter, this inventory grows through incoming 35% of the current posistorathers count. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock has outgoing 22% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
I'll build this model. Let me load the required tools first.

Model built and verified. Simulation could not produce data in this environment (the run returned no variables), so the report below is from structural inspection.

Structure: 3 modules, 18 variables, 18 causal links

Module pablanksills

  • pablanksills.count — stock, init 110, units pablanksills
  • pablanksills.pablanksill growth — inflow = pablanksill growth fraction * count
  • pablanksills.pablanksill growth fraction = 0.06 (1/quarters)
  • pablanksills.pablanksill losses — outflow = pablanksill loss rate
  • pablanksills.pablanksill loss rate = 18 (pablanksills/quarters)

Module posistorathers

  • posistorathers.count — stock, init 70, units posistorathers
  • posistorathers.new posistorathers — inflow = posistoraother arrival rate
  • posistorathers.posistoraother arrival rate = 25
  • posistorathers.posistoraother departures — outflow = posistoraother departure fraction * count
  • posistorathers.posistoraother departure fraction = 0.35 (1/quarters)

Module crypterals

  • crypterals.count — stock, init 95, units crypterals
  • crypterals.new crypterals — inflow = crypteral arrival rate
  • crypterals.crypteral arrival rate = 18
  • crypterals.crypterals from posistorathers — inflow = crypteral conversion fraction * posistorathers count
  • crypterals.posistorathers count — ghost of posistorathers.count (naming convention followed: period replaced with space)
  • crypterals.crypteral conversion fraction = 0.35 (crypterals/(posistorathers*quarters))
  • crypterals.crypteral outflow — outflow = crypteral outflow fraction * count
  • crypterals.crypteral outflow fraction = 0.22 (1/quarters)

Specs: 0–40 quarters, dt 0.25, Euler, time units quarters. No unit warnings and no errors were reported by the engine. Every variable carries units and documentation; no arbitrary constants are embedded inside flow equations — each rate is a named auxiliary.

Causal relationships extracted

All 18 links are recorded with polarity, including the one cross-module coupling: posistorathers.count → (ghost) → crypterals.crypterals from posistorathers → crypterals.count (+).

Structural critique

One issue worth flagging, which I deliberately did not "fix": pablanksills has a proportional inflow (6% of stock) against a constant outflow (18/quarter). At the initial level of 110 the outflow exceeds the inflow (6.6 vs 18), so the stock declines at an accelerating rate and will cross zero analytically around quarter 7.6, then go negative. Normally I would add first-order control on the outflow so it slows as the stock nears zero — but the background information states a flat eighteen-pablanksill loss with no such control, and inventing that structure would introduce a causal relationship the source does not contain. Since this is a causal-extraction exercise, I preserved the stated formulation exactly. Say the word if you want the non-negativity handled structurally, or the horizon shortened to the physically meaningful range.

The other two stocks are well-behaved first-order goal-seeking structures (proportional outflows), and cannot go negative.

What next — shall I run feedback analysis, adjust the time horizon, or add non-negativity to pablanksills.count?

Simultaneously, each week the stock experiences losses of a constant three ocs.  Meanwhile, we begin with forty proptimatires. Every week, this inventory increases due to exactly five new proptimatires. Simultaneously, each week the stock has outgoing 25% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we have on hand eighty priaries. Every week, this inventory gets replenished by 10% of the current proptimatires count. Simultaneously, each week the stock suffers depletion of 5% of whatever houtals are currently available.  Meanwhile, we have on hand sixty houtals. Every week, this inventory receives new additions of exactly seven new houtals. Simultaneously, each week the stock is reduced through 8% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model built and pushed. The simulation run in this environment returned no time-series data (run eval-run-failed-1 came back empty), so I'm reporting structure only — no behavioral claims.

Structure: 4 modules, 4 stocks, 8 flows

proptimatires (units: proptimatires)

  • proptimatires.count — stock, init 40
  • + new proptimatires = new proptimatires per week (= 5 proptimatires/Weeks)
  • − departing proptimatires = count * proptimatires departure fraction (= 0.25 1/Weeks)

ocs (units: ocs)

  • ocs.count — stock, init 25
  • + new ocs = proptimatires count * ocs gain fraction from proptimatires (= 0.15 ocs/proptimatires/Weeks)
  • − lost ocs = ocs loss rate (= 3 ocs/Weeks, constant)
  • Ghost: ocs.proptimatires count → alias of proptimatires.count

priaries (units: priaries)

  • priaries.count — stock, init 80
  • + replenished priaries = proptimatires count * priaries gain fraction from proptimatires (= 0.10 priaries/proptimatires/Weeks)
  • − depleted priaries = houtals count * priaries depletion fraction from houtals (= 0.05 priaries/houtals/Weeks)
  • Ghosts: priaries.proptimatires count, priaries.houtals count

houtals (units: houtals)

  • houtals.count — stock, init 60
  • + new houtals = new houtals per week (= 7 houtals/Weeks)
  • − reduced houtals = count * houtals reduction fraction (= 0.08 1/Weeks)

Specs: 0–52 Weeks, dt 0.25, Euler. All 21 causal edges are recorded with polarities; no hard-coded numbers appear inside any flow equation — every value is a named constant. No errors or unit warnings were returned.

Causal edges extracted (cross-module)

  • proptimatires.count → ocs.new ocs (+), via the ocs-module ghost
  • proptimatires.count → priaries.replenished priaries (+), via the priaries-module ghost
  • houtals.count → priaries.depleted priaries (+), via the priaries-module ghost

No other cross-module influence is stated in the background, so none was added.

Structural critique

Two formulations are worth flagging, both faithful to the source text rather than defects in transcription:

  1. ocs.lost ocs is a fixed 3 ocs/week with no dependence on ocs.count, so the ocs stock has no first-order control on its outflow and can in principle be driven negative if the ocs inflow falls below 3.
  2. priaries.depleted priaries depends only on houtals.count, never on priaries.count — priaries is a pure integrator of two exogenous rates with no first-order control either. If depletion exceeds replenishment persistently, priaries will go negative.

The background states these mechanisms explicitly, so I did not add limiting structure — doing so would introduce causal links the source does not contain. Say the word if you want first-order control added on either outflow, and I'll do it as a labeled deviation from the source text.

Next steps I'd suggest: rerun the simulation in a live client to confirm the trajectories, or have me pull feedback-loop information once a successful run exists.

Simultaneously, each hour the stock suffers depletion of 40% of its current amount. Simultaneously, each hour the stock has outgoing 10% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows thirty illigents. Every hour, this inventory benefits from 40% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock is reduced through a constant five illigents.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows sixty-five yelbs. Every hour, this inventory is enhanced by 10% of the current outrances count. Simultaneously, each hour the stock is reduced through 12% of whatever trazes are currently available.  Meanwhile, our records indicate eighty-five trazes. Every hour, this inventory grows through incoming exactly fifteen new trazes. Simultaneously, each hour the stock loses 18% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
The model is built and pushed to the client. Four modules, each with a stock named count, all cross-module references as ghosts.

outrances (stock outrances.count = 150 outrances)

  • inflow new outrances = outrance arrival rate (20 outrances/hour)
  • outflow outrance depletion = count * outrance depletion fraction (0.4 /hour)
  • outflow outrance outgoing = count * outrance outgoing fraction (0.1 /hour)

illigents (stock illigents.count = 30 illigents)

  • ghost illigents.outrances count ← outrances.count
  • inflow illigent arrivals = outrances count * illigent gain fraction (0.4 illigents/(outrance·hour))
  • outflow illigent removal = illigent removal rate (5 illigents/hour)

yelbs (stock yelbs.count = 65 yelbs)

  • ghosts yelbs.outrances count ← outrances.count, yelbs.trazes count ← trazes.count
  • inflow yelb arrivals = outrances count * yelb gain fraction (0.1 yelbs/(outrance·hour))
  • outflow yelb losses = trazes count * yelb loss fraction (0.12 yelbs/(traze·hour))

trazes (stock trazes.count = 85 trazes)

  • inflow new trazes = traze arrival rate (15 trazes/hour)
  • outflow traze losses = count * traze loss fraction (0.18 /hour)

Specs: 0–24 hours, DT 0.125, Euler. All 25 variables carry units and documentation; 24 causal links are recorded with polarities (all rate/fraction/stock-to-flow links positive, all outflow-to-stock links negative). get_current_model returned no errors and no unit warnings.

Every arbitrary constant from the background is abstracted into a named parameter, so no raw numbers appear inside flow equations. All flows are marked uniflow, since arrivals, depletion, removals and losses are physically one-directional.

Note on execution: run_model returned run eval-run-failed-1 with no variable data — the simulation engine returned nothing in this environment, so I have no behavioral results to report. Structurally, one thing worth flagging: yelbs.count has no dependence on itself in either of its flows (arrivals are driven by outrances, losses by trazes), so nothing in the specified structure prevents it from crossing zero. That is exactly what the background describes, so I have left it literal rather than adding control structure the source does not mention.

Next steps I would suggest: re-run the simulation once the engine is available, then check yelbs.count for a negative crossing and decide whether to keep the literal formulation or add first-order control on yelb losses.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In our organization, we begin with one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory gains from 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each year the stock gets diminished by a constant three whatajigs.  Meanwhile, we begin with two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory grows through incoming 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock is reduced through 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we start the period with two hundred whoziewhats. Every year, this inventory gets replenished by 5% of the current balacks count. Simultaneously, each year the stock loses 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we have on hand twelve funkados. Every year, this inventory receives new additions of 5% of the current whoziewhats count. Simultaneously, each year the stock loses 3% of whatever maxabizers are currently available.  Meanwhile, we start the period with eighty-eight maxabizers. Every year, this inventory receives new additions of 5% of the current funkados count. Simultaneously, each year the stock gets diminished by 3% of whatever whoziewhats are currently available.

supportingInfo.explanation:
Model built. Five top-level modules, one per object, each with a count stock, one inflow, one outflow, named rate constants, and ghosts for every cross-module driver.

whatajigs

  • whatajigs.count — stock, init 100 whatajigs
  • inflow whatajig growth = whatajig growth fraction (0.05 1/Year) * count
  • outflow whatajig loss = whatajig loss rate (3 whatajigs/Year, constant)

balacks

  • balacks.count — stock, init 200 balacks
  • ghost balacks.whatajigs count ← whatajigs.count
  • inflow balack arrival = balack arrival fraction (0.05) * whatajigs count
  • outflow balack departure = balack departure fraction (0.03 1/Year) * count

whoziewhats

  • whoziewhats.count — stock, init 200 whoziewhats
  • ghost whoziewhats.balacks count ← balacks.count
  • inflow whoziewhat replenishment = whoziewhat replenishment fraction (0.05) * balacks count
  • outflow whoziewhat loss = whoziewhat loss fraction (0.03 1/Year) * count

funkados

  • funkados.count — stock, init 12 funkados
  • ghosts funkados.whoziewhats count ← whoziewhats.count, funkados.maxabizers count ← maxabizers.count
  • inflow funkado addition = funkado addition fraction (0.05) * whoziewhats count
  • outflow funkado loss = funkado loss fraction (0.03) * maxabizers count

maxabizers

  • maxabizers.count — stock, init 88 maxabizers
  • ghosts maxabizers.funkados count ← funkados.count, maxabizers.whoziewhats count ← whoziewhats.count
  • inflow maxabizer addition = maxabizer addition fraction (0.05) * funkados count
  • outflow maxabizer loss = maxabizer loss fraction (0.03) * whoziewhats count

29 causal relationships are recorded with polarity and reasoning, covering every stated cause-effect link: each stock→its own proportional flow, each fraction/rate→its flow, each flow→its stock (+ inflow, − outflow), and the four cross-object drivers (whatajigs→balack arrival, balacks→whoziewhat replenishment, whoziewhats→funkado addition and →maxabizer loss, funkados→maxabizer addition, maxabizers→funkado loss).

Validation: no errors and no unit warnings reported. Every rate is a named constant — no numeric literals appear inside any flow equation. Specs: 0–50 Years, DT 0.25, Euler.

One caveat: mcp__builtin__run_model returned run eval-run-failed-1 with zero variables, so no simulation data was produced in this environment and I cannot report behavior or check the stocks for negative values. Structurally, note that funkados.count and maxabizers.count have outflows driven entirely by other stocks with no dependence on their own level — as written in the background, neither has first-order control on its own drain, so they are structurally capable of going negative. I have left this exactly as specified rather than adding structure the background does not state.

Next steps: re-run the simulation once the engine is available, then inspect the funkado and maxabizer trajectories; after that I can pull feedback information for a dominance analysis.

supportingInfo.explanation:
The model represents three distinct inventory stocks: Marticatenes, Refluppers, and Exemintes.

  1. Marticatenes Subsystem: Accumulates via a constant replenishment rate of 10 units/month and decays via a first-order negative feedback balancing loop with a fractional loss rate of 20% per month.
  2. Refluppers Subsystem: Accumulates via an inflow driven directly by the Marticatenes stock level (20% of current Marticatenes per month) creating an inter-system causal link, while draining via a constant outflow rate of 8 units/month.
  3. Exemintes Subsystem: Accumulates via a constant replenishment rate of 8 units/month and drains via a first-order balancing feedback loop governed by a 10% monthly loss fraction.

All numerical parameters have been modularized into separate auxiliary variables to ensure robust structural design.
supportingInfo.title: Multi Stock Inventory Dynamics and Feedback Model

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: In our organization, the baseline inventory shows thirty-five povals. Every day, this inventory increases due to 30% of the current dominitoxings count. Simultaneously, each day the stock loses 20% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows ninety auspongs. Every day, this inventory benefits from 20% of the current povals count. Simultaneously, each day the stock is reduced through a constant twelve auspongs.  Meanwhile, our records indicate forty-five dominitoxings. Every day, this inventory benefits from exactly twelve new dominitoxings. Simultaneously, each day the stock has outgoing 30% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
System Structure and Feedback Loops

The model captures the dynamics across three interconnected inventory stocks: dominitoxings, povals, and auspongs.

  1. Dominitoxings Subsystem:

    • Maintained by an exogenous constant inflow of 12 units/day and governed by a first-order negative feedback balancing loop via a 30% per day proportional outflow.

  2. Povals Subsystem:

    • Receives an inflow driven by 30% of the dominitoxings stock (a unidirectional coupling from dominitoxings to povals) and drains via a first-order negative feedback loop of 20% per day.

  3. Auspongs Subsystem:

    • Driven by an inflow proportional to 20% of the povals stock (unidirectional coupling from povals to auspongs) and depleted by a constant outflow rate of 12 units/day.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: At the warehouse, the baseline inventory shows one hundred ten pablanksills. Every quarter, this inventory is enhanced by 6% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock has outgoing a constant eighteen pablanksills.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows seventy posistorathers. Every quarter, this inventory grows through incoming exactly twenty-five new posistorathers. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock suffers depletion of 35% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, our records indicate ninety-five crypterals. Every quarter, this inventory increases due to exactly eighteen new crypterals. Every quarter, this inventory gains from 35% of the current posistorathers count. Simultaneously, each quarter the stock has outgoing 22% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation: This model captures three distinct inventory dynamics within the warehouse system: 1) Pablanksills Inventory operates with a reinforcing feedback loop driven by a 6% quarterly growth rate and a balancing drain from a constant outflow of 18 units per quarter. 2) Posistorathers Inventory is driven by a constant inflow of 25 units per quarter and a first-order balancing feedback depletion loop of 35% per quarter. 3) Crypterals Inventory features two inflows—a constant quarterly inflow of 18 units and a cross-coupled inflow driven by 35% of the posistorathers inventory level—counterbalanced by a first-order decay outflow of 22% per quarter. All empirical rates and parameters have been fully abstracted into auxiliary variables adhering to System Dynamics best practices.

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: At the warehouse, there are initially twenty-five ocs. Every week, this inventory is enhanced by 15% of the current proptimatires count. Simultaneously, each week the stock suffers depletion of a constant three ocs.  Meanwhile, we begin with forty proptimatires. Every week, this inventory receives new additions of exactly five new proptimatires. Simultaneously, each week the stock has outgoing 25% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows eighty priaries. Every week, this inventory increases due to 10% of the current proptimatires count. Simultaneously, each week the stock gets diminished by 5% of whatever houtals are currently available.  Meanwhile, the baseline inventory shows sixty houtals. Every week, this inventory benefits from exactly seven new houtals. Simultaneously, each week the stock suffers depletion of 8% of its current amount.

supportingInfo.explanation:
This model captures the multi-inventory system dynamics across four interconnected stocks: ocs, proptimatires, priaries, and houtals.

  1. Proptimatires Dynamics: Governed by a constant inflow (5 units/week) and a standard first-order negative feedback balancing loop (25% depletion per week).
  2. Houtals Dynamics: Governed by a constant inflow (7 units/week) and a first-order negative feedback balancing loop (8% depletion per week).
  3. Ocs Dynamics: Enhanced through a unidirectional coupling from proptimatires (15% per week) and depleted at a constant rate of 3 units/week.
  4. Priaries Dynamics: Driven by an inflow coupled to proptimatires (10% per week) and an outflow coupled across subsystems to houtals (5% per week).

All parameters are modeled as explicit auxiliary variables to avoid hardcoded empirical constants.
supportingInfo.title: Interconnected Warehouse Inventory Dynamics Model

additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge: Throughout the process, our records indicate one hundred fifty outrances. Every hour, this inventory benefits from exactly twenty new outrances. Simultaneously, each hour the stock suffers depletion of 40% of its current amount. Simultaneously, each hour the stock loses 10% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we have on hand thirty illigents. Meanwhile, we start the period with sixty-five yelbs. Every hour, this inventory increases due to 10% of the current outrances count. supportingInfo.explanation: This model represents the multi-inventory dynamics described in the background information across four primary state stocks: outrances, illigents, yelbs, and trazes. First-order negative feedback loops regulate outrances and trazes via proportional depletion/loss outflows. In addition, cross-stock couplings are created where the outrances stock drives the replenishment flows of illigents and yelbs, and the trazes stock governs the outflow drain from yelbs. All arbitrary rates and proportions have been modularized into explicit auxiliary parameters to adhere to standard system dynamics best practices.

Simultaneously, each year the stock suffers depletion of a constant three whatajigs.  Meanwhile, our records indicate two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory receives new additions of 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock is reduced through 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, there are initially two hundred whoziewhats. Every year, this inventory benefits from 5% of the current balacks count. Simultaneously, each year the stock decreases by 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we begin with twelve funkados. Every year, this inventory is enhanced by 5% of the current whoziewhats count. Simultaneously, each year the stock is reduced through 3% of whatever maxabizers are currently available.  Meanwhile, we begin with eighty-eight maxabizers. Every year, this inventory gains from 5% of the current funkados count. Simultaneously, each year the stock decreases by 3% of whatever whoziewhats are currently available.

supportingInfo.explanation:
This model captures the multi-tier inventory cascade described in the system narrative.

  1. Whatajigs Subsystem: Modeled as an accumulating stock initialized at 100 with a reinforcing feedback loop from 5% annual self-growth (whatajigs growth) and a constant outflow of 3 units per year (whatajigs depletion).
  2. Balacks Subsystem: Modeled as a stock initialized at 200 with an inflow driven by 5% of whatajigs count (balacks additions) and a balancing outflow loop of 3% of its own stock (balacks reduction).
  3. Whoziewhats Subsystem: Modeled as a stock initialized at 200 with an inflow driven by 5% of balacks count (whoziewhats additions) and a balancing outflow loop of 3% of its own stock (whoziewhats reduction).
  4. Funkados Subsystem: Modeled as a stock initialized at 12 receiving inflow equal to 5% of whoziewhats (funkados enhancement) and drained by an outflow equal to 3% of maxabizers (funkados reduction).
  5. Maxabizers Subsystem: Modeled as a stock initialized at 88 receiving inflow equal to 5% of funkados (maxabizers gain) and drained by an outflow equal to 3% of whoziewhats (maxabizers reduction).

All parameters are parameterized via auxiliary variables to adhere to the strict no-hardcoded-constant rule.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.
            
            Epidemiologists understand that infectious disease spread follows well-established patterns that typically evolve over daily intervals. 
            The susceptible population becomes exposed when they come into contact with infectious individuals. 
            After an incubation period, exposed individuals become infectious and can transmit the disease. 
            Infectious individuals then recover and develop immunity, or in some cases may die from the disease.
            The basic reproduction number (R0) determines how many new infections each infectious person generates.
            Public health interventions like vaccination can move people directly from susceptible to recovered,
            while social distancing measures reduce the contact rate between infectious and susceptible individuals.
            Contact tracing and quarantine can remove exposed individuals from circulation before they become infectious.
            Disease progression involves distinct compartments of people moving through the infection cycle.
            
            Use these variable names: 
            susceptible, exposed, infectious, recovered, infecting, incubating, recovering, contacts, vaccination

supportingInfo.explanation:
Structural Overview

The model implements a classical SEIR (Susceptible-Exposed-Infectious-Recovered) epidemiological structure with public health intervention pathways (vaccination).

  1. Susceptible Population (susceptible): Individuals deplete via two outflows: the infection flow (infecting) and immunization (vaccination).
  2. Exposed Compartment (exposed): Captures latency and the incubation delay before individuals become active disease vectors. It accumulates via infecting and drains via incubating.
  3. Infectious Compartment (infectious): Represents active transmission capability. It accumulates via incubating and empties via recovering.
  4. Recovered Compartment (recovered): Represents immune individuals who either successfully fought off the infection or bypassed infection via vaccination.

Feedback Loops

  • Epidemic Contagion Loop (Reinforcing / R): As infectious individuals rise, contact with susceptible individuals increases infecting, expanding exposed and eventually adding more infectious individuals.
  • Susceptible Depletion & Herd Immunity (Balancing / B1 & B2): As people move through infection to recovery, or directly via vaccination, the susceptible pool diminishes. This lowers transmission probability per contact and terminates epidemic growth.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.
            
            Healthcare systems have limited capacity that affects patient outcomes during health crises that unfold over weekly cycles.
            Patients requiring care enter the system through admissions, but bed capacity limits how many can be treated.
            When demand exceeds capacity, patients face delays or are turned away, potentially worsening their condition.
            Healthcare workers are the key resource - they can treat patients but also become sick themselves,
            reducing available capacity. Staff burnout increases when workload is high, leading to turnover.
            Hospitals can surge capacity by opening additional beds and hiring temporary staff, but this takes time.
            Recovery times vary - some patients recover quickly while others require long-term care.
            The system involves managing patient flows, workforce dynamics, and available bed resources.
            
            Use these variable names:
            patients, available beds, healthcare workers, workload, burnout, staff turnover.

supportingInfo.explanation:
The model represents the systemic capacity limits, workforce burnout loop, and surge response of a healthcare system facing health crises over weekly cycles. Key archetypes and dynamics captured include:

  1. Burnout Reinforcing Feedback (Eroding Goals / Downward Spiral): As patient admissions rise relative to healthcare workers, the workload per worker increases. High workload triggers burnout accumulation, which elevates staff turnover. Staff departures deplete healthcare workers, which further exacerbates the workload on remaining personnel in a vicious feedback loop.
  2. Balancing Surge Adjustments with Delays: The hospital seeks to counteract shortages through hiring and bed surges. Both staff hiring and bed expansion adjust towards desired targets based on patient load, but are constrained by operational time delays (staff hiring delay and bed adjustment time).
  3. Capacity Constraints (Limits to Growth): Occupancy ratio regulates admission fraction via a non-linear graphical function. When hospital occupancy exceeds 100% of available beds, incoming patient demand is constrained, representing diversion or delayed care.
  4. Equation Compliance: All equations adhere strictly to standard XMILE conventions (underscores for variable references), eliminate hard-coded constants in favor of explicitly parameterized auxiliaries, enforce non-negative uniflow constraints on all physical rates, and use smooth formulations without conditional branching.

testParams.prompt: Please give me a quantitative model that captures the key causal processes described in the background information.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I'm trying to understand the key causal mechanisms that drive this system's behavior over time.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
Please rely on the following expert knowledge as much as possible when creating your model.
            
            Transportation engineers recognize that building more roads often fails to reduce congestion due to induced demand effects that emerge over annual planning cycles.
            When new road capacity is added, it initially reduces travel time and congestion. However, this improvement
            attracts new drivers who switch from other routes, times, or modes of transport. Some people who previously
            didn't make trips now find driving more attractive. Over time, this increased traffic volume can return
            congestion to previous levels or even make it worse. The phenomenon demonstrates that transportation is not
            just about moving vehicles, but about the complex behavioral responses to changes in the system.
            Traffic also creates negative externalities like air pollution and noise, which affect quality of life.
            The system involves road infrastructure, traveler behavior, and traffic volume dynamics.
            
            Use these variable names: 
            road capacity, travelers, travel time, congestion.

supportingInfo.explanation: The model captures the classic 'Fixes that Fail' and 'Shifting the Burden' system archetypes underlying traffic congestion and induced demand. When roadway congestion rises, transport planners construct additional road capacity. While this initially reduces congestion and shortens travel time, the improved travel conditions dramatically increase driving attractiveness. This unlocks latent demand from the potential traveler pool, inducing new travelers to adopt driving. As the traveler stock and resulting traffic volume grow, congestion returns to prior levels while generating increased environmental externalities such as noise and air pollution.
supportingInfo.title: Induced Demand Traffic Dynamics and Road Capacity

testParams.prompt:
Please add the following to my model...
Throughout the process, the baseline inventory shows one hundred whatajigs. Every year, this inventory is enhanced by 5% growth relative to its current size. Simultaneously, each year the stock loses a constant three whatajigs.  Meanwhile, our records indicate two hundred balacks. Every year, this inventory is enhanced by 5% of the current whatajigs count. Simultaneously, each year the stock has outgoing 3% of whatever existing_store_lambda are currently available.  Meanwhile, our records indicate two hundred whoziewhats. Every year, this inventory is enhanced by 5% of the current balacks count. Simultaneously, each year the stock loses 3% of its current amount.  Meanwhile, we begin with twelve funkados. Every year, this inventory is enhanced by 5% of the current whoziewhats count. Simultaneously, each year the stock is reduced through 3% of whatever maxabizers are currently available.  Meanwhile, we start the period with eighty-eight maxabizers. Every year, this inventory gets replenished by 5% of the current funkados count. Simultaneously, each year the stock gets diminished by 3% of whatever existing_store_mu are currently available.

supportingInfo.explanation: Added the newly described stock and flow subsystems: whatajigs, balacks, whoziewhats, funkados, and maxabizers. All constant values have been abstracted into explicit auxiliary parameter variables following professional system dynamics guidelines. A reinforcing feedback loop acts on whatajigs growth, while a balancing feedback loop acts on whoziewhats loss. Furthermore, an oscillatory balancing feedback loop is formed between funkados and maxabizers, where funkados stimulates maxabizer replenishment and maxabizers drives funkados reduction. External drivers from existing lambda and mu stores connect directly to the outflows of balacks and maxabizers, respectively.

testParams.prompt: Using your knowledge of how the American Revolution started and the additional information I have given you, please give me a feedback-based explanation for how the American Revolution came about. Your response must include at least 10 variables.

additionalParameters.problemStatement: I am trying to understand how the American Revolution started. I'd like to know what caused hostilities to break out.
additionalParameters.backgroundKnowledge:
The American Revolution was caused by a number of factors, including:
Taxation
The British imposed new taxes on the colonies to raise money, such as the Stamp Act of 1765, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and playing cards. The colonists were angry because they had no representatives in Parliament.
The Boston Massacre
In 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in Boston, killing five people. The massacre intensified anti-British sentiment and became a propaganda tool for the colonists.
The Boston Tea Party
The Boston Tea Party was a major act of defiance against British rule. It showed that Americans would not tolerate tyranny and taxation.
The Intolerable Acts
The British government passed harsh laws that the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. One of the acts closed the port of Boston until the colonists paid for the tea they had ruined.
The French and Indian War
The British wanted the colonies to repay them for their defense during the French and Indian War (1754–63).
Colonial identity
The colonists developed a stronger sense of American identity

supportingInfo.explanation:
The outbreak of the American Revolution is modeled through the lens of the Escalation archetype and reinforcing feedback dynamics.

  1. The Debt and Taxation Trigger: Following the French and Indian War, the British government faced massive debt, motivating aggressive taxation policies (e.g., the Stamp Act). This exogenous pressure directly fed into colonial grievances due to a lack of parliamentary representation.

  2. The Escalation Reinforcing Loop:

    • Growing Colonial Grievance combined with emerging Colonial Identity and Solidarity stimulated organized Colonial Defiance and Resistance (e.g., the Boston Tea Party).
    • This defiance alarmed British authorities, who responded with coercive measures (the Intolerable Acts, port closures, and troop garrisoning in Boston).
    • The accumulation of British Coercive Enforcement produced flashpoint incidents like the Boston Massacre, which further accelerated Colonial Grievance.

  3. Tipping Point into Hostilities: As both British enforcement and Colonial resistance mutually amplified one another through this reinforcing loop, the Hostilities Escalation Index climbed rapidly, culminating in armed clash at Lexington and Concord.
supportingInfo.title: Dynamics of American Revolutionary Outbreak
